## [ALVISI-SP-13] SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks

**Citation:** Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Alessandro Epasto, Silvio Lattanzi, Alessandro Panconesi. "SoK: The Evolution of Sybil Defense via Social Networks." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2013. Pages 382-396 (as paginated in text, pp. 383-397). DOI 10.1109/SP.2013.33.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~lorenzo/papers/AlvisiSoK.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper unifies social-graph Sybil defense — distinguishing forged identities from genuine ones by analyzing the graph structure of a social network rather than by a central authority — under one framework and states which structural property that framework can safely rely on. It shows that four candidate structural properties of a social graph (node-degree distribution, network diameter, clustering coefficient, conductance) can each be defeated cheaply by an adversary who inserts identities via preferential attachment (an inserted node connects to existing node v with probability proportional to v's degree), except conductance, which the paper defines as the ratio of edges leaving a vertex set to the sum of degrees inside that set. It then reduces universal Sybil defense (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, GateKeeper) to a random-walk membership test: an honest verifier and a candidate node each sample a random edge from a short random walk (length order log n, where n is graph size), and a match indicates same-graph membership with a probability derivable from the birthday paradox. The paper then reframes the goal from universal defense (classify every node in the network) to local defense, called Problem 1: given an honest seed node u, find the largest connected subset S containing u whose internal mixing time (the walk length after which a random walk lands on a uniformly random edge) is short and whose cut to the rest of the graph is sparse enough (at most o(|S|/mixing time) edges) that S can be found by a local algorithm without traversing the whole graph. It solves this with ACL (Andersen-Chung-Lang), a Personalized PageRank random walk with a jump-back probability alpha to the seed, approximated by a push-flow algorithm (APPR) with error parameter epsilon, then degree-normalized to rank every other node by trust from the seed's perspective.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| SybilLimit precision decays once attack edges exceed the theoretical bound | Preprocessed Facebook-New Orleans graph (63,392 nodes / 816,886 edges before preprocessing, reduced to 40,757 nodes / 632,597 edges by removing all nodes with degree below 5); attack-edge insertion probability p swept 0.01 to 0.10; SybilLimit configured with 1.5*sqrt(m) random walks of length 1.5*log(n) |
| Preprocessing removes 85%+ of nodes on WikiTalk | WikiTalk graph: 92,117 nodes / 360,767 edges raw, reduced to 13,069 nodes / 133,343 edges after removing degree-below-5 nodes |
| ACL tolerates denser attacks than SybilLimit: ACL at p=0.05 attack strength performs comparably to SybilLimit at p=0.01 | Facebook-New Orleans graph, attack strength p swept 0.01-0.10, ACL configured with alpha=10^-3, epsilon=10^-6 (10^-7 for DBLP), precision/recall averaged over 10 randomly chosen seeds |
| ACL achieves high precision at high recall without preprocessing on Facebook, DBLP, Epinions, WikiTalk; SybilLimit's precision degrades to varying degrees without preprocessing and performs poorly on DBLP even preprocessed | Four graphs: DBLP (718,115 nodes / 2,786,906 edges), Epinions (26,588 / 100,120), Facebook (63,392 / 816,886), WikiTalk (92,117 / 360,767); attack edge probability p=0.01 |
| Under a targeted-attachment attack (fixed number of attack edges g=50,000 connecting to honest nodes chosen at random until g edges obtained, then gamma=10,000 additional Sybil nodes added in a Barabasi-Albert scale-free topology), ACL and the Mislove community-detection algorithm are near-perfect and outperform GateKeeper, SybilLimit, SybilGuard | Facebook-New Orleans graph, g=50,000, gamma=10,000 |
| Under the RenRen-observed attack pattern (isolated Sybil nodes each connected via many attack edges rather than a single well-connected Sybil cluster), every tested defense performs close to random (0.5 probability that a random honest node ranks above a random Sybil node) | Facebook-New Orleans graph; measured probabilities: SybilLimit 0.45, SybilGuard 0.44, Mislove 0.34, GateKeeper 0.49, ACL 0.37 |
| Yang et al.'s RenRen heuristic (flag as Sybil any account whose friendship-acceptance rate is below 50% and whose clustering coefficient is below 1/100) identifies over 98% of Sybils with a false-positive rate under 0.5% | RenRen social network, as reported by Yang et al. and cited by this paper, not independently re-measured here |
| A conductance-based defense layer built on friendship-acceptance-rate monitoring bounds the fraction of edges a Sybil node can spend on attack edges without detection: at honest-acceptance probability p=0.10 and flag threshold T=0.50, each Sybil node must hold at least 7 links to other Sybil nodes per attack edge to avoid detection | Derived bound (Proposition 3): fraction of edges that may be attack edges is p(1-T)/(T-p); example values p=0.10, T=0.50 taken from Yang et al.'s RenRen thresholds |

### Parameters
- alpha (ACL jump-back probability to seed): set to 10^-3 in experiments; theory sets alpha = (10*mixing time)^-1 for a subset S
- epsilon (ACL/APPR approximation error, trading running time against precision, running time O(1/(alpha*epsilon))): 10^-6 for Facebook, Epinions, WikiTalk; 10^-7 for DBLP (chosen so every node in the attacked graph receives non-zero weight)
- SybilLimit random-walk count: 1.5*sqrt(m) walks (m = edge count)
- SybilLimit random-walk length: 1.5*log(n) (n = node count)
- Preprocessing threshold: nodes with degree below 5 are iteratively removed before running SybilLimit-family protocols
- Attack-edge insertion probability p: swept 0.01 to 0.10 across experiments
- Targeted-attachment attack: g (fixed attack-edge count) = 50,000; gamma (added Sybil node count) = 10,000; Sybil sub-topology generated by Barabasi-Albert preferential attachment

### Stated limitations
The paper states that the two assumptions underlying universal random-walk Sybil defense (honest-region mixing time of O(log n), and a sparse cut between honest and Sybil regions) do not hold in the measured graphs: preprocessing to raise mixing time removes over 85% of nodes on WikiTalk, and removed nodes are treated as Sybil by the protocol even though the paper states it is unclear how they can safely use or contribute resources. ACL solves only the local problem (finding one seed's community, Problem 1); the paper states that a universal Sybil defense for a community-structured network remains an open problem. ACL and every other tested random-walk method perform close to random-guessing (0.34-0.49 probability) against the RenRen-observed attack pattern of many isolated Sybil nodes each with several attack edges, rather than one well-connected Sybil cluster with few attack edges — the paper states this vulnerability to multiple-attack-edges-per-node is fundamental to conductance-based methods, following a proof by Yu et al. Multi-seed ranking merging (Cao et al.'s approach) has no proven theoretical guarantee even under all-honest seeds, because seeds near the honest/Sybil boundary can produce an adversarial probability distribution over Sybil nodes with unknown effect on the merged ranking. The friendship-acceptance-rate defense layer is stated to be circumventable by an adversary who issues friendship requests preferentially to other Sybil-controlled nodes.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
ACL requires each honest verifying node to hold, or be able to sample, a local view of the social graph reachable by random walk from itself; it does not require a global, centrally computed graph snapshot at query time, but the paper's own experiments compute walks over a fully materialized graph. ACL's guarantee (Theorem 3) is conditioned on the target subset S having a power-law degree distribution and a cut of size o(|S|/mixing-time of S) to the rest of the graph; a caller supplying a graph without these properties receives no proven guarantee. The ranking is seed-relative: it requires the caller to supply one honest seed per verifying viewpoint, and results do not merge across seeds without losing the proven guarantee (per the multi-seed discussion above). Any system consuming ACL's ranking to admit or reject identities must set alpha from an estimate of the target community's mixing time, which the paper does not show how to measure without already possessing a labeled honest/Sybil partition.

### Contradicts
Community-detection-based Sybil defense is often described as solved by this line of work; the paper itself states this is false in general — Mislove's greedy conductance-heuristic algorithm can be forced by an adversary using only two attack edges (from one honest node v to two Sybil endpoints) to admit an entire attacker-constructed Sybil chain deterministically. No other corpus entry directly disagrees with this paper's measurements as of this batch.

## [ALWEN-EUROSP-17] Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing
**Citation:** Joël Alwen, Jeremiah Blocki. "Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2017. DOI 10.1109/EuroSP.2017.47.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/759.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/759.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The paper reduces the memory an attacker needs to evaluate a data-independent memory-hard function (iMHF) — a key-stretching function, used to slow brute-force password guessing, whose memory-access pattern does not depend on the secret input and so resists timing side-channel attacks — well below the memory the honest algorithm uses, for Argon2i-A (the Password Hashing Competition winner), Argon2i-B (the version proposed to the Internet Research Task Force as a password-hashing standard), and Balloon Hashing. An iMHF's evaluation corresponds to pebbling a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which each node is a memory block and each edge is a data dependency: computing a node's label requires holding its parents' labels in memory. The attack, extending Alwen and Blocki's CRYPTO 2016 construction, computes a small depth-reducing set S of graph nodes such that deleting S from the DAG leaves only short paths; an attacker recomputes the values in S on demand instead of storing them, trading extra computation for a large memory reduction, at attack quality (the ratio of the honest algorithm's cost to the attack's amortized cost, where a ratio above 1 counts as a working attack) that grows with the number of memory blocks. The paper's own contribution is threefold: extending the theoretical attack to Argon2i-B (not previously analyzed), for which it proves attack quality Θ(N^0.2) by constructing a depth-reducing set of size Θ(N^(4/5)) that leaves a residual graph of depth N^(3/5) (N being the total number of memory-block computations, τ passes times σ table size); introducing heuristics — a smaller depth-reducing set construction and an "XOR compression" trick — that improve the attack's concrete efficiency even when the attacker's on-chip memory bandwidth is bounded; and simulating the attack on randomly sampled instances of all three algorithms to measure memory consumption for practical parameter ranges (up to 16-24 GB) and for varying limits on attacker parallelism. Cost is measured as energy complexity (an estimate of the physical energy an attack hardware implementation would consume), which the paper states tightly approximates area-time complexity for the class of attacks considered.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Argon2i-B attack quality at 1 GB, τ=6 passes | Reduces cost by a factor of 2 | Simulated attack on random Argon2i-B DAGs, memory parameter M=1GB, "paranoid" pass count from the IRTF proposal; 10 random graph samples per data point, results varying only in the 2nd-3rd significant digit across samples |
| Passes needed to defeat the attack at 1 GB | More than 10 passes (τ>10) required for the attack to fail against 1 GB Argon2i-B | Same simulation setup; compared against the IRTF proposal's own maximum recommended "paranoid" setting of 6 passes |
| Argon2i-B attack quality, minimal-memory recommended setting | Approximately 5 at 1 GB, approximately 9.3 at 16 GB | τ=1 pass, parameters chosen by the IRTF proposal's own stated selection procedure (maximize memory for a fixed time budget, which yields τ=1 in memory-rich/impatient-user settings) |
| Argon2i-A attack quality at τ=4 passes | Greater than 4 | Simulated attack, n and σ varied 2^17-2^24 nodes, τ∈{1,3,4}, compared directly against Argon2i-B under the same parameters (Figure 2) |
| Balloon Hashing (BH) vs Argon2i-B | BH attack quality increases faster with memory usage than Argon2i-B's at matched n and τ; BH is stated to be less resistant than Argon2i-B | Label size B=512 bytes for BH vs B=1024 bytes (Blake2b) for Argon2i-B; τ=1, n=2^24 gives M=8GB for BH vs M=16GB for Argon2i-B under equal node counts |
| Maximum attacker parallelism required | 1,324 cores for the hardest tested Argon2i-B instance (τ=1, M=16GB); 1,496 cores for the hardest Argon2i-A instance (same M, τ) | Across the full simulated parameter sweep, n∈{2^17,...,2^24}, τ∈{1,3,4,6,10,20} for Argon2i-B/BH, τ∈{1,3,4} for Argon2i-A |
| On-chip memory bandwidth required, worst case | About 2 TB/s (M=1GB, τ=1 pass); about 0.6 TB/s for 4-pass Argon2i-B at 1GB | Derived assuming 1.5 GB/s bandwidth needed per Blake2b compression-function core (extrapolated from an implemented 4-core, 8-thread Argon2i-B measurement of 5.8 GB/s aggregate [Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, Table 4]); compared against then-current AMD Radeon R9 Fury (512 GB/s) and emerging Samsung HBM2 (>1 TB/s) hardware |
| Effect of bounding parallelism | Attack quality for Argon2i-B peaks near parallelism p=200 and can decrease beyond that point; for Argon2i-A quality rises almost monotonically with p, flattening at higher p | Fixed M=1GB (σ=2^20), p tested at {25,50,100,200,500,750,1000}, τ∈{1,4,7,10}, 10 random graph instances per configuration |
| Multi-lane Argon2i attack quality | Attack quality >1.18 against 4-lane Argon2i-B (τ=4, σ=2^17, p=4), versus no working attack (quality <1, specifically 0.89) against the equivalent single-lane 4-pass Argon2i-B at the same per-lane memory | Hand-selected attack parameters (gap=32, #layers=256, g=13,970); demonstrates the Argon2i multi-lane parent-selection rule (parents drawn across lanes) reduces resistance to this attack relative to running independent single-lane instances |
| iXOR (indegree-21, XOR-and-high-indegree hardening) attack quality | With the paper's added "XOR compression" heuristic, 3-pass iXOR and 6-pass Argon2i-B show roughly equivalent attack quality | iXOR = Argon2i-A modified to draw 20 additional random parents per node and XOR their labels before compression, modeling the Corrigan-Gibbs et al. hardening technique used in BH-Double-Buffer |

### Parameters
- Memory parameter σ (table size) and timing parameter τ (pass count): swept over n=στ ∈ {2^17, 2^18, ..., 2^24} and τ ∈ {1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 20} for Argon2i-B and BH; τ ∈ {1, 3, 4} for Argon2i-A.
- Compression-function output/label size B: 1024 bytes for Argon2i (Blake2b-based); 512 bytes for Balloon Hashing (except a 1344-byte variant using SHA3, not the one plotted).
- Attacker parallelism p, explicitly bounded in one experiment set: {25, 50, 100, 200, 500, 750, 1000} at fixed M=1GB; {25, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000} in the fixed-runtime (n=2^24) variant.
- Assumed memory bandwidth per attacker compute core: 1.5 GB/s, taken as a reference point derived from an implemented Argon2i-B measurement of 5.8 GB/s on 4 cores.
- iXOR indegree: 21 (1 sequential parent plus 20 random parents), matching the original BH-Double-Buffer construction's indegree.
- Multi-lane example parameters: τ=4, σ=2^17, p=4 lanes (n=2^19).
- Number of random graph samples per data point: 10, with reported variation confined to the 2nd-3rd significant digit of measured attack cost.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their understanding of Argon2i-A and Argon2i-B security remains incomplete after this work, and list as open questions whether the attack on Argon2i-B can be further improved and whether a matching lower bound on Argon2i-B's energy complexity can be proved. They state the multi-lane attack result is not fully optimized: they conjecture attack quality on multi-lane Argon2i-A and Argon2i-B can be improved further with additional parameter and heuristic tuning, and explicitly leave this as future research rather than a result they establish. The paper notes it focuses its main simulation results on the single-lane variant of each iMHF because, combined with the "trivial" (independent-instance) approach to parallelism, single-lane constructions are more resistant to this attack than the Argon2i design's cross-lane parent-selection rule — meaning the headline attack-quality numbers understate the effect against the deployed multi-lane configuration. The authors state that prior observers (the Argon2 authors and others) had argued the original Alwen-Blocki attack does not threaten real-world Argon2 security because of large constants hidden in the asymptotic bounds and because a literal hardware implementation would need memory bandwidth beyond then-available technology; the current paper's stated purpose is to test, not assume, those objections, and it reports the concrete simulated numbers rather than asserting the asymptotic result alone.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A system choosing Argon2i-B (or another data-independent MHF) as a password-hashing or key-stretching primitive must select the pass count τ knowing that quality-2 or better memory-reduction attacks exist against low pass counts at practical memory sizes (e.g., τ=6 at 1GB), so the choice of τ trades directly against user-perceived latency: the paper states that increasing τ multiplies running time by τ, and that human users have limited tolerance for authentication delay (on the order of 1-2 seconds cited as the tolerance window in the source text). Any parameter-selection procedure for this class of MHF needs an explicit joint choice of memory σ and passes τ; the paper states the IRTF proposal's own selection procedure (fix memory first from available hardware, then pick the maximum τ affordable in the time budget) tends to produce τ=1 in memory-rich or impatience-constrained deployments, which the measured results show is the parameter region most vulnerable to this attack. A deployment relying on the multi-lane parallel Argon2i construction for throughput must account for the measured finding that cross-lane parent selection reduces attack resistance relative to running independent single-lane instances in parallel; choosing single-lane Argon2i and parallelizing across independent instances instead preserves the stronger resistance this paper measures. Any claim that a hardening technique (such as XOR-and-high-indegree) increases attacker cost needs re-verification under this paper's optimized attack, because the XOR-compression heuristic introduced here is shown to substantially reduce the naive cost increase that technique otherwise imposes.

### Contradicts
The paper contradicts the informal industry consensus, attributed in its own text to the Argon2 designers (Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich) and to Khovratovich and Aumasson, that the original Alwen-Blocki (CRYPTO 2016) attack "does not present a threat to the real world security of Argon2-B (or BH)" because of large asymptotic constants and infeasible hardware bandwidth requirements; this paper's simulated results show the attack reduces cost by a factor of 2 against Argon2i-B at 1 GB memory and τ=6 passes, within the IRTF proposal's own recommended parameter space, and states the IRTF proposal's security analysis had omitted this attack from consideration. No contradiction with another paper in this corpus was found (BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16, the Argon2 paper itself, is the object of this critique rather than an independent measurement disagreement — see BIRYUKOV-EUROSP-16's entry for the corresponding attribution).

## [AMBATI-SACMAT-26] SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities

**Citation:** Sushanth Ambati, Kainat Adeel, Jack Myers, Nikolay Ivanov. "SoK: Self-Sovereign Digital Identities." ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies (SACMAT), 2026. DOI: 10.1145/3750555.3811903.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06896 (arXiv:2603.06896v2 [cs.CR], 11 Mar 2026)
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06896
**Domain:** E

### What it does
This is a systematization of knowledge (a structured survey that classifies existing work rather than proposing a new mechanism) on self-sovereign digital identity (SSDI), a paradigm in which a user, rather than a service provider or a federated identity broker (such as Google or Facebook), holds their own authentication keys and data and presents them on demand as digital credentials. The paper follows a five-step method: it reviews eight prior surveys published 2018-2023 to establish what has already been systematized; it draws on 80 sources (active SSDI projects, peer-reviewed papers, standards-body reports, and privacy-advocacy manifestos) to distill six recurring adoption challenges; it structurally classifies 47 scientific publications proposing SSDI systems along five dimensions (system type, trust infrastructure, cryptographic technique, which of the six challenges each addresses, evaluation method); it evaluates 12 production-deployed SSDI systems along five self-sovereignty dimensions; and it synthesizes five forward-looking research frontiers from the first four steps.

The six challenges it identifies: (1) identity binding — establishing that one decentralized identifier (DID, a self-generated identifier not issued by any central authority) corresponds to one real-world individual or organization, addressed in the literature by credential-based binding (a trusted issuer such as a government or university attests to the correspondence), web-of-trust binding (peers vouch for one another across a social graph), or biometric binding (tying identity to a physical characteristic); (2) key management and protocol immaturity — users must generate, store, back up, rotate, and recover their own cryptographic keys with no central password-reset mechanism, and over 100 registered DID methods remain largely non-interoperable; (3) usability — the shift from username-and-password to key-based authentication and selective disclosure (revealing only specific attributes of a credential) imposes cognitive load unfamiliar to typical users; (4) oversight and regulation — legal frameworks such as GDPR's right to be forgotten assume a centralized party capable of deleting data, in tension with immutable ledger anchoring, and no single party exists for law enforcement to serve a subpoena on; (5) critical-mass adoption — a cold-start problem in which users will not adopt SSDI credentials until verifiers accept them, and verifiers will not integrate verification until enough users hold credentials; (6) single infrastructure dependence — the great majority of proposed systems anchor identity to one specific blockchain, so a consensus failure, a 51% attack, or a smart-contract vulnerability in that one chain endangers every identity anchored to it, a risk the paper calls meta-centralization because it exists at the ecosystem level even when the chosen chain is itself internally decentralized.

| Papers relying on implementation benchmarks (throughput, latency, gas cost) as sole evaluation | 23 of 47 (49%) | Same 47-paper corpus |

| Real-world SSDI deployments achieving full support on all five self-sovereignty dimensions (user key control, permissionless issuance, credential portability, selective disclosure, revocation resistance) | 0 of 12 | Assessment of 12 production-deployed or advanced-pilot SSDI systems (Sovrin, EU Digital Identity Wallet, British Columbia VON, DIF ION, SpruceID, uPort Veramo, Jolocom, Trinsic, Truvera/Dock, KILT, Ping Identity/ShoCard, IDunion), five dimensions scored fully/partially/not supported per system |
| Real-world SSDI projects fully operational as of February 2026 | 3 of 12 (25%) | Same 12-project cohort, status assessed from code repositories and/or public websites |
| Real-world SSDI projects defunct | 3 of 12 (25%) | Same 12-project cohort |
| Real-world SSDI projects inactive | 2 of 12 (17%) | Same 12-project cohort |
| Real-world SSDI projects under active development or partial deployment | 4 of 12 (33%) | Same 12-project cohort |
| World population lacking any officially recognized identity | over 1 billion | Cited from World Economic Forum figures, not independently measured by this paper |

### Parameters
Not applicable — this is a literature systematization with no runnable mechanism or tunable parameter of its own. The classification scheme applied to the 47-paper corpus used five fixed dimensions (type, trust infrastructure, cryptographic technique, which of 6 challenges addressed, evaluation method) and the 12-deployment assessment used five fixed self-sovereignty dimensions (key control, permissionless issuance, portability, selective disclosure, revocation resistance), each scored fully / partially / not supported.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that the scientific literature it surveyed treats usability "as an afterthought or ignore[s] it entirely," with only 2 of 47 papers reporting any user study, and calls this "a critical gap" because "systems that are not evaluated with real users risk optimizing for the wrong objectives." Key recovery is stated as "arguably the most critical unsolved problem": social-recovery schemes (a quorum of trusted contacts restoring access) introduce their own trust assumptions and coordination overhead, and hardware-backed key storage (secure enclaves, hardware security modules) protects keys at rest but does not solve backup if the device is lost or destroyed. Sybil resistance (preventing one actor from registering multiple identities) has no solution accepted as satisfactory among the three surveyed approaches: credential-based binding reintroduces dependence on a centralized issuing authority, web-of-trust binding is vulnerable to collusion and has bootstrapping problems in sparse networks, and biometric binding is irreversible once compromised and raises privacy concerns. The paper's own real-world evaluation found every one of the 12 deployed systems makes at least one compromise against full self-sovereignty, government-backed systems in particular sacrificing permissionlessness and revocation resistance by design because governments require the ability to revoke a credential. GDPR's right-to-be-forgotten conflicts with immutable ledger anchoring, and the paper states the legal sufficiency of the common workaround (storing only hashes on-chain, personal data off-chain) "remains contested." The paper explicitly frames its five-dimension deployment assessment as "a first step" toward a sovereignty-assurance framework, not a completed one, and identifies formalizing such a framework as future work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A credential-based identity-binding approach requires an external, already-trusted issuing authority (a government, university, or employer) willing to attest off-protocol that a given DID corresponds to a specific real-world entity; the protocol itself supplies no mechanism to establish that correspondence. A web-of-trust binding approach requires an existing social graph dense enough to avoid the bootstrapping failure the paper states occurs in sparse networks, and requires that colluding participants be detectable or economically discouraged elsewhere in the system, since the mechanism itself does not resist collusion. Key recovery via social recovery requires a quorum of contacts the user selects in advance to remain reachable and honest at the moment of recovery; hardware-backed key storage requires a physically available replacement device or backup channel, since the paper states it does not itself solve loss-of-device backup. Any mechanism anchoring identity to a single blockchain inherits that chain's consensus-failure and governance-crisis risk for every identity anchored to it, so avoiding this single-infrastructure dependence requires either a ledger-agnostic design or migration tooling across ledgers, for which the paper states "the current landscape falls far short" of existing cross-ledger interoperability standards. A design using zero-knowledge proofs for selective disclosure requires wallet software and verifier software to agree on a standardized proof format across DID methods, which the paper states does not yet exist.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational:** Mühle, Grüner, Gayvoronskaya, Meinel. Survey identifying essential SSI components (DIDs, verifiable credentials, distributed ledgers) — one of the earliest SSI surveys, cited as an architectural-overview baseline this SoK extends with challenge- and deployment-level analysis.
- **Foundational:** Der, Jähnichen, Sürmeli. Early position paper on SSI opportunities and challenges, cited as anticipating several of this SoK's six challenges without a systematic survey methodology.
- **Competing:** Stokkink, Ishmaev, Epema, Pouwelse. "TrustChain"-style peer-to-peer SSDI system (paper [132] in this SoK's numbering) — one of only 4 of 47 surveyed systems avoiding blockchain dependency entirely; explicitly argued by its authors that a "truly self-sovereign" system should not depend on any single ledger, cited by this SoK as not having achieved significant adoption.
- **Competing:** Zaeem, Khalil, Lamison, Pandey, Barber. "On the usability of self sovereign identity solutions," University of Texas at Austin Center for Identity Technical Report 21-02, 2021 — one of the only empirical usability studies of SSDI found in the 47-paper corpus; source of the finding that users found onboarding confusing and expressed anxiety about losing private keys.
- **Attack-or-critique:** Giannopoulou — critical sociopolitical analysis questioning whether SSI decentralization empowers users or merely relocates power to different intermediaries, cited by this SoK as a sociopolitical-perspective survey it builds on.
- **Superseded-by:** none identified — this is itself the most recent (2026) SoK in the domain.

- "Key recovery is arguably the most critical unsolved problem."
- "the vast majority of SSDI proposals rely on a single blockchain or distributed ledger as their trust anchor."
- "only 3 of the 12 surveyed projects (25%) were fully operational."
- "adopting the SSDI label without delivering its core properties" (describing "sovereignty washing").
- "usability is a precondition for adoption, not a secondary concern."

## [ANDONI-ARXIV-26] Efficient Algorithms for Adversarially Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
**Citation:** Alexandr Andoni, Themistoklis Haris, Esty Kelman, Krzysztof Onak. "Efficient Algorithms for Adversarially Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search." arXiv:2601.00272, 2026. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2601.00272.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.00272
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00272
**Domain:** B

### What it does
This paper gives algorithms that answer Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) queries correctly with high probability even when an adversary chooses both the searched dataset and every query adaptively, after seeing every prior answer — a threat model under which the paper shows ordinary randomized nearest-neighbor data structures can be forced to fail. The (c,r)-ANN problem (Definition 1.1) is: given a dataset S of n points in a metric space, a radius r, and an approximation factor c, build a data structure that, for a query point q, returns some point within distance c*r of q if any point within distance r of q exists, and otherwise may answer "no such point." Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH), the standard oblivious solution, groups points so that nearby points collide in the same hash bucket with higher probability than far points; a prior attack (Kapralov et al., 2024, cited but not reproduced in this corpus) is stated to show that an adaptive adversary needs only a number of queries polynomial in log(n) to learn enough about an LSH structure's internal hash functions to make it fail on a subsequent query.

The paper's adversarial-robustness model (Definition 3.1) is a game: the adversary picks the dataset S; the algorithm preprocesses S using private internal randomness the adversary cannot see; then, over Q rounds, the adversary picks each query using the full history of previous queries and answers, and the algorithm must answer correctly in every round with probability at least 1 - delta over its own randomness, for the run to count as delta-adversarially-robust. The dataset may also be updated (points added or deleted) obliviously, meaning the adversary fixes the update schedule in advance rather than adapting it to the algorithm's answers.

Three constructions are given, all working by preventing the adversary from learning the algorithm's internal randomness rather than by hiding the output (unlike the noise-adding techniques used for numeric estimation problems, which the paper states do not apply to search problems because the output must be an actual dataset point, not a perturbable number):
1. Fairness-based robustness (Theorem 1.2): building on prior work on "fair" ANN algorithms that select a valid answer uniformly at random from the qualifying candidates (Aumuller et al., 2022), the paper proves that any exact fair ANN algorithm is automatically adversarially robust, because uniform random selection is a form of statistical independence across queries that denies the adversary a learnable signal.
2. Search-to-decision via bucketing (Theorem 1.3): the search problem is reduced to a weak decision problem (does a point within r exist? does one within c*r not exist?) that can be solved by an oblivious LSH structure and then made robust with differential-privacy techniques (Hassidim et al., 2022) — maintaining Θ(sqrt(Q)) independent copies of the decision structure and combining their answers privately (via subsampled aggregation, avoiding a private-median step the prior framework needed). The dataset is partitioned into buckets of about sqrt(n) points each, a robust decider is run per bucket to find which bucket holds a qualifying point, and that bucket is then searched exhaustively for the final answer.
3. Concentric-annuli construction (Theorem 1.4): to remove the sqrt(n) floor the bucketing method imposes on query time, the (r, c*r) annulus around a query is split into several smaller concentric sub-annuli, the fair algorithm from construction 1 is run within each sub-annulus, and a counting argument guarantees at least one sub-annulus has low enough point density that the fair algorithm terminates quickly with probability at least 0.9; a differentially private selection step then picks a favorable sub-annulus to run the final (held-out) query on, without revealing which internal randomness the selection is based on to the adversary.

A separate "for-all" family of algorithms (Theorem 1.5 and Appendix D) targets a stronger, different guarantee: with probability at least 0.99, the built data structure answers every possible query correctly (not merely each of Q adaptively chosen queries with per-round failure probability delta), by discretizing the metric space into a covering and running enough independent LSH hash functions that a union bound over all points in the covering succeeds. This is stated to apply only to low-dimensional metric spaces, defined here as the regime d = O(sqrt(Q)), as opposed to the high-dimensional regime d = omega(sqrt(Q)) the fairness/privacy constructions target.

### Measured results
Every figure in this paper is a proved asymptotic bound over an abstract computational model, not an empirical measurement; there is no implementation, dataset, or run reported anywhere in the text. The bounds and the exact model conditions each depends on are:

| Result | Bound | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Standard oblivious LSH (baseline, not robust) | Query time O~(d * n^rho), space O~(n^(1+rho)) | d-dimensional metric space, n points, rho = rho(c) in (0,1) a constant fixed by the approximation factor c and the LSH construction; for the Hamming cube {0,1}^k with the best known construction, rho = 1/(2c-1) (Andoni and Razenshteyn, 2015) |
| Theorem 1.2 (fairness-based robustness) | Space O~(n^(1+rho(c)) * log(nQ)) bits; query time O~(d * (n^rho(c) + n(q,cr)/n(q,cr)+1... i.e. depends on the density ratio D) * log(nQ)) | n(q,r) is the count of dataset points within radius r of query q ("S-density"); query time depends on D = n(q,cr)/n(q,r), the ratio of far-ball to near-ball density around q, which the adversary can make arbitrarily large by constructing an adversarial dataset — this is stated as the construction's weakness |
| Theorem 1.3 (bucketing / search-to-decision) | Query time O~(d * n^(1/(2-rho))); space O~(sqrt(Q) * n^(2/(2-rho))); update time O~(d * n^(rho/(2-rho)) * sqrt(Q)); success probability at least 1 - Theta(delta) over Q queries | Same rho(c) as above; independent of dataset density (assumption-free), unlike Theorem 1.2; query time is always at least O(sqrt(n)) regardless of how close c pushes rho toward 0, which the paper states as this construction's limitation |
| Theorem 1.4 (concentric annuli) | Query time O~(d * n^beta) with probability at least 1 - delta, space O(sqrt(Q) * n^(1+beta)), update time O~(d * n^beta * sqrt(Q)), where beta = min over positive integers k of max(rho(c^(1/k)), 1/k) | For the Hamming hypercube specifically, rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) makes beta = Theta(log(log(c))/log(c)), which the paper states goes to 0 as c grows, unlike Theorem 1.3's exponent 1/(2-rho(c)), which does not |
| Theorem 1.5 (for-all guarantee, Hamming hypercube) | Space O~(d * n^(1+rho+o(1))); query time O~(d * n^rho); correctness on every possible query simultaneously with probability at least 0.99 | rho = 1/(2c-1); d-dimensional Hamming hypercube {0,1}^d specifically; the paper states this family's space complexity scales with an extra factor of d relative to the adaptive-adversary algorithms above, "making them intractable for high-dimensional metric spaces," and that these algorithms must be tailored per metric space rather than generalizing |
| Comparison to concurrent work (Feng et al., 2025) | Feng et al.'s algorithm: query time O(d * s * n^rho); space O(sqrt(Q) * s * n^(1+rho)); update time O~(d * n^rho * s * sqrt(Q)), where s = n(q,cr), the raw near-ball density (not a ratio) | The paper states its own Theorem 1.2 depends additively on the density ratio D (which is strictly smaller than Feng et al.'s s), and that this dependency does not affect the space complexity of its own algorithms (which grow only by an added factor of sqrt(Q)), whereas Feng et al.'s query time depends multiplicatively on s |

### Parameters
- n: dataset size (number of points).
- d: dimensionality of the metric space.
- c: the ANN approximation factor (c >= 1); larger c generally drives rho(c), and therefore query-time exponents, toward 0.
- r: the target radius defining a "near" neighbor; c*r is the radius defining the discard threshold.
- Q: the total number of adaptive queries the algorithm must remain robust against; several constructions' space costs scale with sqrt(Q).
- delta: the per-construction failure probability bound (adversarially-robust constructions) or, for the for-all family, the paper fixes a concrete constant success probability of 0.99 rather than a tunable delta.
- rho(c): the LSH quality exponent, metric-space- and construction-dependent; explicit closed form given only for the Hamming hypercube under the best known LSH construction, rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) (cited to Andoni and Razenshteyn, 2015).
- beta (concentric-annuli construction): beta = min_{k in positive integers} max(rho(c^(1/k)), 1/k), a derived quantity from rho and c, not an independently chosen parameter.
- Regime split: high-dimensional d = omega(sqrt(Q)) is where the fairness/decision/annuli constructions (Theorems 1.2-1.4) are the paper's contribution; low-dimensional d = O(sqrt(Q)) is where the for-all constructions (Theorem 1.5, Appendix D) apply instead.

### Stated limitations
Theorem 1.2's query time is stated to depend on the density ratio D between the c*r-ball and r-ball around a query, and the paper states the adversary can construct a dataset where this ratio is large, "severely degrading performance" — this is an explicit, named weakness of the fairness-only construction, not merely an unoptimized bound. Theorem 1.3's query time is stated to always be at least O(sqrt(n)) regardless of how favorable c is, which the paper calls not ideal given that oblivious LSH methods can push the query-time exponent arbitrarily close to 0 by increasing c. The for-all family (Theorem 1.5, Appendix D) is stated to have space complexity that scales by an extra factor of d, "making them intractable for high-dimensional metric spaces," a direct consequence of needing enough independent hash functions to union-bound over every possible query; the paper also states these for-all algorithms "lack the generality of their adaptive counterparts" because each is tailored to a specific metric space rather than working generically. The adversarial-robustness game defined here (Definition 3.1) treats updates to the dataset as oblivious — chosen in advance by the adversary, not adaptively based on the algorithm's answers — and the paper states it is "not concerned with robustness" against adaptively chosen updates, only queries. The conclusion states three explicit open questions the paper does not resolve: whether matching time/space lower bounds exist for robust ANN algorithms, whether the fairness-to-robustness link generalizes to estimation problems beyond search, and — stated directly — that "a practical implementation of our approach and the nuances it presents in a real system are also important avenues to investigate," meaning no implementation or systems-level evaluation exists in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every construction requires the algorithm's setup-phase and per-query internal randomness to be genuinely private from the adversary (Definition 3.1 states the adversary "may know the code for A but not the specific instance of R_setup"); a real deployment must therefore supply a source of randomness the querying party (or anyone observing the querying party's queries and answers) cannot predict or reconstruct — the proofs give no robustness guarantee if this randomness leaks through a side channel the model does not account for. The bucketing and concentric-annuli constructions both require access to a differential-privacy composition and amplification toolkit (the Laplace mechanism, privacy amplification by subsampling, and adaptive/parallel composition theorems, all cited to prior differential-privacy literature and used, not re-derived, as noted in Appendix B) — a system adopting this mechanism needs a correct implementation of these DP primitives, since the robustness proof is built on their guarantees holding exactly. The fairness-based construction (Theorem 1.2) requires an existing exact fair ANN algorithm as a subroutine (cited to Aumuller et al., 2022) that returns a uniformly random valid neighbor, not merely the closest one, so a system without such a subroutine cannot use this construction directly. The bucketing and annuli constructions both require maintaining sqrt(Q) or more independent copies of an underlying LSH-based decision structure simultaneously, so a deployment must know (or bound) Q, the number of future adaptive queries it needs to remain robust against, in advance, since the space cost is stated as a function of Q rather than being unboundedly extensible. The for-all algorithms require the metric space to be discretizable into a bounded covering (explicit constructions given only for the Hamming hypercube and l_p spaces), so applying them to an arbitrary or unbounded metric space is out of scope as stated.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. Section 2.1 states its own results differ from Feng et al. (2025), a concurrent and independent paper solving the same problem, in that Feng et al.'s query time scales multiplicatively with a raw near-ball density count while this paper's scales additively with a density ratio — an explicit, attributed disagreement in approach and bound shape between two papers on the same problem, not a contradiction discovered within this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- Kapralov, Mousavifar, Ozgur (or coauthors), 2024, attack on standard LSH data structures under adaptive queries — attack (the motivating result this paper responds to; states an adaptive adversary needs only a polylogarithmic number of queries to defeat unmodified LSH).
- Feng, Feng, Li, Song, Woodruff, Zhang, "On Differential Privacy [robust ANN]," 2025 — competing (concurrent, independent solution to the same robust-ANN problem, compared directly in Section 2.1 and Table 1).
- Hassidim, Kaplan, Mansour, Matias, Stemmer, 2022 — foundational (the differential-privacy robustification-via-aggregated-copies framework this paper's bucketing and annuli constructions build on).
- Aumuller, Har-Peled, Mahabadi, Pagh, Silvestri, "Sampling a Near Neighbor in High Dimensions — Who is the Fairest of Them All?," ACM Transactions on Database Systems 47(1), 2022 — foundational (defines and studies the fair-ANN algorithms this paper's Theorem 1.2 invokes as a subroutine).
- Beimel, Kaplan, Mansour, Nissim, Saranurak, Stemmer, "Dynamic Algorithms Against an Adaptive Adversary: Generic Constructions and Lower Bounds," STOC 2022 — foundational (source of the cited lower bound that robust search algorithms for certain problems are inherently slower than oblivious ones).
- Andoni and Razenshteyn, "Optimal Data-Dependent Hashing for Approximate Near Neighbors," STOC 2015 — foundational (source of the explicit rho(c) = 1/(2c-1) LSH construction used as the concrete example throughout).
- Cherapanamjeri and Nelson, 2020 and 2024 — foundational (prior discretization/net-based techniques for for-all-guarantee ANN and robust distance estimation, which Appendix D's construction refines).
- Ben-Eliezer, Jayaram, Woodruff, Yogev, 2022b — foundational (formalized adversarial robustness for streaming algorithms; source of the adversarial-robustness game definition adapted here as Definition 3.1).
- Pham and Pagh, 2016, and Wei, 2022 — competing (Las Vegas LSH constructions with no false negatives, stated to remain vulnerable to adversaries who inflate their expected runtime, per Kapralov et al., 2024).

## [ANGEL-SP-18] PIR with compressed queries and amortized query processing
**Citation:** Sebastian Angel, Hao Chen, Kim Laine, Srinath T. V. Setty. "PIR with compressed queries and amortized query processing." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2018. Pages 962-979. DOI 10.1109/SP.2018.00062.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/1142.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/1142.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
This paper (the system is called SealPIR in the text, though the paper's own title does not use that name) makes single-server computational Private Information Retrieval (PIR) cheaper on two axes: the size of the query a client sends, and the per-query computation a server performs when many queries from the same client arrive together. Ordinary computational PIR built on Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), of which the paper's baseline XPIR is an instance, requires the server to hold the database as a d-dimensional hyperrectangle of ciphertext-encrypted elements; the client's query, under the prior approach (Stern's protocol, which XPIR implements), must contain one ciphertext per candidate position along one dimension, so a database of n elements arranged with dimension d needs roughly the d-th root of n ciphertexts in the query. SealPIR replaces this multi-ciphertext query with a single compressed ciphertext plus a server-side procedure called EXPAND: using a technique built on ciphertext substitution (a property of the underlying FHE scheme, here the SEAL library's implementation of the Fan-Vercauteren, FV, encryption scheme), the server homomorphically expands the client's one compressed ciphertext back into the same d ciphertexts XPIR would have required, without the client ever having to send them explicitly. This shrinks client-to-server query bandwidth without changing what the server ultimately computes over. The second technique, probabilistic batch codes (PBC), lets a server answer several PIR queries from the same client (for a batch of k desired elements) using less total computation than running k independent single-element PIR queries. A PBC encodes the n-element database by replicating each element into w candidate positions ("buckets") chosen by w independent hash functions (a construction called Cuckoo hashing when the specific reverse-hashing allocation strategy of Cuckoo hashing is used to place elements into buckets), producing m = w times n total encoded elements across b buckets; to retrieve k desired elements, the client maps its k indices to b buckets using the matching consumer-side hashing procedure (this mapping can fail, returning an explicit failure marker, with a computable failure probability) and issues one PIR query per bucket rather than one per original element, and the server runs standard single-query PIR independently on each bucket.

### Measured results
All measurements on Microsoft Azure H16 server instances (16-core 3.6 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2667, 112 GB RAM) and F16s client instances (16-core, 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673, 32 GB RAM), Ubuntu 16.04, compiled with Rust nightly 1.25, across three Azure data centers (West US, South India, West Europe). Each experiment run 10 times with averaged results; standard deviations reported as under 10% of the mean in every case. The paper reports hardware as multi-core (16-core) instances but does not state explicitly, for the microbenchmarks in Figure 9, whether the implementation used a single thread or multiple threads of that 16-core machine; this detail could not be verified from the text.

Microbenchmarks (Figure 9), 288-byte database elements, FHE ciphertext polynomial degree 2048 with 60-bit coefficient modulus, comparing XPIR (dimension d=2 and d=3) against SealPIR (d=2):

| Database size (n, elements) | Metric | XPIR d=2 | XPIR d=3 | SealPIR d=2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65,536 | Client query generation (ms) | 13.83 | 4.98 | 3.37 |
| 1,048,576 | Client query generation (ms) | 55.14 | 12.74 | 3.37 |
| 65,536 | Query network size (KB) | 4,384 | 1,632 | 64 |
| 1,048,576 | Query network size (KB) | 17,536 | 4,064 | 64 |
| 65,536 | Server answer computation (s) | 0.21 | 0.27 | 0.13 |
| 1,048,576 | Server answer computation (s) | 2.12 | 2.52 | 2.01 |
| 65,536 | Answer network size (KB) | 256 | 1,824 | 256 |
| 1,048,576 | Answer network size (KB) | 256 | 1,952 | 256 |

Query size reduction over XPIR is 274 times at d=2 and 63 times at d=2-vs-d=3 comparison basis, for larger databases. SealPIR's EXPAND procedure adds 11% to 38% server CPU overhead relative to answering a query vector directly (no query compression), but keeps total server answer time comparable to XPIR at the same database size.

Response-time measurements deploying the PIR server in Azure US West and clients under four network conditions, retrieving one 288-byte element, compared against scp (secure copy, downloading the whole database) as a naive-PIR baseline: intra-datacenter (about 3.4 Gbps, measured with iperf), inter-datacenter (client in South India, about 800 Mbps), home network (client in South India, rate-limited to 20 Mbps via the Linux tc traffic-control utility, chosen to match the reported 18.7 Mbps mean US download speed from a cited Akamai report), and mobile network (client in South India, rate-limited to 10 Mbps via tc, chosen to approximate reported average US mobile carrier data speeds). At intra-datacenter bandwidth, scp gives the lowest response time; SealPIR is competitive with both XPIR variants except at the largest tested database size (2^22 elements), where SealPIR falls behind because its EXPAND optimization forces a small plaintext modulus at that size, increasing the number of plaintexts needed. At lower bandwidth (home and mobile conditions), SealPIR's lower network consumption yields up to a 42% reduction in response time relative to the compared schemes.

Throughput (Figure 11), server in Azure US West, 4 to 256 concurrent clients across South India and EU West, database of 2^20 elements of 288 bytes each, experiment designed so the server's CPU or WAN link (not the client or a specific inter-datacenter link) is the bottleneck: XPIR with d=2 saturates at 9 requests/second; SealPIR saturates at 7 requests/second (23% lower throughput than XPIR d=2 in this comparison); against XPIR with d=3, SealPIR achieves about 50% higher throughput. Both SealPIR and XPIR achieve more than 20 times the throughput of naive PIR via scp, because scp's bottleneck is network bandwidth rather than CPU.

Probabilistic Batch Code (PBC) benchmark (Figure 12), database of 2^20 elements, 288 bytes each, SealPIR (t=2^20) as the underlying single-query PIR library, comparing mPIR (SealPIR plus PBC with Cuckoo hashing, w=3 hash functions, b=1.5k buckets) against Pung's own multi-retrieval scheme, at batch sizes k = 16, 64, 256: at k=256, mPIR gives a 2.6 times reduction in server CPU cost for answering queries compared to Pung's scheme, and a 40.5 times reduction compared to running k independent single-query PIR instances. mPIR is 6 times more network-efficient (combined upload and download) than Pung's scheme at the measured batch sizes. mPIR's estimated Cuckoo-hashing failure probability is about 2^-40 for k > 200 (closer to 2^-20 for smaller k), lower than Pung's stated 2^-20 failure probability.

End-to-end case study porting SealPIR and mPIR into the Pung private-messaging system (256K simulated users, 32 real clients, remainder simulated by pre-populating the server database with random messages, closed-loop round-based operation), each client sending one message and retrieving k messages per round, k up to 256: at k=64, the modified system ("Pung+MS," using both mPIR and SealPIR) achieves 3.1 times the throughput, in messages per minute, of the original Pung implementation. Per-client network cost for one round at k=16 falls from 279 MB (original Pung) to 7.7 MB (Pung+MS), a reduction the paper states as over 36 times.

### Parameters
- FHE ciphertext polynomial degree N: 2048, with 60-bit ciphertext coefficient modulus q (SEAL uses q = 2^60 - 2^18 + 1; XPIR uses q = 2^61 - i times 2^14 + 1 for various i), chosen following XPIR's published security estimates based on the Albrecht-Player-Scott hardness analysis.
- Database element size: 288 bytes throughout the main evaluation, chosen to match the message size used by the Pung system in the case study.
- Plaintext modulus t: 2^23 as the default SealPIR setting (a larger t lowers network and computation cost but risks decryption failure from excess noise growth, so t is lowered in some experiments, e.g. to 2^20 for the PBC benchmarks, to guarantee correct decryption).
- XPIR packing parameter alpha: 14 elements packed per XPIR plaintext, chosen to have roughly the same effect as SealPIR's t=2^23 setting for 288-byte elements under the paper's security parameters.
- PIR dimension d: tested at d=2 and d=3 for XPIR; SealPIR evaluated at d=2 in the main comparisons.
- PBC parameters (Cuckoo-hashing variant): w=3 independent hash functions, b=1.5k buckets for a batch size of k, following prior empirical analysis of Cuckoo hashing failure rates cited from other work.
- Batch size k for multi-query PIR: tested at 1 (no amortization baseline), 16, 64, and 256.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that determining the exact failure probability and constant factors of Cuckoo hashing analytically remains an open problem in the literature it cites, so its own failure-probability figures (2^-40 for k > 200, 2^-20 for smaller k) are described as empirical estimates from prior work rather than proven bounds. The paper states that under a malicious (not merely semi-honest) server, the server controls where database elements are placed and so can deliberately place specific elements at index combinations that make GenSchedule always fail for a client requesting that combination, opening what the paper calls a "selective failure" attack analogous to one already known in single-query PIR; the paper states this requires additional mechanisms (making the client's externally visible reaction independent of query success or failure) to convert an information-leaking failure into a mere availability failure, but the paper does not implement or measure such a mechanism. The paper states SealPIR falls behind XPIR in response time specifically at the largest tested database size (2^22 elements) under high-bandwidth (intra-datacenter) conditions, because its EXPAND optimization there forces a smaller plaintext modulus and more plaintexts. The paper states, as future work rather than a solved problem, that CPU costs could be further reduced using a matrix-multiplication aggregation technique from prior work (Beimel et al.) not implemented in this paper, and that PBC bucket-allocation strategies studied here are drawn from online load-balancing literature (elements arriving one at a time) rather than from strategies specific to the offline setting (all elements available at once) that PBC actually operates in, leaving offline-optimized allocation as an open direction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The client must already know, before issuing a query, which numeric index or indices in the database it wants; the paper states three alternative external mechanisms an application must supply to produce that index (a Bloom filter shared out of band, as in the Pung system; a PIR-by-keyword scheme; or the client independently simulating the server's Cuckoo-hashing placement given a shared pseudorandom seed), none of which SealPIR or the PBC construction itself provides. Multi-query batching (mPIR) requires the client and server to agree in advance on the batch size k and the hashing parameters (w, b) used to construct and consume the PBC; a client that does not know these parameters cannot correctly map its desired indices to buckets. The scheme's privacy guarantee (the server cannot tell which index was retrieved) holds under a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) server for the analysis given; the paper states that a fully malicious server breaks a distinct property (whether a client's chosen batch of indices can be retrieved at all) unless a system built on this scheme separately adds the selective-failure countermeasure described above. mPIR's failure mode (GenSchedule returning an explicit failure marker for a chosen index set) is visible to the client before any PIR query is issued, so a system relying on mPIR must have a defined recovery behavior (retry with different indices, retrieve fewer elements, or otherwise) built into its application logic, since the paper does not mandate a single response to a schedule failure.

### Contradicts
The prior-pass claim (recorded in the target-retrieval registry's rationale) that this paper reports a throughput of "102 MB/s" with no attached experimental condition is not supported anywhere in this paper's text: no figure or table in the paper states a MB/s throughput number at all. The paper's own throughput results are stated in requests per second (7 for SealPIR, 9 for XPIR d=2, both saturating at a 2^20-element, 288-byte-element database under a specific multi-client, multi-datacenter deployment) or in messages per minute (Pung case study), never in MB/s; the "102 MB/s" figure attributed to this paper should be treated as unverified against the primary source and possibly misattributed from a different PIR paper. No other cross-corpus contradiction found.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: C. Aguilar-Melchor, J. Barrier, L. Fousse, M.-O. Killijian. "XPIR: Private information retrieval for everyone." PoPETs 2016 — the direct baseline this paper's every microbenchmark, response-time, and throughput comparison is measured against.
- competing: S. Angel, S. Setty. "Unobservable communication over fully untrusted infrastructure" (Pung), USENIX OSDI 2016 — the private-messaging system this paper modifies for its end-to-end case study; holds Pung's original custom multi-query PIR scheme this paper's mPIR is compared against.
- foundational: J. Stern. Untitled CPIR protocol referenced as "Stern's protocol" (Figure 1's source construction), cited as the basis for both XPIR and SealPIR's per-dimension query structure.
- foundational: A. Beimel et al. Matrix-multiplication aggregation technique for multi-query PIR, cited as an unimplemented future optimization for reducing SealPIR's CPU cost.
- competing: Y. Ishai et al. Subcube batch code construction, cited as the batch-coding approach underlying Pung's multi-retrieval scheme, against which the paper's own probabilistic batch code is compared in Figure 5.
- attack: M. R. Albrecht, R. Player, S. Scott. "On the concrete hardness of learning with errors." Journal of Mathematical Cryptology, 2015 — the hardness-estimation basis for this paper's and XPIR's choice of FHE security parameters.

## [ASTHANA-PHD-14] PAC'nPost: A Peer-to-Peer Micro-blogging Social Network

**Citation:** Harshvardhan Asthana. "PAC'nPost: A Peer-to-Peer Micro-blogging Social Network." PhD thesis, University College London, 2014.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1457379/1/Harshvardhan%20Asthana%20thesis%20-%20submitted.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title, author, and abstract)
**Source URL:** https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1457379/1/Harshvardhan%20Asthana%20thesis%20-%20submitted.pdf
**Domain:** B

### What it does
PAC'nPost lets a node in an unstructured peer-to-peer network retrieve the short posts ("micro-blogs") of the users it follows, and search all published micro-blogs by keyword, without a central server and without directly contacting the nodes it follows. It builds on the probably approximately correct (PAC) search architecture, in which a node retrieves an item with a target accuracy by querying a fixed number z of random peers, provided the item has already been replicated onto a computable fraction of the network. The framework's problem is to replicate every newly created post onto enough nodes, fast enough, without flooding the network with copies (a mechanism the thesis calls rapid-yet-restrained dissemination) and without a central coordinator, given that microblog creation happens continuously and at a high rate rather than as a single one-off rumor.

Every node in the network periodically (every s seconds) sends a request to z randomly chosen peers, naming the list of user IDs it follows and the identifier of the latest post from each it has already retrieved. Each queried node answers by returning, from its own local storage, the most recent post from every followed user it has stored, plus its own most-recently-published post, plus the current contents of a small local structure called the transfer buffer. The transfer buffer holds a bounded number of recently encountered posts that the node has not yet decided to stop forwarding; a post the node chooses not to place in the buffer is permanently excluded from further forwarding by that node (called "stifling," borrowed from epidemic/gossip terminology). Buffer membership is decided per post with a probability that decays with the post's age, P(select) = e^(−t/β), where t is the post's age in seconds and β is a tunable "dissemination parameter" — a larger β keeps older posts eligible for forwarding longer, increasing both the post's final replication and each node's bandwidth. A post is eligible for buffer selection only during its first sr seconds after publication (a fixed replication window), after which no node will forward it further regardless of buffer decisions already made. When a post is first published, its origin node immediately sends it to z (or, in the bandwidth-optimized variant, a separate initial-seeding count zs) random peers, giving the post a head start on this stifling process before ordinary scheduled queries take over its spread.

Retrieval accuracy, µ, defined as the probability of finding a specific post by querying z random nodes given it has been replicated onto r of n total nodes, follows µ = 1 − (1 − r/n)^z, the same relation underlying the PAC search architecture cited from the thesis's own earlier ICTIR 2011 paper (Asthana, Fu, Cox). This equation determines the replication fraction r/n required for a chosen target accuracy at a chosen query fan-out z, and the thesis inverts it to compute the number of nodes queried needed for a required accuracy, or vice versa. Keyword search reuses the identical query mechanism: a query for a keyword is broadcast to the same z random peers, each of which searches its local micro-blog collection using the BM25 ranking algorithm and returns its own top-k ranked results, which the querying node merges by BM25 score into a single top-k list.

To decouple the replication rate from the query interval s (in the base design the two are coupled because replication happens only via ordinary scheduled queries), the thesis's Chapter 4 variant introduces a separate role, "replicators": at every iteration, a node is admitted into the replicator set with a probability that also decays with the age of its most-recent locally-stored post, e^(−(t−1)/δ) for parameter δ, and each replicator independently forwards its own transfer buffer contents to zr additional random nodes per iteration — mimicking the "eager push" primitive of classical gossip protocols while still using the transfer-buffer stifling mechanism to support many concurrent, independently-aged rumors (one per post) rather than a single global rumor.

Chapter 5 adds a two-step algorithm for detecting a trending keyword — one occurring in posts at an elevated rate — without any node having access to global post-creation statistics. Step one: on each scheduled query, each queried node reports the top-j most frequent keywords (by cumulative count) found in its local keyword-storage sets covering the most recent (s+t) iterations, where t is the number of consecutive iterations a keyword must appear in to count as trending; the querying node sums frequencies across the z responses. Step two: on the following scheduled query, the node asks the same z peers for the specific iteration numbers at which any keyword whose combined frequency exceeds w times the median frequency (w a system parameter) was observed; merging the returned iteration numbers lets the node compute a trending fraction σ — the proportion of the required t consecutive iterations in which the keyword was actually observed — and treat the keyword as trending once σ exceeds a threshold.

| Non-uniform (power-law, γ=0.68) follower/posting-rate replication of high- vs. regular-popularity users' posts separately gives only marginal bandwidth reduction versus uniform replication (e.g., 9.46 MB vs 10.35 MB at n=10,000, p(h)=0.01α) | Top-1% of nodes assigned 20% of all follower edges and (in the tested split) up to 50% of post-creation probability; analytical optimum per Eqs. 4.1-4.3 applied separately to each population |

| Illustrative (non-simulated, analytically computed) per-node memory: 1.93 MB soft-state-equivalent storage capacity for 900 MB of allocated post storage compressed at ~0.1 KB/post, yielding 9 million storable compressed posts per node and 75 million system-wide unique posts at 12% replication, sufficient to retain all posts created over 340 days at n=100,000 and 2.5 posts/sec system-wide creation rate | Assumes 1 GB contributed disk space/node, 90%/10% storage/index split, 1 KB/post uncompressed, FIFO eviction on capacity exhaustion — a capacity calculation, not a measured retention duration |

All simulation results above ran the actual PAC'nPost node logic in a discrete-iteration simulator, not an emulated network testbed; no real-network deployment or wide-area measurement is reported anywhere in the thesis.

### Parameters
Target accuracy µ: fixed at 95% throughout ("the most important decision" the designer makes, per the thesis; a lower target trades directly against replication or query count). Nodes queried per request, z: 25 in the base design (Chapters 3, 5); optimized to 15-16 (n=10,000) or 45-51 (n=100,000) as a function of query interval s in the bandwidth-optimized design (Chapter 4). Query interval, s: 30 seconds (base design, chosen to resemble Twitter's user experience) or 60-120 seconds (bandwidth-optimized design). Replication window, sr: 30 seconds (time a post is allowed to spread before being deemed available for retrieval). Dissemination parameter β: swept from 4.9-15.0 across experiments depending on n and target accuracy; determines exponential post-selection-into-buffer probability e^(−t/β). Maximum transfer buffer size, |T|max: unbounded in initial experiments, then capped at 25 (Chapter 3) or 100 (Chapter 4, decoupled design). Post creation rate, α: 25 posts/iteration (10x an assumed Twitter baseline of 4,600 tweets/sec over 200 million users) as the default; 125 posts/iteration (50x-500x baseline depending on n) tested as a spike condition; also expressed as α=2.5×10^-4 posts/node/iteration for the bandwidth model. Followers per node, f: fixed at 35 uniformly, based on Kwak et al.'s reported 1.47 billion links over 41.7 million Twitter users; later relaxed to a power-law distribution with exponent γ=0.68 (top 1% of nodes hold 20% of all follower edges). Post size, cb: 1,000 bytes (500 UTF-8 characters at 2 bytes/character). Per-contact protocol overhead, ct: 64 bytes (empty TCP/IP packet). Per-followed-peer specifier cost, cn: 8 bytes. Per-node contributed disk: 1 GB, split 90% post storage / 10% index. Churn model: session lengths exponentially distributed with mean 60 seconds under the "heavy churn" test; Poisson-arrival joins balance exponential-exit departures, holding active population roughly constant at 50,000 of 100,000 total. Seeding parameter zs: 25-105 tested (Chapter 4), trading off against β for a fixed target replication. Replicator-selection parameter δ: 0.66 in the reported decoupled-design simulations. Replicator fan-out zr: 7-9 (n=10,000) or 7-8.5 (n=100,000) in the decoupled-design simulations. Trending-keyword parameters: t=10 consecutive iterations to qualify as trending, w=10 (frequency threshold multiplier over median), j=1-3 (number of keyword-frequency pairs returned per query), y=5%-15% (fraction of posts carrying the injected trending keyword in test scenarios).

### Stated limitations
The thesis states PAC'nPost provides no mechanism for a user to delete or recall a published post once it has spread; a "recall/delete mechanism" is listed as future work. It states that the fixed-capacity, first-in-first-out (FIFO) storage area at each node means older posts are eventually evicted and permanently lost from the network once no node retains a copy, and that "an archiving strategy needs to be considered" — no such strategy is designed or evaluated in the thesis. The two-step trending-keyword algorithm is stated to require significant additional bandwidth (up to 37.73% overhead in the tested multi-keyword configuration) when tuned to detect multiple simultaneous trending keywords, which the authors state is future work to reduce. The thesis states BM25 is not an optimal ranking function for very short documents (micro-blog posts sized like SMS messages, ~140 characters) because term-frequency weighting is largely uninformative at that length, and states that query-independent features (publisher popularity, follow-relationship distance) would be a better ranking signal — not implemented or evaluated, only proposed as future work. The thesis states the framework is vulnerable to two forms of content pollution: false-identity disinformation and spam; it states these malicious posts would not appear in a user's followed-post timeline (because that timeline is restricted to accounts the user follows) but could appear in keyword-search results, and states that no defense is implemented — a "system of complaints" is sketched as a possible future direction but explicitly noted to itself require a decentralized reputation mechanism whose complaint-submitter's own reliability must also be assessed, which the thesis states is unsolved and left as future work rather than designed. The trending-keyword mechanism's susceptibility to spam abuse (a spammer inserting the trending keyword into unrelated posts to be retrieved by searches on that keyword) is stated explicitly as a known, unaddressed vulnerability, also deferred to future work. The non-uniform (popularity-weighted) replication scheme is stated to yield only marginal bandwidth savings versus uniform replication, in contrast to distributed web search, because the thesis's own periodic-polling retrieval model requires every node to keep querying for both high- and low-popularity content on every cycle, which the authors state erodes the benefit non-uniform document distribution provides in a more static distributed-search setting. The system-bandwidth calculation for mobile devices (6.64 KB/sec sustained upload+download) is stated by the authors to be "currently not viable for a mobile phone," with the only proposed mitigation being to have a mobile app communicate through a separate always-on desktop node rather than the phone itself directly participating.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
PAC'nPost requires an underlying peer-sampling/membership service that supplies each node with a partial, near-uniformly-random view of the network and periodically refreshes that view by exchanging entries with other nodes; the thesis names Cyclon, the overlay management system of Jelasity et al., and Brahms as examples that could supply this, but does not itself implement or evaluate any of them, so the correctness of PAC'nPost's random-peer-selection assumption depends entirely on whichever such service is deployed beneath it. It requires every participating node to follow at least one other peer, because a node that follows nobody never issues the scheduled queries that also carry replication traffic via the transfer buffer; the thesis states that if a newly published post is seeded only to nodes that follow nobody, that post fails to replicate — an explicitly acknowledged (if "very unlikely") failure mode. The keyword-search accuracy measurement depends on a centralized "gold standard" database that mirrors every published post, used only for evaluation, not for production operation — a real deployment has no such oracle and cannot itself measure retrieval or keyword-search accuracy against ground truth. The bandwidth-optimized (decoupled) design and the trending-keyword mechanism both assume the underlying transfer-buffer/stifling mechanism from the base design already functions and is running on every node; the trending-keyword mechanism specifically piggybacks its extra request/response fields onto the already-scheduled query and therefore inherits every precondition (working peer-sampling service, non-empty follow lists, honest response content) that the base retrieval mechanism requires. Retrieval-accuracy measurement throughout assumes queried nodes answer truthfully and completely from their actual local storage; no experiment introduces a node that misreports its stored content, forges a keyword-frequency count, or omits available posts, so none of the measured accuracy or bandwidth figures characterize behavior under such a node.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5). The thesis's own two-page WWW 2012 companion paper (Asthana and Cox, "PAC'nPost: A Framework for a Micro-blogging Social Network in an Unstructured P2P Network") is stated by the registry's own retrieval-justification note to be too short to state the mechanism in implementable detail; this thesis is the correct full-length source for citing PAC'nPost mechanism details and measured figures, and any prior citation of numeric results to the WWW 2012 paper alone should be checked against this thesis instead. The thesis's own claim that existing DHT-based peer-to-peer social networks (PeerSoN, eXO, Cuckoo, My3) "do not address how a keyword search across all published data could be performed" and "assume a tight-knit community of peers" is the thesis authors' characterization of those systems, not a verified fact from this batch — retrieving those papers directly would be needed to confirm or contradict it.
