## [BIRYUKOV-SP-13] Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization

**Citation:** Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov, Ralf-Philipp Weinmann. "Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2013. DOI 10.1109/SP.2013.15.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cryptolux.org/images/2/25/Tor-HS-deanonymization.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cryptolux.org/images/2/25/Tor-HS-deanonymization.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper demonstrates three attacks against Tor hidden services (a Tor hidden service publishes a rendezvous descriptor to a small set of relays instead of a public IP address, so a client reaches it only through the Tor network). First, an attacker computes future rendezvous-descriptor identifiers and precomputes relay key pairs whose fingerprints land immediately after those identifiers on the fingerprint ring Tor uses to assign descriptor storage, then runs relays with those keys so the attacker's own relays become the hidden service's descriptor-storage points (hidden service directories, HSDirs). Injecting the relays into every second gap of the ring lets the attacker capture every descriptor published network-wide. Second, controlling a hidden service's rendezvous descriptor storage or its guard node lets the attacker count descriptor fetch requests, which the paper uses as a proxy for the number of distinct clients that used the hidden service in the counted period. Third, an attacker who additionally controls a Tor relay acting as a hidden service's entry guard (the fixed first hop of every circuit the hidden service builds) forces the hidden service to open a rendezvous circuit to an attacker-controlled rendezvous point; the rendezvous point sends a distinctive count of relay cells (50 padding cells) back down the circuit, and the guard node recognizes the resulting cell-count and timing signature on any circuit passing through it, which identifies the immediately preceding relay as the hidden service's own entry point and, when the guard is one hop from the hidden service's own machine, reveals its IP address directly.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 59,130 descriptor publication requests, 58,389 descriptors fetched, 24,703 with unique public keys, ~1.5% encrypted | 50 Amazon EC2 instances running 1,200 Tor relay processes (24 relays per instance) for 25 hours, November 2012 |
| ~3% of hidden descriptors estimated missed | Verified against a 120-hidden-service sample from public sources; 4 relays from the sample were absent from the harvested set |
| 39,824 unique onion addresses collected, cost reduced to USD 57 | Second harvesting run, 58 EC2 micro instances, relays set to 0-1 Bytes/sec reported bandwidth to avoid attracting client traffic unrelated to the attack |
| Estimated botnet size 12,000-30,000 infected machines | Derived from descriptor-fetch counts of 1,408-4,977 requests/day for one hidden service (command-and-control channel), 13-29 July, capped at one fetch per 24 hours per machine because Tor caches descriptors for 24 hours |
| Silk Road: 15,185-19,284 descriptor requests/day; DuckDuckGo: 502-549 requests/day | Four consecutive days, 9-12 November 2012, measured by controlling one of each service's three responsible HSDir relays |
| Average gap between consecutive HSDir fingerprints on the ring: 10^44.8, minimum 10^42.16 | One randomly selected Tor consensus document, November 2012; finding a key fingerprint that falls in such a gap took a few minutes on a multi-core computer |
| Guard-identification attack: 8, 6, 5 correct identifications from ~36,000 rendezvous cells over 1h20m; second run: 5, 2, 1 correct identifications from ~16,000 rendezvous cells over 40 minutes | Two hidden services operated by the authors, attacker running one guard-adjacent (middle) relay and one rendezvous point |
| Cell-count traffic signature (3 cells up / 53 cells down) observed on 0 of 748,846 circuits examined | Circuits passing through one guard node the authors operated, used to establish the signature's false-positive rate |
| 90% probability of deanonymizing a long-running hidden service within 8 months, for EUR 8,280 (~USD 11,000) | Renting 23 relays of the EUR 45/month "EcoServer Large X5" class, each independently having ~0.6% average monthly probability of being chosen as one of a hidden service's three guards; combined chance per hidden service of 13.8% per guard-rotation attempt |

### Parameters
- Hidden service directory (HSDir) set size: 3 relays per descriptor replica, 2 replicas published, so 6 HSDirs total per hidden service.
- HSDir flag acquisition delay: 25 hours of consensus presence required before a relay is trusted as an HSDir.
- Consensus validity window: published hourly, fresh for 1 hour, valid for 3 hours total; clients fetch the next consensus in the interval (fresh-until + 45 min, valid-until − 10 min).
- Guard set size: 3 guards chosen initially; replaced only when fewer than 2 remain reachable; each guard's tenure is a random duration between 30 and 60 days.
- Maximum Tor relays per IP address admitted to the consensus: 2 (enforced by directory authorities; used in the attack by running additional "shadow" relays on the same IP that do not appear in the consensus until an active relay drops out).
- Attacker resource used for full-network descriptor harvesting: R = N / (12 × 2) IP addresses, where N is the number of HSDirs in the network (derived from the need to cover every second gap on the fingerprint ring, in two ring passes per day, with 2 relays per IP).

### Stated limitations
The paper's descriptor-count-based population estimates are approximate: multiple power cycles of one machine in a day overcount that machine, and the 24-hour descriptor cache means a machine that stays on for multiple days is undercounted. The authors state the guard-identification method proposed for encrypted introduction points cannot distinguish between hidden services once the full descriptor set for comparison is unavailable to the attacker. The authors state their proposed fixes are "nothing more than stop-gap measures" and that hidden services need a more complete redesign. The paper does not measure detection resistance of the attacker's own relays against countermeasures the Tor directory authorities might apply beyond the flag-assignment change already made in response to this work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any rendezvous/directory design that assigns responsibility for storing a lookup record deterministically from a public identifier (a fingerprint ring keyed by a hash of the identifier, here) gives an adversary who can compute future identifiers the ability to precompute keys that land adjacent to that identifier and, by running relays with those keys, capture the storage role before the legitimate publisher does. Any capacity- or reputation-gated onboarding delay (the 25-hour HSDir-flag wait, here) bounds only the attacker's setup latency, not the number of identities the attacker can eventually operate, when the identity-creation cost itself is close to free (running a Tor relay process). A guard-node or fixed-entry-hop mechanism that keeps the same relay as a client's or service's first hop for weeks concentrates all of that period's deanonymization risk onto whichever party operates that one relay; the risk is proportional to the probability of an adversary being selected in the guard-selection weighting, which this paper measures directly for one bandwidth class.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch measures Tor hidden-service directory assignment or guard-selection probability directly; JOHNSON-CCS-13 and SUN-USENIXSEC-15 measure Tor circuit compromise from different adversary positions (autonomous-system-level and relay-operator-level traffic correlation, and BGP-level routing manipulation) and do not overlap with this paper's descriptor-harvesting or guard-identification figures.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Dingledine, Mathewson, Syverson. "Tor: The second-generation onion router." USENIX Security Symposium, 2004.
- foundational: Øverlier, Syverson. "Locating hidden servers." IEEE S&P, 2006.
- competing/related: Elahi, Bauer, AlSabah, Dingledine, Goldberg. "Changing of the Guards: A framework for understanding and improving entry guard selection in Tor." WPES 2012. (already a target in this batch: ELAHI-WPES-12)
- attack: Bauer, McCoy, Grunwald, Kohno, Sicker. "Low-resource routing attacks against Tor." WPES 2007.
- attack: Murdoch. "Hot or not: Revealing hidden services by their clock skew." ACM CCS 2006.
- attack: Zander, Murdoch. "An improved clock-skew measurement technique for revealing hidden services." USENIX Security Symposium 2008.
- foundational: Douceur. "The Sybil attack." IPTPS 2002.

- "we could have lost about 3% of hidden descriptors"
- "None of the circuit exhibited the trafﬁc pattern of 3 cells up the circuit and 53 cells down the circuit"
- "the probability to deanonymize a long-running hidden service... is more than 90%, for a cost of... USD 11,000"
- "the above suggestions are nothing more than stop-gap measures"

## [BONEH-ASIACRYPT-16] Balloon Hashing: A Memory-Hard Function Providing Provable Protection Against Sequential Attacks
**Citation:** Dan Boneh, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Stuart Schechter. "Balloon Hashing: A Memory-Hard Function Providing Provable Protection Against Sequential Attacks." ASIACRYPT, 2016 (revised May 12, 2017). DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-53887-6_8.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/027.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/027.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
A memory-hard function forces any evaluator to use a large amount of working memory, so that an attacker checking many candidate passwords against a stolen password-hash file cannot substitute cheap computation for expensive memory and thereby parallelize the attack cheaply on custom hardware. Balloon Hashing achieves this with a data-independent memory-access pattern (the sequence of memory addresses touched during evaluation does not depend on the password), which prevents an attacker who can observe a victim's memory-access trace (for example, through a cache-timing side channel) from learning anything about the password. The algorithm takes a password, a salt, a space-cost parameter `s_cost` (buffer size in blocks), and a time-cost parameter `t_cost` (number of mixing rounds `r`), and runs in three steps: (1) Expand — fill an `s_cost`-block buffer with pseudo-random bytes by repeated hashing of the password and salt; (2) Mix — perform `r` rounds over the buffer, where each round updates every block to the hash of the previous block, the block's current contents, and `δ` (delta) other blocks chosen by a pseudorandom function of the salt and position (not of the password); (3) Extract — output the last block of the buffer. The construction uses only a standard (non-memory-hard) cryptographic hash function `H` as its compression-function subroutine, modeled as a random oracle for the security proof, so any hash function whose output size matches or exceeds its internal state size can be substituted.

The paper's security proof works by mapping the algorithm's computation to a data-dependency graph — a directed acyclic graph with one vertex per random-oracle query, edges representing which prior outputs a later query depends on — and applying a graph-pebbling argument: an adversary "graph-respecting" if it queries the random oracle for a value only once all of that query's input values are already computed and held in memory. The proof shows the Balloon data-dependency graph, built by stacking random "sandwich graphs," satisfies well-spreadedness and expansion properties with high probability over the choice of random oracle, and that these properties force any graph-respecting adversary using space `S` and time `T` to satisfy `S · T ≥ n²/32` for an `n`-block computation. A technique from Dwork, Naor, and Wee then extends this bound from graph-respecting adversaries to arbitrary adversaries in the random-oracle model.

### Measured results
All experimental figures from an Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) at 3.40 GHz with 8 GiB RAM, code compiled with gcc 4.8.5 at `-O3`, using the OpenSSL 1.0.1f implementation of SHA-512 and reference implementations of Blake2b, ECHO, and SHA-3/Keccak, all algorithms compared using Blake2b as the underlying compression function for consistency, each measurement averaged over 32 trials.

- Minimum buffer size for a given hashing throughput (Figure 5, two security-parameter settings): at a target authentication rate of 100 hashes/second on a four-core machine (25 hashes/second/core, one core doing the measured single-core work), one-round Balloon hashing (`r=1`, "Normal Security," `δ=3`) needs a 2 MiB buffer, and eight-round Balloon hashing (`r=8`, "Strong Security") needs a 256 KiB buffer, both instantiated with Blake2b. Under the same 100-hashes/second target, single-pass Argon2i (v1.2.1, also instantiated with Blake2b) permits an attacker to use only roughly 1.5 MiB — smaller than Balloon's 2 MiB buffer at the comparable round setting — which the authors state as evidence Balloon simultaneously gives better performance and a stronger memory-hardness guarantee than Argon2i at matched parameters.
- Argon2i attack, space reduction with no measured computation-time increase: the paper's pre-computation-based attack computes `n`-block single-pass Argon2i using `n/4` blocks of storage (expected value; the paper's own empirical Figure 4 shows the attack achieving `n/5` blocks in practice, tighter than the idealized `n/4` analysis predicts) against the Argon2i design document's claimed 7.3× computational penalty at `n/4` space (Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, Argon2 design document Table 2) — the paper's attack incurs no computational penalty at that same space budget. For multi-pass Argon2i (default: 3 passes) the attack's expected space usage tends to `n/e ≈ n/2.7` blocks as pass count grows, against the design document's claimed 16,384× penalty at `n/3` space (Argon2i design document, Section 5.4) for the same space class — again with no computational penalty measured by this attack.
- Compression-function throughput comparison (Figure 6, buffer sizes 16 KiB to 4 MiB): Blake2b and ECHO (the latter exploiting AES-NI instructions) outperform SHA-3 and SHA-512 by "a bit less than a factor of two" in bytes written per second when used as the Balloon compression function, on the same test machine; the paper's plotted curves also mark the machine's L1, L2, and L3 cache boundaries as visible throughput inflection points, though no numeric cache sizes are stated in the text extracted.
- Pre-computation table cost for the Argon2i attack: at most `8·p·n` bytes on a 64-bit machine for `p`-pass, `n`-block Argon2i (one 8-byte timestamp per generated block); for the single-pass case the paper computes the combined table-plus-buffer cost as `8n + 1024(n/4) = 8n + 256n` bytes against the `1024n` bytes Argon2i's straightforward implementation requires — stated as still a substantial reduction.

### Parameters
- `δ` (delta), dependencies per block per mixing round: the main theorem is stated for `δ=3` (giving bound `S·T ≥ r·n²/32`) and for `δ=7` combined with `S < n/64` (giving the stronger bound `S·T ≥ (2r−1)·n²/32`). The reference pseudocode (Figure 1) sets `delta = 3` as its example value; the paper states the real construction uses `δ ≥ 3`.
- `s_cost` (space cost / buffer size in blocks) and `t_cost` (time cost / number of mixing rounds `r`): both user-specified with no fixed recommended values; block size is set equal to the output size of the underlying compression function `H`.
- Hash function `H`: instantiated in experiments with Blake2b, SHA-3/Keccak (rate 1344, operating on 1344-bit blocks), SHA-512, and ECHO (512-bit blocks for the latter three); the construction is stated to be agnostic to this choice provided `H`'s internal state size is at least as large as its output size.
- `M`-core parallel variant: defined as the XOR of `M` independent single-core Balloon evaluations on the same password with `M` different salt suffixes; computing it is argued to require computing `M` full single-core instances, with no numeric `M` fixed.
- Comparison baselines' parameters, as configured for Figure 5: bcrypt at cost factor 12; PBKDF2-SHA512 at 10^5 iterations.

### Stated limitations
The proof's `S·T ≥ n²/32` (or the `δ=7` variant's tighter bound) is a single-instance, sequential-adversary guarantee: it lower-bounds the space-time product of computing the Balloon function once, and treats an adversary limited to one random-oracle query per time step; the authors state a password-guessing attacker in practice makes billions of evaluations and may have thousands of cores in parallel, which the underlying definition does not model. Alwen and Blocki's result, cited by this paper, shows no perfectly memory-hard function with a password-independent access pattern exists under the amortized, parallel adversary model (the parallel random-oracle model, pROM); their special-case attack computes Balloon in the pROM using an amortized time-space product of roughly `O(n^(7/4))`, weaker than the sequential `Ω(n²)` guarantee. The composed construction the authors recommend (Balloon composed with scrypt) defends against memory-access-pattern leakage and against the parallel pROM attack separately but not simultaneously — an attacker with both capabilities at once defeats the composition, which the authors state explicitly. The Argon2i time-space lower bound the paper proves in Appendix F (`S·T ≥ n²/1536` for single-pass, `n`-block Argon2i) is stated by the authors to be weaker than the Balloon bound and to leave open the possibility of an attack saving a further factor of 1536 in space with no increase in computation time. The paper's Argon2i attack analysis is restricted to the single-threaded instantiation; the authors state they "have not tried to extend it to the many-threaded variant." The attack targets Argon2i v1.2.1, the version that won the Password Hashing Competition; the authors state they notified the Argon2i designers and that a later specification version incorporates a design change intended to prevent the attack.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The security proof requires the compression function `H` to behave as a random oracle; a real deployment substitutes a concrete hash function and inherits whatever gap exists between that function and true random-oracle behavior. The proof further requires `H`'s internal state size to be at least as large as its output size — the paper states this specifically to avoid an unspecified pitfall detailed in its Appendix B.3, meaning a compression function violating this size relationship voids the stated memory-hardness guarantee. The parallel-attack-resistant composed construction (Balloon then scrypt) requires running the password through the data-independent algorithm first and the data-dependent algorithm second — the ordering is stated explicitly and is not argued to be secure in the reverse order. Any system relying on this paper's provable memory-hardness guarantee against parallelized attackers must treat the sequential-model guarantee as inapplicable to a many-core attacker and instead rely on the weaker, separately-cited pROM results (amortized `Ω(n²/log n)` at best, per Alwen, Blocki, and Pietrzak, not proven achieved by Balloon itself) if resistance to parallel attack is a requirement.

### Contradicts
The paper's own experimental result contradicts a claim in the cited Argon2i (v1.2.1) design document: that document states computing `n`-block single-pass Argon2i in `n/4` space incurs a 7.3× computational penalty, and that computing three-pass Argon2i in `n/3` space incurs a 16,384× penalty; this paper's measured attack computes both in the stated space budgets with no computational penalty. No other paper in this corpus was found to report Argon2i or Balloon Hashing figures.

- **[19]** Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, "Argon2 design document" (version 1.2.1) — foundational and directly attacked; the source of the 7.3× and 16,384× penalty claims this paper's attack contradicts.
- **[21]** Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, "Argon2 design document" (later version) — superseded-by direction: the design change the authors state was made in response to being notified of this paper's attack.

## [BONEH-CRYPTO-18] Verifiable Delay Functions
**Citation:** Dan Boneh, Joseph Bonneau, Benedikt Bünz, Ben Fisch. "Verifiable Delay Functions." CRYPTO, 2018.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
A verifiable delay function (VDF) forces anyone computing it to spend a specified minimum number of sequential computation steps, even given an unbounded number of parallel processors, while letting any third party check the output in far less time than the computation itself took. A VDF is a triple of algorithms. Setup(security parameter, delay parameter t) produces public parameters that fix the input and output domains. Eval takes an input x and, after t sequential steps, outputs a value y and a proof pi. Verify takes x, y, and pi and accepts or rejects in time much shorter than t. The paper defines the security property a VDF must have as sigma-sequentiality: no adversary limited to parallel time sigma(t) on any polynomial number of processors can distinguish a correct output from a random string with more than negligible advantage, even after an unbounded pre-computation phase before the challenge x is known. Four candidate constructions are given. First, a theoretical construction from incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), in which a prover updates a succinct proof of correctness at each step of an underlying sequential function so the full proof is ready immediately after the computation finishes; this achieves sigma(t) = (1-epsilon)t - O(1) sequentiality given a tight IVC scheme, itself built from succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs). Second, a candidate built from injective permutation polynomials over finite fields whose inverse requires computing a polynomial greatest common divisor (GCD), a computation the paper states is sequential in the polynomial's degree on any machine with fewer than a stated number of processors; this is called a "weak VDF" because the honest evaluator itself needs greater-than-polylogarithmic parallelism to run in the stated delay. Third, a practical efficiency technique that plugs a "time-asymmetric encoding" (a function cheap to invert but expensive to compute forward) into the IVC construction as the repeated sequential step, so the SNARK proof only needs to verify inversion rather than the forward computation, cutting the arithmetic complexity the SNARK must verify per step. Fourth, an exponentiation-based construction in a group of unknown order (an RSA group whose factorization nobody knows, or a class group of an imaginary quadratic order) that is secure only against an adversary bounded to a fixed amount of pre-computation done before the challenge is issued, trading the strength of the general sigma-sequentiality guarantee for a much shorter proof than the IVC-based constructions produce.

### Measured results
This is a construction and proof paper; it reports no deployed-system benchmark. Its quantitative figures are analytical or micro-benchmark extrapolations tied to a stated construction and hardware model, not an end-to-end system measurement.

| Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Computing one modular square root of a 256-bit prime takes about 45,000 clock cycles | Extrapolated by the paper's authors from a cited external report of 30 million square-root iterations for a 256-bit prime taking 10 minutes on a single 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7 |
| Computing SHA-256 for a 256-bit output takes about 864 clock cycles | Same Intel Core i7 class of hardware, cited from an external source, given as the comparison baseline |
| The best known arithmetic circuit for SHA-256 uses 27,904 multiplication gates | Cited from an external source as the baseline for the "Sloth++" SNARK-verification efficiency comparison |
| Sloth++ construction requires verifying only 4 arithmetic gates over the SNARK field per roughly 89,000 parallel-time evaluation cycles | Uses a degree-2 field extension and a non-arithmetic coordinate-swap permutation; stated as yielding "over a 7,000 fold improvement" in SNARK verification complexity versus a SHA-256 hash chain for the same wall-clock delay, even crediting the attacker a factor-100 ASIC speedup on the modular square root step |
| Permutation-polynomial variant needs to verify about 16 gates per 100,000 (10^5) parallel-time evaluation cycles | Requires the honest evaluator to use 10^5-way parallelism to run the polynomial GCD computation at that rate; stated as a further factor-15 improvement over Sloth+, contingent on assuming no adversary can amass more than 10^14 parallel processors for the polynomial-GCD algorithm |
| Bounded-pre-computation group-exponentiation construction: worked numeric example uses an RSA modulus N of about 4096 bits and a preprocessing security parameter B = 2^30 | The paper states this concrete choice as an example, not as a measured optimum; B bounds how many challenges the fixed public parameters can securely answer before requiring re-generation |
| The paper's example assumes an evaluator possessing an NVIDIA Titan V GPU can perform up to 10^14 pipelined arithmetic operations per second | Cited as the basis for treating the B = 2^30 preprocessing bound as "reasonable" for that hardware, not as a measured throughput of the constructed VDF itself |

### Parameters
- Delay parameter t: the number of sequential steps Setup fixes (or, in the incremental variant, that Eval specifies within a single set of public parameters).
- sigma(t), the achieved sequentiality: (1-epsilon)t - O(1) for the tight-IVC-based construction; t - o(t) for the polynomial-GCD-based weak VDF under Assumption 2 (no algorithm computes the GCD of two degree-d univariate polynomials in fewer than O(d^2) parallel steps).
- Preprocessing security parameter B for the bounded-pre-computation exponentiation construction: worked example B = 2^30; determines both public-parameter size (encoding key holds B group elements) and how many challenges may be safely answered before regenerating parameters.
- RSA modulus size for the bounded-pre-computation construction: worked example 4096 bits, with prime factors chosen as strong primes.
- SNARK field size for the IVC-based practical constructions: p is approximately 2^128 in the base pairing-based SNARK; the Sloth-family improvement instead matches the iterated function's field to the SNARK field Fq with q approximately 2^256.
- Sloth++ field-extension degree r = 2 over Fp, chosen so verifying one iteration costs exactly 4 multiplication gates over Fp.

### Stated limitations
The security of using a VDF-based delay to protect a proof-of-work blockchain randomness beacon "remains an informal conjecture due to the lack of a complete game-theoretic model capturing miner incentives in Nakamoto-style consensus protocols," so no formal bound on the required delay parameter against a profit-motivated miner is given. The polynomial-GCD-based construction is stated to be only a "weak VDF": the honest evaluator itself must use super-polynomial parallelism (not merely poly-logarithmic) to complete in the stated delay, because the polynomial's degree must be super-polynomial in the security parameter to block an adversary from running the polynomial-time GCD algorithm on polynomially many processors. The bounded-pre-computation exponentiation construction is explicitly stated to not satisfy the paper's own VDF security definition: the authors describe a concrete pre-computation attack requiring tB group operations and O(sB) space that grants a parallel adversary a factor-s speedup, and state the construction "is secure for only B challenges, after which new public parameters need to be generated." The paper states that using a group of unknown order without a trusted setup (by sampling a sufficiently large random RSA-form modulus N) forces N to be large enough to make factoring hard, and that this larger N both gives an adversary more opportunity to parallelize the group arithmetic and increases the verifier's running time, compared to a trusted-setup modulus. Sloth, a prior construction the paper builds on, is stated not to meet the paper's VDF definition because its output, a t-bit number, requires time proportional to t simply to read, so verification cannot run in the paper's required polylogarithmic time. The paper states that the class of proof-of-replication constructions it enables is "quite delicate to formally define" and had at the time of writing been developed further only in unpublished follow-up work.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A VDF-based randomness beacon requires the network to post public parameters (from Setup) before any challenge is issued, and requires whoever evaluates the VDF to have no way to learn the challenge input earlier than every other party, since the entire security argument rests on the evaluator needing t sequential steps starting from when the input becomes known. The trusted-setup variants (the IVC-based construction using a pairing-based SNARK, and the RSA-modulus exponentiation construction using a modulus with unknown factorization) require a one-time setup ceremony run by a party trusted to discard the corresponding secret (the SNARK toxic waste, or the RSA factorization); an alternative that avoids this trusted party is to use the class group of an imaginary quadratic order, which the paper states has an efficient public setup, at the cost of the larger-modulus tradeoffs described above. The bounded-pre-computation construction's security assumption is violated if an adversary can run a pre-computation of size proportional to B group operations between the time the public parameters are published and the time the challenge is issued, so any deployment must bound or monitor that interval. Using a VDF as the time-asymmetric encoding inside a proof-of-replication protocol requires modeling the VDF as an ideal cipher (an oracle that is a bijection from a random subset of inputs to outputs and takes T sequential steps per query) rather than merely as sigma-sequential, which is a strictly stronger requirement the paper states is needed for that specific application and not automatically satisfied by every construction in the paper.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch (BONEH-CRYPTO-18, WESOLOWSKI-EUROCRYPT-19, EVERSPAUGH-USENIXSEC-15, DAVIDSON-POPETS-18, SIRIVIANOS-USENIXATC-07, SHENG-NDSS-24) reports a conflicting measurement of the same quantity; WESOLOWSKI-EUROCRYPT-19 is a distinct construction the present paper's related-work section does not discuss (this paper predates or is contemporaneous with it), so there is no basis in this text for a contradiction claim between the two.

### References worth retrieving

- Pietrzak, K., "Simple verifiable delay functions." Cryptology ePrint Archive, Report 2018/627. — competing (contemporaneous group-of-unknown-order VDF construction requiring a trusted setup, cited as the construction this paper's exponentiation-based construction is "subsumed by" in terms of security but improves on for proof size)
- Wesolowski, B., "Efficient verifiable delay functions." Cryptology ePrint Archive, Report 2018/623. — competing (a distinct group-of-unknown-order VDF construction; both listed in this paper's bibliography as reference [73] and [65] respectively; this is the paper retrieved separately as WESOLOWSKI-EUROCRYPT-19 in this corpus)
- Dziembowski, S., Faust, S., Kolmogorov, V., Pietrzak, K., "Proofs of space." CRYPTO. — foundational (proof-of-space primitive combined with VDFs in the paper's resource-efficient-blockchain and proof-of-replication applications)

## [BOSHMAF-NDSS-15] Íntegro: Leveraging Victim Prediction for Robust Fake Account Detection in OSNs
**Citation:** Yazan Boshmaf, Dionysios Logothetis, Georgos Siganos, Jorge Lería, Jose Lorenzo, Matei Ripeanu, Konstantin Beznosov. "Íntegro: Leveraging Victim Prediction for Robust Fake Account Detection in OSNs." NDSS, 2015.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2015/integro-leveraging-victim-prediction-robust-fake-account-detection-osns
**Source URL:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2015/integro-leveraging-victim-prediction-robust-fake-account-detection-osns
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Íntegro ranks accounts in an online social network (OSN) so that real accounts are placed above fake accounts in the ranked list even when fakes have deliberately friended real users who accept requests from strangers (victims), an adversary strategy that defeats prior ranking schemes relying purely on the assumption that fake accounts stay sparsely connected to real accounts. The mechanism has three stages.

First, a victim classifier trained with a random forest algorithm on low-cost, readily available profile features (friend count, photo count, feed-item count, account age, and similar attributes that require no expensive backend query) predicts, for every real account, the probability that it will accept friend requests from fakes (a vulnerability score). Second, every edge in the social graph is reweighted according to the vulnerability scores of its two endpoints: an edge incident to a predicted victim is assigned a low weight relative to edges between two accounts unlikely to be victims, using the formula w(vi, vj) that depends on the vulnerability scores p(vi) and p(vj) and two tuning constants alpha and beta. Third, trust (a numeric quantity, analogous to the trust used by prior random-walk-based rankers) is initialized on a set of manually verified trusted accounts (seeds) selected across communities detected by the Louvain method, then propagated through the weighted graph for omega = O(log n) iterations of power iteration (n is the number of nodes), and each account's degree-normalized trust after omega iterations becomes its rank; accounts are sorted by this rank in descending order.

Because edges into the fake region carry low weight whenever they pass through a predicted victim, the total amount of trust that can flow from the real region into the fake region is bounded by the sum of the weights on attack edges (edges directly joining a real and a fake account), called vol(E_a), regardless of how many attack edges exist — this is the mechanism's core robustness property, contrasted against prior schemes (SybilRank) whose bound instead grows with the raw count of attack edges.

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Íntegro production precision at Tuenti, lowest-ranked 20K accounts | 95% | deployment on Tuenti's daily-active-user graph, several million nodes, tens of millions of edges (exact counts masked per non-disclosure agreement), snapshot of 6 February 2014; 96.6% of nodes and 94.2% of edges in one giant connected component, evaluation restricted to that component |
| SybilRank precision, same interval | 43% | same graph and evaluation |
| Tuenti's existing user-based abuse-reporting system, hit rate | 5% | same deployment; assumes all fakes eventually get reported |
| Victim-classifier AUC (area under ROC curve), Facebook dataset | 0.70 (40% better than random) | 9,646 real users initially collected in 2011 who received friend requests from fakes, re-validated June 2013, reduced to 8,888 after excluding 7.9% disabled/deactivated accounts; 18 low-cost profile features; 10-fold cross-validation |
| Victim-classifier AUC, Tuenti dataset | 0.76 (52% better than random) | 60,000 real users who received friend requests from fakes, 50% victims, collected 10 February 2014 from live production cache; 14 low-cost profile features (fewer available fields than Facebook) |
| AUC sensitivity to training-set size | no significant AUC increase above 40,000 feature vectors | cross-validation on the Tuenti dataset |
| Ranking AUC under targeted-victim infiltration | Íntegro-RF sustained AUC > 0.92, at most 0.07 decrease as attack edges increased; SybilRank degraded toward ~0.7 | Facebook graph replaying 65 real socialbots' recorded infiltration (n=2,991 nodes, m=11,952 edges), timestamped attack edges added incrementally, averaged over at least 10 runs, 95% confidence intervals |
| Ranking AUC under random-victim infiltration | same pattern: Íntegro-RF AUC > 0.92, up to 30% relative improvement over SybilRank; SybilRank degraded toward ~0.7 | synthetic fake region of 3,068 fakes / 36,816 friendships (small-world graph model) attached to the second Facebook graph (6,136 real accounts, 38,144 friendships) by 35,306 random attack edges (n=9,204, m=110,266) |
| Distant-seed attack (attacker targets accounts k hops from all trusted seeds) | SybilRank slightly better than Íntegro for k<3; Íntegro better for k≥3 | Facebook graph, varying k from 1 to 5 |
| Random-seed attack (attacker victimizes randomly chosen trusted seeds) | ranking quality of both systems degrades as victimized-seed count rises from 1 to 100 | Facebook graph |
| Community detection on Tuenti GCC | 42 communities found in 5 Louvain iterations, modularity 0.83, largest community 220,846 nodes, 15 communities exceeding 50,000 nodes | Tuenti giant connected component after preprocessing |
| Fake-account rate in newly joined accounts (deferred by the design) | 6% of a 100-account random manual sample were fake; most successful single fake account had 103 victims | accounts that joined Tuenti in the 30 days before the 6 February 2014 snapshot |
| Estimated manual-inspection cost avoided | Tuenti's 5% hit rate would need 1,267 person-hours to discover 19,000 fake accounts via user reporting alone | stated comparison against Íntegro's deployment, given as a derived estimate rather than a separately measured quantity |
| Computational cost | O(n log n) end-to-end, where n = number of accounts | derived from an m = O(n) assumption justified by the platform-enforced friend-count caps (5,000 on Facebook, 1,000 on Tuenti); victim classification and trust propagation each independently cost O(n log n), community detection costs O(n), ranking/sorting costs O(n log n) |
| Theoretical security bound (Theorem 4.1) | number of fake accounts ranking similar to or higher than real accounts after O(log n) iterations is O(vol(E_a) log n) | assumes the real region is fast-mixing and the attacker establishes attack edges uniformly at random; proof given in a cited companion technical report, not reproduced in full in this paper |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested / notes |
|---|---|---|
| Edge-weight exponent alpha | 0.5 (illustrative example) | governs how strongly a low vulnerability score suppresses edge weight |
| Edge-weight multiplier beta | 2 (illustrative example) | paired with alpha in the weighting formula |
| Propagation iterations omega | O(log n); worked example uses omega = ceil(log2(9)) = 4 | terminated early, before convergence to the graph's true mixing time, which the paper states is much larger than O(log n) for typical social networks |
| Trusted-seed count | minimum one seed per detected community; exact count in the Tuenti deployment set by available manual-verification resources | Tuenti evaluation manually verified 0.05% of nodes in each detected community as trusted |
| Feature count used by victim classifier | 18 features (Facebook), 14 features (Tuenti) | listed in Table I with per-dataset relative-importance (RI) scores; friend count has RI 100.0% (Facebook) and 84.5% (Tuenti) |
| Classifier training-set size (final) | 40,000+ feature vectors | AUC did not improve significantly beyond this size in cross-validation |

### Stated limitations
The authors state two design limitations inherited from SybilRank and similar power-iteration ranking schemes. First, Íntegro's design is stated to apply only to undirected social graphs, because directed graphs have a substantially smaller mixing time than their undirected counterparts, making short random walks unsuitable for robust ranking on directed graphs. Second, Íntegro defers ranking newly joined accounts because their sparse initial connectivity would otherwise place them at low rank and generate false positives; the authors measured that only 7% of new users active in the prior 30 days on Tuenti had more than 46 friends (versus a platform average of 254), and that 6% of a 100-account random sample of these deferred new accounts were fake. The authors explicitly state that handling this trade-off (excluding new accounts versus risking false positives against them) is an operational decision left to the platform operator, and note a vouching-based alternative exists in other published fake-account detection designs for admitting legitimate new users, without evaluating it themselves. The authors state Íntegro is not a standalone fake-account detection system but is intended to complement existing detection mechanisms; in the Tuenti deployment it operated alongside a separate feature-based detection system and the existing user-reporting system. The community-detection step explicitly does not rely on the assumption that fake accounts form tightly-knit communities among themselves — the authors state this assumption does not always hold and that fakes can evade community-based detection by keeping sparse connectivity among themselves, and Íntegro is designed to tolerate an attacker who befriends either real or fake accounts without restriction.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Íntegro requires a set of manually verified trusted accounts (seeds) distributed across the graph's detected communities; verification is performed by human analysts, and the paper states the number of seeds selectable is bounded by available manual-verification resources, with a stated minimum of one seed per detected community. It requires a community-detection step (the Louvain method, run before rate adjustment) over the full social graph to prevent inter-community sparsity from starving the trust-propagation process. It requires training data for the victim classifier consisting of real accounts already known to have accepted friend requests from fakes, plus a defined feature set of low-cost profile attributes that must be available for every account for the resulting feature vectors to be complete — the paper states 4 of the 18 Facebook features had no equivalent field in the Tuenti dataset. It requires the underlying graph to be undirected, per the stated limitation above. It requires an operational policy decision, external to the mechanism itself, on how to treat newly joined accounts during the deferral window, since the mechanism assigns them uninformatively low rank by design. Its security bound (Theorem 4.1) is proved only for an attacker establishing attack edges uniformly at random against a fast-mixing real region; the paper's own seed-targeting experiments show the bound's practical behavior changes under a resourceful attacker who instead targets accounts near or overlapping the seed set, with SybilRank slightly outperforming Íntegro at small attacker-to-seed distances (k<3).

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper explicitly disputes a property commonly assumed by community-detection-based fake-account approaches — that fake accounts necessarily form tightly-knit communities among themselves — citing evasion by sparse self-connectivity as a documented counter-strategy; this is a claim about other systems' assumptions, not about a specific paper in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Q. Cao, M. Sirivianos, X. Yang, T. Pregueiro, "Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Networks" (SybilRank) [ref 13] — the direct comparison baseline throughout, using an unweighted power-iteration ranking with an O(n log n) bound growing with the raw count of attack edges rather than their total weight
- competing: G. Danezis, P. Mittal, "SybilInfer" [ref 18] — Bayesian-inference-based fake account probability assignment, O(n (log n)^2) time per trusted account, stated to provide no analytical worst-case bound on fakes outranking real accounts
- competing: H. Yu, M. Kaminsky, P. B. Gibbons, A. Flaxman, "SybilGuard" [ref 16], and H. Yu, P. B. Gibbons, M. Kaminsky, F. Xiao, "SybilLimit" [ref 17] — modified-random-walk detection, O(sqrt(m*n) log n) time in a centralized setting; SybilLimit already in this corpus as YU-SP-08
- competing: GateKeeper [ref 20] — flow-based detection improving on SumUp, requires balanced-graph assumptions, O(n log n) time per trusted account ("ticket source")
- competing: B. Viswanath et al., using Mislove's greedy local-community-expansion algorithm [ref 19] to partition real and fake regions — O(n^2) time, evadable by sparse intra-fake-region connectivity
- foundational: Y. Boshmaf, I. Muslukhov, K. Beznosov, M. Ripeanu, "The Socialbot Network: When Bots Socialize for Fame and Money," ACSAC 2011 [ref 7] — source of the timestamped-attack-edge Facebook dataset reused in the targeted-victim infiltration experiment
- foundational: Louvain method for community detection [ref 54] — the community-detection algorithm used for both seed selection and evaluation of the trust-propagation graph structure

### Verbatim extracts
"Íntegro resulted in up to an order of magnitude higher precision in fake account detection" — deployment result summary.
"Íntegro achieved 95% precision, as compared to 43% by SybilRank and 5% by Tuenti's user-based abuse reporting system" — the three-way production comparison.
"the number of fake accounts that rank similar to or higher than real accounts after O(log n) iterations is O(vol(Ea) log n)" — Theorem 4.1's statement.
"Íntegro's design is limited to only undirected social graphs" — stated limitation.
"Íntegro is not a stand-alone fake account detection system" — stated scope limitation.
"fakes can easily evade detection if they establish sparse connectivity among themselves" — stated limitation of community-detection-based approaches, motivating Íntegro's design choice not to rely on that assumption.

## [CAO-NSDI-12] Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services
**Citation:** Qiang Cao, Michael Sirivianos, Xiaowei Yang, Tiago Pregueiro. "Aiding the Detection of Fake Accounts in Large Scale Social Online Services." USENIX NSDI, 2012.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi12/nsdi12-final22.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi12/nsdi12-final22.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilRank ranks the users of an online social network (OSN) by their likelihood of being a fake
account (Sybil), so that the operator can direct limited manual-inspection effort toward the
lowest-ranked accounts first, rather than relying only on user abuse reports.

The mechanism starts from a small set of trust seeds — accounts manually confirmed non-Sybil —
and distributes an initial amount of trust equally among them. It then runs power iteration (a
standard technique for repeatedly propagating a value across a graph by matrix multiplication) to
simulate a random walk: at each iteration, every node splits its current trust evenly among its
neighbors and sums what its neighbors send it. This is run for w = O(log n) iterations, where n
is the node count, and then stopped before the walk reaches its true stationary distribution — an
early-terminated random walk. Because Sybil accounts are assumed to connect to the honest region
through only a limited number of attack edges (edges between a Sybil and a non-Sybil user), that
narrow connection is a bottleneck: trust seeded in the non-Sybil region cannot yet spread
uniformly into the Sybil region within O(log n) steps, so non-Sybil users retain higher
degree-normalized trust (a node's trust divided by its own degree) than Sybil users at
termination. SybilRank ranks nodes by degree-normalized trust rather than raw trust, which the
paper states removes a Sybil's advantage from artificially inflating its own degree and gives
each non-Sybil node close to the same degree-normalized score, since after O(log n) power
iterations trust within the well-connected non-Sybil region approaches its own local stationary
distribution (trust proportional to degree).

Because a single well-connected OSN often contains multiple weakly-interconnected communities,
SybilRank additionally applies the Louvain community-detection method to partition the graph and
places multiple trust seeds inside each detected community (in the deployment, roughly 100 nodes
inspected total across communities in an 11-million-node graph), rather than seeding trust only
in one dominant community; this prevents communities distant from a single seed set from being
starved of trust and misclassified as Sybil. A final stage annotates ranked-list intervals with
the measured proportion of confirmed fakes within each interval (from manual sampling), letting
the operator choose where in the ranked list to spend inspection effort or how often to issue
CAPTCHAs, rather than relying on a single Sybil/non-Sybil cutoff, which the paper states no
social-graph defense can currently produce with an acceptable false-positive rate.

The paper proves (Theorem 1, full proof in a companion technical report not examined here) that
when an attacker establishes g attack edges at random into a fast-mixing (mixing time O(log n))
non-Sybil region, the total count of Sybils that rank above non-Sybil users, summed over the
whole network, is O(g log n) — a bound the paper states holds for any number of trust seeds.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Deployed on the complete Tuenti social graph: 1,421,367,504 edges, 11,291,486 nodes, 11,216,357 in the giant connected component; 595 communities found via Louvain, 25 of them >100K nodes; ~100 nodes manually inspected total to pick trust seeds | Tuenti (Spain's largest OSN at the time), snapshot from August 2011 |
| Of the 2,000 lowest-ranked users manually inspected, 100% were confirmed fake | Same Tuenti deployment |
| Across the lowest 200K ranked users (sampled 100 users per 50K-user interval, up to 650K users disclosed), ~90% were confirmed fake, versus ~5% for Tuenti's existing user-abuse-report method — stated as an 18-fold efficiency increase | Same deployment; described by the authors as directly related to the precision metric from collaborative filtering |
| Fake proportion falls abruptly above the 200K mark: ~90% → ~50% → ~10% moving up the ranked list | Same deployment |
| Simulated ranking quality: at 1,500 attack edges into a 5,000-node Sybil region on the Facebook sample (regular-attack topology), a non-Sybil node still ranks above a random Sybil with 70% probability (area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve) | Facebook sample graph (10,000 nodes, 40,013 edges), 50 trust seeds, averaged over 100 runs |
| SybilRank outperforms SybilLimit, SybilInfer, Mislove's community detection (CD), GateKeeper, and EigenTrust on area under the ROC curve and on false positive/negative rates, across regular and scale-free attack structures on all 8 test graphs | 8 social graphs from Table 1 (sizes 7,115–18,772 nodes), Sybil region of 5,000 nodes with attack-edge count varied from a small value up to a value large enough to degrade all schemes; d=4 non-attack edges per Sybil; 20% fixed false-rate pivot for ROC comparisons; 100 runs averaged |
| EigenTrust has "at least 20% higher false positive and negative rates than SybilRank in most of the attack scenarios" | Same simulation setup |
| SybilInfer shows a steep area-under-ROC-curve drop near 500 attack edges on Facebook under the regular attack | Same simulation setup; attributed to uncertain convergence of SybilInfer's Metropolis-Hastings sampling within its O(n log n)-step termination |
| EigenTrust's normalized area under the ROC curve decreases as Sybil-internal (non-attack) edge count per Sybil rises from 4 to 40, while SybilRank's improves under the same change | Facebook graph, regular attack, 100/500/1,000 attack edges tested for each scheme |
| EigenTrust concentrates high degree-normalized trust near seeds (>9,400 of 10,000 non-Sybil nodes fall below trust value 2 at distance >2 hops); SybilRank keeps roughly uniform degree-normalized trust regardless of seed distance | Synthetic scale-free graph, regular attack with 10,000 attack edges, 5 seeds, total trust set to 2m |
| In a 5-community synthetic graph (one 2,000-node core plus four 2,000-node satellite communities linked to the core by 500 edges each, average degree 10), distributing 50 seeds across all communities (10 each) outperforms confining all 50 seeds to the core community, for SybilRank, EigenTrust, and Mislove's CD alike; SybilRank remains most accurate under both seeding strategies | Synthetic multi-community graph, attack edges varied 0–5,000 |
| Under a targeted attack (200 attack edges connected to the k non-Sybil nodes nearest a trust seed, k varied 1,000–10,000), all schemes degrade as k shrinks (attack edges concentrate nearer the seed); SybilRank degrades least but still degrades at small k | Facebook graph, 5,000-node regular-attack Sybil region |
| Hadoop/MapReduce prototype processes a 160-million-node synthetic scale-free graph in under 33 hours, with execution time increasing almost linearly with graph size across sizes from 10M to 160M nodes, using O(log n) power iterations | Amazon EC2 cluster of 11 m1.large instances (1 master, 10 slaves) |
| Mean random-walk length needed to reach a fixed total variation distance of 0.01 from the stationary distribution is much longer for confirmed Sybils than for random users in the same community (random-user walks mostly <100 steps) | 25 Louvain-detected Tuenti communities >100K nodes; 1,000 random users and 100 confirmed Sybils sampled per community |

### Parameters
- Power iterations w: set to O(log n); the paper does not report the specific integer used for the Tuenti deployment (11.2M-node graph) beyond the asymptotic form, stating only that measured Sybil random-walk lengths (Figure 11) exceeded the power-iteration count SybilRank actually used.
- Trust seeds K: 50 used in the main simulated comparisons (1 chosen from the top-10 highest-degree non-Sybil nodes, 49 random non-Sybil nodes); for schemes supporting only a single seed, 1 randomly chosen top-10-degree node is used for a fair comparison. In the Tuenti deployment, seeds are chosen per Louvain-detected community after manual verification of ~4 candidate nodes per community (25 communities >100K nodes).
- Attack-edge count g: varied per experiment; up to 1,500 (Facebook, regular attack) and up to 15,000 (synthetic scale-free graph) in the ranking-quality comparison; 10,000 in the seed-distance experiment; 0–5,000 in the multi-community experiment; 200 in the targeted-attack experiment.
- Non-attack (intra-Sybil) edges per Sybil, d: fixed at 4 in the main attack-strategy simulations; varied 4–40 in the EigenTrust-comparison experiment (Figure 7).
- Sybil region size: fixed at 5,000 nodes in all simulated attacks, described as chosen to "stress-test each scheme."
- ROC fixed false-rate pivot: 20%, used to compute the corresponding other false rate for comparison across schemes.
- Total variation distance for mixing-time measurement: 0.01, used to define the walk length compared between Sybils and random users in each Tuenti community.
- EigenTrust reset probability: 0.15, run to convergence (not early-terminated), following the cited EigenTrust paper's own setting.

### Stated limitations
The paper states SybilRank's central limitation is inherent to the open nature of OSNs: a fake
account that succeeds in befriending many real users accumulates trust and is ranked as non-Sybil,
which is why the fake proportion in the Tuenti-ranked list falls sharply above the 200K mark. It
states that no social-graph-based Sybil defense, including SybilRank, can currently produce a
binary Sybil/non-Sybil classification with an acceptable false-positive rate, so a fixed
ranked-list pivot cannot substitute for manual inspection — SybilRank instead reports the fake
proportion per ranked-list interval so an operator can allocate inspection effort. It states its
own security guarantee (Theorem 1) is derived under the assumption that attack edges are placed
uniformly at random by the Sybils, not under the more effective targeted-attack strategy of
placing attack edges close to trust seeds; the paper's own targeted-attack experiment (Section 6.5)
shows all schemes, including SybilRank, degrade as the targeting gets closer to the seed. It states
that whether real social networks' non-Sybil mixing time is truly O(log n), or has an unknown
larger constant factor, or grows faster than O(log n), is unresolved, citing two independent
measurement studies that found some social networks mix slower than expected; SybilRank's
robustness to this uncertainty is qualified, not eliminated — the paper states SybilRank does not
depend on the absolute mixing time value, only on the non-Sybil region mixing faster than the full
graph including Sybils, but concedes that using too few iterations relative to the true non-Sybil
mixing time risks starving trust to non-Sybil users poorly connected to any seed. For the Tuenti
deployment, the paper states it could not evaluate SybilRank with the same false positive/negative
and ROC metrics used in simulation, because manually labeling ground truth at Tuenti's scale was
infeasible, and states it could not disclose the exact fraction of network-wide fakes SybilRank
misses, citing confidentiality constraints. It states pre-processing (pruning extremely-high-degree
nodes' edges and deferring very recent accounts) was required before applying SybilRank to Tuenti
to control two identified sources of error — well-maintained high-degree fakes and low-connectivity
new honest accounts — meaning the deployed system is not the unmodified base algorithm.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires the operator to hold the complete social graph as an undirected graph, and requires an
initial manually verified set of non-Sybil trust seeds (drawn per detected community, not
globally) before the mechanism can run at all. Requires the non-Sybil region of the graph to be
well-connected, non-bipartite, and fast-mixing relative to the full graph including Sybils
(mixing time strictly less than that of the full graph), which is a property of the graph
structure that must be verified for a given deployment, not assumed by construction — the paper's
own Tuenti section measures an approximation of this gap rather than asserting it. Requires Sybils
to be limited in the number of attack edges they can form into the non-Sybil region; the paper
states this assumption can fail if fake accounts can cheaply befriend large numbers of real users,
and that the mechanism's accuracy specifically degrades for accounts that do so, regardless of any
other property of the account. Requires a downstream process (human review, or an automated
challenge such as a CAPTCHA) to consume the ranked list and its per-interval fake-proportion
annotations, because SybilRank itself produces a ranking and an approximate fake-density curve,
not an admission or suspension decision. Community detection (the paper uses the Louvain method)
must be re-run to identify the graph's community structure before seed placement, adding an O(m)
preprocessing cost (m = edge count) ahead of the O(n log n) trust-propagation and ranking cost.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus. This entry corrects a claim commonly associated with
this line of work: SybilRank's security guarantee (Theorem 1) is stated only for the case where
attack edges are placed uniformly at random; the paper's own experiments (Section 6.5) show
detection accuracy is measurably worse under a targeted-attack placement strategy, so a categorical
claim that SybilRank bounds Sybil rank under any adversarial edge-placement strategy is not
supported by this paper.

## [CASTRO-OSDI-02] Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks
**Citation:** Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Ayalvadi Ganesh, Antony Rowstron, Dan S. Wallach. "Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks." USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 2002.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://people.mpi-sws.org/~druschel/publications/security.pdf
**Source URL:** https://people.mpi-sws.org/~druschel/publications/security.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This paper makes a structured peer-to-peer overlay (a network in which each node holds a small routing table and a lookup for a key is forwarded hop by hop toward the node or nodes responsible for that key) deliver a message to every correct replica root for a key with high probability, even when a bounded fraction of nodes actively try to prevent delivery. It decomposes the problem into three mechanisms, each closing one attack the paper demonstrates against overlays that lack it.

First, certified node-identifier (nodeId) assignment: a set of certification authorities (CAs), which can be offline and uninvolved in day-to-day operation, sign a certificate binding a node's randomly assigned nodeId to its public key and IP address. This stops an attacker from choosing a nodeId, which the paper shows otherwise lets an attacker place itself as the sole custodian of a target key's replicas or as every routing-table entry of a targeted victim.

Second, a constrained routing table alongside the normal proximity-optimized one: every constrained-table slot must hold the live nodeId numerically closest to a publicly computable point in the identifier space, a rule independent of network-measured proximity and therefore not manipulable by an attacker who intercepts or fakes proximity probes. The paper demonstrates that without this constraint, an attacker's routing-table updates propagate malicious entries faster than honest ones do, and derives that the fraction of faulty entries in a node's table after processing one further update is at least (1 − f)·f + f, strictly greater than the starting fraction f, so repeated updates push the faulty fraction toward one.

Third, secure message forwarding: a node routes a lookup using the fast proximity-aware table, then applies a routing failure test to the returned set of prospective replica roots. The test compares the average numerical distance between consecutive nodeIds in the sender's own neighbor set (call it µ_p) against the same statistic computed over the returned prospective root set (µ_rn), because faulty nodeIds cluster less densely than the full honest population would. The set is accepted (test returns negative) only if every certificate in it is valid and µ_rn ≤ µ_p × γ, where γ is a tunable threshold. If the test returns positive, or if no response arrives before a timeout, the sender falls back to redundant routing: it sends r message copies through r different members of its own neighbor set (a technique the paper calls neighbor set anycast for overlays, such as Pastry and Chord, whose replica roots cluster in one node's neighbor set rather than spreading uniformly over the identifier space), collects signed certificates from any node that reports the destination's root in its own neighbor set, and iterates up to three times to assemble the definitive replica set.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Probability of routing to a correct replica root drops from near 1 at f=0 to 65% at f=10%, for N=100,000 nodes | Pastry, closed-form model σ ≈ (1−f)^(log_2b N), b=4, validated against simulation with error below 2% (Figure 3) |
| At f=20% and N=100,000, success probability is 65% with b=4 and 75% with b=6 (larger b reduces hop count at the cost of larger routing tables) | Same closed-form model applied to Pastry/Tapestry-style routing with varying base b |
| Chord (fixed b=1) reaches only 42% success at f=20%, N=100,000, under the same model | Same model, Chord's fixed digit base |
| Routing-failure-test minimum error rate α=β=0.0008 at γ=1.72 | Simulation, 100,000 random nodeIds, f=c=0.3 (fraction and collusion bound both 0.3), n=256 distance samples at sender, k=l=32 root-neighbor samples |
| Under a nodeId-suppression attack (attacker leaves the overlay to thin nodeId density near the sender or the root neighbor set), minimum achievable error exceeds 0.001 once c ≥ 0.2, even with 256 samples | Simulation, same 100,000-node setup, c=f swept |
| At γ=1.23, l=32, 256 samples, target false-negative rate β=0.001: false-positive rate α=0.12 without a nodeId-suppression attack and α=0.77 under a nodeId-suppression attack, at c=0.3 | Simulation, 100,000 nodeIds |
| Probability of reaching all correct replica roots via redundant routing with neighbor set anycast exceeds 0.999 for f ≤ 0.3 | Simulation and closed-form model, N=100,000, b=4, l=r=32 |
| Overall reliability target Σ > 0.999 achievable for f ≤ 0.18 with γ=1.8, l=16 (redundant routing invoked only 0.5% of the time when there are no faults); for f ≤ 0.25 with γ=1.58, l=32 (redundant routing invoked 0.4% of the time with no faults) | Simulation, N=100,000, two named parameter scenarios |
| Extra bandwidth for a negative routing-failure test: 5.6 KB with l=32, 2.9 KB with l=16 (message headers excluded) | Computed from message counts and PSS-R signature sizes: 1024-bit modulus nodeId certificates at 128 bytes each |
| Redundant routing, best case (all root neighbors gathered in one round): 22 KB extra bandwidth with l=32, 7 KB with l=16; under attack: fewer than 451 messages with l=32, f=0.25, fewer than 188 messages with l=16, f=0.18, with roughly 12 KB (l=32) or 1 KB (l=16) of additional bytes for nodeId lists | Same 100,000-node analytic setting, PSS-R 64-byte signed nonces |
| Checked iterative routing (rejected alternative): minimum hop-test error α=β≈0.35 at c=0.3, 256 samples; combining it with Pastry's constrained routing table improved end-to-end success from below 0.3 to 0.4 at c=0.3, N=100,000, b=4, l=32, but added 2.7 extra hops per route on average from false positives | Simulation, same 100,000-node setting |
| BFT-replica-group correctness: with r=32 replicas and f=0.2 (20% of overlay nodes compromised), probability that a given replica group of 32 has fewer than 1/3 faulty replicas is under 93%; combined with routing success this yields only 72% overall probability of correctly reaching a 32-node replica group at N=100,000 | Closed-form binomial-distribution calculation, cited as the reason the paper's own authors rejected a Lynch-Malkhi-Ratajczak-style full-BFT-replicated-overlay alternative |

The paper's own headline conclusion: the combination of certified nodeIds, constrained routing tables, and the routing-failure-test-plus-redundant-routing primitive "allow us to tolerate up to 25% malicious nodes while providing good performance when the fraction of compromised nodes is small" — stated as the paper's summary claim, distinct from and not identical to any single numbered figure above; treat it as the paper's own qualitative headline, not an additional independent data point.

### Parameters
- f: fraction of nodes in the overlay that are faulty/malicious.
- c: upper bound on the fraction of faulty nodes that can collude (c ≤ 1, and α, β are shown to depend on c but not on f directly).
- γ: routing-failure-test threshold controlling the tradeoff between false-positive rate α and false-negative rate β; values used in experiments range from 1.23 to 1.8 depending on target security level.
- l: neighbor set size (also root-neighbor-set size k in most experiments, k=l); values tested: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 as sample counts, with l itself tested at 16 and 32 for the end-to-end scenarios.
- n: number of nodeId-distance samples the sender uses to compute µ_p; tested at 32, 64, 128, 256, with 256 used as the paper's primary operating point.
- b: digit base for the routing table (controls table size versus hop count); tested at b=4 (Pastry's typical default) and b=6; Chord is fixed at b=1.
- N: overlay size; tested at 1,000, 10,000, 100,000, and 1,000,000 for the base routing-success model, with 100,000 used for all routing-failure-test and redundant-routing simulations.
- r: number of redundant-routing message copies sent per lookup, set equal to l in the reported experiments.

### Stated limitations
The paper states explicitly that "the security and performance of our techniques was fully evaluated only in the context of Pastry; a full evaluation of the techniques in other protocols is future work" — the CAN, Chord, and Tapestry adaptations described are design sketches, not evaluated implementations. The paper states the routing failure test's own accuracy is undermined by a nodeId suppression attack it identifies as "unavoidable": an attacker can leave the overlay to thin nodeId density near the sender (raising the false-negative rate β) or near the destination root (raising the false-positive rate α), can alternate between the two, and the paper states honest nodes have no way of detecting which mode is in effect. The paper states two further routing-failure-test attacks — collecting certificates of departed nodes to inflate a set's apparent density, and mixing controlled and correct nodeIds within one prospective root set — and offers a mitigating certificate-confirmation protocol but does not fully close either. The paper states its own hop-test variant of checked iterative routing has a high minimum error (≈0.35) because it relies on a single density sample at each hop, and rejects the technique after finding no measurable improvement when combined with redundant routing, attributing the failure to iterative routes being less independent of one another than recursive routes. The paper states it does not have a model for the effect of proximity-manipulation attacks on the locality-aware (non-constrained) routing table, and states only a belief, not a proof, that such attacks are hard to mount for small f. The self-certifying-data reduction the paper proposes does not remove the need for secure routing when inserting new objects, verifying an object's absence, or handling node joins — the paper states these cases still require the full secure routing primitive.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The certified-nodeId mechanism requires an external certification-authority infrastructure whose public keys are distributed out of band (the paper suggests bundling them with node software, as browsers bundle root certificates), and requires a certificate-revocation or reissuance path for any node whose IP address changes, since the paper binds nodeId certificates to IP addresses specifically to block certificate-swapping among colluding attacker-controlled nodes. The constrained-routing-table mechanism requires that the overlay's routing table slots be defined by a public, verifiable function of node identifiers (a point p in the identifier space), which forecloses proximity as the sole neighbor-selection criterion for that table; a system wanting both proximity optimization and this defense must maintain two separate tables, as this paper does. The routing failure test requires every node in a neighbor or root-neighbor set to hold a valid nodeId certificate that the testing node can check, so it depends on the certified-nodeId mechanism as a precondition — the test's stated accuracy figures (the α/β values in the measured-results table) hold only once nodeIds are already unforgeable. Self-certifying data as a way to reduce reliance on secure routing requires an independent per-object integrity mechanism (a content hash or an owner signature) supplied by the application layer, since routing itself does not embed integrity checking; the mutable-object extension the paper sketches additionally requires a Byzantine-fault-tolerant replication algorithm run by the replica group holding the object.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Cross-reference: URDANETA-CSUR-11 (the survey citing this paper) restates several of these figures (the 0.77/0.12 false-positive pair, the 2.7-extra-hops figure, the Condie et al. 80%-poisoning figure attributed to a different paper) faithfully to the conditions given here; a downstream synthesis step should cite this entry, not the survey's paraphrase, for any of the numbers in the table above.

### Verbatim extracts
- "allow us to tolerate up to 25% malicious nodes while providing good performance"
- "the probability of successful routing is only 65% when there are 100,000 nodes"

- "nodeId suppression attacks can increase α to 0.77 ... without nodeId suppression attacks the value of α is only 0.12"
- "the probability of success is greater than 0.999 for f ≤ 0.3"
- "improves from below 0.3 to 0.4 ... but it adds an extra 2.7 hops"
- "a full evaluation of the techniques in other protocols is future work"
- "there is a nodeId suppression attack that seems to be unavoidable"
