## [CHASE-CCS-19] SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less Trust

**Citation:** Melissa Chase, Apoorvaa Deshpande, Esha Ghosh, Harjasleen Malvai. "SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less Trust." ACM CCS, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3363202.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/607.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/607.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
SEEMless lets a user detect whether the messaging provider serving her public key to her contacts is showing everyone the same key (non-equivocation), so a compromised or coerced provider cannot silently insert its own key for a man-in-the-middle attack, while also letting key changes take effect in well under a minute instead of the roughly one-hour delay the paper attributes to prior work. It formalizes a privacy-preserving verifiable key directory (VKD): a stateful directory that, at each discrete round (epoch), accepts a batch of username-to-public-key registrations and updates, and produces a short cryptographic commitment to the current directory state. A client queries the directory for a username and receives the current public key plus a proof that the key is bound to the published commitment, without the proof revealing anything about other users' keys (zero-knowledge, with a well-defined leakage function). The construction keeps two append-only zero-knowledge sets (aZKS) built on a Patricia trie: an "all" aZKS holding every version of every (username, key) pair ever issued, and an "old" aZKS holding retired key versions; verifying that a key is current means proving membership in "all" and non-membership in "old." Both aZKS root commitments are chained into a Merkle tree of per-epoch commitments (replacing the plain hash chain used by CONIKS), which the paper states shortens the audit-proof cost. A verifiable random function (VRF) hides which entry in the trie corresponds to which username by mapping the username to a pseudorandom label, so an observer of the tree structure cannot tell how many times a given user has updated her key without also holding a proof; SEEMless uses three VRF evaluations per query response (versus CONIKS's one) as the mechanism enforcing this stronger label-privacy property. Auditors — any party, not a privileged role — verify between consecutive epochs that the aZKS commitments were correctly appended to the Merkle tree and that both aZKS grew append-only; the paper states one honest auditor per adjacent epoch pair is sufficient for the non-equivocation soundness guarantee to hold. A persistent authenticated data structure ("Persistent Patricia Trie," PPTr) stores only the state of each tree node that actually changed at each epoch, rather than the whole tree, which the paper credits with letting the same construction run entirely in RAM at scales where CONIKS's implementation exhausted memory.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Server update time at 10M registered users | 0.28 s average | 1,000 new registrations and 1,000 key updates per epoch, batch inserted every 100k-user increment; Linux VM, 2.30GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673, 125GB RAM, 64GB JVM heap for server-side |
| aZKS commitment insertion into the epoch Merkle tree | 61 microseconds | After 10M server epochs have passed; cost estimated using the Patricia trie structure from CONIKS as an over-estimate |
| Offline per-request VRF computation cost | 1.3 ms (registration, 1 VRF call) to 2.5 ms (update, 2 VRF calls) | Computed between epochs, not counted against online update time; VRF built on Secp384r1 with Bouncy Castle, Icart's function for hashing to the curve, SHA-384 |
| CONIKS scalability limit in the same test harness | Heap exhaustion at ≈4.5M users | Same Linux VM/JVM configuration as the SEEMless server-update test; CONIKS's Java implementation could not proceed further with frequent epochs, attributed to repeated copying of its Patricia trie |
| Query proof generation/verification time at 10M users | SEEMless: 6.03 ms (server prove) / 10.51 ms (client verify); CONIKS: 2.01 ms / 3.47 ms | Averaged over 100 users, 10 trials each; VRF cost dominates (compute/prove/verify VRF averaged 1.3/1.9/3.4 ms over 5,000 trials, used as simulated constants); SEEMless needs 3 VRF proofs per query vs. CONIKS's 1 |
| Query proof size at 10M users | ≈8,600 bytes average (SEEMless); up to 3x that for CONIKS is stated as the expected ratio because CONIKS uses 1 authentication path vs. SEEMless's 3 | Includes username, public key, key commitment and opening, VRF proof, and Patricia-trie authentication path |
| KeyHistory bandwidth, 10 special users updating 10 times, 1M regular users (R), 1M epochs | SEEMless: ≈1.09 MB per fully-verifying user (vs. ≈1.03 MB at 100k epochs); CONIKS: ≈576.8 MB over the same span | Special users (S) update at regular intervals; regular users (R) register once per epoch as a load control |
| KeyHistory bandwidth, 20 updates over 5 months, 200k epochs fixed, |R|=1M | SEEMless: ≈2.01 MB total to verify full key history, verified in under 0.05 s (excluding VRF cost) | Includes username/key bytes (at least 1,000 bytes per update) sent for the user to verify used values |
| KeyHistory verification time, non-caching, at 100k epochs | CONIKS: over 349 s; SEEMless comparable figure not separately isolated in this row (see Figures 7-8 in source) | 10 special users, 1M regular users, 10 key updates by special users |
| KeyHistory verification time at 1M epochs | CONIKS: 3,495 s without VRF caching, 71 s with caching | Same experiment configuration, increased epoch count |
| KeyHistory verification time, 200k epochs fixed, varying update count | CONIKS: over 699 s without caching, over 14 s with caching (constant regardless of update count since CONIKS's cost is epoch-count-driven) | Same S/R population sizes |
| Client-side VRF cache size after 20 updates over 1M epochs | ≈2.8 KB | Derived from the paper's formula `[2i + 2^(floor(log i)+1) + log t - (floor(log i)+1)] x 32 bytes`, i = number of user updates, t = number of server epochs |
| Server-side VRF-proof cache for 10M users at 20 updates each | ≈28 GB | Caching the VRF proof for each of 10M users' latest key version |
| Server-side VRF-value+proof cache to answer Query without recomputation | 1.44 GB over 10M registered users | 3 x 48-byte VRF value per user (48 bytes = the VRF value size stated), current key only |
| Auditor bandwidth and time per adjacent-epoch audit | Less than 4.24 MB (upper bound, includes double-counted nodes), under 5 MB stated informally, verified in under 0.3 s | Simulated using the actual "all"/"old" aZKS hash-recomputation counts from the 10M-user experiment: under 47k new hashes (0.17 s) for "all," under 17k new hashes (0.05 s) for "old," plus leaf downloads (192 KB) and an upper bound on unchanged-subtree-root downloads (4.04 MB) |

### Parameters
- VRF construction: Secp384r1 elliptic curve, Bouncy Castle library, Icart's function for hashing to the curve, SHA-384, with the input hashed twice (`SHA384(0||input)` and `SHA384(1||input)`) and Icart applied to both hashes, because applying Icart once does not give an output indistinguishable from random.
- VRF value size: 48 bytes.
- VRF calls per operation: 1 for a new registration; 2 for a key update (one for the new key entering the "all" aZKS, one for the old key entering the "old" aZKS); 3 total per Query response in SEEMless versus 1 in CONIKS.
- Epoch length: not fixed by the construction; the paper's own experiments treat half-a-minute epochs as a realistic working assumption (525,600 minutes/year approximated by 1M epochs), and states the epoch length is not bounded by blockchain block time when a blockchain is used only for periodic root-commitment posting.
- Test scale range: up to 10M registered users for Query and server-update experiments; up to 1M "regular" users and 10 "special" users, up to 1M epochs, for KeyHistory experiments.
- Auditing granularity: one audit unit covers one pair of adjacent epochs; parallel auditors can each cover disjoint adjacent-epoch pairs.

### Stated limitations
The paper places specific trust assumptions on users and the surrounding system, listed under "Model Assumptions": it assumes the user's device can store her current secret key but may be lost or re-imaged, losing that secret; it assumes the user has some out-of-band way to authenticate to the service provider (a second factor, e.g., a text message or phone call), stated as already required by existing end-to-end encryption systems and therefore not an added attack surface; it assumes the server enforces access control on who may query whose key; and it assumes the user can recognize approximately when she last updated her key, to notice if the log lists updates she does not recognize. It assumes Alice, Bob, and the server keep approximately synchronized clocks. It assumes some external mechanism (a blockchain post, as in Catena, or a gossip protocol, as in CONIKS) exists so that different users' views of the current root commitment do not silently diverge; the paper explicitly leaves that mechanism outside SEEMless itself. The paper explicitly defers to future work: usability studies for the end-user interface exposing VKD verification, and storage optimizations such as moving inactive users' cached VRF values to disk rather than keeping them all in RAM. Server-side caching of every user's VRF proof (to avoid recomputing on Query) is stated to require ≈28 GB at 10M users with 20 updates each — an increasing, not bounded, cost as update counts grow, which the paper does not resolve inside this construction. The paper states Keybase's competing design assumes users hold multiple trusted devices and manage long-term cryptographic signature keys themselves, and states its own authors' judgment that "for an end user, it is incredibly difficult to manage keys" under that assumption — this is the paper's own stated opinion about a different system's user-facing usability, not a measurement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A working SEEMless deployment needs at least one honest auditor examining every adjacent pair of epochs; the non-equivocation soundness guarantee is stated as conditional on that minimum, and auditing can be distributed arbitrarily across many independent parties without coordination since each adjacent-epoch check is independent. The system needs an external, out-of-band mechanism ensuring all clients' views of the current root commitment do not fork silently — SEEMless does not supply this itself; the paper names a blockchain post (as in Catena) or a gossip protocol (as in CONIKS) as options, and states client software must periodically interact with whichever mechanism is chosen (for a blockchain option, checking the chain at least as often as the "vulnerability window" the deployment is willing to tolerate, since a misbehaving server is caught only at the next post). The user's client software must persist her current key locally between sessions to detect equivocation, since the whole non-equivocation guarantee depends on the user's own device being the source of truth for what her key currently is; a device that never independently remembers this cannot detect a server showing a different party the wrong key. The system assumes the user or her software has an out-of-band, already-established authentication channel to the service provider (e.g., a second factor) independent of the VKD itself — SEEMless does not create or replace this channel. The server needs synchronized-enough clocks with clients to make epoch boundaries meaningful to all parties. Any component relying on SEEMless's stronger label-privacy property (hiding how many times a user has updated relative to CONIKS) inherits the added VRF cost (3x the VRF calls per query) as an explicit privacy/performance trade-off — a caller not needing that specific privacy property gets no benefit from paying this cost.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Cross-reference: Parakeet (MALVAI-NDSS-23, same batch) presents its own reimplementation of this paper's aZKS construction and measures markedly worse persistent-storage numbers than SEEMless's own self-reported figures here (Parakeet reports ≈66 minutes, 47 storage accesses, to insert 100k users into a 300k-user set with a MySQL-backed persistent layer, versus this paper's RAM-only 0.28-second update-time figure at 10M users). This is not a contradiction of a shared measurement — the two papers measure different storage backends (SEEMless's own experiments run entirely in RAM; Parakeet's SEEMless reimplementation adds a MySQL persistence layer) and different operations, so the discrepancy reflects added persistent-storage cost, not a disputed figure for the same configuration. A reader combining the two entries should not average or directly compare these two sets of numbers as if they described the same experimental setup.

### References worth retrieving
- Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, Freedman. "CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users." USENIX Security 2015 (cited as [20]) — foundational; the direct predecessor this paper extends and benchmarks against throughout.
- Bonneau. "EthIKS: Using Ethereum to Audit a CONIKS Key Transparency Log." (cited as [3]) — competing; the paper states EthIKS weakens CONIKS's privacy guarantee and makes per-operation blockchain invocation "quickly infeasible" at scale — a specific cost claim worth independently verifying.
- Tomescu, Devadas. "Catena: Efficient Non-equivocation via Bitcoin." IEEE S&P 2017 (cited as [26]) — competing/complementary; the blockchain-commitment-posting mechanism this paper explicitly proposes integrating with for root-commitment consistency.
- Eskandarian, Messeri, Bonneau, Boneh. "Certificate Transparency with Privacy." (cited as [9]) — foundational; adjacent transparency-log line of work the paper cites as related but distinct.
- Micali, Rabin, Kilian. "Zero-Knowledge Sets." (cited as [21]) — foundational; the underlying zero-knowledge-set primitive the aZKS construction generalizes.
- Keybase.io, "Protocol Security Review" and "Managing Teams and Keys with Keybase" (cited as [15], [16]) — competing; the deployed auditable-key-directory system compared on user-key-management assumptions.

## [CHOR-JACM-98] Private Information Retrieval
**Citation:** Benny Chor, Oded Goldreich, Eyal Kushilevitz, Madhu Sudan. "Private Information Retrieval." Journal of the ACM, 1998. DOI 10.1145/293347.293350.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/PS/pir.ps — NOTE: the retrieved PostScript file's own embedded metadata (dvips source comment `%%Title: focs.dvi`, 10 pages) identifies it as the FOCS 1995 conference extended-abstract typesetting of this paper, not a re-typeset of the JACM 1998 journal version the citation in the target registry names. Title and all four authors match the registry record exactly; the theorems, proofs, and reference list extracted below are the FOCS 1995 content. Where the JACM 1998 journal version adds material beyond the FOCS extended abstract, that added material is not reflected here. The source file is raw dvips PostScript (glyph-placement commands, not linear extracted text); every quantity below was reconstructed by concatenating the file's parenthesized glyph strings and reading the result, cross-checked against the paper's own theorem numbering.
**Source URL:** https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/PS/pir.ps
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Private information retrieval (PIR) lets a user fetch one bit (or block) from a database without
the database learning which bit was fetched. The paper defines PIR for the multi-server, replicated
setting: k identical, non-communicating copies of an n-bit string x are held by k databases DB_1,
..., DB_k; the user wants bit x_i without any single database learning i. Privacy is defined as
follows: for every database DB_l, every possible database content x, and any two indices i and j,
the communication that DB_l observes must be identically distributed whether the user wants x_i or
x_j — an unconditional (not computational-hardness-based) guarantee, since no cryptographic
assumption appears in any of the paper's protocols. The paper's motivating fact, stated and proved,
is that a single database achieves this only by sending the user the entire n-bit database, so every
construction in the paper depends on having at least two non-colluding copies.

Mechanism (basic two-database scheme, Section 3.1): the user picks a uniformly random subset S of
[n] (each index included independently with probability 1/2), sends S to DB_1 and the symmetric
difference of S with the singleton {i} to DB_2. Each database replies with the exclusive-or (XOR) of
the bits at its received index set. The user XORs the two replies to recover x_i. Each database sees
only a uniformly random subset of [n], independent of i, so neither learns which bit was retrieved;
this scheme sends n bits total (no better than trivial download) but is the base case generalized
below.

Mechanism (multi-database cube scheme, Section 3.2): for k = 2^d databases, embed the n-bit string
in a d-dimensional hypercube of side length n^(1/d), associate the target index i with a d-tuple of
cube coordinates, and associate each of the 2^d databases with a distinct binary string of length d
indicating which "side" of each cube dimension it queries. Each database is asked for the XOR of
bits in a uniformly random d-dimensional subcube, with the subcubes across databases correlated so
that XORing all k replies recovers x_i; each individual database sees a uniformly distributed
subcube description, revealing nothing about i. Total communication is 2^d * (d * n^(1/d) + 1).

Mechanism (covering-codes scheme, Section 3.3, Theorem 1): improves the constant number of databases
needed for a given exponent by mapping database indices to codewords of a covering code — a set of k
binary strings of length d such that every binary string of length d is within Hamming distance 1 of
some codeword — instead of requiring all 2^d corners of the cube. For any (d, k) pair admitting a
radius-1, k-word covering code of {0,1}^d, there exists a k-database PIR scheme with communication
complexity k + (2d + (d-1)*k) * n^(1/d). Instantiated at d=3 with the 2-word covering code
{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)} of {0,1}^3, this gives the paper's headline two-database scheme with communication
O(n^(1/3)). At d=4, a 4-word covering code gives a four-database scheme; the paper tabulates the best
known covering codes up to d=8 (citing Honkala's bounds) together with the resulting communication
complexity for each.

Mechanism (polynomial-interpolation scheme, Section 4, Corollary 6): represents the user's desired
index i implicitly via a low-degree polynomial over a finite field GF(q); the user sends field
elements derived from k-1 random polynomials to each of k databases, and each database returns one
field-element evaluation of a related polynomial built from the database contents. Interpolating the
k received values (using that the sum of k such polynomials, evaluated at 0, equals x_i) lets the
user recover the bit while each individual database sees only field elements from polynomials whose
free terms are uniformly random. This scheme generalizes to arbitrary constant k with communication
complexity k * (s + k*sqrt(n) + k) * log_2(q), where s is a function of k and n stated explicitly for
k=2 through k=4 and asymptotically for k >= 5; for general constant k this gives O(n^(1/k))
communication, and is asymptotically better than the covering-codes scheme except at k=2 and k=4,
where covering codes remain superior (O(n^(1/3)) versus O(n^(1/2)) for k=2, matching orders for k=4).

Mechanism (polylogarithmic-database scheme, Section 4, Theorem 14): setting the number of databases
to grow with n — specifically (1/3)*log_2(n) + 1 databases — the same polynomial-interpolation
framework yields communication complexity (1/3)*(1+o(1)) * log_2^2(n) * log_2(log_2(2n)),
polylogarithmic in n. More generally (Theorem 14), for any integer function t(n) and any d(n) =
c*t(n) for constant c > 1, there exists a t-private information-retrieval scheme for d(n) databases
with communication O(t(n) * c^(sqrt(n))) [the paper's own stated bound, sqrt applied to n inside the
c-exponent form as printed]; and for d(n) = t(n)*log_2(n), a t-private scheme exists with
communication polylog(n) * t(n).

Mechanism (privacy against coalitions, Section 7): the schemes above guarantee privacy only against
any single database observed in isolation ("1-private"); the paper states explicitly that in every
scheme given, any two databases jointly can extract information about i from their combined queries,
and in some schemes two colluding databases can fully recover i. Section 7 generalizes the
polynomial-interpolation scheme to guarantee privacy against any coalition of up to t colluding
databases: using t(k-1)+1 databases, field elements distributed via t random degree-t polynomials per
user query (rather than one), and interpolation at t(k-1)+1 points, the resulting scheme is proved
t-private with communication complexity (t(k-1)+1) * (s+1) * log_2(q), reducing to the 1-private
scheme's parameters when t=1.

Mechanism (block retrieval, Section 6): Propositions 10-11 and Corollaries 12-13 show how to convert
a scheme retrieving a single bit per query into one retrieving an m-bit block at m times the
per-block communication of retrieving a single bit from a database of size scaled by m, and,
separately, that for block length ℓ >= n the basic two-database scheme (Section 3.1) gives a
one-round protocol with total communication exactly 4*ℓ — a constant-factor (4x) overhead over
non-private transfer once the retrieved block is at least as large as the database being queried
against.

### Measured results
This is a theoretical paper: every "result" below is a proven asymptotic communication-complexity
bound for a stated construction under stated parameters (number of databases, privacy level, field
size), not an empirical measurement from a running system. No hardware, dataset, or implementation is
described; Section 5 ("Numeric Results," referenced as Figure 2) numerically compares the
covering-codes and polynomial-interpolation schemes at specific database counts and sizes (k = 2, 4,
7, 16; n = 2^20, 2^30, 2^40), but the paper's own tabulated bit-counts for those combinations could
not be reliably recovered from the retrieved PostScript source's glyph-placement encoding (table
cells are positioned by absolute coordinates rather than linear text flow, which the extraction
method used here does not reconstruct), so no specific figure from that table is recorded here. The
paper's own qualitative conclusion from that table is recorded as a comparative finding, not a
number: for k=2, the covering-codes scheme is superior to the polynomial-interpolation scheme
(matching the asymptotic result that covering codes give O(n^(1/3)) versus polynomial interpolation's
O(n^(1/2)) at k=2); for k=4, k=7, and k=16, the polynomial-interpolation scheme is superior,
increasingly so for larger n.

| Scheme | Databases (k) | Privacy level | Communication complexity | Condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trivial single-database | 1 | none possible beyond full download | n bits | Proved as a lower bound: any 1-database scheme with privacy requires communicating the whole n-bit database |
| Basic two-database XOR scheme (Section 3.1) | 2 | 1-private | n bits (no improvement; base case for later constructions) | one round, XOR-based |
| Cube scheme (Section 3.2) | k = 2^d, any d >= 1 | 1-private | 2^d * (d*n^(1/d) + 1) | one round, XOR-based |
| Covering-codes scheme (Theorem 1) | k = size of a radius-1 covering code of {0,1}^d | 1-private | k + (2d + (d-1)*k) * n^(1/d) | requires a known radius-1, k-word covering code for the chosen d; volume bound requires k >= 2^d/(d+1) |
| Covering-codes scheme instantiated at d=3, k=2 | 2 | 1-private | O(n^(1/3)) | codewords {(0,0,0),(1,1,1)}, a Hamming-perfect code |
| Polynomial-interpolation scheme (Corollary 6) | any constant k >= 2 | 1-private | k * (s + k*sqrt(n) + k) * log_2(q), giving O(n^(1/k)) | q a prime power >= k+1; s given explicitly for k=2 (s = sqrt(n)+2), k=3 (s = sqrt(2) * cube-root(n) + 3), k=4 (s = cube-root(6) * fourth-root(n) + 3), and asymptotically s = (k-1) * k-th-root(n) for k >= 5 |
| Polylogarithmic-database scheme (Theorem 14, specific case) | (1/3)*log_2(n) + 1 | 1-private | (1/3)*(1+o(1)) * log_2^2(n) * log_2(log_2(2n)) | asymptotic in n; the paper states this is close to optimal given the state of knowledge on 1-private schemes at the time |
| General t-private scheme (Theorem 14, general case 1) | d(n) = c*t(n), constant c>1 | t-private (survives coalitions of up to t databases) | O(t(n) * c^sqrt(n)) [as stated in the paper] | any integer function t(n) |
| General t-private scheme (Theorem 14, general case 2) | d(n) = t(n)*log_2(n) | t-private | polylog(n) * t(n) | any integer function t(n) |
| t-private coalition-resistant polynomial scheme (Section 7) | t*(k-1)+1 | t-private, any coalition of up to t databases | (t*(k-1)+1) * (s+1) * log_2(q) | reduces to the 1-private Corollary 6 scheme's parameters at t=1 |
| Block-retrieval overhead, block length ℓ >= n (Corollary 13) | 2 | 1-private | 4*ℓ total communication | one round, built from the Section 3.1 two-database scheme via Proposition 10 |
| Lower bound, two databases, single binary query each | 2 | 1-private | user messages must have length linear in n | proved only for the restricted case of a single binary query per database, stated by the authors as a limited but illustrative lower bound |

Related-work comparison the paper itself draws: Pudlak and Rodl's construction (unrelated
motivation, complexity theory) yields an equivalent two-database PIR scheme with o(n) communication,
more precisely O(n*log_2(log_2(n))/log_2(n)) — an improvement over the trivial n-bit bound but weaker
than this paper's O(n^(1/3)). Babai, Kimmel, and Lokam's independent, concurrent work yields, for
general k, total communication O(k*n^(H_2(1/(k+1)))) where H_2 is binary entropy; at k=2 this gives
O(n^(H_2(1/3))) which the paper approximates as O(n^0.92), better than the Pudlak-Rodl bound but
still worse than this paper's O(n^(1/3)) result at k=2.

### Parameters
Number of databases k: instantiated at k=2 (headline result), general constant k, k=2^d for the cube
scheme, and k growing as (1/3)*log_2(n) for the polylogarithmic scheme. Field size q: any prime power
with q >= k+1 for the polynomial-interpolation scheme. Privacy coalition bound t: t=1 (standard
"1-private," the default across Sections 3-6) generalized to arbitrary t in Section 7. Block length
ℓ: the block-retrieval overhead result is stated specifically for ℓ >= n. Covering-code radius: fixed
at 1 throughout Theorem 1's construction (the paper notes larger radii, e.g., 2 or 3, are applicable
in principle but does not work out their resulting complexity in the extracted text). Dimension d for
the covering-codes scheme: tabulated by the paper (Figure 1, not independently recoverable in this
extraction) for d up to 8, using the best covering codes known at the time, citing Honkala's bounds;
the paper notes the d=3 and d=7 codes used are Hamming codes, which are perfect codes (all
radius-1 balls around codewords are disjoint).

### Stated limitations
Every scheme in Sections 3 through 6 guarantees privacy only against a single database observed in
isolation (1-privacy); the paper states explicitly that in all of these schemes, any two databases
that pool their received queries obtain some information about the desired index i, and in some of
the schemes two colluding databases can fully recover i. The stronger t-private construction of
Section 7 requires t*(k-1)+1 databases for the same underlying k-database polynomial scheme,
increasing communication accordingly, so the paper's own t-private bound is a large-constant-factor
cost for coalition resistance rather than a free upgrade. The paper's own lower-bound result (Section
8 discussion) is explicitly limited: it applies only to the very restricted case of two databases
where the user is permitted a single binary (one-bit) query to each database; the authors state this
"is very restricted with respect to what we want," i.e., it does not establish a general lower bound
for schemes with longer per-database queries, and no stronger general lower bound is proved in this
extended-abstract version. The paper does not address a computational (cryptographic-hardness-based)
relaxation of privacy anywhere in the extracted text — every scheme here provides unconditional,
information-independent privacy against one (or t) databases, with no discussion of a single-database
computational PIR variant; that direction is developed only in later, separate papers (Kushilevitz
and Ostrovsky, FOCS 1997, is the earliest single-server construction and is not this paper).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every scheme (Sections 3-6) requires at least two physically or organizationally separate copies of
the database that do not communicate their received queries to each other; the 1-privacy guarantee is
voided the moment any two of the k databases pool what they each received, since the paper states
directly that colluding pairs can extract information about, and in some schemes fully recover, the
desired index. A design wanting resistance to coalitions of up to t colluding database operators must
use the Section 7 construction specifically, provision t*(k-1)+1 separate database replicas instead
of k, and accept the correspondingly larger per-query communication; the ordinary Corollary 6 scheme
gives no partial coalition resistance at any intermediate t. Every database replica must hold an
identical, static copy of the n-bit string x for the stated bit-recovery correctness proofs to apply;
the paper's protocols are not proven correct against a database that returns an answer to a
different data content than the one the other replicas hold. The user must generate and send
uniformly random field elements or subsets on every query (the source of the privacy guarantee); a
weakened randomness source at the user directly weakens the proved privacy bound, though the paper
does not itself analyze partial-randomness degradation. The described one-round protocols require no
persistent per-user server-side state and no shared secret key between user and database — privacy
holds unconditionally for any adversary, without a cryptographic hardness assumption — so a system
built on these schemes does not need a key-management or key-distribution component for the PIR layer
itself, unlike later single-server, cryptographic-assumption-based PIR schemes.

### Contradicts
None found within the extracted text; this is the field's foundational multi-server PIR paper and the
paper positions its own results as new upper bounds against the prior related work it cites (Pudlak
and Rodl; Babai, Kimmel, and Lokam), not as contradicting them. Cross-paper in this corpus: this
paper's results concern multi-server, non-colluding-server PIR exclusively; MENON-SP-22,
HENZINGER-USENIXSEC-23, and MENON-USENIXSEC-24 in this corpus all address single-server PIR (a
setting this paper does not construct a scheme for, and does not claim is impossible — it simply is
not addressed in the extracted text), so no direct numeric comparison applies between this entry and
those three.

### References worth retrieving
- Pudlak, Rodl, "Modified Ranks of Tensors and the Size of Circuits," STOC 1993 — foundational
  (the first construction, via an unrelated complexity-theory motivation, implying a two-database PIR
  scheme with o(n) communication, the direct predecessor this paper improves on for k=2).
- Babai, Kimmel, Lokam, "Simultaneous Messages vs. Communication," STACS 1995 (appeared) — competing
  (an independent, concurrent construction giving O(k*n^(H_2(1/(k+1)))) communication for general k,
  the paper's own stated comparison point, better than Pudlak-Rodl but worse than this paper's bound).
- Beaver, Feigenbaum, "Hiding Instances in Multioracle Queries," STACS 1990 — foundational (introduces
  low-degree polynomial techniques this paper's polynomial-interpolation scheme, Section 4, builds
  on and cites as its starting point).
- Beaver, Feigenbaum, Kilian, Rogaway, "Security with Low Communication Overhead," CRYPTO 1990 —
  foundational (further develops the polynomial technique; the paper states its Section 4.2 scheme is
  an improved variant of a construction derivable from this paper's Remark 5.2).
- Abadi, Feigenbaum, Kilian, "On Hiding Information from an Oracle," Journal of Computer and System
  Sciences 39:1, 1989 — foundational (the instance-hiding model, related to but distinct from this
  paper's PIR model, discussed explicitly in the related-work section).
- Honkala, "Modified Bounds for Covering Codes," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 37:2, 1991 —
  foundational (the source of the best-known covering-code sizes this paper's Theorem 1 construction
  and Figure 1 table depend on).
- Rivest, Adleman, Dertouzos, "On data banks and privacy homomorphisms," in Foundations of Secure
  Computation, 1978 — foundational (early work on computing over encrypted/hidden data, cited in the
  paper's introductory discussion of related privacy models).

"achieving this type of privacy requires communicating the whole database, or n bits."
"a two database scheme with communication complexity of O(n^1/3)."

## [COHEN-IPTPS-03] Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
**Citation:** Bram Cohen. "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent." Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems, presented at IPTPS 2003. May 22, 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf
**Source URL:** https://bittorrent.org/bittorrentecon.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
BitTorrent redistributes the upload cost of serving a file from a single host to the set of concurrent downloaders, by having every downloader upload pieces of the file it already holds to its peers while it continues downloading pieces it lacks. This removes the requirement that hosting a file with an unbounded number of downloaders needs unbounded upload capacity at one machine.

A file is published by placing a small static .torrent file (containing the file's length, name, per-piece SHA1 hashes, and the address of a tracker) on an ordinary web server, and starting at least one seed, a peer that already holds the complete file. The tracker is a lightweight coordination point reached over HTTP: a downloader reports what file it wants and what port it listens on, and the tracker replies with a list of other peers downloading the same file, drawn at random rather than through any peer-selection heuristic that would bias the resulting connection graph toward a structured or power-law shape. Peers connect directly to each other over these tracker-supplied addresses; the tracker never routes file data itself.

Each file is divided into fixed-size pieces (a quarter megabyte in the deployments described), and each piece is further divided into 16-kilobyte sub-pieces for pipelined transfer over TCP, with a fixed number of sub-piece requests (five) kept outstanding at any time to keep the TCP connection saturated. A peer reports to every connected peer which pieces it currently holds, and only reports a piece as held once its SHA1 hash has been checked. Piece download order follows four combined rules. Once a sub-piece of a given piece has been requested, all remaining sub-pieces of that same piece are requested next, ahead of sub-pieces from any other piece, so that complete pieces finish quickly. Subject to that priority, a peer downloads whichever piece is held by the fewest of its own peers ("rarest first"), which keeps rare pieces from disappearing when the peers holding them leave, and keeps every peer's held-piece set useful to upload to others. At the very start of a download, before a peer has anything to upload, pieces are instead selected at random rather than by rarity, because a rare piece is more likely to be held by only one peer and so download more slowly than a piece obtainable in parallel sub-piece chunks from many peers. Near the end of a download, once every remaining needed sub-piece is already requested from some peer, a peer additionally requests all remaining sub-pieces from every peer that has them ("endgame mode"), and cancels the redundant in-flight requests as each sub-piece arrives, to avoid a single slow peer stalling completion.

Upload allocation among peers is governed by a choking algorithm run independently by each peer. Choking is a temporary refusal to upload to a given connected peer; it does not close the connection, so the choked peer can resume receiving without renegotiation. A peer always unchokes a fixed number of other peers (four, by default), chosen by highest current download rate received from them, recomputed once every ten seconds, a period the author states is long enough for TCP to ramp a new transfer up to its available capacity. Current download rate is calculated as a rolling 20-second average, rather than a long-term cumulative total, because bandwidth availability is stated to shift quickly as other transfers start and stop. Independent of that four-way rule, one additional connection is always unchoked regardless of its current download rate, called the optimistic unchoke, and which connection holds that role rotates every third recompute period (30 seconds); this lets a peer discover whether an otherwise-unused connection would in fact yield a better download rate than the currently favored ones, in the same role that always cooperating on the first move plays in a repeated prisoner's-dilemma strategy. If a peer receives no data for over a minute from a peer it was formerly downloading from, it marks that peer as having "snubbed" it and stops uploading to it except via the optimistic-unchoke slot; because this can produce more than one concurrent optimistic unchoke, it speeds recovery when a peer's download rate has collapsed. Once a peer has finished downloading and has no download rate left to measure, it instead prioritizes uploading to peers to which it has the best upload rate, to keep utilizing upload capacity productively.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| At a real large deployment of a single file over 400 megabytes, the number of complete downloaders ("seeders") reached at least 1,000 at one point in time | Field observation from one real BitTorrent deployment (figure 1 in the source), no controlled experiment; the paper states the actual number of completed downloads over the full period was "probably several times" 1,000, without giving a number |
| The largest known real-world BitTorrent deployments, as of the paper's writing (2003), had over 1,000 simultaneous downloaders | Field observation, unspecified file(s) and time period, no measurement methodology given |
| Tracker bandwidth overhead is about one-thousandth of total bandwidth used in a deployment, expected to fall to about one ten-thousandth with unspecified future protocol extensions | Field estimate from real deployments, no methodology, hardware, or run count given; the ten-thousandth figure is a stated expectation, not a measurement |
| Simply having peers announce their held-piece sets produces "less than a tenth of a percent" bandwidth overhead while reliably utilizing all available upload capacity | Stated as a general property of the piece-announcement protocol, no experimental setup, dataset, node count, or run count given |

None of these figures come with node counts, topology, dataset composition, or run counts sufficient to reproduce them; the paper is a design and mechanism description supported by informal field observation of real deployments, not a controlled experiment.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Tested range |
|---|---|---|
| Piece size | "typically a quarter megabyte" | Not otherwise specified |
| Sub-piece size | "typically sixteen kilobytes" | Not otherwise specified |
| Pipelined outstanding sub-piece requests | "typically five" | Not otherwise specified |
| Default number of unchoked peers | Four | Not otherwise specified |
| Choking-decision recompute interval | Ten seconds | Justified as long enough for TCP to reach full transfer capacity; not otherwise varied |
| Optimistic-unchoke rotation interval | Thirty seconds (every third ten-second recompute period) | Justified as enough time for upload to reach capacity, download to reciprocate, and download to reach capacity in turn; not otherwise varied |
| Download-rate averaging window used for choking decisions | Rolling 20-second average | Contrasted against a former implementation that used long-term net transfer totals, stated to have performed worse; no quantitative comparison given |
| Snub threshold | No data received from a peer for over one minute | Not otherwise specified |

### Stated limitations
The paper states that erasure codes had been suggested by other work as a technique for the piece-verification and distribution problem, but that BitTorrent's much simpler fixed-piece SHA1-hash approach "has proven to be workable" instead, without a quantitative comparison of the two approaches. It states that for deployments with a single seed whose upload capacity is well below that of the aggregate downloaders, and for deployments where the original seed is eventually taken offline, a piece can become completely unavailable if rarest-first replication does not spread it in time; the paper presents rarest-first as reducing but does not claim eliminating this risk. It does not report a formal robustness or fairness analysis of the choking algorithm; the claim that seeking pareto efficiency through tit-for-tat "tend[s] to have" properties of full resource utilization, consistent download rates, and resistance to non-contributing peers is presented as a consequence of a cited general economic argument, not as a property proven or measured for BitTorrent specifically. The paper does not model or measure adversarial peer behavior (for example peers that upload junk data, or coordinate to defeat the choking algorithm); it addresses only unmodified good-faith peer behavior under high churn.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
BitTorrent's choking mechanism requires a bidirectional TCP connection between any two peers exchanging pieces, since choking blocks only the upload direction while leaving the same connection able to resume downloading without renegotiation. It requires the tracker to supply peer lists chosen at random rather than through a structured peer-selection rule, since the paper attributes BitTorrent's churn robustness to the resulting random-graph topology and explicitly attributes the fragility of power-law peer graphs (produced by many other peer-selection algorithms) to their vulnerability to segmentation after modest churn. It requires a piece-integrity check (the per-piece SHA1 hash from the .torrent file) to exist before a peer is willing to advertise or serve that piece to others, since the reported piece set doubles as the input that both piece selection (rarest-first) and choking-partner selection operate on. It requires a mechanism outside the wire protocol (the choking algorithm is stated to not be part of the BitTorrent wire protocol itself) to select which unchoked peers to reciprocate with, meaning any peer-selection or reputation input other than recent observed download rate would have to be added at that separate layer, not the protocol itself. The rarest-first piece-selection policy requires each peer to know, from its own connected peers' advertised piece sets, which pieces are locally rare; this signal comes from the same piece-announcement messages the choking algorithm's traffic accounting does not use, so a peer that withheld its held-piece set from others to preserve privacy would prevent both the choking algorithm's income signal to it, since others would not know to reciprocate, and rarest-first's ability to protect that peer's pieces from disappearing.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch reports figures for BitTorrent's choking algorithm or tracker overhead.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: M. Castro, P. Druschel, A.-M. Kermarrec, A. Nandi, A. Rowstron, A. Singh, "SplitStream: High-bandwidth content distribution in cooperative environments," IPTPS 2003 — a tree-structured alternative distribution approach cited by Cohen as not utilizing the upload capacity of leaf nodes, the direct architectural alternative BitTorrent's mesh-based piece exchange is implicitly compared against.
- foundational: A.-L. Barabási, "Linked: The New Science of Networks," Perseus Publishing, 2002 — cited as the source for the claim that random graphs have good robustness properties, underlying the paper's argument for the tracker's random peer selection.
- attack/critique context: E. Adar, B. A. Huberman, "Free riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 — cited as establishing the general peer-to-peer fairness problem BitTorrent's tit-for-tat choking is designed to solve; also cited directly by VISHNUMURTHY-P2PECON-03 in this batch for the same freeloading motivation.
- foundational: P. Maymounkov, D. Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002 — cited only for the observation that real deployments experience very high peer churn (peers connecting for minutes to a few hours), not for any mechanism BitTorrent reuses.

### Verbatim extracts
- "Simply having peers announce what they have results in less than a tenth of a percent bandwidth overhead"
- "The current scaling bottleneck (which hasn't actually been reached) appears to be the bandwidth overhead of the tracker."
- "Currently that's about a thousandth the total amount of bandwidth used"
- "Ten seconds is a long enough period of time for TCP to ramp up new transfers to their full capacity."
- "30 seconds is enough time for the upload to get to full capacity, the download to reciprocate"

## [CORRIGANGIBBS-SP-15] Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users
**Citation:** Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Dan Boneh, David Mazieres. "Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2015. Pages 321-338. DOI 10.1109/SP.2015.27.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.henrycg.com/files/academic/papers/oakland15riposte.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.henrycg.com/files/academic/papers/oakland15riposte.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Riposte lets a large number of clients anonymously post fixed-length messages to a shared bulletin board maintained by a small set of minimally trusted servers, so that no server, and no network eavesdropper who observes all client-server traffic, can determine which client wrote which message. Messaging proceeds in fixed time epochs. To write, a client picks a row index in a shared database table and secret-shares a write vector that is zero everywhere except at that row (where it holds the client's message) across the servers, one share per server; a coalition of servers smaller than a protocol-specific threshold learns nothing about the message or the write location from its own shares. Instead of sending a full-length share vector (which would need to be as long as the whole database, an approach the paper calls the "first-attempt" construction and rejects for bandwidth cost), the client encodes its write using a distributed point function (DPF): a compact key, of size proportional to the square root of the table length L rather than L itself, that each server locally expands (via a pseudorandom generator, using AES-based symmetric-key operations in the two-server variant, or DDH-based elliptic-curve operations in the s-server variant) into its own share of the same all-zero-except-one-row vector. Riposte calls this technique "PIR run in reverse": ordinary Private Information Retrieval (PIR) lets a client read a hidden row privately; Riposte's DPF-based write lets a client set a hidden row privately. Servers accumulate every client's share vector by simple vector addition over the epoch; at epoch end, the summed table, containing every client's message in its own row, is revealed, but no server can attribute any row to any specific client because the sum was computed homomorphically over secret shares.

Riposte defines two variants trading server count for security assumption. The three-server variant uses two database servers plus one audit server and needs only that no two of the three collude; it detects and rejects a malformed client write (a write that is not actually zero-except-one-row, which would otherwise let one malicious client corrupt every row and deny service to everyone) using a computationally cheap multi-party protocol among the servers based on the Poly1305 keyed hash function and Pedersen commitments, run before the write is admitted. The s-server variant tolerates s-1 out of s servers behaving arbitrarily (Byzantine), at the cost of the more expensive DDH-based DPF and, in its full design, client-generated zero-knowledge proofs of well-formedness instead of the multi-party check.

### Measured results
Implemented in Go, source published; measured on the DeterLab network testbed, on commodity servers running Ubuntu 14.04 with four-core AES-NI-enabled Intel E3-1260L CPUs and 16 GB RAM. Network topology: 100 Mbps links among server nodes, 1 Gbps links among the eight client nodes and between client and server switches, 20 ms round-trip latency between every pair of nodes; eight client machines used multiple threads to saturate the servers with write requests. Error bars in the paper's figures report the standard deviation of throughput measurements across repeated runs (run count not stated).

Three-server variant (two database servers plus one audit server, no two colluding), fully implemented including the audit protocol, so throughput figures include the cost of detecting and rejecting malformed writes, using 160-byte database rows (chosen as the smallest 32-byte multiple large enough for a 140-byte Tweet), AES-128-CTR as the pseudorandom generator, Poly1305 for the audit protocol's keyed hash, and TLS for link encryption:

| Database table size (160-byte rows) | Write throughput |
|---|---|
| 64 rows | 751.5 requests/second |
| 65,536 rows | 32.8 requests/second |
| 1,048,576 rows (about 168 MB) | 2.86 requests/second |
| 2.3 million rows (377 MB table) | 1.4 requests/second |

The measured upper bound on throughput from the servers' AES pseudorandom-generator speed (a Go AES benchmark) is 605 MB/s; the paper states migrating the performance-critical code from Go to C using OpenSSL (reported OpenSSL AES throughput of 3.9 GB/s on the same hardware) could raise throughput by up to 6 times. At very small table sizes, TLS connection setup, not cryptographic computation, limits throughput to roughly 900 requests per second.

Effect of the square-root-size distributed point function versus a naive full-length write vector, holding total table size fixed at 10 MB while varying the table's width-to-height ratio: the DPF-optimal table shape achieves 38.4 requests per second; the naive-construction extreme (client sends a vector as large as the database) achieves 0.05 requests per second, a 768-times difference in this specific comparison. Elsewhere the paper describes the general bandwidth-efficient DPF as giving a 32-times speedup over the naive approach.

Total data transferred per write request scales sub-linearly with table size: at a 2.5 GB table, one database server transfers a total of 1.23 MB to process a single write request (against a naive-construction bound of transferring the full table size, i.e. 2.5 GB, per write).

Writing into a 377 MB table (2.3 million 160-byte rows) requires each client to upload less than 1 MB of data to the servers; the paper states a two-server Dining-Cryptographers-network (DC-net) based system would require each client to upload more than 750 MB of data for the equivalent write, though no citation gives the specific measured DC-net system this comparison figure was computed from.

s-server variant (Byzantine-tolerant, s-1 out of s servers may be malicious), implemented without the zero-knowledge disruption-resistance proofs (so these figures are stated as an upper bound on that variant's real throughput), using a DDH-based seed-homomorphic pseudorandom generator over the NIST P-256 elliptic curve, 160-byte rows, eight servers: at a table size of 1,024 rows, the cluster processes one request every 3.44 seconds; the paper computes that a table of one million rows would take nearly one hour per request under this construction (compared to 0.3 seconds for the three-server, AES-based variant at a comparable table size). Varying the number of servers from two to ten at fixed table sizes (16-row and 64-row tables) produces only a slight decrease in throughput, attributed to the workload being CPU-bound rather than network-bound.

Large-anonymity-set demonstration: a three-server Riposte cluster with a 65,536-row database table, run continuously for 32 hours, processed 2,895,216 write requests total, at an average rate of 25.19 requests per second. The paper computes that with this table size and the collision-rate technique of Section III-B, a table of 65,536 rows supports up to 0.3% of anonymity-set members writing per epoch while keeping the write-collision rate under 5%, so reaching a roughly 1,000,000-user anonymity set with a three-server cluster and a 65,536-row table requires a time epoch of at least 11 hours.

Scale comparison against Twitter's reported 2013 throughput of 5,700 140-byte Tweets per second (approximately 5,000 Riposte-equivalent 160-byte messages per second): at a one-million-row table, the measured three-server cluster processes 2.86 write requests per second (from the table above), so the paper computes that matching Twitter's Tweet volume at anonymity-set sizes of hundreds of thousands of clients would need roughly 1,750 times more computing power, i.e. about 5,250 servers split across three non-colluding data centers, or, accounting for the audit server needing only string comparisons, closer to 4,000 servers total. This is a derived projection, not a separately measured deployment.

The paper states prior DC-net-based anonymity systems (citing Dissent) scaled to 5,120 clients, and prior verifiable-shuffle-based systems (citing Bayer and Groth) scaled to 100,000 clients, as points of comparison for its own 2,895,216-client demonstration; these two figures are attributed to those other systems' own publications, not independently re-measured by this paper.

### Parameters
- Row (message) length: 160 bytes in every reported experiment, chosen as the smallest 32-byte multiple that holds a 140-byte Tweet; the paper notes throughput depends only on total table size (rows times row length), so a 4096-byte-row email application would reach 2.86 requests/second at a table size of 40,960 rows instead of 1,048,576.
- Server count for the three-server variant: exactly 3 (two database servers, one audit server); security holds as long as no two of the three collude.
- Server count s for the general s-server variant: tested at s = 8 in the throughput-vs-table-size experiment (Figure 6) and varied from 2 to 10 in the throughput-vs-server-count experiment (Figure 7).
- Time epoch length: not fixed by the protocol; the paper computes a required minimum of at least 11 hours to reach a roughly 1,000,000-client anonymity set with a 65,536-row table at a 0.3% per-epoch write rate and under 5% collision rate.
- Anonymity-set-to-writer ratio: the paper's collision-rate analysis (Section III-B, referenced but not re-derived here) ties this ratio to table size and target collision rate; 0.3% of the anonymity set writing per epoch is the value used in the 65,536-row worked example.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its threat model trusts all servers for availability (a server can always deny service by refusing to run the protocol) though not for privacy or correctness; disruption resistance in this paper is defined only against malicious clients, and the paper states explicitly it does not try to prevent servers themselves from corrupting the database state. The s-server variant's reported throughput is stated as an upper bound only, because the zero-knowledge proofs needed to make that variant resistant to malicious-client disruption were not implemented; the paper estimates the added cost as an additional order-square-root-of-L elliptic-curve operations per server, which it states would almost certainly be dwarfed by the linear-in-L elliptic-curve cost of updating the database table, but this added cost was not measured. The paper states three specific open problems it leaves unsolved: whether an (s, s-1)-distributed-point-function construction for s greater than 2 exists using only symmetric-key operations (the three-server variant already achieves this only for s=2); whether disruption resistance is achievable without a non-colluding audit server, using no public-key primitives; and whether any DPF construction allows processing a write request in amortized time sublinear in the database length L. The large-anonymity-set demonstration (2,895,216 users over 32 hours) is stated by the paper to require both hours-scale messaging latency tolerance and a read-heavy workload (few writers relative to readers); the paper states these two conditions hold for whistleblowing and microblogging but does not claim the demonstrated scale for lower-latency or write-heavy applications.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The security property (no server learns which client wrote which row) holds only under the stated non-collusion assumption: no two of the three servers collude in the three-server variant, or no more than s-1 of s servers collude in the general variant; any system composing Riposte as a subcomponent must independently ensure operationally that the servers it selects do not collude, since Riposte itself provides no mechanism to enforce or detect collusion. A system relying on Riposte's large-anonymity-set property must accept messaging latency on the order of the epoch length (hours, in the paper's own worked example), and must supply a mechanism to generate "empty" read-only write requests from non-writing participants, since the anonymity-set-inflation technique described in Section VI-C depends on read-only clients submitting indistinguishable dummy writes into a fixed database row. The write-collision mitigation (Section III-B, cited but not fully re-derived in this extraction) requires the system to tolerate a nonzero message-loss rate from collisions (under 5% in the paper's worked example) and requires knowing or bounding the number of concurrent writers per epoch to size the table and epoch length correctly; a downstream component that cannot tolerate any message loss cannot rely on the collision-based capacity model as stated. The DPF-based write mechanism requires every server to independently and correctly expand its DPF key using its own pseudorandom generator (AES-based or DDH-based, depending on variant) with no coordination among servers beyond the client-issued keys; a component relying on Riposte must supply a fixed, agreed table row length in advance, since Riposte's per-write bandwidth cost is a function of that fixed row length and the table's row count.

### Contradicts
None found among papers currently in this corpus. Internally, the paper's headline claim ("millions of users" in the title, 2,895,216-client demonstration) applies only to the specific read-heavy, latency-tolerant, three-server configuration; it does not hold for the s-server variant, whose measured throughput at large table sizes (nearly one hour per request at one million rows) is far below the three-server figures and is explicitly labeled an upper-bound estimate rather than a full implementation result.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: D. Chaum. "The Dining Cryptographers problem: Unconditional sender and recipient untraceability." Journal of Cryptology, 1988 — the original Dining Cryptographers network (DC-net) construction Riposte's client/server write protocol is described as inspired by.
- competing: D. I. Wolinsky, H. Corrigan-Gibbs, A. Johnson, B. Ford. "Dissent: Accountable anonymous group messaging" (and the later Dissent system referenced as scaling to 5,120 clients) — the paper's own stated prior-scale comparison point for DC-net-based systems; holds the comparison numbers this paper's scaling claim is measured against.
- competing: S. Bayer, J. Groth. "Efficient zero-knowledge argument for correctness of a shuffle." EUROCRYPT 2012 — cited as the prior verifiable-shuffle-based system scaling to 100,000 clients, the second scale comparison point.
- foundational: B. Chor, N. Gilboa. "Computationally private information retrieval." STOC 1997 — origin of the distributed-point-function-adjacent PIR technique Riposte's "reverse PIR" write mechanism is built from.
- foundational: B. Chor, E. Kushilevitz, O. Goldreich, M. Sudan. "Private information retrieval." Journal of the ACM, 1998 — foundational PIR definition Riposte's reverse-PIR framing depends on.
- competing: S. Goel, M. Robson, M. Polte, E. Sirer. "Herbivore: A scalable and efficient protocol for anonymous communication" — a DC-net scaling approach (partitioning users into small groups) the paper contrasts its own single-large-anonymity-set approach against.
- foundational: H. Corrigan-Gibbs, D. I. Wolinsky, B. Ford. "Proactively accountable anonymous messaging in Verdict" — prior disruption-resistance work using zero-knowledge proofs, cited as more expensive than Riposte's multi-party disruption check.

### Verbatim extracts
- "a three-server Riposte cluster can build an anonymity set of 2,895,216 users in 32 hours."
- "the system handles 751.5 write requests per second" (64-row table).
- "the total data transfer in a Riposte cluster scales sub-linearly with the database size."
- "DPFs yield a 768× speed-up" (naive versus bandwidth-efficient construction, fixed 10 MB table).
- "we do not try to prevent servers from corrupting the database state."
- "these performance figures thus represent an upper bound on the s-server protocol's performance."
- "Does there exist an (s,s−1)-DPF construction for s>2 that uses only symmetric-key operations?"

## [CORTESGOICOECHEA-ARXIV-24] Scalability Limitations of Kademlia DHTs when Enabling Data Availability Sampling in Ethereum

**Citation:** Mikel Cortes-Goicoechea, Csaba Kiraly, Dmitriy Ryajov, Jose Luis Munoz-Tapia, Leonardo Bautista-Gomez. "Scalability limitations of Kademlia DHTs when enabling Data Availability Sampling in Ethereum." arXiv, 2024. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2402.09993.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.09993
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.09993
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper determines whether a Kademlia distributed hash table (DHT — a data structure that maps keys to the network addresses of the nodes storing their values, using node-to-node routing) can serve as the content-location mechanism for Ethereum's proposed Data Availability Sampling (DAS — a scheme letting a node verify a large block is fully published by successfully retrieving a small random subset of its erasure-coded pieces). It builds a discrete-event DHT simulator ("py-DHT") reproducing Kademlia's routing-table structure, lookup and provide (store-announcement) operations, and configurable network-condition parameters (connection failure rates, latency ranges, and a "gamma" overhead parameter modeling the added delay a node experiences from serving many concurrent connections). It validates the simulator against a live measurement tool ("looking-up-ipfs") run against the production InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) Kademlia DHT, then uses the validated simulator to project DHT behavior at Ethereum-scale request volumes the live network was not tested at.

Ethereum's DAS proposal (DankSharding) erasure-codes each block into a 256x256 grid, extended in both directions to 512x512 samples so any half of the samples in a row or column suffice to reconstruct that row or column (and thus the whole block) via Reed-Solomon encoding. Each of the 262,144 resulting samples (512 bytes of data plus 48 bytes of a KZG polynomial-commitment proof) would be addressed and located through the DHT, keyed by a Beacon Node's identifier and the segment's position, rather than through IPFS-style provider records that first ask who holds the content and only then fetch it. A sampling node issues 80 concurrent lookups for randomly selected samples (the number the paper states as sufficient for high-probability reconstruction confidence on a 512-by-512 encoded block) and DAS verification is complete only when every one of the 80 succeeds.

### Measured results

| Operation | Condition | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Lookup hops, live IPFS network | 100 sets of 80 concurrent DHT lookups, real IPFS DHT, AWS Paris VM (4 CPU, 8 GB RAM, 50 GB SSD), 3 Oct 2023 | 99% of lookups completed in under 18 hops; a 1% tail reached up to 100 hops |
| Lookup hops, simulator | 100 sets of 200 concurrent lookups, k=20, alpha=3, beta=20, fast-failure (connection-refusal) rate 10% | 99th percentile 12-14 hops; concurrency-overhead parameter had negligible effect on hop count |
| Lookup latency by region, live IPFS | Probelab Team's regional IPFS measurements, k=20, alpha=3, beta=20 | 90th percentile latency: 700 ms (US), 700 ms (Europe), 1.7 s (South America), 1.5 s (Africa, figure as stated in the paper) |
| Lookup latency, live IPFS | 100 rounds of 80 concurrent lookups, IPFS network | 90% completed between 600 ms and 1.2 s |
| DHT provide (seeding) latency, simulator | 1,000 concurrent provide operations from a single node, network of 12,000 nodes, k=20 | Completed within 20 seconds only under low network overhead; requires higher-end hardware to sustain even that |
| DHT provide (seeding) latency, simulator | 10,000 concurrent provide operations from a single node, same network | The cumulative distribution shows the DHT reaching a throughput bottleneck (no numeric completion time given for this run) |
| DHT provide (seeding) latency, simulator, worst case | 262,144 concurrent provide operations (a full DankSharding block) from a single node, best-case simulated per-connection delay factor of 0.015 ms | 10-14 minutes to complete, roughly 50 to 70 times the 12-second Ethereum slot deadline |
| DHT provide (seeding) latency, live IPFS | 100 sets of 80 concurrent CID (content identifier) provide operations, real IPFS network, 80-second timeout per set | Only about 20% of the 100 sets completed within 70 seconds; about 67% of sets were cut off by the 80-second timeout |
| Per-node storage load under a naive seeding scheme | 262,144 block segments (512 columns x 512 rows) seeded across roughly 13,000 active Ethereum nodes (the paper's stated current network figure), k=20, alpha=3 (the paper's stated standard Kademlia parameters) | 403.29 segments per node on average, every 12 seconds |
| Provide-operation hop count | Same seeding scenario | Median 8 to 10 hops to notify the k closest nodes to a segment's key |

Bottleneck mechanism identified: because Kademlia's routing table keeps the most stable, longest-observed nodes (its k-buckets prefer long-lived contacts, following the original Kademlia paper), the 250-300 nodes in a seeding node's routing table are contacted first on every provide operation and become the most heavily loaded nodes in the network under a high-volume single-seeder workload; the routing table does not change fast enough during a 12-second window to redistribute this load.

### Parameters
- k (replication factor / k-bucket size): 20 (paper's stated standard Kademlia value, used throughout the experiments).
- alpha (maximum concurrent lookup connections per client): 3, matching the value the paper states IPFS uses.
- beta (number of closer peers returned per lookup response): 20.
- Fast error rate (fraction of connections refused outright): varied; 10% used in the reported hop-count simulation.
- Slow error rate (fraction of connections that time out): configurable in the simulator; no single value stated as used across all reported runs.
- Gamma (incremental per-additional-connection overhead delay): varied across simulated runs (Figures 7-10); the best-case value used for the 262,144-sample worst-case run was 0.015 ms per connection.
- Network size: 12,000 simulated nodes for the seeding experiments; approximately 13,000 stated as the live Ethereum active-node count at time of writing; under 500 nodes is stated as the network size used in a prior throughput study (Dabek et al., cited as [11]) that this paper contrasts itself against.
- Sample size: 512 bytes of data plus 48 bytes of KZG proof per DAS sample; 262,144 total samples per block (512x512 grid).
- Concurrent lookups per sampling node: 80 (DAS verification requirement) in the live-network validation runs; 200 in some simulator-only runs (Figures 5, 7).
- Hardware: simulation runs on a Ryzen 5900X CPU, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD; live IPFS benchmark runs on an AWS cloud VM in Paris with 4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, 50 GB SSD, dated 3 October 2023.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that a single node (a block proposer or builder) seeding all 262,144 samples cannot complete within the 12-second Ethereum slot deadline under any simulated configuration it tested, because the seeding node's own routing table becomes the bottleneck. It states that alternative seeding by multiple validators, each responsible for the segments in the GossipSub topics they subscribe to, still risks correlating a node's DHT-observed activity with the topic subscriptions of the validators it hosts, compromising validator anonymity, and that this correlation risk is unresolved in the paper. It states that the internal parameters of any deployed Ethereum DAS DHT were not yet fixed at the time of writing. It states that Dabek et al.'s prior DHT-throughput work does not account for the overhead of a network the scale of Ethereum's, having tested under 500 nodes. It states, as future work, an intention to evaluate DHT viability under DAS protocol variants less constrained by the 12-second slot deadline than the one analyzed here.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Requires a fixed per-operation deadline (the paper's is the Ethereum 12-second slot time) against which any DHT-based content-location mechanism's seeding and lookup latency must be measured; a mechanism whose seeding time scales with the number of items to publish from a single node, as Kademlia's provide operation does here, cannot meet a fixed per-round deadline once item count crosses a threshold the paper places between 1,000 and 10,000 concurrent provides on a 12,000-node network.
- Requires, for the anonymity property DAS assumes (that no observer can correlate which node holds which validator's samples), that neither the DHT's node-ID-to-content mapping nor its topic-subscription pattern leak validator identity; the paper identifies this as unresolved for both single-seeder and multi-seeder GossipSub-based designs.
- Requires a routing-table refresh policy elsewhere in the system if the accelerated-routing-table alternative (crawling the whole network to skip iterative lookups) is used, because refreshing frequently enough to track churn means crawling the network more often, which the paper states is incompatible with Ethereum's preference for low connection counts to limit bandwidth use.
- Requires the erasure-coding scheme (Reed-Solomon, per the paper) to guarantee reconstruction from any half of a row's or column's extended samples; the DHT-location mechanism only has to deliver enough of those samples, not all of them, which is the precondition making sampling-based (rather than full-retrieval) verification meaningful.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. No other paper in this batch measures the same Kademlia deployment (IPFS) under the same operation; STEINER-CCR-07 and GUMMADI-SIGCOMM-03 examine a different Kademlia deployment (KAD/eMule) and different metrics (attack cost, routing geometry) respectively, not seeding throughput.

### References worth retrieving
- Competing: F. Dabek et al., "Designing a DHT for Low Latency and High Throughput," NSDI (cited as [11]) — a prior DHT-throughput-improvement paper this paper explicitly contrasts its own larger-network results against; tested under 500 nodes.
- Foundational: P. Maymounkov, D. Mazieres, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric," IPTPS 2002 (cited as [28]) — already in this corpus per BRIEF.md section 7.
- Competing: Bernhard Heep, "R/Kademlia: Recursive and topology-aware overlay routing," ATNAC 2010 (cited as [22]) — this is the HEEP-ATNAC-10 key already in this batch; the paper cites it as reducing iterative-lookup overhead relevant to the seeding bottleneck it identifies.
- Competing: Elias Rohrer, Florian Tschorsch, "Kadcast: A Structured Approach to Broadcast in Blockchain Networks," AFT 2019 (cited as [37]) — extends recursive Kademlia for efficient broadcast, cited as a candidate mitigation for the seeding-cost problem.
- Competing: Zoltan Czirkos, Gabor Hosszu, "Solution for the broadcasting in the Kademlia peer-to-peer overlay" (cited as [10]) — same broadcast-extension family as Kadcast.
- Foundational/measurement: Dennis Trautwein et al., "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web," ACM SIGCOMM 2022 (cited as [44]) — the primary IPFS measurement paper this work's live-network validation builds on.
- Attack/critique-adjacent (privacy): "The IPFS DHT Reader Privacy Upgrade" (cited as [41], a design discussion of double-hashing stored records to reduce query exposure) — directly relevant to the validator-anonymity requirement stated above.
- Competing: Alfonso De la Rocha, David Dias, Yiannis Psaras, "Accelerating content routing with bitswap" (cited as [15]) — the BitSwap alternative to DHT-based content routing the paper discusses as an existing IPFS workaround.
- Competing/independent measurement: Dennis Trautwein et al., "IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide" (cited as [45]) — a proposed fix for slow DHT provide operations, the closest published attempt at the same seeding-latency problem this paper measures.
- Foundational: Alexandros G. Dimakis et al., "Network coding for distributed storage systems," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 56(9), 2010 (cited as [17]) — cited as showing erasure coding combined with DHTs reduces bandwidth for retrievability.
- Superseded-by/emerging-alternative: "PeerDAS proposal" (cited as [31]) and "SubnetDAS proposal" (cited as [40]) — both are stated in the paper's own conclusion as emerging designs that avoid the DHT-seeding bottleneck this paper identifies, at the stated cost of either a reduced sample count (PeerDAS) or weakened query unlinkability (SubnetDAS).
