## [COX-SOSP-03] Samsara: Honor Among Thieves in Peer-to-Peer Storage
**Citation:** Landon P. Cox, Brian D. Noble. "Samsara: Honor Among Thieves in Peer-to-Peer Storage." ACM SOSP, 2003. DOI 10.1145/945445.945458.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://courses.cs.duke.edu/fall05/cps296.1/papers/samsara-sosp03.pdf
**Source URL:** https://courses.cs.duke.edu/fall05/cps296.1/papers/samsara-sosp03.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Samsara forces a node that requests storage from a peer to consume no more space than it contributes, without a trusted third party, a currency system, or a certified identity. It converts every asymmetric storage relationship into a symmetric one. When node A stores an object on node B, B must in return hold a claim from A: a placeholder block equal in size to the space B consumed, computed so that A can prove it is physically stored but B never has to store a local copy to verify it. A claim is built from a chain of SHA1 hashes seeded by a secret passphrase P and a private symmetric key K: the storage space is logically filled with hash values h_i = SHA1(P, i), and a claim C_i is the encryption under K of 26 consecutive hash chunks (25 full 20-byte hashes plus the first 12 bytes of the 26th). Because the claim is derived from a keyed hash chain, the claim owner (A) can recompute it on demand without storing it, while the holder (B) can produce it only by actually having reserved the corresponding space. Each side periodically queries the other to confirm the exchanged data or claim is still held: the querying node sends an initial value h0 and a list of n objects to verify, and the responder chains h0 through each object with SHA1 (h1 = SHA1(h0, object1), h2 = SHA1(h1, object2), and so on) and returns only the final hash h_n, so verification costs one hash value in bandwidth regardless of how many objects are checked. A node that fails a query is punished probabilistically rather than immediately: each replica site independently discards the failed node's object with probability p_i, where p_i = (1/(r−i+1))^(r−i+1) for the i-th consecutive failed query and r is the system's normative replication factor, so an honest node with a transient outage loses at most a fraction of its replicas and can rebuild from survivors, while a node that keeps failing queries loses data at a rate that grows super-exponentially with consecutive failures. When local storage runs short, a node reduces its claim-storage overhead by claim forwarding: it replaces the claim it is holding for a downstream peer with a claim it itself is owed from an upstream peer, extending a dependency chain; if a forwarded claim eventually returns to the node that originally issued it, a dependency cycle forms and the claim is removed from the system entirely, restoring space with no loss of enforcement.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Data transfer time, tree load | samsarad outperforms scp for store-data phase; claims storage adds ~10 s | Tree load = 1,676 files, 13 MB total (openssl-0.9.7a source tree); archive load = same data as one 13 MB file; 550 MHz Pentium III Xeon, 256 MB RAM, 10k RPM SCSI Ultra-wide disk (4.7 ms seek, 3.0 ms rotational latency, 41 MB/s peak throughput), switched 100 Mb/s Ethernet; 10 trials per experiment, buffer cache flushed between trials |
| Query compute/verify time | Data-query compute time equals verify time; claims-query compute takes longer than verify (verify is in-memory only) | Same testbed and loads as above, measured after data copied and caches flushed |
| Space overhead at 100% utilization | Claim overhead reduced to <0.02% of global storage, for both collection-based and DHT replication | Simulated 5,000-node network built on SimPastry, replication factor 4, one object per node sized equal to a claim, utilization varied 50%-100% |
| Cycle frequency | Collection-based replication: 86-180 cycles across utilization range; DHT replication: 4-37 cycles | Same 5,000-node simulation; collection-based clusters nearby nodes (more cycles), DHT replicates across random ID-space ranges (fewer cycles) |
| Chain length at 100% utilization | 69% of chains shorter than 4, 79% shorter than 8; one observed chain reached 3,822 nodes out of 5,000 | Same 5,000-node simulation, DHT and collection-based replication compared |
| Object loss vs. chain length cap | At 8% permanent failure rate: 0.13% objects lost with chains capped at 4, 0.30% lost with chains capped at 8. At 16% failure rate: 1.1% lost at cap 4, 3.3% lost at cap 8 | 5,000-node network, DHT replication, unlimited storage capacity, aggressive claims transfer up to the stated forwarding cap, failures modeled as permanent and simultaneous |
| Object loss vs. utilization | At 50% utilization, conservative claim transfer: 0.28% of objects lost even at 16% permanent simultaneous node failure | Same 5,000-node DHT simulation; conservative vs. aggressive claims-transfer policy compared at 50% and 80% utilization across failure rates 1%-16% |

### Parameters
- Claim size: 4,096 bytes (implementation default).
- Replication factor r: 4 in the simulation study; r=5 used in the worked probability examples in the design section.
- Discard probability for the i-th consecutive failed query: p_i = (1/(r−i+1))^(r−i+1); tested against r = 5, 6, 7, 10 in the analytic figure.
- Pastiche node's assumed object population for the worked examples: 2,000,000 objects, about 32 GB of state.
- Query response hash: SHA1, 20-byte hash chunks.
- Symmetric encryption key K and passphrase P: node-local secrets, sizes unspecified beyond hash-chunk boundaries.
- Storage utilization tested: 50%, 57%, 67%, 80%, 100% (space-overhead and chain-length experiments); 50% and 80% (reliability-vs-utilization experiment).
- Permanent node failure rate tested: 1%, 2%, 4%, 8%, 16%.
- Chain-forwarding caps tested in the reliability-vs-chain-length experiment: 1, 2, 4, 8, unlimited.

### Stated limitations
The authors state Samsara targets greedy users, not arbitrarily malicious ones, and does not stop a node that promises to store data and then immediately discards it, nor prevent a node from refusing service once it detects a restore is in progress. Samsara enforces that consumption is matched by an equal claim but does not force a node to ever accept storage requests from others: if every node refuses to store anything but the claims it receives, no data is ever stored anywhere. The claim-and-query mechanism is stated to apply only to non-renewable resources such as storage and memory; the authors say they cannot see how to build an equivalent placeholder for a renewable resource such as bandwidth or processor cycles, because monitoring the resource's use would itself consume it. Forwarding weakens reliability for as long as a chain stays open, and the authors state it is unclear how to induce claim cycles (which restore reliability) without either constraining replica-site choice or first creating a chain; they list this as an open direction. The reliability simulations are stated to be pessimistic because they model every failure as permanent, whereas the cited failure-rate study found permanent failures far less frequent than transient ones. The implementation's free-space lists are described as linearly searched and single-level, with no fragmentation handling or placement optimization, and all stores are whole-object grained rather than claim-block grained.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Samsara requires that objects are replicated across multiple independent sites so that a probabilistic per-replica discard on a failed query does not destroy the only copy of an object; the punishment mechanism assumes replication is already the availability strategy, not an add-on. It requires periodic bidirectional querying between every pair of nodes in a storage relationship (the querying schedule in the paper's worked example runs daily for the first three days, then weekly), so it needs a live channel between peers and a component that keeps track of who currently holds a claim for whom (Samsara's location, storage, and replica lists). It assumes an underlying storage-placement layer (in the paper, Pastiche over Pastry) decides where replicas go; Samsara sits below that layer and does not perform lookup or routing itself, so it requires the calling storage system to supply replica-site selection. It assumes each node behaves honestly toward its own interest in retaining its own data — a node forwarding a claim remains liable for it, so correctness of the incentive depends on the assumption that a node protects its own stored objects by punishing failures on claims it is holding, not on any external auditor. It does not require certified identity or a public-key infrastructure for its core exchange, but its Sybil-attack resistance argument (an alias gains no advantage from a forwarded claim because it must still produce the claim on demand) depends on the object-storage mechanism, not the identity layer, carrying that guarantee.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper's own related-work section distinguishes its no-identity, no-payment, no-symmetry design from CFS, PAST, Cooper's data trading, Ngan's audit-based accounting, Fileteller's micropayments, and SHARP, each of which requires certified identity, symmetric placement, or a trusted clearance/authentication step Samsara does not need; these are the authors' own comparisons, not measurement disagreements.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: L. P. Cox, C. D. Murray, B. D. Noble. "Pastiche: Making backup cheap and easy." OSDI, 2002, pp. 285-298. (Samsara is built as a storage layer beneath this system.)
- **Foundational**: A. Rowstron, P. Druschel. "Pastry: Scalable, distributed object location and routing for large-scale peer-to-peer systems." Middleware, 2001, pp. 329-350.
- **Competing**: F. Dabek, M. F. Kaashoek, D. Karger, R. Morris, I. Stoica. "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS." SOSP, 2001, pp. 202-215. (Quota enforcement via IP-address identification, no contribution-proportional quota.)
- **Competing**: A. Rowstron, P. Druschel. "Storage management and caching in PAST, a large-scale, persistent peer-to-peer storage utility." SOSP, 2001, pp. 188-201. (Smartcard-issued, trusted-third-party quota enforcement.)
- **Competing**: M. Lillibridge, S. Elnikety, A. Birrell, M. Burrows, M. Isard. "A cooperative Internet backup scheme." USENIX ATC, 2003, pp. 29-42. (Source of the grace-period attack Samsara's probabilistic discard is designed to defeat; requires symmetric storage.)
- **Competing**: J. Ioannidis, S. Ioannidis, A. D. Keromytis, V. Prevelakis. "Fileteller: Paying and getting paid for file storage." Financial Cryptography, 2002, pp. 282-299. (Micropayment-based accounting, requires a third party to provision and clear payments plus secure identities.)
- **Competing**: B. F. Cooper, H. Garcia-Molina. "Peer-to-peer resource trading in a reliable distributed system." IPTPS, 2002, pp. 319-327. (Data trading of equal amounts, requires symmetric storage relationships.)

(Distributed accounting via random audits; requires certified identities and detects inflated capacity claims only near full utilization, unlike Samsara's per-exchange detection.)
- **Competing**: Y. Fu, J. Chase, B. Chun, S. Schwab, A. Vahdat. "SHARP: An architecture for secure resource peering." SOSP, 2003. (No global certified identity, like Samsara, but requires offline pairwise authentication and allows asymmetric exchange with non-local punishment.)
- **Attack**: J. R. Douceur. "The Sybil attack." IPTPS, 2002, pp. 251-260. (Samsara's claim-forwarding argument is checked against this attack directly in the text.)

- **Foundational**: W. J. Bolosky, J. R. Douceur, D. Ely, M. Theimer. "Feasibility of a serverless distributed file system deployed on an existing set of desktop PCs." SIGMETRICS, 2000, pp. 34-43. (Source of the transient-vs-permanent failure-rate claim the reliability simulation relies on.)

## [CRITES-CCS-25] SyRA: Sybil-Resilient Anonymous Signatures with Applications to Decentralized Identity
**Citation:** Elizabeth Crites, Aggelos Kiayias, Markulf Kohlweiss, Amirreza Sarencheh. "SyRA: Sybil-Resilient Anonymous Signatures with Applications to Decentralized Identity." ACM CCS, 2025. DOI 10.1145/3719027.3744806.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/379.pdf (IACR ePrint 2024/379, pre-publication text of the CCS 2025 paper)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/379
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SyRA (Sybil-Resilient Anonymous signatures) lets a user sign messages under a context-specific pseudonym so that two signatures from the same user in the same context are linkable to each other, while signatures from the same user across different contexts reveal nothing that connects them, and each real-world identity can obtain at most one working key. The construction, SASSI (SyRA via Stateless Issuing), realizes this without any issuer having to retain a per-user record after issuance.

A set of n issuers jointly holds shares of one secret key isk. A user proves possession of a real-world identity string s to a threshold t of the n issuers, using an abstract personhood relation the paper leaves unspecified so the construction stays compatible with different real-world identity checks (a signed government certificate, a biometric reading, or an OAuth identity token are all named as possible instantiations). The t issuers then jointly compute, via a distributed verifiable random function (VRF, a function whose output is indistinguishable from random but comes with a proof that it was computed correctly from a hidden key), a pair of values deterministically derived from s and isk: (g^(1/(s+isk)), ĝ^(1/(s+isk))). This pair is the user's secret key. Because the pair is a deterministic function of s and isk, an issuer needs to store nothing after issuance to prevent a repeat issuance from producing a different key — recomputing the function on the same s always yields the same key, so a second issuance attempt on the same identity string yields no new capability. The user then signs a message for a context ctx by evaluating a second VRF using their secret key, producing a pseudonym T = e(h(ctx), û) via a bilinear pairing, and proves in zero knowledge that T was computed correctly. Because T is deterministic in (s, ctx), two signatures under the same identity and context always carry the same T, giving intra-context linkability, while T under two different contexts is pseudorandom and unlinkable to any adversary who does not hold s. The two VRF layers use asymmetric (Type-III) bilinear pairing groups; the paper extends the Dodis-Yampolskiy VRF construction to asymmetric groups to support this.

### Measured results
Performance was measured on one machine: a MacBook Pro with an M3 Max processor, 16-core CPU, 48 GB RAM, macOS 15.1, implementation in Rust 1.83, using the BLS12-381 elliptic curve. Reported figures are median times over 10 iterations per configuration.

| Metric | Value | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Signature generation time | 10.42 ms | includes context switching |
| Signature verification time | 11.24 ms | — |
| Signature size | 5.703 KB | — |
| Share aggregation by user (threshold issuance) | 1.08–1.29 ms | rises with issuer-set size, from 5–10 issuers (t=5, n=10) to 150–300 issuers (t=150, n=300) |
| Threshold issuance protocol time among issuers | 0.0651 s to 72.6 s | same six configurations: (t,n) = (5,10), (15,30), (30,60), (50,100), (70,140), (150,300); threshold t fixed at n/2 |

Issuance time rises from 0.0651 s at (t=5, n=10) to 72.6 s at (t=150, n=300); share-aggregation time rises far more slowly, from 1.08 ms to 1.29 ms over the same range. The threshold issuance evaluation assumed an honest-majority adversary corrupting at most t_c = n/2 − 1 participants.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Issuance threshold t | n/2 | fixed ratio across all six configurations tested |
| Total issuers n | 10 to 300 | six point values: 10, 30, 60, 100, 140, 300 |
| Adversary corruption bound (issuance evaluation) | n/2 − 1 | honest-majority assumption, not varied |
| Elliptic curve | BLS12-381 | not varied |

### Stated limitations
The authors state, as an explicit assumption in a footnote, that SyRA with a single centralized malicious issuer cannot provide privacy, because that issuer could impersonate any user with identity s and trace their signatures — privacy holds only when at least t of the n issuers behave honestly. They leave as an open question whether a construction relying solely on symmetric pairings (avoiding the asymmetric-group requirement) is achievable, noting that both symmetric pairing groups and DLIN-based encryption available as one such alternative reduce performance. Adaptive corruption of issuers is left for future work, and the leak-signatures adversarial interface's information exposure under adaptive corruption is stated as an open question, including whether key-evolving VRFs could reduce it. Comprehensive credential revocation is stated to be out of scope; the paper sketches an initial mechanism (publishing one group element û per revoked identity) but states this mechanism does not provide forward security in a non-interactive manner, because revealing û retroactively links all of that user's past pseudonyms. Extending SyRA to attribute-based credentials with better efficiency than the composition approach given (running SyRA and a separate attribute-based credential scheme side by side) is left for future work. The paper does not evaluate the personhood-relation-checking step itself (verifying a government certificate, biometric reading, or OAuth token) — the performance numbers cover only the cryptographic issuance and signing steps once a valid witness for the personhood relation is already available.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
SyRA requires an external mechanism supplying the personhood relation R_s — a way to verify that a claimed real-world identity string s is genuinely tied to one physical person and not previously used. The paper explicitly does not build this: it lists a signed government certificate (e.g., an X.509 attribute certificate over a national ID), a biometric reading (citing Worldcoin), or an OAuth/OpenID identity token (citing zkLogin) as possible instantiations, but the security of Sybil resistance is only as strong as whichever personhood check is plugged in. SyRA requires a set of n issuers of which at least a threshold t (t = n/2 in the evaluated configurations) act honestly; if fewer than t issuers are honest, both privacy and, per the ideal-functionality definition, Sybil resistance guarantees fail. The construction requires no communication channel from the issuers to a persistent state store — issuers hold only their long-term VRF key share and need not retain any per-user record — but each issuance protocol run does require the participating threshold of issuers to be online simultaneously to jointly compute the distributed VRF, using oblivious-transfer-based multiparty multiplication. Verification of a SyRA signature requires the verifying party to already hold the correct issuer verification key ivk for the session; the paper states it does not assume a public-key infrastructure for issuer verification keys or authenticated channels between verifiers and issuers, so a verifier using an incorrect ivk receives no guarantee from the construction. Detecting repeated signatures under the same identity and context requires a verifier to maintain a local key-value store mapping observed pseudonyms T to contexts.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. On the specific point the target record flagged for verification — whether the issuer is a genuinely new trusted party rather than a removed one — the paper does not claim to eliminate the trust requirement; it claims only to remove the requirement that issuers retain state, while still requiring a threshold t of n issuers to be honest for both privacy and Sybil resistance to hold. This is a narrower claim than "no trusted party" and should not be represented as the latter.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: A. Maram et al., "CanDID: Can-Do Decentralized Identity with Legacy Compatibility" — the paper states CanDID is the only prior attempt at the same issuer-state problem, using a shared PRF evaluation obfuscation, but requires each issuer to hold state linear in the number of credentials
- competing: F. Baldimtsi, K. K. Chalkias, Y. Ji, J. Wang et al., "zkLogin: Privacy-Preserving Blockchain Authentication with Existing Credentials" — paper states zkLogin does not provide Sybil resistance in either of its two operating modes
- competing: J. Park et al. (2023), "ZK Address Abstraction" — paper states this scheme also does not address Sybil resistance
- foundational: Y. Dodis, A. Yampolskiy (2005), the Dodis-Yampolskiy verifiable random function, extended here to asymmetric (Type-III) bilinear groups
- foundational: C. Gurkan et al. (2021), verifiable unpredictable function (VUF) construction the second VRF layer is inspired by
- competing: A. Sonnino, M. Al-Bassam, S. Bano, S. Meiklejohn, G. Danezis (2019), "Coconut: Threshold Issuance Selective Disclosure Credentials" — paper states Coconut does not provide guarantees the construction here does
- competing: J. Doerner et al. (2023), Threshold BBS+ signatures for distributed anonymous credentials
- foundational: R. Zhang et al. (2020), DECO, a three-party protocol (prover, verifier, TLS server) used here as one candidate mechanism to realize the personhood relation from legacy web services
- competing/attack: Worldcoin whitepaper (2023) — biometric (iris) personhood instantiation, cited as an alternative to certificate- or OAuth-based personhood

### Verbatim extracts
"failure to do so would permit a trivial attack against Sybil resilience" — on why issuers historically needed a persistent identity-to-credential mapping.
"our issuers can be stateless" — the construction's core claim.
"zkLogin ... does not provide Sybil resilience" — explicit statement about a competing system.
"privacy, since in that case, the issuer could always impersonate a real-world user" — the centralized-malicious-issuer limitation.
"Revocation ... is out of scope of this paper and an interesting direction for future work."
"this will not provide forward security, at least in a non-interactive manner" — on the sketched revocation mechanism's limitation.

## [DAVIDSON-POPETS-18] Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
**Citation:** Alex Davidson, Ian Goldberg, Nick Sullivan, George Tankersley, Filippo Valsorda. "Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2018 (3):164-180. DOI 10.1515/popets-2018-0026.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://petsymposium.org/popets/2018/popets-2018-0026.pdf
**Source URL:** https://petsymposium.org/popets/2018/popets-2018-0026.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Privacy Pass lets a client redeem one unlinkable anonymous token per rate-limited action, obtained in a batch of N tokens after passing a single challenge (a CAPTCHA in the deployed case), so a server can rate-limit or gate repeated access without learning which of the client's earlier challenge-passes any later redemption corresponds to. The mechanism is a verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function (VOPRF): an oblivious PRF is a two-party protocol letting a client obtain F_k(x) for a server-held key k without revealing x to the server, and "verifiable" means the client also gets a proof that the server used the same key k it committed to. The client generates N random token values t_1...t_N, computes T_i = H1(t_i) for a hash-to-curve function H1, blinds each with a random exponent r_i to get a blinded token, and sends the batch to the server together with proof of having passed the challenge. The server signs each blinded token under its own private key and produces one non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (a batched discrete-log-equality, or DLEQ, proof) that every signature in the batch used the same private key, rather than one DLEQ proof per token; the client verifies this single batched proof and unblinds each signed token to recover N usable (t_i, W_i) pairs, where W_i = the PRF evaluation F_k(t_i). To redeem a token later, the client presents an unspent pair (t, W) together with a MAC computed over request-binding data R using a key derived from W; the server recomputes F_k(t) from its own key, checks that t has not been redeemed before, and verifies the MAC to confirm the client actually holds a validly signed token, without either side ever having linked this redemption to the earlier signing session that produced it. This unlinkability follows from the OPRF's message-hiding property (the server never saw t or T_i unblinded during signing) plus the one-more-token security property, which the paper proves under a standard hardness assumption and which guarantees a client holding l signed tokens cannot construct l+1 valid ones. Key rotation invalidates old tokens: the server periodically retires old signing keys and clients must obtain fresh tokens under a key still on the server's accepted-key list, which the paper recommends keeping to about 2-3 concurrently accepted keys to limit how far the user base is split across key-specific anonymity sets.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Cryptographic microbenchmarks, NIST P-256 elliptic curve, JavaScript client / Go server implementation, N tokens per batch swept at N = 5, 10, 15, ..., 100, 100 repeated trials per N | Client: token generation (GenToken + Blind) = 120 + 64N ms; DLEQ verification = 220 + 110N ms; total signing request = 340 + 180N ms; total redemption request = 57 ms (constant, independent of N). Server: signing = 0.04 + 0.20N ms; DLEQ proof generation = 0.32 + 0.55N ms; total signing = 1.48 + 0.87N ms; total redemption = 0.8 ms (constant) |
| Message size overhead, same benchmark setup, N tokens per batch | Signing request (client to edge): 57 + 63N bytes; signing response (edge to client): 295 + 121N bytes (about double the request size because the JavaScript client compresses elliptic-curve points but the Go server does not, to avoid making the client perform expensive point decompression); redemption request: 396 bytes (constant); for N = 30, total additional communication load stated as under 6 KB |
| Cloudflare production deployment, browser extension released 8 November 2017, figures averaged over a 7-day window ending 28 November 2017 (20 days after release) | Chrome users: 8,499; Firefox users: 3,489 (excludes manually-installed copies). Cloudflare accepted 1.6 trillion requests per week on average, of which 780 billion came over the Tor network. 1.04% of all requests globally were served a CAPTCHA challenge, versus 17% of Tor-network traffic — stated by the authors as evidence of disproportionate challenge exposure for Tor users |
| Same deployment window, redemption-phase operating load | Redemption phases peaked at 2,000 per second globally and 200 per second for Tor users; 515 million requests globally contained a Privacy-Pass clearance cookie, of which 34.5 million (22.58% of Tor-originated requests) came from the Tor network |
| Same deployment window, median request/response sizes | Tor-user request/response sizes: 700-800 bytes / 5-6 KB; median CAPTCHA submission and response sizes: under 1 KB — the paper notes these figures differ slightly from the controlled benchmarks above because they include Cloudflare-specific data not modeled in the benchmark harness |
| Token-batch size deployed in production vs. server-supported maximum | Cloudflare issues N = 30 tokens per solved challenge in the initial deployment, chosen as a balance of usability, performance, and token-hoarding risk, though the server supports up to N = 100; the paper states this upper bound of 100 means accumulating 1,000,000 tokens for a denial-of-service stockpile would require a minimum of 10,000 CAPTCHA solutions |

### Parameters
- Elliptic curve: NIST P-256.
- Token batch size N: benchmarked at N = 5, 10, 15, ..., 100 in 5-token increments; deployed value N = 30; server-enforced maximum N = 100.
- Key rotation interval: the paper recommends short rotation periods "such as 3-4 days" to bound how long a stockpiled token batch of signed tokens remains redeemable.
- Number of concurrently accepted signing keys: recommended at 2-3, to limit the degree to which multiple active keys split the anonymity set of token holders into smaller, more identifiable groups.
- Threat/security model: security proofs are given in the random oracle model, and one-more-token security is stated to follow from "a standard assumption" without the paper stating that assumption's name at the point cited in the main text (developed in the paper's Section 5.4.3 proof).

### Stated limitations
The paper states its protocol does not defend against a monster-in-the-middle (MitM) adversary during the signing phase: because tokens carry no client-binding metadata (by design, to avoid deanonymization via that metadata), a MitM that intercepts a client's completed-challenge signing request can substitute its own blinded tokens and receive signed tokens without having solved the challenge itself; the paper's stated mitigation is only that this requires a renewable source of challenge solutions to exploit repeatedly, not a cryptographic fix. Token accumulation ("farming") is stated as a residual risk enabling stockpiling for a denial-of-service attack; the paper's countermeasures are operational limits (the 100-token signing cap, and key rotation on the order of days) rather than a protocol-level prevention. Token exhaustion is stated as possible: an embedded sub-resource that repeatedly triggers redemption can drain a client's stored tokens; the paper's mitigation (rate-limiting redemptions per URL, tracked client-side) is described as reducing rather than eliminating the attack, and a stronger fix (blacklisting URLs after one redemption attempt) is stated as "not implemented at time of writing." The paper states a structural anonymity limit shared with all such registration-based systems: early-adopter clients belong to a small anonymity set, and a server that signs tokens for very few clients (or immediately after a key rotation) can narrow a later redemption to one of a small number of possible signers; the paper states this makes the scheme, like Tor itself, "only really effective when the number of users is quite large." The paper explicitly states its threat model does not defend against a verifier (the edge/CDN) colluding with the token issuer to break unlinkability, nor against a client that shares its tokens with other parties — both are named directly by the target registry's citation as out of scope, and correspondingly this paper's security proofs (Section 5, unlinkability and one-more-token security) are stated relative to an honest-but-possibly-curious single verifier-issuer, not a colluding pair. Double-spending protection is stated to require each service to implement its own redemption-index check (a hash table or Bloom filter over spent tokens); the paper does not measure the storage or lookup cost of this index at Cloudflare's request volume, only recommends it be present.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The protocol requires the server to run and maintain a signing key, publish a small, low-churn list of currently accepted verification commitments (2-3 keys recommended) so clients whose tokens were signed under a recently-rotated-out key can still redeem before those tokens expire, and requires some out-of-band or globally-consistent channel for distributing key-rotation updates; the paper suggests "beacons or other globally visible and consistent locations, such as the Tor consensus" for this, but states the initial deployment instead updates commitments directly inside the browser extension. It requires the calling application (the "challenge" the client must first pass) to supply the actual work-based anonymity guarantee: Privacy Pass tokens are only as scarce as the challenges that produce them, so the mechanism composes with any challenge type (the paper's deployment uses a CAPTCHA) but supplies no scarcity of its own. It requires the redeeming server to maintain a double-spend index across every previously redeemed token value t, and the paper states each service's own redemption index must be separate from every other service's, since services must "use their own private keys for signing tokens so that tokens cannot be spent multiple times across different services." It requires the client to be able to store unspent token pairs locally between the signing and redemption phases (the browser extension's local storage in the deployed case) and to track, per domain, whether a token has already been spent, since the paper's own mitigation for the token-exhaustion attack depends on this per-domain spend tracking being available and enforced client-side.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Jarecki, S., Kiayias, A., Krawczyk, H., "Round-optimal password-protected secret sharing and T-PAKE in the password-only model." — foundational (originates the oblivious PRF and DLEQ-proof-based verifiable OPRF construction this paper adapts directly, including the batched DLEQ-proof extension)
- Henry, R., Goldberg, I., "Formalizing anonymous blacklisting systems." — competing (formalizes multiple anonymous blacklisting/whitelisting approaches for the same Tor-CAPTCHA-denial problem, including blind-RSA-based designs and "Nymble-like" trusted-third-party designs the paper explicitly declines to adopt because they require an extra trusted party)
- Henry, R., Goldberg, I., "Batch proofs of partial knowledge." — foundational (source of the batching technique the paper's batched DLEQ proof adapts, cited as showing batch verification is possible for this proof family)
- Liu, Z., Liu, Y., Winter, P., Mittal, P., et al., "TorPolice: ..." — competing (a privacy-preserving access-control mechanism for Tor-originated connections, contrasted as narrower in scope than this paper's general browser-based solution)
- Lofgren, P., Hopper, N., "BNymble: More anonymous..." — competing (a Nymble-family anonymous-blacklisting system using a trusted third party, part of the design space the paper positions itself against)
- Chaum, D., "Blind signatures for untraceable payments." — foundational (originates the blind-signature primitive the paper's VOPRF-based token scheme is compared against as a heavier-weight alternative construction)
- Papadopoulos, D., Wessels, D., Huque, S., et al., "..." (elliptic curve verifiable random functions) — foundational (cited as closely related work in constructing elliptic-curve verifiable random functions, informing the paper's own VOPRF construction choices)

### Verbatim extracts
- "does not add any significant overheads to either the client or server"
- "1.04% were challenged in general globally, though 17% of Tor traffic is challenged"
- "such privacy solutions are only really effective when the number of users is quite large"
- "1, 000, 000 tokens would require minimum 10, 000 CAPTCHA solutions"

## [DAVIDSON-POPETS-23] FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
**Citation:** Alex Davidson, Goncalo Pestana, Sofia Celi. "FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval." Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs), 2023. DOI 10.56553/POPETS-2023-0022.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/981.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/981.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
FrodoPIR lets a client download one item from a server-held database, at a server-chosen index, without revealing to the server which index the client read. The server cannot distinguish a query for index i from a query for any other index. The construction splits into an offline phase and an online phase. In the offline phase the server derives a pseudorandom Learning-With-Errors (LWE) matrix A (dimension n times m, from a lambda-bit seed) and multiplies it by the database (arranged as an m by omega matrix D) to produce a public parameter matrix M = A times D; the client independently derives the same A from the published seed and, per future query, samples a secret vector and computes preprocessed values that do not depend on which index will later be queried. Because this preprocessing is client-independent (the server does the same work once no matter how many clients query later) and query-independent (the client does the same work once no matter which index it will later query), a single offline computation amortizes across every client and every query. In the online phase the client picks the actual query index, adds a small correction to one entry of its preprocessed vector, and sends the modified vector; the server computes one vector-matrix multiplication against its database and returns the result; the client subtracts its own secret to recover the requested item. Security rests on the Matrix-LWE assumption: an adversary given the query vector cannot distinguish which index was targeted.

### Measured results
All computation measured single-threaded on an Amazon EC2 t2.2xlarge (8 CPU cores, 32 GB RAM), except Table 7 which uses a c5n.2xlarge to match a comparison paper's hardware. Database elements are 1 KB (w = 2^13 bits) unless stated otherwise. Security parameter n = 1774 (conservative setting for 2^52 client queries at 128-bit security) unless stated otherwise.

Non-amortized performance by database size (Table 6, 1 KB elements, single client, single server, lattice dimension n = 1774):

| log2(m) items | Client download, offline (KB) | DB preprocessing (s) | Client query (KB, online) | Server response (KB, online) | Server response time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 5682 | 104.6 | 256 | 3.203 | 45.0 |
| 17 | 5682 | 206.3 | 512 | 3.203 | 94.5 |
| 18 | 5682 | 429.1 | 1024 | 3.203 | 188.4 |
| 19 | 6313 | 936.4 | 2048 | 3.556 | 417.9 |
| 20 | 6313 | 1895.2 | 4096 | 3.556 | 825.4 |

Server response size grows less than 3.6 times the original 1 KB element across all measured database sizes, versus 128 times for SOnionPIR and 320 times for PSIR at the same 2^20-element database size, comparison run on the same t2.2xlarge hardware with each client making 500 queries.

Financial cost, at $0.09 per GB of server-to-client transfer and $0.0464 per CPU hour (AWS on-demand pricing, August 2022): offline database preprocessing for a 2^20-element database costs slightly above 1 US cent (a one-time, globally amortizable cost); the online per-query cost is about 0.001 cent at the largest measured database size.

Comparison against Spiral (Menon and Wu) on a shared c5n.2xlarge instance, single-threaded, at three database shapes (Table 7):

| Database shape | Metric | Spiral | FrodoPIR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Query size | 14 KB | 4 MB |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Response size | 20 KB | 912 B |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Server computation time | 1.37 s | 0.16 s |
| 2^20 items x 256 B | Throughput | 196 MB/s | 1.56 GB/s |
| 2^18 items x 30 KB (FrodoPIR extrapolated from 2^16 items for memory reasons) | Server computation time | 17.69 s | 4.27 s |
| 2^18 items x 30 KB | Throughput | 434 MB/s | 1.76 GB/s |
| 2^14 items x 100 KB | Server computation time | 4.58 s | 0.89 s |
| 2^14 items x 100 KB | Throughput | 358 MB/s | 1.76 GB/s |

FrodoPIR wins on computation throughput at every measured shape; Spiral wins on response-size-to-element ratio and bandwidth when elements are large (30 KB or 100 KB).

Reducing the LWE dimension n from 1774 to 1572 or 1288 (Table 10, log2(m) = 16 and 20, same t2.2xlarge hardware): bandwidth (client download) falls by more than 11% at n = 1572 and by 27% at n = 1288, relative to n = 1774, at both database sizes; client derivation of the matrix A falls by about 20% at the smaller dimensions.

Applied worked example, Google SafeBrowsing-style URL blocklist checking, using a single 2^18-element, 1 KB-element database shard with the parameters of Table 5 at m = 2^18, on the same t2.2xlarge instance (Table 8): offline client download 180 KB, database preprocessing 28.6 s, online client query 1024 KB, online server response 0.1 KB, online server response time 5.223 ms.

Comparison against the two-server PIR constructions of Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs (dpfPIR, ooPIR) and against the non-private baseline, all scaled to 1 billion users, using each scheme's stated per-query latency to derive server counts (Table 9):

| Indicator | Non-private | dpfPIR (2-server) | ooPIR (2-server) | FrodoPIR (1-server, estimated) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Servers needed for 1B users | 143 | 9047 | 1348 | 9778 |
| Latency (ms) | 90 | 122 | 91 | 90 |
| Client running time (s/month) | 0.5 | 0.8 | 8.0 | 1272.0 |
| Online communication (MB/month) | 3.0 | 3.6 | 9.0 | 539.7 |
| Max client storage (MB) | 4.5 | 4.5 | 26.1 | 30.69 |

FrodoPIR's server count and per-client monthly bandwidth are both worse than the two-server schemes in this specific comparison; the paper attributes this to the SafeBrowsing usage pattern (many small, frequent queries against a large database) rather than to a general FrodoPIR weakness, and states this comparison, unlike Table 7, is not a favorable case for FrodoPIR's design.

### Parameters
- LWE modulus q = 2^32 (fixed across all reported parameter sets, chosen to match 32-bit unsigned integer arithmetic).
- LWE dimension n: 1774 used as the primary conservative setting (128-bit security for up to 2^52 client queries); 1572 and 1288 tested as less conservative alternatives (Table 10) trading security margin for bandwidth.
- Plaintext modulus rho: 2^10 for database sizes m <= 2^18, 2^9 for m > 2^18 (Table 5).
- Number of tolerated queries before matrix A must be re-derived, l (script-l): 2^52 in the primary parameter sets.
- Error distribution chi: uniform ternary.
- Element size w: 1 KB (2^13 bits) in the main experiments (Section 6); 256 B, 30 KB, and 100 KB tested in the Spiral comparison (Table 7).
- Per-client number of preprocessed queries c: 500, fixed across the amortization comparisons with SOnionPIR and PSIR.
- Improvement factor kappa = (log(rho) times m) / (n times log(q)): reported as 13.0 to 187.6 across the five parameter rows of Table 5, rising with m.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the main limitation of FrodoPIR is that online client query size grows linearly in the database size m, unlike SOnionPIR and PSIR whose online query sizes grow more slowly; at m = 2^20, the client query reaches 4 MB. A second stated limitation is that the server's transformed database representation is roughly 3 times the size of the original database. The paper states this can be mitigated (query size, not the 3x storage factor) by sharding the database into s parallel instances, at the cost of a client download that grows by a factor of s and a public-parameter download per shard. The paper states it does not provide a fully optimized implementation: it explicitly excludes computational optimizations such as sub-cubic matrix multiplication and query batching, leaving them as unexplored future work. The paper states it does not evaluate the "DoublePIR" optimization of concurrent work (Henzinger et al.) applied to FrodoPIR, though it states the underlying observation should apply. The paper states its security analysis assumes a semi-honest (not malicious) server, and that no attack against the specific Matrix-LWE variant used is currently known, but does not prove none exists.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The client must know, before the online phase, the specific numeric index it wants to query; the paper states elsewhere (Section 7, referring to Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs) that mapping a real-world key (such as a URL hash) to that index requires a separate mechanism the client downloads out of band, distinct from the FrodoPIR protocol proper. The scheme requires an offline phase before any query: the client must download the server's public parameters (the seed and matrix M) before making its first query, so a client cannot query cold. Database updates require the server to redistribute updated public parameters for whichever shard changed, and require every client to re-run preprocessing for that shard before it can query updated data; this couples update frequency to client-side computational and bandwidth allowance. The security guarantee (128-bit, against up to 2^52 or 2^32 queries depending on chosen n) decays as the server answers more queries against the same matrix A, and the server must eventually resample A to reset the guarantee; the paper assumes, under its semi-honest model, that the server does this resampling honestly. The scheme provides no defense if multiple non-colluding servers are required elsewhere in a design: it is explicitly single-server, so a system relying on FrodoPIR cannot also assume the multi-server non-collusion property that dpfPIR and ooPIR rely on.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at time of writing. The paper's own Table 9 comparison contradicts an unqualified claim that FrodoPIR is cheaper than multi-server PIR in general: for the SafeBrowsing workload specifically, FrodoPIR uses more servers, more client compute time per month, and more monthly bandwidth than the two-server dpfPIR and ooPIR schemes of Kogan and Corrigan-Gibbs. The general throughput and financial-cost advantage claimed in Sections 6.1-6.2 holds against single-server stateful competitors (SOnionPIR, PSIR) under the amortized multi-client comparisons, not against multi-server schemes.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: A. Henzinger, M. M. Hong, H. Corrigan-Gibbs, S. Meiklejohn, V. Vaikuntanathan. "One server for the price of two: Simple and fast single-server private information retrieval" (SimplePIR/DoublePIR), Cryptology ePrint 2022/949 — concurrent work using the same LWE mechanism; not yet in this corpus.
- competing: M. H. Mughees, H. Chen, L. Ren. "OnionPIR: Response efficient single-server PIR" — this is the SOnionPIR baseline compared against in Figures 6-7.
- competing: S. Patel, G. Persiano, K. Yeo. "Private stateful information retrieval" (PSIR) — the second single-server baseline compared against.
- competing: S. J. Menon, D. J. Wu. "SPIRAL: fast, high-rate single-server PIR via FHE" — the Table 7 comparison target for large database elements.
- competing: H. Corrigan-Gibbs, A. Henzinger, D. Kogan. "Single-server private information retrieval with sublinear amortized time" (CHKPIR), EUROCRYPT 2022 — the sublinear-online-time comparison in Section 6.2.
- competing: D. Kogan, H. Corrigan-Gibbs. Two-server PIR constructions (dpfPIR, ooPIR) for SafeBrowsing, cited as [54] — source of the Table 9 comparison numbers and the usage-model assumptions (query rate, update rate) FrodoPIR's SafeBrowsing example reuses.
- foundational: E. Boyle, N. Gilboa, Y. Ishai. "Function secret sharing: Improvements and extensions" — underlies distributed-point-function PIR-by-keyword approaches discussed as an alternative to FrodoPIR's index-based model.
- attack: M. R. Albrecht, R. Player, S. Scott. "On the concrete hardness of learning with errors" — the lattice-hardness estimator FrodoPIR's security parameters are derived from.

- "the server response size compared with the original 1KB data element" grows "< 3.6× overhead."
- "SOnionPIR (128×) and PSIR (320×)" response-size overhead at the same database size.
- "Clearly, FrodoPIR involves heavier usage costs compared to all known solutions" (SafeBrowsing comparison).

## [DUCAS-TCHES-18] CRYSTALS-Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme

**Citation:** Léo Ducas, Eike Kiltz, Tancrède Lepoint, Vadim Lyubashevsky, Peter Schwabe, Gregor Seiler, Damien Stehlé. "CRYSTALS-Dilithium: A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme." IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (TCHES) 2018(1), 238-268. DOI: 10.13154/TCHES.V2018.I1.238-268.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/633.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/633.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Dilithium is a digital signature scheme (a mechanism letting a holder of a private key produce, for any message, a value that anyone holding the matching public key can check was produced by that key) whose unforgeability rests on the hardness of two lattice problems, Module Learning With Errors (MLWE, a generalization of the Learning With Errors problem to structured polynomial-ring modules) and Module Short Integer Solution (MSIS). It differs from earlier compact lattice signature schemes (NTRU-GPV, BLISS) by avoiding discrete Gaussian sampling entirely: those schemes draw secret randomness from a discrete Gaussian distribution during signing, and the paper cites three separate side-channel results ([BHLY16], [EFGT17], [PBY17]) showing that securely implementing that sampling step in constant time is error-prone in practice. Dilithium replaces Gaussian sampling with rejection sampling over uniform distributions, which the paper states is "easily implementable in constant-time" — an implementation where the sequence of operations executed does not depend on secret data, closing the timing side channel.

The scheme follows the "Fiat-Shamir with Aborts" paradigm (originating in Lyubashevsky's 2009 scheme). Key generation produces a public matrix A and a public value t = As1 + s2, where s1 and s2 are small-coefficient secret vectors; the public key stores only the high-order bits of t (dropping the low d=14 bits per coefficient), shrinking the public key. To sign a message M, the signer samples a masking vector y, computes w1 as the high-order bits of Ay, derives a challenge c = H(M || w1) via a hash function modeled as a random oracle, computes a candidate response z = y + c·s1, and restarts the entire signing attempt (rejection sampling) whenever z or a related bound exceeds fixed thresholds (γ1, γ2, β) — a step that leaks no information about the secret because an accepted z's distribution is independent of s1, at the cost of a variable number of signing attempts per message signed. Because the public key withholds the low bits of t, the verifier cannot recompute w1 exactly from a candidate signature (z, c) alone; the signer therefore transmits a small "hint" — the positions where dropped low-order bits of c·t0 would have caused a carry into the high-order bits — as extra signature bytes, letting the verifier reconstruct the needed high bits without full knowledge of t.

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Public key size vs. prior most efficient non-Gaussian lattice scheme ([BG14]) | 2.5x smaller (saves over 2 KB) | Same security level, at the expense of about 100 additional signature bytes versus [BG14] |
| Signature size vs. [BG14] | approximately 100 bytes larger | Same comparison as above |
| Key generation, reference implementation, recommended parameters | 386,268 median CPU cycles | Intel Core i7-4770K (Haswell), 3500 MHz fixed clock, hyperthreading and Turbo Boost off, Debian stable, Linux kernel 3.16.0, gcc 6.3.0; median of 10,000 executions |
| Signing, reference implementation, recommended parameters | 1,804,738 median cycles / 2,326,829 average cycles | Same hardware/software; 32-byte message; average exceeds median because rejection sampling occasionally requires extra signing attempts |
| Verification, reference implementation, recommended parameters | 409,904 median cycles | Same hardware/software |
| Key generation, AVX2-optimized, recommended parameters | 218,724 median cycles | Same hardware, AVX2 vector instructions |
| Signing, AVX2-optimized, recommended parameters | 789,926 median cycles / 1,035,284 average cycles | Same hardware, AVX2 |
| Verification, AVX2-optimized, recommended parameters | 209,292 median cycles | Same hardware, AVX2 |
| Number-theoretic-transform (NTT) speed-up from new AVX2 scheduling technique | roughly 2x over previously published AVX2 NTT implementations | Same Haswell hardware; specific counts in the paper's Table 1 |
| Public key / signature size, recommended parameters | 1,472 bytes / 2,701 bytes | (k,l)=(5,4), q=8,380,417, at claimed 125-bit classical security level (Table 2/3) |
| Comparison: SPHINCS (stateless hash-based signature) | signature ~41,000 bytes, public key 1,056 bytes, signing 51,636K cycles, verification 1,451K cycles | Benchmarked on Intel Xeon E3-1275 (Haswell) per the cited authors' own reported figures, at 128-bit claimed security, timing-attack-protected |
| Comparison: TESLA-I (standard-lattice, non-structured) | public key 12 MB, signature 2,444 bytes, signing 143,402K cycles, verification 19,284K cycles | Intel Core i7-4770K (Haswell), 98-bit claimed security, timing-attack-protected |
| Comparison: MQDSS (multivariate) | public key 72 bytes, signature 40,952 bytes, signing 8,510K cycles, verification 5,752K cycles | Intel Core i7-4770K (Haswell), 128-bit claimed security, timing-attack-protected |
| Comparison: Rainbow(16,32,32,32) (multivariate) | public key 145,500 bytes, signature 48 bytes, signing 68K cycles, verification 22K cycles | Xeon E3-1245 v3 (Haswell), 128-bit claimed security, timing-attack-protected |
| BKZ block-size to break the MSIS instance underlying the signature, recommended parameters | block-size 475 required, estimated at 138-bit best-known classical bit-cost, 125-bit estimated quantum, 98-bit "best plausible" bit-cost | Estimate from the paper's own lattice-reduction cost model (Table 2), not an executed attack |
| BKZ block-size to break the MLWE instance underlying the public key, recommended parameters | block-size 485 required, 141-bit best-known classical, 128-bit best-known quantum, 100-bit best plausible bit-cost | Same estimation method, recommended parameter set |

### Parameters
Four named parameter sets (weak, medium, recommended, very high), all sharing modulus q=8,380,417 and coefficient-drop parameter d=14 and challenge weight (number of nonzero coefficients in c) 60, and each varying: γ1=(q-1)/16=523,776 and γ2=γ1/2=261,888 fixed across all four sets; module dimensions (k,l) = (3,2) weak, (4,3) medium, (5,4) recommended, (6,5) very high; secret-coefficient bound η = 7, 6, 5, 3 respectively; rejection-sampling bound β = 375, 325, 275, 175; hint-count bound ω = 64, 80, 96, 120; expected number of signing-loop repetitions (derived from the scheme's own Eq. 5) = 4.3, 5.9, 6.6, 4.3. The paper states signing was benchmarked with a 32-byte message. The paper states an alternative parameterization sampling from a Gaussian distribution instead of uniform could save roughly 10-15% in signature size, but states this "does not justify the added complexity of securely implementing the scheme" — a value judgment attributed to the authors, not a measured constraint.

### Stated limitations
The security reduction (Dilithium's unforgeability reduces to the hardness of MLWE and MSIS) holds in the classical random oracle model via the forking lemma, and the paper states explicitly that "the reduction does not transfer over to the quantum setting" because the forking lemma's rewinding step has no known quantum analogue; the paper argues around this by introducing an intermediate problem (SelfTargetMSIS) that has a tight reduction to unforgeability under quantum reductions, but this reduction to SelfTargetMSIS from the base MSIS/MLWE problems is itself non-tight in the classical random oracle model. The paper states its own classical reduction is non-tight and offers only an empirical, not a proof-theoretic, argument that this does not matter in practice (citing that Schnorr and GQ signatures, which have similarly non-tight reductions, set parameters ignoring the non-tightness with no known resulting attack). The paper states it does not know whether the sketched attack against l-infinity-norm SIS (its Appendix C.3) is optimal, describing an unstudied combinatorial variant that might improve the attack, and explicitly states "we leave [this] to future work" rather than resolving it. It states there exist no constant-time implementations of the Gaussian-sampling-based competing schemes (NTRU-GPV, BLISS) "to the best of our knowledge," citing one contemporaneous partial fix ([MW17]) that it states still uses side-channel-vulnerable lookup tables. Benchmarked signing time is variable per invocation (median differs materially from average, e.g. 1,804,738 vs. 2,326,829 cycles at the recommended parameter set) because rejection sampling forces a variable, secret-dependent-in-distribution-only number of loop iterations; this variability is by design (it is what removes the discrete-Gaussian side channel) but means worst-case signing latency is not a fixed constant.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Verifying a Dilithium signature requires the verifier to reconstruct the high-order bits of Az-ct using the signer-supplied hint bytes, so any transport or storage layer carrying a Dilithium signature must preserve those extra hint bytes alongside (z, c) — dropping them makes verification impossible, not merely less efficient. The scheme's hash function H, modeled as a random oracle mapping (message, w1) to a challenge c, must be instantiated with a function with no exploitable algebraic relationship to the underlying MLWE/MSIS structure; the paper's own security argument (the SelfTargetMSIS problem) depends on assuming no such relationship exists, which is an assumption about the hash function choice, not a proof. The scheme requires an implementation that runs signing and verification in constant time to realize its side-channel-resistance goal; the paper achieves this design property but explicitly does not claim to have audited hardware-level side channels (power, electromagnetic) beyond timing. Any protocol composing Dilithium as a component needs to budget for a variable per-signing-attempt cost (rejection sampling: an expected 4.3 to 6.6 repetitions depending on parameter set) rather than a single fixed-cost signing operation, and needs to carry the larger of the two combined sizes (public key + signature, 1,472 + 2,701 = 4,173 bytes at recommended parameters) versus the alternative post-quantum schemes the paper benchmarks, when key and signature are both transmitted (the paper names TLS certificate chains as the motivating case for minimizing this sum).

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational:** V. Lyubashevsky, "Fiat-Shamir with Aborts: Applications to Lattice and Factoring-Based Signatures," Asiacrypt 2009 — origin of the abort-based signing paradigm Dilithium is built on.
- **Foundational:** S. Bai, S. Galbraith, "An Improved Compression Technique for Signatures Based on Learning with Errors," CT-RSA 2014 [BG14] — the immediately prior scheme whose public key Dilithium reduces by a factor of ~2.5 at a 100-byte signature-size expense; direct predecessor and comparison baseline.
- **Competing:** L. Ducas, A. Durmus, T. Lepoint, V. Lyubashevsky, "Lattice Signatures and Bimodal Gaussians" (BLISS), CRYPTO 2013 [DDLL13] — a competing NTRU-lattice signature scheme with smaller signature/key sizes but no known constant-time implementation due to discrete Gaussian sampling; direct comparison in Table 3.
- **Competing:** V. Lyubashevsky, D. Prest, "Quadratic Time, Linear Space Algorithms for Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization and Gaussian Sampling in Structured Lattices" (NTRU-GPV instantiation) [DLP14] — the smallest-output competing lattice signature scheme, same side-channel caveat.
- **Competing:** D. J. Bernstein, D. Hopwood, A. Hülsing, T. Lange, R. Niederhagen, L. Papachristodoulou, M. Schneider, P. Schwabe, Z. Wilcox-O'Hearn, "SPHINCS: Practical Stateless Hash-Based Signatures," Eurocrypt 2015 [BHH+15] — the stateless hash-based signature comparison point (41 KB signatures, ~51.6 million signing cycles), cited by this paper as the most conservative standard-model alternative.
- **Competing:** E. Alkim, N. Bindel, J. Buchmann, Ö. Dagdelen, E. Eaton, G. Gutoski, J. Krämer, F. Pawlega, "Revisiting TESLA in the Quantum Random Oracle Model" [ABB+17] — the standard-lattice (non-algebraically-structured) signature comparison point, with a 12 MB public key.
- **Competing:** M.-S. Chen, A. Hülsing, J. Rijneveld, S. Samardjiska, P. Schwabe, "From 5-Pass MQ-Based Identification to MQ-Based Signatures," Asiacrypt 2016 [CHR+16] (MQDSS) — multivariate signature scheme with a tight reduction to the MQ problem, comparison point in Table 3.
- **Attack-or-critique:** P. Kirchner, P.-A. Fouque, "Revisiting Lattice Attacks Using Focus Groups" [KF17] — cited as recently exploiting NTRU lattices' geometric structure for improved attacks against large-modulus/small-secret variants, motivating this paper's choice of Module-LWE/MSIS over NTRU as the hardness assumption.
- **Attack-or-critique:** G. Barthe, S. Belaïd, T. Espitau, P.-A. Fouque, B. Grégoire, M. Rossi, M. Tibouchi, "Masking the GLP Lattice-Based Signature Scheme at Any Order" [BHLY16], and similar entries [EFGT17], [PBY17] — the side-channel results this paper cites as the specific motivation for avoiding discrete Gaussian sampling.

### Verbatim extracts
- "our scheme has a public key that is 2.5X smaller than the previously most efficient lattice-based schemes."
- "the reduction does not transfer over to the quantum setting."
- "we leave to future work" (regarding whether the sketched l-infinity-SIS attack is optimal).
- "to the best of our knowledge no constant-time implementations of these schemes exist" (regarding Gaussian-sampling NTRU-based competitors).
- "does not justify the added complexity of securely implementing the scheme" (regarding Gaussian sampling's 10-15% size saving).
- "Dilithium is SUF-CMA secure based on the hardness of the standard MLWE and MSIS lattice problems."

## [DURUMERIC-IMC-15] Neither Snow Nor Rain Nor MITM...: An Empirical Analysis of Email Delivery Security

**Citation:** Zakir Durumeric, David Adrian, Ariana Mirian, James Kasten, Elie Bursztein, Nicolas Lidzborski, Kurt Thomas, Vijay Eranti, Michael D. Bailey, J. Alex Halderman. "Neither Snow Nor Rain Nor MITM...: An Empirical Analysis of Email Delivery Security." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2015. DOI 10.1145/2815675.2815695.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://conferences2.sigcomm.org/imc/2015/papers/p27.pdf
**Source URL:** https://conferences2.sigcomm.org/imc/2015/papers/p27.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper measures how completely deployed mail-transport encryption and authentication protocols are, by scanning the mail-server configurations of the Alexa Top Million domains and by analyzing a year of Gmail's own SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, the protocol that relays messages between mail servers) handshake logs. It also measures two live network attacks against mail confidentiality: an on-path attacker corrupting the STARTTLS command during an SMTP handshake to force the connection to fall back to unencrypted transport (a downgrade attack, possible because STARTTLS fails open to cleartext on any error), and an attacker returning falsified DNS MX (mail exchange) records to redirect a sender's connection to an attacker-controlled server. The authors detect STARTTLS downgrading by sending a deliberately malformed STARTTLS command to servers across the public IPv4 address space and checking whether the server echoes back the exact bytes sent or a corrupted variant, which reveals a middlebox that rewrote the command in transit.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Gmail: 80% of outgoing messages and 60% of incoming connections used STARTTLS | Snapshot as of 26 April 2015, Google's own SMTP handshake logs excluding spam |
| Gmail STARTTLS growth: outbound 52% to 80%, inbound 33% to 60% | January 2014 to April 2015, same dataset |
| 792,494 of the Alexa Top Million domains (79.25%) have operational mail servers; of those, 648,030 (81.8%) support STARTTLS | MX-record lookup and SMTP/STARTTLS handshake scan of the Alexa Top Million domains, 26 April 2015, using ZMap |
| Five third-party mail providers transport mail for 25% of the Top Million domains: Gmail 15.9%, GoDaddy 4.6%, Yandex 1.6%, QQ 1.4%, OVH 1.1% | Same Alexa Top Million domain scan; all five support inbound STARTTLS |
| 414,374 domains (52% of domains with SMTP servers, 64% of STARTTLS-supporting domains) present certificates that validate against the Mozilla NSS root store, but only 0.6% present a certificate matching the recipient's own domain name | Same scan |
| Five SMTP server implementations account for 97% of identifiable Top Million mail servers: exim 34% (Top Million) / 24% (public IPv4), Postfix 18%/21%, qmail 6%/1%, sendmail 5%/4%, Exchange 4%/12% | Installed each implementation's latest version on Ubuntu 14.04.1 LTS (Exchange documentation used instead of installation) and tested default STARTTLS behavior |
| 14.1 million IPv4 hosts had TCP port 25 open, 8.85 million responded as SMTP servers, 4.62 million (52% of responsive SMTP servers) completed a STARTTLS handshake | Public IPv4 TCP SYN scan on port 25, 20 April 2015, from the University of Michigan, using ZMap |
| 41,405 SMTP servers across 4,714 autonomous systems (ASes) and 191 countries show evidence of STARTTLS command corruption, transiting mail for 2,563 Top Million domains | Same IPv4 scan; detected via 623,635 hosts (14% of hosts that failed the TLS handshake) that echoed back the received command, of which 5,756 showed corrupted bytes, plus 35,649 more found via corrupted STARTTLS advertisement in the EHLO response |
| 96.13% of mail transiting from Tunisia to Gmail affected by STARTTLS stripping; 8 more countries above 10%, 16 more above 5% | Fraction of inbound Gmail messages originating from IPs identified as stripping TLS, measured 20-27 April 2015 |
| 178,439 of 8,860,639 responsive public DNS servers (2.01%) returned an invalid or falsified MX or A record for one of gmail.com, yahoo.com, outlook.com, qq.com, or mail.ru | Ten repeated IPv4-wide ZMap scans querying MX and A records for the five domains, 25 April 2015, from the University of Michigan |
| DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) validation failure rate for inbound Gmail messages: 10.65% in November 2013, 6.14% in April 2015 | Gmail's own validation logs, two snapshots |

### Parameters
- SPF (Sender Policy Framework), DKIM, and DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) are the three authentication extensions measured; no numeric threshold parameter is set by the authors themselves — all figures are observed deployment states, not configured experimental variables.
- Scan dates: Alexa Top Million domain scan 26 April 2015; IPv4 STARTTLS-stripping scan 20 April 2015; IPv4 DNS-falsification scan 25 April 2015; provider-encryption spot check against 19 webmail/ISP providers, date given only as "as of" the study's April 2015 window.
- Gmail transparency-report and paired cipher/authentication dataset window: January 2014 to April 2015.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their STARTTLS-corruption scanning methodology "does not comprehensively find all servers where STARTTLS is blocked," because it depends on a server echoing back the received command (only 14% did), cannot detect stripping that applies only to outgoing messages, and cannot detect a middlebox that removes the STARTTLS advertisement entirely rather than corrupting it in place — so the reported 41,405-server figure is stated as an underestimate. The Gmail-log dataset is stated to be "noticeably skewed towards a handful of large web mail providers" (Yahoo, Outlook, and large ISPs relaying bulk personal mail), so its aggregate percentages do not represent the long tail of small mail operators uniformly. The authors state end-to-end encryption (PGP, S/MIME) "does not address many of the challenges" they measure, because it leaves sender, recipient, and subject metadata exposed at the SMTP transport layer regardless of message-body encryption. The paper identifies as an open problem how to authenticate mail sent through mailing lists, because in-transit message modification invalidates DKIM signatures and blocks large providers from publishing a DMARC reject policy.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A store-and-forward relay protocol that fails open to cleartext on any handshake error (STARTTLS's behavior, as measured here) requires every relay hop, not just the endpoints, to correctly negotiate encryption, because a single corrupting hop anywhere on the path suffices to force cleartext delivery for that message, and the sender has no protocol-level signal that this occurred. Certificate-based server authentication for a mail relay requires either DNSSEC-protected MX records or an equivalent authenticated-name-resolution mechanism, because a certificate that matches only the MX hostname (the common deployment pattern measured here, 34.2% of trusted certificates) provides no protection if the attacker can also falsify the DNS response that supplies that hostname. A provider-concentration mitigation such as third-party mail hosting requires the hosting provider to hold a certificate valid for its client's domain, which the authors state creates an impersonation risk if the hosting provider's systems are separately compromised.

### Contradicts
The paper's own comparison notes that Foster et al. (2015, concurrent, comparing Top Million domains from the 2013 Adobe breach data) found higher adoption rates (89% STARTTLS, 85% SPF, 68% DMARC among popular providers) than this paper's Alexa Top Million figures (81.8% STARTTLS among domains with mail servers); the authors attribute the difference to Foster et al. sampling popular providers rather than the general domain population, not to a measurement disagreement. No other paper in this batch measures SMTP transport-security deployment or DNS-record falsification for mail, so no cross-paper numeric contradiction exists in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Klensin. "Simple mail transfer protocol." RFC 5321, 2008.
- foundational: Hoffman. "SMTP service extension for secure SMTP over transport layer security." RFC 3207, 2002.
- competing/independent-measurement: Foster, Larson, Masich, Snoeren, Savage, Levchenko. "Security by any other name: On the effectiveness of provider based email security." ACM CCS 2015.
- independent-measurement: Rijs, van der Meer. "The state of StartTLS." June 2014 (116 Dutch organizations).
- competing methodology: Holz, Braun, Kammenhuber, Carle. "The SSL landscape: A thorough analysis of the X.509 PKI using active and passive measurements." IMC 2011.
- foundational (scanning tool): Durumeric, Wustrow, Halderman. "ZMap: Fast Internet-wide scanning and its security applications." USENIX Security 2013.
- attack/related: Duan, Weaver, Zhao, Hu, Liang, Jiang, Li, Paxson. "Hold-on: Protecting against on-path DNS poisoning." Workshop on Securing and Trusting Internet Names, 2012.

### Verbatim extracts
- "only 35% successfully conﬁgure encryption, and 1.1% specify a DMARC authentication policy"
- "highlighting seven countries where more than 20% of inbound Gmail messages arrive in cleartext"
- "Five providers are used for mail transport by 25% of the Top Million domains"
- "only 0.6% are valid for the recipient domain"
- "our scanning methodology does not comprehensively ﬁnd all servers where STARTTLS is blocked"
- "end-to-end mail encryption... does not address many of the challenges we discuss"
