| Detection performance for all methods degrades on sparse graphs relative to dense graphs of the same modularity, because fewer low-frequency eigenvalues remain isolated from the high-frequency bulk on sparse graphs | Synthetic SBM comparison: dense case N=3,000/k=2/d_ave=20/c_out=1 versus sparse case N=3,000/k=2/d_ave=5/c_out=1, spectral distributions of each shift matrix plotted directly (not detection AUC) |

### Parameters
- Filter kernel forms (Table I in the source): CIA h(lambda)=(1-alpha)/(1-alpha(1-lambda)) on the random-walk Laplacian L_rw; SybilRank h(lambda)=(1-lambda)^Gamma on L_rw; SybilWalk h(lambda)=1/lambda on the augmented normalized Laplacian L_aug; SybilSCAR-C h(lambda)=1/lambda on the maximum-degree-normalized Laplacian L_max; SybilSCAR-D h(lambda)=1/lambda on L_rw; SybilBelief an ideal low-pass filter on the Bethe-Hessian matrix H(r)
- SybilHeat filter kernel: heat kernel h(lambda)=e^(-s*lambda); scaling parameter s=8 used in the reported experiments (larger s attenuates high-frequency components more strongly, no stated tested range beyond this single value)
- SybilHeat shift matrix: regularized Laplacian L_tau = I - D_tau^(-1/2) A D_tau^(-1/2), regularization parameter tau set equal to the graph's average degree d_ave, following a cited prior recommendation
- Chebyshev polynomial approximation order K: used to reduce SybilHeat's per-computation cost from O(N^3) (full eigendecomposition) to O(K|E|); specific K value used in experiments not given in the retrieved text
- CIA restart parameter alpha: 0.85
- SybilRank iteration count Gamma: floor(log N)
- SybilSCAR residual prior probability theta: 0.5
- Synthetic-graph parameters: N=1,000, k=2 communities, average degree d_ave=5, theta_i=1 (SBM, homogeneous degree) or theta_i ~ Uniform(3,7) (DCSBM, heterogeneous degree); 10% of each community's nodes labeled; all synthetic results averaged over 100 runs
- Real-graph labeling: max(3, floor(0.1*N)) nodes labeled per side (benign/Sybil), using the largest connected component of each of 4 named benchmark community-detection graphs
- Community detectability threshold used as the reference boundary: (c_in - c_out)/2 > sqrt((c_in + c_out)/2) for SBM, per a cited conjecture; an analogous DCSBM-specific bound is used for the degree-heterogeneous case

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own theoretical framework builds directly on a prior work by the same authors that covered only two methods (CIA and SybilBelief) and could not explain performance differences arising from degree heterogeneity or modularity differences between graphs; this paper extends that coverage to five methods but the extension is still confined to methods expressible as a linear shift-matrix/filter-kernel pair, so it does not by construction cover nonlinear detection methods. The paper states explicitly that SybilHeat's own performance could likely be improved further by a different filter kernel or shift matrix than the ones chosen, meaning the paper itself does not claim SybilHeat as an optimum, only as one point satisfying the two derived necessary conditions. It states, citing existing studies, that learning node features and edge weights (as opposed to relying purely on labeled-node reputation propagation over an unweighted graph) would further improve detection performance, which SybilHeat as presented does not do. SybilSCAR-D is excluded from the empirical comparison because the paper found its convergence unstable, a limitation of that specific baseline method rather than of the paper's own proposed method. The theoretical detectability threshold used throughout (equation 3, and its DCSBM analogue) is stated as a conjecture from a cited prior paper, not a proof, though the paper's own empirical spectral-clustering results are consistent with it.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every method covered by this framework, including SybilHeat, requires a set of pre-labeled benign nodes and, for methods other than SybilRank and CIA (which use only one label type each), a set of pre-labeled Sybil nodes as well; the paper's own experiments assume these labels arrive already correct except in the explicit noise-robustness tests, and do not address how a deployed system obtains them. The framework's guarantee that low-frequency eigenvectors carry community-structure information holds only in the graph regime the paper analyzes (SBM or DCSBM-generated, or empirically similar real graphs) above the stated detectability threshold; below that threshold the paper's own results show SybilBelief's accuracy collapses sharply, so a system relying on it needs an independent estimate of whether its deployment graph is in the detectable regime. SybilHeat's Chebyshev approximation requires the shift matrix (the regularized Laplacian) and the average degree d_ave to be computable from a graph the caller supplies in full, since tau is set from that same average-degree statistic; a system that cannot expose global degree statistics, or that only has a partial or streaming view of the graph, cannot use this scaling rule as given. The paper's stated computational-cost improvement (O(K|E|) versus O(N^3)) presumes the caller can perform repeated sparse matrix-vector multiplications against the full edge set, meaning a system embedding SybilHeat needs the entire graph materialized somewhere it can run that computation, not merely local per-node views.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch regarding the paper's own reported figures. This paper reframes, rather than contradicts, GONG-TIFS-14 (SybilBelief) and its family: it derives that SybilBelief's strong noise robustness and strong detectable-region performance follow mathematically from its filter kernel being an ideal (hard cutoff) low-pass filter, while its collapse below the detectability threshold follows from the same kernel discarding all high-frequency information, including the marginal signal that remains available in weakly modular graphs; GONG-TIFS-14 itself did not identify this shared cause and reported the individual behaviors as separate empirical observations. This is a structural explanation building on GONG-TIFS-14's numbers, not a factual contradiction of them, since GONG-TIFS-14's own datasets and community-structure sweep are consistent with the pattern this paper attributes to filter-kernel shape.

## [GAO-CNS-18] SybilFuse: Combining Local Attributes with Global Structure to Perform Robust Sybil Detection
**Citation:** Peng Gao, Binghui Wang, Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Sanjeev R. Kulkarni, Kurt Thomas, Prateek Mittal. "SybilFuse: Combining Local Attributes with Global Structure to Perform Robust Sybil Detection." IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (CNS), 2018. DOI 10.1109/CNS.2018.8433147.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.06772
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.06772
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilFuse ranks nodes in a social network by likelihood of being a Sybil identity, combining two information sources that prior work used only separately: local per-node and per-edge attributes, and global graph structure. It trains local classifiers on node- and edge-level features to produce local trust scores, then propagates those scores through the graph using a weighted variant of two established structure-propagation mechanisms — random walk and loopy belief propagation (LBP, an iterative message-passing inference procedure on graphical models that can produce approximate marginal probabilities even when the graph contains cycles). Because the propagation weights come from the trained local classifier's confidence rather than being fixed a priori, the method is designed to remain effective when the graph-structural assumptions ("strong trust network," "fast-mixing honest region") that prior structure-only defenses require do not hold.

Mechanism: (1) local trust score computation — extract discriminative node features from available account attributes (in the paper's own Twitter evaluation, since only structural data was accessible, three purely structural proxy features were used: the fraction of a node's incoming follow requests it accepts, the fraction of its outgoing follow requests that get accepted, and its local clustering coefficient), train a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel on a small labeled sample, and output the classifier's probabilistic confidence as each node's local trust score; edge trust scores use a default constant (0.9 in the paper's experiments) to model homophily (the tendency of connected accounts to resemble each other) when edge-level features are not separately extractable from the available data. (2) weighted score propagation — feed the local scores as either a weighted random walk (SF-RW) or a weighted loopy belief propagation pass (SF-LBP) over the full graph, so a node's final score integrates its own local signal with the local signals of everything structurally connected to it. (3) output — either threshold the final scores (a threshold obtained via cross-validation on training data) to produce a binary Sybil/benign label, or rank all nodes ascending by score so a human analyst reviews the most-suspicious accounts first.

### Measured results
| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Robustness to local-classifier error, synthetic network | Preferential-attachment-generated benign (1,000 nodes) and Sybil (500 nodes) regions, average degree 10 in each region, 1,000 attack edges, simulated local trust scores sampled in [0.1, 0.9] at controlled false-positive/false-negative rates (0.5 decision threshold), edge trust scores fixed at default 0.9 | With node trust scores: for FPR = FNR <= 0.3, both SF-RW and SF-LBP achieve >0.98 accuracy and Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). With edge trust scores (1 benign + 1 Sybil trusted seed, node scores 0.9/0.1 for seeds, 0.5 default elsewhere): >0.92 accuracy and AUC under the same error bound. Performance improves as classifier error falls, as attack-edge count falls, and as Sybil-node count rises; SF-LBP consistently outperforms SF-RW across all tested settings |
| Labeled real-world Twitter network, moderate scale | 8,167 nodes, 54,146 edges after converting a directed follower network from [Yang et al., WWW 2012] to undirected by keeping only bidirectional edges; ground truth: 7,358 verified benign, 809 Sybil nodes; SVM trained on 50 benign + 50 Sybil randomly sampled nodes; edge scores default 0.9 | Sybil nodes emit 40,010 attack edges total (49.5 per Sybil on average); 53.4% of Sybils are isolated (connect only to benign nodes), emitting 37.0% of attack edges; 41.2% of Sybils form one largest connected component (42.8% of attack edges); 5.4% form small connected groups (20.2% of attack edges); 5,546 benign nodes (75.4% of all benign nodes) are "victims" (benign nodes directly connected to a Sybil) |
| Sybil-ranking performance, same 8,167-node network | Compared against SVM alone, SybilRank (SR), CIA, SybilBelief (SB), SybilSCAR (SS), Integro (INT), Integro with a hypothetical perfect victim predictor (INT-PF), four ensemble combinations, and random guessing (RG); ranking evaluated as fraction of true Sybils among the top-K ranked nodes | SF-RW's average fraction-of-Sybils improvement over SR, CIA, INT is 44.8, 16.2, 54.3 percentage points respectively. SF-LBP's average improvement over RG, SVM, SR, CIA, INT, SB, SS is 85.7, 57.5, 85.9, 57.4, 95.5, 36.5, 13.4 percentage points respectively; SF-LBP achieves >98% Sybil coverage up to the top 400 ranked nodes. INT's victim predictor achieved 18.3% precision, 19.6% recall on this network, and INT-PF (perfect victim prediction) performed only slightly better than random guessing, because Integro's edge-downweighting formula suppresses score propagation through victims, and 75.4% of benign nodes here are victims |
| Composition of top-500 ranked nodes by Sybil type | Same network; Sybils categorized as isolated, in the largest connected component (LCC), or in other small connected groups | SVM ranks isolated Sybils best (74.6% of all Sybils it surfaces are isolated); global structure-based methods rank LCC Sybils best (71.2% SR, 66.4% CIA, 62.4% SB, 71.6% SS of surfaced Sybils are LCC members); SF-LBP performs best at ranking both isolated and LCC Sybils simultaneously |
| Large-scale labeled Twitter network | 21,297,772 nodes, 265,025,545 edges after undirected conversion, from a Twitter follower-network snapshot [Kwak et al., WWW 2010]; ground truth obtained by re-crawling every account via Twitter's API: 145,156 (0.7%) suspended (labeled Sybil), 1,911,482 (9.0%) deleted (excluded, status unknown), remainder active (labeled benign); local-score SVM trained on 3,000 benign + 3,000 Sybil sampled nodes; same three structural features as the smaller network | Network modularity of the benign/Sybil partition: 0.0042 (modularity >0.3 is the threshold Clauset et al. state indicates real community structure, so this partition is not a detectable community by that standard); 77,917 connected components in the Sybil region, 50% of Sybils isolated, 45% forming the largest connected component, remainder in small (<20-node) groups; the largest-connected-component-plus-benign partition has modularity only 0.0046; 18,414,469 total attack edges, averaging 127 attacked benign nodes per Sybil; 90% of attack edges concentrate on 3% of benign nodes (hypothesized to be celebrity accounts that follow back indiscriminately) |
| AUC on the large-scale Twitter network | Same 21M-node network, same compared methods | SR 0.57, CIA 0.80, INT 0.48, INT-PF 0.54, SB 0.74, SS 0.74, SF-RW 0.81, SF-LBP 0.85 |
| Sybil-ranking fraction on the large-scale Twitter network, top 1K nodes | Same network | SF-LBP's improvement over SR, CIA, INT, INT-PF, SB, SS: 54.8, 46.5, 55.1, 55.1, 55.1, 53.9 percentage points respectively (one reported figure of 55.1% appears against three different baselines) |
| Ground-truth check against Twitter's own suspension policy | Manual review of the top-100 nodes ranked by SF-LBP on the large-scale network | 71 were already suspended by Twitter; of the 29 still-active accounts, 24 (82.8% of the 29) showed spam/low-quality-profile characteristics consistent with being Sybil but had evaded Twitter's own detection, 3 were judged genuinely benign, 2 were inconclusive due to protected account settings |

The paper's own robustness experiment (synthetic network) does not compute an accuracy figure for SF-RW specifically, stating that random-walk-based final scores are "typically very low" in absolute terms, making a fixed threshold unreliable; only AUC is reported for SF-RW in that experiment.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range/notes |
|---|---|---|
| Basic synthetic network size (robustness experiment) | 1,000 benign, 500 Sybil nodes, average degree 10 in each region, 1,000 attack edges | held as the "basic setup" while one factor was varied at a time |
| Local classifier error rate (FPR = FNR), synthetic robustness experiment | swept 0 to 0.4 | 0-0.4 |
| Edge trust score default | 0.9 | fixed across all experiments; used to "model homophily" wherever edge features could not be extracted |
| Node trust score for trusted seeds (edge-score experiments) | 0.9 (benign seed), 0.1 (Sybil seed), 0.5 (default, all other nodes) | one benign + one Sybil seed sampled per run |
| SVM kernel | RBF, via LIBSVM | fixed |
| Training-set size, moderate Twitter network | 50 benign + 50 Sybil nodes, randomly sampled | fixed |

| Modularity threshold for "significant community structure" (cited from Clauset et al.) | 0.3 | used as an external reference point, not tuned |

### Stated limitations
Existing structure-only Sybil defenses that SybilFuse compares against are stated by the authors to require assumptions the large-scale Twitter measurement directly shows are violated: a "strong trust network" (limited attack-edge count) and, for two of them, a fast-mixing benign region implying a well-connected giant community. The paper's own modularity measurement (0.0042, rising to only 0.0046 even restricted to the largest Sybil connected component) is presented as direct evidence the benign and Sybil regions on this real Twitter graph cannot be treated as separable communities, which the authors state is why prior structure-only methods perform poorly there. Integro's victim-prediction approach is stated to degrade toward random-guess performance even under a hypothetical perfect victim predictor once the true victim fraction is large (75.4% here), because its edge-downweighting formula then suppresses propagation broadly rather than selectively. The authors state that a strategic adversary aware of SybilFuse's specific local features could evade the local classifier by mimicking benign local statistics, but argue (without a corresponding experiment) that doing so requires denser Sybil-to-Sybil connectivity that then becomes more detectable by the structure-propagation stage; they state periodic retraining of local classifiers is advisable to track evolving attack behavior, without measuring an optimal retraining interval. Ground truth is bounded by Twitter's own detection policy: nodes not suspended by Twitter are labeled benign by default, and the authors' own manual audit of the top-ranked-but-still-active accounts found 82.8% of a 29-account sample showed Sybil-like characteristics, meaning the paper's own accuracy figures against this ground truth likely undercount true Sybil detection since some labeled "benign" nodes are actually undetected Sybils. Deleted accounts (9.0% of the large network) were excluded from training and evaluation because the authors could not determine whether deletion was user- or platform-initiated. The paper cites (Liu et al., ACM CCS 2015) that gradual movement of attack edges over time defeats seed-propagation-based defenses like SybilInfer and SybilRank under a churn attack requiring the attacker to know the trusted seed locations and for those locations to remain stable over an attack window; the authors argue but do not experimentally demonstrate that SybilFuse resists this because it does not propagate exclusively from fixed trusted seeds.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a source of local, per-node (and ideally per-edge) attribute data sufficient to train a supervised classifier; when such attributes are unavailable, as in the paper's own Twitter evaluations, the method falls back to purely structural proxy features (accepted-request ratios, clustering coefficient) and a constant default for edge scores, which is a degraded configuration of the method rather than its intended input. Requires a labeled training sample of both benign and Sybil nodes (50+50 or 3,000+3,000 in the paper's experiments) obtained from some ground-truth source external to the algorithm itself — the paper's own ground truth comes from Twitter's platform-level suspension decisions, an external, centrally-operated classifier the paper's method is itself layered on top of. Requires the ability to periodically re-run and retrain, since the authors' own discussion states resistance to both social churn and strategic feature-mimicking depends on the system administrator refreshing trusted seeds or retraining classifiers on a schedule the paper does not specify. Places no requirement on graph fast-mixing or on a bounded count of attack edges, unlike the structure-only defenses (SR, SB, SS) it compares against — this is the paper's central claimed structural advantage, evidenced by its performance holding up on a network the authors show fails the fast-mixing and strong-trust-network assumptions those other methods require.

### Contradicts
The target-registry's description of this paper (used to select it for retrieval) states it was evaluated "on a Tuenti dataset" — the retrieved full text contains no mention of Tuenti anywhere; its two labeled evaluation networks are both derived from Twitter data (an 8,167-node network built from Yang et al.'s WWW 2012 spammer-network crawl, and a 21-million-node network built from Kwak et al.'s WWW 2010 Twitter crawl). This is a mismatch between the registry's prior description and the paper's actual content, not a mismatch of the retrieved file's identity (title and authors both match the registry entry exactly).

Beyond that, none found among other entries in this corpus. This paper's own re-implementation-free citation of prior methods' reported assumptions (strong trust network, fast mixing) is consistent with, not contradictory to, WEI-INFOCOM-12's explicit statement of the same two assumptions for SybilDefender.

## [GHOSH-HOTPETS-14] A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays
**Citation:** Mainak Ghosh, Miles Richardson, Bryan Ford, Rob Jansen. "A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays." Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs), 2014.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://dedis.cs.yale.edu/dissent/papers/hotpets14-torpath.pdf
**Source URL:** https://dedis.cs.yale.edu/dissent/papers/hotpets14-torpath.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
TorPath lets the participants of one Tor (The Onion Router, an anonymity network that routes traffic through a multi-relay circuit so no single relay learns both a client's identity and its destination) circuit jointly generate cryptographic proof of how much end-to-end goodput (successfully delivered payload throughput) that specific circuit carried, without any centralized bandwidth authority, so that proof can back the minting of a companion currency (TorCoin) proportional to measured transfer rather than to a self-report. The construction has two layers. TorPath first replaces Tor's directory servers with a decentralized group of assignment servers that assemble a circuit (one client plus an entry, middle, and exit relay) for each client through a three-stage protocol: in Group Initialization, clients and relays each submit a temporary public key onion-encrypted (successively encrypted in layers, one per assignment server, so no single server can read the innermost content alone) under all assignment servers in the forming consensus group; in Verifiable Shuffle, the consensus group jointly and verifiably permutes each column of the resulting key matrix using the Neff shuffle (a shuffle whose correctness -- that the output is a permutation of the input without revealing the permutation -- any observer can verify), so each output row becomes one anonymous circuit's four temporary keys with no single participant learning which real identity holds which key; in Path Lookup, each participant learns only the IP address of its immediate circuit neighbor by a second onion-encrypted, shuffled exchange, so a client learns only its entry relay and each relay learns only its adjacent circuit member. Each assigned circuit receives a Circuit Identifier formed from the hash of the shuffle matrix and the circuit's row index. TorCoin then runs a proof-of-bandwidth protocol on top of an assigned circuit: every m Tor packets, each of the four circuit participants commits to a fresh temporary hash value, the values accumulate into a shared blob as they pass from client to exit relay and back, and once the blob is fully formed and signed by all four participants using their circuit-specific temporary keys, the client checks whether a hash of the assembled blob has enough low-order zero bits to count as a mined coin (a Bitcoin-style proof-of-work check, applied to a value that could only have been assembled by all four participants having actually forwarded traffic to each other, rather than to arbitrary computation); because each of the four contributions is revealed only after all parties have committed to their own hash first, no strict subset of the four participants can reconstruct the blob on their own to mint coins without the others' cooperation. A valid coin's sequence number must be exactly one more than the last coin recorded from that circuit's identifier on the blockchain (Bitcoin's distributed, append-only transaction ledger, reused here to prevent a coin from that circuit being claimed twice), and is capped by a fixed, publicly known per-circuit coin limit. The mined coin is split with one third of its value paid to each of the three relays via the standard Bitcoin transfer protocol.

### Measured results
| Measurement | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Per-round TorCoin protocol packet overhead: 1,752 bytes total, broken into a first client-to-entry packet of 34 bytes, entry-to-middle of 66 bytes, middle-to-exit of 98 bytes, exit-to-middle return of 324 bytes, middle-to-entry return of 518 bytes, and entry-to-client return of 712 bytes | Measured by simulating message passing through a set of relays using the Python Twisted framework, with keys, hashes, and signatures assumed uniformly 32 bytes each; described by the authors as "Preliminary Results," with no stated relay count, run count, or real-network deployment. |
| TorCoin protocol overhead as a fraction of Tor traffic: approximately 5% when the packet-count interval m is 10 or more | Derived from the 1,752-byte per-round overhead against a standard Tor cell size of 514 bytes, so one round trip of 6 cells (entry-middle-exit and back) carries 514 x 6 = 3,084 bytes of base traffic; this is an arithmetic derivation from the simulated overhead figure and the fixed Tor cell size, not an independently measured network run. |

### Parameters
- m (the number of Tor packets between successive rounds of TorCoin proof-of-bandwidth generation): the paper states m greater than or equal to 10 yields roughly 5% overhead, and states m can be tuned in further experimentation to trade transmission efficiency against incentive granularity for relay operators; no other specific value is tested or recommended.
- Consensus-group quorum size: given only as an illustrative example ("if there are 10 assignment servers in the network, we might require at least 6 of them to participate"), not a value the paper adopts as a recommendation.
- Consensus-group size n (number of clients gathered before a shuffle proceeds): stated as configurable, trading a larger anonymity set against longer circuit-assignment wait time; no numeric value given or tested.
- Per-circuit TorCoin mint limit (the cap on coins any one assigned circuit may mine): stated to exist and to be recorded in the blockchain for verification, with no numeric value given.
- Assumed key/hash/signature length in the overhead measurement: 32 bytes.
- Standard Tor cell size used in the overhead derivation: 514 bytes.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the Neff shuffle used for circuit assignment is complex and requires several rounds of communication among assignment servers, and states this cost is tolerated only under the unverified expectation that assignment servers will number fewer than 10 and be well-provisioned; the paper offers a workaround (using conventional Tor circuits immediately, then transitioning to TorCoin circuits once assigned) for latency-sensitive users rather than a measured latency figure. TorPath's circuit-assignment mechanism is stated to be incompatible with the deployed Tor network because it requires route assignment and access control that ordinary Tor relays and directory servers do not implement, though the authors state a single physical machine could run both a standard Tor relay and a TorPath/TorCoin service simultaneously. The Neff shuffle applied per-position can assign the same physical relay to more than one position (for example, both entry and middle) on the same circuit; the authors state this should be rare with a reasonable number of participating relays and consider it no worse than Tor's existing risk of one operator controlling multiple relays on a circuit by chance, and explicitly defer building any detection mechanism for it to future work. The paper explicitly states that Bitcoin's transaction layer offers only limited payment anonymity and that this limitation is inherited unmodified by TorCoin, presenting Zerocoin, Mixcoin, and CoinShuffle only as candidate, unimplemented fixes to that separate problem. The design as specified always assigns three fresh relays per circuit rather than persisting a stable entry relay across circuits (Tor's actual practice, adopted for a different reason -- limiting a client's cumulative exposure to malicious entry relays over time); the authors sketch a persistent-entry-relay variant of the assignment matrix but state it comes at the cost of a higher chance of forming an all-colluding circuit, without giving a numeric bound on that increase.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Verifying that a claimed TorCoin corresponds to real bandwidth transfer requires a reader to hold the full public consensus log of shuffle matrices produced by assignment servers, since a Circuit Identifier is checked against that log and the four temporary public keys it names; a system without persistent access to that log cannot independently audit a coin. Assignment-server honesty is assumed only in majority: the adversary model states the design tolerates a minority of assignment servers being controlled by an adversary, with the rest merely honest-but-curious (they follow the protocol but may try to infer private information from what they see), and the anonymity and coin-integrity guarantees are stated to hold conditional on that majority assumption. The mechanism assumes that at most half of the temporary keys across the network belong to colluding participants, under which condition the paper computes that only 1/16 (1/2^4, since a circuit has four positions) of assigned circuits are fully colluding and able to mint coins for zero genuine bandwidth transfer; a higher colluding fraction was not analyzed by the paper and would raise this fraction. The mining check itself requires that the underlying transport reliably deliver each of the four onion-forwarded commit/reveal messages per round in order, since a message lost or reordered on the forward or return path prevents the blob from being validly formed and signed by all four participants. Anything reading TorCoin balances for a reward or reputation purpose downstream must treat coin possession as proof of goodput on one specific, now-identified circuit at mint time, not as a general, ongoing measure of a relay's capacity or honesty, since the mechanism produces no per-relay aggregate score, only per-circuit, per-round proofs.

### Contradicts
None found within this paper's own claims; the authors describe their own overhead figures explicitly as preliminary and simulated, not as a production measurement, so no later paper's field measurement of TorCoin overhead should be read as confirming or refuting a claim this paper does not make. No other entry in this batch reports a comparable bandwidth-backed incentive currency to compare numerically.

### References worth retrieving
- Nakamoto, "Bitcoin: A peer-to-peer electronic cash system," 2008 -- foundational (the base blockchain and proof-of-work construction TorCoin's mining and double-spend-prevention protocol adapts).
- Jansen, Johnson, Syverson, "LIRA: Lightweight Incentivized Routing for Anonymity," NDSS 2013 -- competing (a prior Tor incentive scheme this paper argues can partition the anonymity set by traffic speed and relies on a trusted central bank for coin assignment, both properties TorCoin is designed to avoid).
- Moore, Wacek, Sherr, "Exploring the potential benefits of expanded rate limiting in Tor: Slow and steady wins the race with Tortoise," ACSAC 2011 -- competing (a prior incentive scheme, Tortoise, this paper argues may compromise client anonymity by making traffic identifiable).
- Jansen, Hopper, Kim, "Recruiting new Tor relays with BRAIDS," CCS 2010 -- competing (a prior relay-recruitment incentive scheme cited among the unsatisfactory prior designs this paper responds to).
- Snader, Borisov, "EigenSpeed: secure peer-to-peer bandwidth evaluation," IPTPS 2009 -- competing (a peer-reported bandwidth measurement scheme this paper contrasts against for relying on self-reporting rather than proof of transfer).
- Neff, "A verifiable secret shuffle and its application to e-voting," CCS 2001 -- foundational (the Neff shuffle, the specific verifiable-shuffle algorithm TorPath uses to assign circuits).
- Jansen, Miller, Syverson, Ford, "From onions to shallots: Rewarding Tor relays with TEARS," HotPETs 2014 -- competing (a contemporaneous alternative Tor relay-reward scheme by an overlapping author set, cited by this paper for extended discussion of incentive-system requirements and tradeoffs).
- Miers, Garman, Green, Rubin, "Zerocoin: Anonymous distributed e-cash from Bitcoin," IEEE S&P 2013 -- competing (cited as a candidate, unimplemented fix for the Bitcoin transaction-anonymity limitation this paper inherits).
- Ruffing, Moreno-Sanchez, Kate, "CoinShuffle: Practical decentralized coin mixing for Bitcoin," HotPETs 2014 -- competing (cited as a second candidate, unimplemented fix for the same Bitcoin transaction-anonymity limitation).

## [GONG-TIFS-14] SybilBelief: A Semi-Supervised Learning Approach for Structure-Based Sybil Detection

**Citation:** Neil Zhenqiang Gong, Mario Frank, Prateek Mittal. "SybilBelief: A Semi-supervised Learning Approach for Structure-based Sybil Detection." IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 2014. DOI 10.1109/TIFS.2014.2316975.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.5035
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilBelief classifies or ranks every node in a social graph as benign or Sybil by propagating a small set of known-benign and, optionally, known-Sybil labels across the graph, using both label types together rather than only one. It models the social graph as a Markov Random Field (a joint probability distribution over one binary random variable per node, benign or Sybil), where each edge (u,v) carries a homophily-strength parameter w_uv expressing that connected nodes tend to share a label, and each node v carries a prior parameter theta_v expressing prior belief about that node's own label before any neighbor information is used. Given the labeled nodes as fixed evidence, SybilBelief approximates each unlabeled node's posterior probability of being benign using Loopy Belief Propagation (an iterative algorithm that computes exact posteriors on tree-structured graphs and is applied as an approximation on general graphs with cycles, since Pearl's original algorithm has no convergence guarantee off trees), where each node repeatedly recomputes a belief by combining messages sent from its neighbors that themselves encode each neighbor's current belief weighted by the edge homophily parameter. The output is a per-node posterior probability used directly for classification (thresholding to benign/Sybil) or for ranking (sorting by probability of being benign). When only one label type (benign or Sybil) is available, the paper adds a "boosting" step that samples nodes uniformly at random from the graph, treats them as if they were the missing label type, runs the full algorithm k times with different random samples, and combines (ensembles) the k results.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| False negatives and false positives both first rise then fall as Sybil region size increases, from a maximum ("accepted Sybil nodes"/"rejected benign nodes") that the paper uses as its worst-case metric | Preferential Attachment (PA) and Erdos-Renyi (ER) synthetic networks, benign region fixed at 1,000 nodes average degree 10, 500 attack edges added uniformly at random, theta_v=0.5, w=0.9, one labeled benign and one labeled Sybil node, averaged over 100 trials |
| PA-generated (scale-free) Sybil regions produce more accepted Sybil nodes than ER-generated Sybil regions at the same attack-edge count (100-500 edges swept); rejected benign nodes stay below 5 (false-positive rate under 0.5%, on a 1,000-node benign region) in all four generator combinations | Same basic synthetic setup, attack edges swept 100-500, generator pairs ER-ER/ER-PA/PA-ER/PA-PA |
| Label site (whether labeled nodes sit at attack-edge endpoints or away from them) has no measurable effect on accepted Sybil nodes across the tested range | Same synthetic setup, four label-site combinations (SI/SII on each side) |
| A phase-transition point exists for the homophily-strength parameter w at approximately w0=0.65; above w0 the algorithm achieves a stable tradeoff between accepted Sybil and rejected benign nodes; performance is independent of theta_l (prior on labeled nodes) once theta_l exceeds 0 | Same synthetic setup, w swept 0.5-1.0 at theta_l=0.5, and theta_l swept 0.0-1.0 at w=0.9 |
| One label per community suffices: accepted-Sybil-node count is stable across a wide range of labeled-benign-node counts (roughly ratio 0.1 to 10 of benign:Sybil labels); it rises sharply only when the labeled-benign-to-labeled-Sybil ratio exceeds 10 or falls below 0.1 | Same synthetic setup, labeled benign and Sybil node counts each swept 1/10/100 against the other |
| SybilBelief tolerates up to 49% incorrect labels: at 49% label noise, accepted Sybil nodes are only about 3x the noise-free count, and rejected benign nodes stay under 3 (false-positive rate under 0.3%); the paper reports 100% accuracy detecting which specific labels were incorrect | Same synthetic setup, 100 labeled benign and 100 labeled Sybil nodes, percent of both types corrupted swept 0-49% (the paper notes 50%+ noise causes any such algorithm to accept unbounded Sybils) |
| Performance is stable as the benign region's community count increases from 1 to 10 (a proxy for larger mixing time / weaker fast-mixing assumption), with rejected benign nodes staying near 0 | Benign region built as k Preferential-Attachment communities each linked to prior communities by 10 random edges, k swept 1-10, one Sybil label and 10 benign labels (one per community) |
| Against real social-graph benign regions, SybilBelief (SB) and its no-Sybil-label boosted variant (SB-B) outperform SybilLimit and SybilInfer by "orders of magnitude" in both accepted Sybil nodes and rejected benign nodes | Facebook New Orleans interaction graph (43,953 nodes / 182,384 edges) as benign region, PA-generated Sybil region, attack edges swept 600-2,000, 100 labeled benign nodes, 1 labeled Sybil node (SybilLimit/SybilInfer results shown only for Facebook because the paper states they do not scale to the larger Slashdot and Email graphs) |
| SybilBelief (SB) and its boosted variant (SB-B) achieve higher AUC (area under the ROC curve, the probability a random benign node ranks above a random Sybil node) than SybilRank and CIA (Criminal account Inference Algorithm) across three real graphs, with the margin growing as attack edges increase; under label noise, SybilRank and CIA's AUC degrades sharply while SybilBelief's stays nearly unchanged | Facebook (43,953 nodes/182,384 edges), Slashdot (82,168/504,230), Email (224,832/339,925) used as both benign and Sybil regions with attack edges added between the two copies, swept roughly 1 to 10,000 (log scale), 100 labeled benign and 100 labeled Sybil nodes (10 of each corrupted in the noise condition), AUC averaged over 10 trials per attack-edge count |
| SybilBelief's computational complexity is stated as O(n*d), where n is node count and d is the number of Loopy Belief Propagation iterations; SybilRank/CIA-family random-walk approaches are stated as O(n log n); the paper reports the two run in similar wall-clock time in its experiments since d and log(n) are close in practice | Comparison stated for the same graphs used in the AUC experiments; no separate wall-clock timing table given in the retrieved text |

### Parameters
- theta_v (prior belief a node is benign, for unlabeled nodes): 0.5 in all experiments (no prior preference)
- theta_l (prior parameter for labeled nodes): fixed at 0.5 by the paper's own convention, since labeled node states are held fixed and theta_v has no effect on them; independently varied in one sensitivity experiment (0.0-1.0) with no effect observed once above 0
- w_uv / w (homophily strength, uniform across all edges in every experiment): 0.9 in the main experiments; phase transition found near w0=0.65 in a sweep from 0.5 to 1.0
- Number of boosting trials k (when only one label type is available): 10 used in the main comparison experiments; k=1 and k=10 both tested in a dedicated boosting experiment
- Basic synthetic setup: benign region 1,000 nodes, average degree 10 (PA or ER generator), 500 attack edges added uniformly at random, 1 labeled benign + 1 labeled Sybil node, results averaged over 100 trials
- Label noise fraction tested: 0% to 49%, in the noise-tolerance experiment
- Number of communities in the community-structure experiment: 1 to 10, each linked to prior communities by 10 random edges
- Real-graph experiments: 100 labeled benign nodes (Sybil classification comparison) or 100 labeled benign + 100 labeled Sybil nodes (ranking comparison); 10 corrupted in noise conditions; attack edges swept 600-2,000 (classification) or roughly 1-10,000 log-scale (ranking)
- CIA restart parameter alpha: 0.85 (value from the original CIA paper, reused here)

### Stated limitations
The paper states explicitly, as an acknowledged limitation, that it did not evaluate SybilBelief or the compared approaches using real Sybil users, because the authors could not obtain a social network with ground-truth benign/Sybil labels; all Sybil regions in the evaluation are synthetic (PA-generated or duplicated benign regions with synthetic attack edges). It states that computing exact posterior probabilities in a general Markov Random Field is NP-hard, and that Loopy Belief Propagation, the approximation method used, has no proven convergence guarantee on graphs with cycles (as opposed to trees), citing Pearl's original observation of possible oscillation; the paper reports only that the approximation performs well empirically in its own experiments. The paper states that at 50% or higher label noise, "any algorithm" would accept an unbounded number of Sybil nodes, implicitly bounding SybilBelief's noise tolerance below that threshold. The homophily assumption itself is stated as a precondition the paper does not guarantee: it cites Yang et al.'s finding that the RenRen social network does not satisfy homophily and states structure-based approaches should not be applied there, contrasted with Cao et al.'s finding that Tuenti's invitation-based network does satisfy it. The paper lists future work explicitly: evaluating with datasets containing real Sybils, and applying the SybilBelief framework to graph-based botnet detection, reputation systems, and private-information inference — none of which are addressed in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
SybilBelief requires a social graph in which the homophily assumption approximately holds (linked nodes tend to share a label); the paper states this needs to be arranged elsewhere in the system, either by using an interaction-derived or tie-strength-derived graph rather than a raw friend graph, or by a preprocessing step elsewhere that detects and removes compromised benign nodes ("front peers") before the graph reaches SybilBelief. It requires at minimum one labeled benign node reachable in the same connected component as the region to be classified, and the paper's own experiments show it needs at least one label per distinct community in the benign region to remain robust to community structure — meaning whatever labeling process feeds it (verified accounts, a machine-learning classifier, or crowdsourced labeling, all cited as possible sources) must cover every community, not just the graph overall. It tolerates label noise up to just under 50% but not beyond, so any upstream labeling pipeline supplying it must be presumed correct on a strict majority of the labels it submits. Its correctness argument for the fraction of successfully detected Sybils is conditioned on attack edges appearing between the benign and Sybil regions at a rate sparse relative to within-region connectivity; the paper does not defend against an attacker with unlimited attack-edge budget, since fast-mixing/sparse-cut-style structural assumptions from the wider Sybil-defense literature still bound what any homophily-based method can achieve.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch. This paper's own presentation corrects a claim it attributes to prior work: it states that requiring the benign region to be fast-mixing (an assumption SybilLimit, SybilInfer, GateKeeper, and SybilDefender make) was shown unsatisfied in real social graphs by Mohaisen et al., a citation this paper relies on rather than an original finding of its own. Cross-reference for later composition checking against ALVISI-SP-13 and VISWANATH-SIGCOMM-10 in this corpus: this paper's synthetic-attack evaluation (uniformly random attack-edge placement) does not include a targeted-attachment adversary, the attack model VISWANATH-SIGCOMM-10 and ALVISI-SP-13 show is measurably more damaging to structure-based defenses than random attachment; SybilBelief's reported "orders of magnitude" improvement over SybilLimit/SybilInfer is measured only under the random-attachment model.

- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman. "SybilGuard" — foundational
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao. "SybilLimit" — competing (direct empirical comparison in this paper)
- Danezis, Mittal. "SybilInfer" — competing (direct empirical comparison in this paper)

## [GONG-USENIXSEC-20] Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting
**Citation:** Jiajun Gong, Tao Wang. "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting." 29th USENIX Security Symposium, 2020.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec20-gong.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec20-gong.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
FRONT and GLUE both hide, from a passive eavesdropper positioned between a Tor client and the Tor network entry node, which webpage a client loaded, by adding dummy packets to the encrypted traffic between the client and a cooperating Tor middle node acting as a defense proxy. Neither defense delays any real packet, so both add zero latency overhead; both add only data overhead (extra dummy packets), which the paper calls "lightweight." FRONT targets the observation that a Website Fingerprinting (WF) classifier extracts most of its useful features from the first few seconds of a page-load trace (the "trace front"). For each trace, the client draws a random count of outgoing dummy packets from a discrete uniform distribution bounded by parameter N_c, and the cooperating proxy independently draws a random count of incoming dummy packets bounded by N_s; each side also draws a random padding-window width from a uniform distribution bounded by W_min and W_max. Each side schedules its dummy packets by sampling arrival times from a Rayleigh distribution with that side's padding-window width as its scale parameter, which concentrates roughly 40% of dummy packets within the first window-width of the trace and tapers the rest, producing a front-loaded burst without a hard cutoff. Because the packet count and window width are redrawn independently for every trace of the same webpage, repeated visits to the same page produce traces with different total lengths and different packet-order patterns, defeating a classifier trained on defended traces. GLUE targets a different attacker step: before running any per-page classifier, the attacker must first segment a continuous traffic stream into per-page traces (find where one page-load ends and the next begins). GLUE inserts dummy "glue traces" between consecutive real page loads so a sequence of separately visited pages appears to the eavesdropper as one long, undivided trace; an attacker must first solve "split decision" (does this stream contain multiple pages at all) and "split finding" (where are the boundaries) before any per-page WF classifier can even run. GLUE also incorporates FRONT noise on the first page of each glued sequence, because the paper found GLUE alone leaves the first page's front insufficiently obscured.

### Measured results
Dataset DS-19, collected by the authors between February and April 2019 using Tor Browser 8.5a7 on Tor 0.4.0.1-alpha, driven by automated command-line browsing on one machine on a university network: Alexa top 100 websites, 100 visits each, as monitored pages, plus 10,000 other pages (after filtering pages that failed to load through Tor) as non-monitored pages. All FRONT results below use open-world evaluation with r = 10 (client visits one monitored page for every ten non-monitored pages) and 10-fold cross-validation, with true/wrong/false positives summed across folds before computing True Positive Rate (TPR), Wrong Positive Rate, False Positive Rate, precision, and F1.

Defense overhead (Table 3), against a no-defense baseline of 0% latency and 0% data overhead:

| Defense | Parameters | Latency overhead | Data overhead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tamaraw | rho_out=0.04, rho_in=0.012, L=50 | 78.43% | 162.93% |
| WTF-PAD | Normal rcv histogram | 0% | 32.71% |
| FT-1 (FRONT) | N_s = N_c = 1700, W_min = 1s, W_max = 14s | 0% | 33.01% |
| FT-2 (FRONT) | N_s = N_c = 2500, W_min = 1s, W_max = 14s | 0% | 48.80% |

F1 score (lower is a more effective defense) on DS-19, by attack (Table 4), against four published attacks: kNN, CUMUL, kFP (k-fingerprinting), and DF (Deep Fingerprinting), with DF's maximum trace length raised to 10,000 (from the 5,000 the DF paper recommends) to accommodate FRONT's dummy packets:

| Defense | kNN F1 | CUMUL F1 | kFP F1 | DF F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No defense | 0.86 | 0.76 | 0.93 | 0.94 |
| Tamaraw | 0.028 | 0.052 | 0.038 | 0.11 |
| WTF-PAD (33% data overhead) | 0.16 | 0.28 | 0.61 | 0.70 |
| FT-1, similar overhead to WTF-PAD | 0.048 | 0.18 | 0.54 | 0.47 |
| FT-2, 49% data overhead | 0.016 | 0.13 | 0.46 | 0.40 |

At matched data overhead against WTF-PAD, FT-1 lowers F1 against every one of the four attacks; against DF specifically, FT-1's F1 (0.47) is roughly two-thirds of WTF-PAD's (0.70).

Mechanism-level comparison against WTF-PAD, same DS-19 dataset: WTF-PAD spends 24% of its dummy-packet budget in the first quarter of a trace and 49% in the first half; FRONT spends 40% in the first quarter and 69% in the first half. The median coefficient of variation of dummy-packet counts injected per webpage class is 42% for FRONT versus 36% for WTF-PAD.

Recall of the kFP attack against FRONT-defended traces by webpage-size quartile (four groups of Alexa-top-100 pages divided by packet count, ranging up to 2039, 4368, 6611, and 28,199 packets per quartile): 24%, 24%, 35%, and 54% respectively; a tenfold increase in webpage size (quartile 1 to quartile 4) raises kFP's recall by 30 percentage points.

GLUE evaluation, same DS-19 dataset split into ATTACK_TRAIN (9,000 instances), SPLIT_TRAIN (2,000 instances), and EVALUATION (9,000 instances), FRONT noise set to N_s = N_c = 1100, glue-trace maximum duration d_max drawn from U(10s, 15s), inter-page dwell time drawn from U(1s, 10s), non-monitored-to-monitored page visit ratio 10:1. Two attacker conditions: told the true number of glued pages l directly ("without split decision"), or required to find l itself ("with split decision").

Without split decision, on undefended (no-GLUE) l-traces, the strongest attack (kFP) achieves 96% TPR and 97% precision at l=2, falling to 82% TPR and 82% precision at l=16. Against GLUE-defended traces, all four attacks fall below 5% TPR by l=16; DF is the best attack at l=2 with 54% TPR, then weakens quickly as l grows. With split decision required, all attacks perform worse than without it, falling below 1% precision by l=16; on undefended traces with split decision required, kFP still achieves 45%-75% TPR and 41%-77% precision across the same l range, since the paper's split-finding procedure exceeds 92% accuracy.

GLUE data overhead (Figure 12), computed from an average webpage load time d_P = 27.30 seconds measured on DS-19, under three assumed client dwell-time distributions: strict (dwell mean d_G = 2.5s, tail mean d_L = 5s) gives 3%-13% overhead depending on l; normal (d_G = 5.5s, d_L = 12.5s) gives 22%-44%; lenient (d_G = 10s, d_L = 20s) gives 35%-53%. Larger l (more pages glued together) reduces overhead within each setting. Measured overhead runs about 5-10 percentage points below the paper's closed-form overhead formula, attributed to uneven bandwidth density in real glue traces.

Impact of removing FRONT noise from the first page of a glued sequence (same l=2 to l=16 setting): with FRONT noise present, all four attacks achieve 20%-60% TPR on the first page; with FRONT noise removed, the same attacks achieve 40%-80% TPR on the first page.

### Parameters
- N_c, N_s (FRONT): client and proxy dummy-packet budgets; tested at N_c=N_s=1700 (FT-1, matched to WTF-PAD's ~33% overhead) and N_c=N_s=2500 (FT-2, 49% overhead); GLUE evaluation used N_c=N_s=1100.
- W_min, W_max (FRONT): padding-window bounds; both FT-1 and FT-2 use W_min=1s, W_max=14s. Appendix A (not extracted here in full) discusses tuning these.
- Rayleigh distribution scale parameter w: set per-trace to the sampled window width w_c (client) or w_s (proxy); about 40% of dummy packets fall within [0, w] by construction (closed-form: integral of the Rayleigh probability density from 0 to w equals ~0.40).
- l (GLUE): number of real pages glued into one apparent trace; evaluated across the range 2 to 16.
- d_max (GLUE): maximum glue-trace duration, drawn from U(10s, 15s) in the main evaluation.
- r (open-world precision definition): ratio of non-monitored to monitored page visits by the client; set to 10 for the FRONT evaluation ("a client that visits one monitored webpage for every ten non-monitored webpages").
- Attack parameters: kNN, kFP, and DF use each attack's own paper-suggested parameters, except DF's maximum trace length is raised from 5,000 to 10,000 to accommodate FRONT's added dummy packets; CUMUL's Support Vector Machine (SVM) parameters are tuned by the authors following CUMUL's own paper's procedure.

### Stated limitations
The paper states FRONT's performance was not sensitive to dataset age (tested on two datasets collected five years apart) or to page-size subsetting, except that it performed worse on very large webpages (consistent with the quartile-recall result above). The paper states it did not explore whether a client's own poor network conditions (where the client's link, not Tor, is the bottleneck) degrade FRONT's effectiveness, and states building FRONT to self-adjust to such conditions is left as future work. For GLUE, the paper states it evaluated an attacker with complete knowledge of the entire database of glue traces, and states it cannot prove that an attacker who instead pursues a strategy of directly detecting glue traces in the client's stream must fail; it offers three specific reasons that attack is difficult (network jitter perturbing scheduled glue-trace timestamps, glue traces being cut off early when the client resumes browsing, and glue traces being drawn from a population meant to resemble real page loads) but leaves the question of whether glue-trace detection is possible as open future work. The paper states it did not design FRONT or GLUE to provide a guarantee against all future attacks, contrasting this with Tamaraw's stronger (but far more expensive) property; it states it cannot prove that its "split decision" and "split finding" problems, which GLUE relies on being hard, are unsolvable in general. The paper proposes but does not implement or measure one deployment component: it proposes that Tor directory servers maintain and distribute large databases of glue traces for clients to draw from, and states only informally ("quite low") that the resulting distribution cost is acceptable, without a measured figure; it separately proposes, without evaluating, an on-the-fly client-side glue-trace generation alternative to eliminate that distribution cost.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Both defenses require a cooperating relay to run the defense logic jointly with the client; the paper specifies this must be the middle node of a three-hop Tor circuit, not the entry or exit node, because the entry node is the position the adversary is assumed to occupy and the exit node and web server must see undefended traffic (the middle node strips dummy packets before forwarding onward). The threat model assumes a purely passive eavesdropper that observes but does not delay, modify, or drop packets; the paper does not evaluate either defense against an active adversary. GLUE's protection depends on the client's own browsing behavior: the number of pages glued (l) and the resulting overhead are functions of how long the client dwells between page loads, so a system deploying GLUE has no fixed overhead figure to budget against and instead exposes a client-controllable range (3% to 53% in the paper's three tested dwell-time regimes). GLUE's proposed production deployment requires an additional infrastructure component not built or measured in this paper: a directory-server-hosted store of pre-generated glue traces that clients download from, which becomes a new object other components must serve, keep available, and refresh. FRONT requires the client and the cooperating proxy to independently and correctly instantiate the same Rayleigh-distribution sampling and the same discrete-uniform packet-count sampling procedure using their own local randomness; the two sides do not coordinate a shared random seed, since the padding schemes for the two directions are described as generated independently.

### Contradicts
None found among papers currently in this corpus. The paper's own comparison contradicts a claim, sometimes made informally elsewhere, that WTF-PAD adequately defends Tor against modern classifiers: Table 4 measures WTF-PAD leaving kFP and DF at 0.61 and 0.70 F1 respectively, effectiveness the paper characterizes as remaining high for those two attacks despite WTF-PAD's overhead.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: M. Juarez, M. Imani, M. Perry, C. Diaz, M. Wright. "Toward an Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense" (WTF-PAD), ESORICS 2016 — the direct lightweight-defense baseline FRONT is compared against throughout.
- competing: X. Cai, R. Nithyanand, T. Wang, R. Johnson, I. Goldberg. "A Systematic Approach to Developing and Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (Tamaraw), ACM CCS 2014 — the heavyweight regularization baseline compared against in Table 3 and Table 4.
- attack: P. Sirinam, M. Imani, M. Juarez, M. Wright. "Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning" (DF), ACM CCS 2018 — the strongest attack used throughout the evaluation; described as having defeated WTF-PAD.
- attack: J. Hayes, G. Danezis. "k-fingerprinting: A Robust Scalable Website Fingerprinting Technique" (kFP), USENIX Security 2016 — one of the four benchmark attacks.
- attack: A. Panchenko et al. "Website Fingerprinting at Internet Scale" (CUMUL), NDSS 2016 — one of the four benchmark attacks.
- foundational: P. Syverson, R. Dingledine, N. Mathewson. "Tor: The Second Generation Onion Router," USENIX Security 2004 — the onion-routing network both defenses are deployed on; already in this corpus as DINGLEDINE-USENIXSEC-04.
- competing: X. Wang, I. Goldberg. "Walkie-Talkie" as introduced by Wang and Goldberg, 2017 — a confusion-category defense using half-duplex browser communication, requiring client knowledge of webpage sizes, contrasted against FRONT's no-extra-infrastructure design in Table 1.
- attack: K. P. Dyer, S. E. Coull, T. Ristenpart, T. Shrimpton. "Peek-a-Boo, I Still See You: Why Efficient Traffic Analysis Countermeasures Fail" (introduces BuFLO), IEEE S&P 2012 — foundational regularization-defense analysis Table 1 compares against.

## [GRUBBS-SP-19] Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks
**Citation:** Paul Grubbs, Marie-Sarah Lacharite, Brice Minaud, Kenneth G. Paterson. "Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2019. DOI 10.1109/SP.2019.00030.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/011.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/011.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
The paper reconstructs the plaintext values or plaintext order of records in an encrypted database
from access-pattern leakage alone — the record identifiers a server returns for each query, without
seeing plaintext query or record content — by treating reconstruction as a statistical learning
problem. This reframing produces attacks whose query count depends only on the desired error
tolerance, not on the number of records or the number of possible plaintext values, which the
authors state as the first attacks with that scale-free property.

Mechanism (approximate order reconstruction, ApproxOrder, the paper's central result): the attacker
observes range queries against the database and, for each query, the encrypted database returns
which stored records fall inside the range. From the sequence of returned record sets the attacker
builds a PQ-tree, a data structure originally used for testing the consecutive-ones property, that
compactly records every ordering constraint the observed queries impose on the records. Reading
maximal-order-preserving groups ("buckets") out of the finished PQ-tree yields the records' order up
to a sacrifice: any two records whose true values differ by at most a fraction epsilon of the value
domain N may be merged into an ungrouped bucket, and records within epsilon N of the domain's two
extremes may be left ungrouped ("sacrificial epsilon-approximate order reconstruction",
epsilon-AOR). The attack requires no assumption about the query distribution — not independence,
not identical distribution, not uniformity — to run; a uniform-distribution assumption is used only
in the paper's own analysis of query count, not in the attack.

Mechanism (approximate value reconstruction, epsilon-ADR, extending order to value): given the
epsilon-AOR bucket structure and an auxiliary model of the database's value distribution (a
probability distribution over N approximating, but not necessarily equal to, the true one), the
attack in three steps: (1) record-rank estimation orients the ordered buckets left-to-right by
comparing the proportion of records estimated above versus below the domain midpoint against the
same proportion computed from the auxiliary distribution, and estimates how many sacrificed records
precede the first bucket; (2) partition estimation converts the estimated rank range of each bucket
into an estimated value-range boundary using order statistics of the auxiliary distribution; (3)
database estimation assigns every record in a bucket the median of the auxiliary distribution
restricted to that bucket's estimated value range.

Mechanism (approximate value reconstruction without order, ApproxValue, an independent attack
requiring i.i.d. uniformly random queries): assumes the database holds at least one record with
value in the range [0.2N, 0.3N] (or its reflection [0.7N, 0.8N]) and uses that anchor record's
observed query-match pattern as a reference to place other records by comparing their match patterns
against it.

### Measured results

| Attack | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| GeneralizedKKNO (sacrificial epsilon-ADR, generalizing Kellaris et al. to sparse databases) | O(epsilon^-4 log epsilon^-1) queries; generic lower bound Omega(epsilon^-4) | Analytical result; any data density, uniformly random range queries |
| ApproxValue (sacrificial epsilon-ADR, requires a record near the 0.2N-0.3N anchor point) | O(epsilon^-2 log epsilon^-1) queries; generic lower bound Omega(epsilon^-2) | Analytical result; any density given the anchor-record requirement, uniformly random range queries |
| ApproxValue, empirical query count at N = 10^6 with the anchor condition met | 500 queries recover almost all records to within 5% error, versus approximately 10^26 queries the KKNO exact-reconstruction attack would need for the same N | Synthetic data, uniformly random range queries |
| ApproxOrder (sacrificial epsilon-AOR, no query-distribution assumption needed to run) | O(epsilon^-1 log epsilon^-1) queries under a uniform-query assumption used only for the analysis; generic lower bound Omega(epsilon^-1 log epsilon^-1) | Analytical result; any density |
| ApproxOrder, empirical, uniform random range queries | At N = 10^6, after 500 queries the attack fully orders records except those differing by less than 2% of the domain size | Synthetic data, results averaged over 500 databases with 500 randomly sampled queries each |
| ApproxOrder, empirical, fixed-width range queries (width in {100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000}) | Behaves as predicted by the epsilon^-1 log epsilon^-1 bound after an initial period bottlenecked by sacrificed-record symmetric values, not bucket diameter | R = 1,000 records, N = 10,000 possible values, results averaged over 500 databases per range-query width |
| ADR from AOR plus auxiliary distribution (Algorithm 4), ZIP code dataset | Percent of records recovered to within 25%/50%/75% of N error: 10 queries → 4%/7%/11%; 25 queries → 2%/4%/7%; 50 queries → 1%/3%/6%; 100 queries → 1%/2%/5%. Baseline (guess the median): 15%/27%/37% | US FAA registered-pilot database, over 61,000 records, N = 9,999 (5-digit ZIP codes); auxiliary model = US Census ZIP-code population data (statistical distance from true distribution approximately 0.51); results averaged over 20 randomly generated query transcripts; run on Ubuntu 16.04, Intel Core i7-6700 at 3.4 GHz, Python 2.7, PQ-tree via a C++ library called through SWIG |
| ADR from AOR plus auxiliary distribution (Algorithm 4), salary dataset | Percent of records recovered to within 25%/50%/75% of N error: 10 queries → 2%/4%/7%; 25 queries → 1%/2%/4%; 50 queries → 1%/2%/3%; 100 queries → 1%/2%/3%. Baseline: 2%/5%/9% | California state public-employee salaries from 2016 (over 248,000 records, values 0-762,000 USD, outliers above 500,000 USD truncated), N = 500,000; subsampled to random 10,000-salary databases per trial; auxiliary model = New York state public-employee salaries from the same year (approximately 120,000 records; statistical distance from CA distribution approximately 0.19); results averaged over 10 subsampled databases x 10 query transcripts each |
| ADR headline figures quoted in the abstract | 50 queries recover the first two ZIP-code digits (often identifying a city) for a majority of records; 100 queries on salaries predict a majority to within 10,000 USD | Same ZIP-code and salary datasets and setup as above |
| Prefix-query reconstruction attack, last-name dataset | With approximately 500 prefix queries (mean 315 to reach the grouping condition in 9 of 10 trials): recovers the first character for over 70% of records. With 40,000 queries: recovers first two characters for over 55%. With 3,000,000 queries: recovers first three characters for over 40%, exactly recovering roughly 1,500 three-character last names | Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) database dump (2016), over 600,000 US law-enforcement personnel records; auxiliary data = US Census last-name frequency statistics; theoretical (epsilon-net) sample-complexity predictions for the same three targets were 1,491 / 120,000 / 6,000,000 queries, substantially higher than what the experiment needed |
| Prefix-query attack applied to the FAA ZIP-code dataset instead of last names | Performed poorly | Same ZIP-code dataset as the range-query experiment; degradation attributed by the authors to the auxiliary Census data poorly modeling the ZIP-code distribution |

### Parameters
Sacrificial-order/sacrificial-value error tolerance epsilon: swept as the independent variable in
every experiment (queries-vs-epsilon plots), not fixed to one value. Domain size N: 10,000 in the
fixed-width synthetic experiment, 9,999 for FAA ZIP codes, 500,000 for CA salaries, 10^6 in the
ApproxValue synthetic test. Record count R: 1,000 in the fixed-width synthetic experiment; over
61,000 for FAA ZIP codes; subsampled to 10,000 per trial for CA salaries; over 600,000 for the
last-name dataset. Range-query widths tested for fixed-width queries: 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000,
5000. Number of query transcripts averaged: 500 databases x 500 queries for the AOR synthetic tests;
20 transcripts for ZIP codes; 10 subsampled databases x 10 transcripts for salaries; 10 trials for
the prefix-query experiment. ApproxValue's anchor-record requirement: at least one record with value
in [0.2N, 0.3N] or its reflection [0.7N, 0.8N]. Hardware for Algorithm 4 and prefix experiments:
Ubuntu 16.04 desktop, Intel Core i7-6700 CPU at 3.4 GHz, Python 2.7, PQ-tree implementation in C++
called via SWIG.

### Stated limitations
The attacks assume the adversary knows the domain size N and the full set of possible queries, but
not the set of records in the database, their count, or that every value in [N] is populated (no
density assumption is required for the general attacks). ApproxValue additionally requires a record
with a value in a specific sub-range of the domain; the authors state this as a mild but real
precondition. The uniform-query-distribution assumption used to state ApproxOrder's O(epsilon^-1 log
epsilon^-1) query bound is used only for the paper's own complexity analysis; running the attack
itself needs no assumption about the query distribution, but the authors note this distinction only
holds cleanly for ApproxOrder, not for ApproxValue or GeneralizedKKNO, which require the queries to
be drawn i.i.d. and uniformly at random to run at all, and the authors state this requirement makes
those two attacks values "as important indicators of what is possible in principle" rather than
"practical, ready-for-use attacks" against a real deployment whose query distribution is unknown and
non-uniform. The heuristic that orients the sorted bucket list (OrientSubsets) chose the wrong
orientation in approximately half of the ZIP-code trials, because the ZIP-code value distribution is
close to flat around the domain midpoint, though the authors note an incorrect choice between only
two possible orientations is "mostly inconsequential" to the eventual error. A fraction of trials
produced a PQ-tree with no Q-node at its first level and were excluded from the reported statistics:
this happened rarely for ZIP codes, in about one-quarter of salary trials at 10 queries, and in about
one-tenth of salary trials at 100 queries; the authors state the attacker can detect this condition
and query further before running the attack. The prefix-query attack performed poorly on the
ZIP-code dataset because the available auxiliary distribution (Census population data) was a poor
model of the true distribution, illustrating that ADR-style attacks needing an auxiliary distribution
degrade when that distribution diverges from the truth. The paper's stated future work: extend the
approach to other query types of practical importance (edit distance, wildcard, substring queries)
and apply further learning-theory results (active or online learning) to access-pattern leakage
attacks and defenses; neither extension is carried out in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A server or peer implementing an encrypted database that returns record identifiers per query — the
minimal access-pattern leakage this paper attacks — must not treat that leakage as safe merely
because the ciphertext and query content are hidden: the epsilon-AOR attack requires only the
sequence of which stored items matched which range query, nothing about query content or plaintext
values, and no assumption that queries are independent or uniformly distributed. A design offering
range queries over encrypted or access-pattern-observable content should assume an observer with
query-response visibility can recover approximate record order using only O(epsilon^-1 log
epsilon^-1) observed queries, scale-free in both record count and domain size. Converting that order
recovery into approximate value recovery (epsilon-ADR) additionally requires the observer to hold, or
construct, an auxiliary distribution over the value domain that approximates the true one; a system
wanting to bound this specific escalation would need to prevent an observer's access to any such
distribution, which is generally infeasible for public distributions (Census data, published salary
tables). The prefix-query result establishes the same requires-only-access-pattern property extends
to prefix queries under an analogous auxiliary last-name-frequency distribution, so a design using
either range or prefix predicates over leakage-observable stored content faces both attack classes.

### Contradicts
The paper does not contradict a claim of its own predecessors' results; it explicitly generalizes and
extends Kellaris, Kollios, Nissim, O'Neill (KKNO16, CCS 2016) and Lacharite, Minaud, Paterson (LMP18,
IEEE S&P 2018), reproducing LMP's O(N log N) dense-database result as a special case at epsilon =
1/N. No claim commonly attributed to this paper needs correction from the text retrieved. Cross-paper
in this corpus: None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Kellaris, Kollios, Nissim, O'Neill, "Generic attacks on secure outsourced databases," CCS 2016 — foundational (KKNO, first exact range-query reconstruction attack; this paper's generalized version and comparison baseline).
- Lacharite, Minaud, Paterson, "Improved reconstruction attacks on encrypted data using range query leakage," IEEE S&P 2018 — foundational/competing (LMP, direct predecessor whose dense-database O(N log N) result this paper reproduces as a special case and whose auxiliary-distribution attack this paper's epsilon-ADR construction is compared against).

- Grubbs, Sekniqi, Bindschaedler, Naveed, Ristenpart, "Leakage-abuse attacks against order-revealing encryption," IEEE S&P 2017 — attack (order-leakage attack on a different encryption scheme, order-revealing encryption, cited on the severity of order leakage).
