## [HEILMAN-USENIXSEC-15] Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network
**Citation:** Ethan Heilman, Alison Kendler, Aviv Zohar, Sharon Goldberg. "Eclipse Attacks on Bitcoin's Peer-to-Peer Network." USENIX Security Symposium, 2015.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-heilman.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-heilman.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This paper takes over every connection a target Bitcoin node makes to the rest of the network (an eclipse attack), by exploiting how bitcoind version 0.9.3 selects which peer addresses to store and to reconnect to, rather than by poisoning a distributed-hash-table routing structure — Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network is unstructured, so the mechanism here is identity forgery against a connection table, not DHT routing-table poisoning. A node with a public IP address stores peer addresses in two on-disk tables: tried (64 buckets of up to 64 addresses each, for peers it has already successfully connected to) and new (256 buckets of up to 64 addresses each, for peers it has only heard about). Each address hashes deterministically to one tried bucket via a per-node secret key and the address's /16 IP prefix ("group"); when a bucket is full, bitcoin eviction picks four addresses from the bucket at random and replaces the oldest of the four with the new one, then moves that evicted address into new.

The attack has three exploitable properties the paper identifies directly in this table structure. First, any node can insert an address into a victim's tried table simply by making an unsolicited incoming connection to the victim from that address, and the eviction rule described above means an attacker's fresher addresses tend to displace older legitimate ones over repeated rounds. Second, a node accepts unsolicited ADDR messages (up to 1,000 addresses each) and inserts their contents directly into new without testing connectivity, so an attacker can flood new with "trash" (unreachable) addresses that eventually overwrite every legitimate entry there. Third, because outgoing-connection selection is biased toward addresses with the freshest timestamps, an attacker who keeps re-touching its own addresses across repeated rounds (each round taking a duration τ_a) can make its addresses look newer than the legitimate ones, whose timestamps grow stale as the attack runs for a duration τ_ℓ. Once the victim restarts — which the paper argues is not a rare event, citing a 25% chance of any given public-IP node going offline within 10 hours, forced software updates, and DDoS-induced restarts as ordinary causes — the victim reconnects using only tried and new, both of which the attacker has already populated, so with high probability all eight of its outgoing connections and its open incoming slots land on attacker-controlled addresses.

The paper derives a closed-form probability of eclipsing a victim, q(f, f′, τ_a, τ_ℓ)^8, as a function of f (the fraction of tried the attacker controls), f′ (the fraction of legitimate addresses still actively connected to the victim when it restarts), and the two time parameters, and validates this model against Monte Carlo simulation and live experiments on real bitcoind nodes.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| An infrastructure attacker with 32 distinct /24 IP blocks (8,192 addresses) or a 4,600-bot botnet can eclipse a victim with at least 85% probability, independent of total network size | Worst-case initial condition: tried and new tables completely full of fresh legitimate addresses (closed-form model, Section 4) |
| The same 8,192 honest, protocol-following addresses joining today's network (approximately 7,200 public-IP nodes at the time of writing) would eclipse a victim by chance with probability only about 0.6% (computed as (8192/(7200+8192))^8) | Comparison baseline computed by the paper, same network-size assumption |
| Without random address selection, an attacker controlling only f=72% of tried reaches 90% eclipse success by investing τ_ℓ=48 hours with τ_a=27-minute rounds; with random selection, reaching 90% requires f=98.7% | Closed-form model, Figure 1, f′ = 8/(64×64) (a full tried table with 8 addresses actively connected pre-restart) |
| A botnet exploiting multiple attack rounds can fill tried to its "initially empty" best case with roughly 6,000 addresses total | Closed-form model (equation 4) confirmed by Monte Carlo simulation, 100 trials per data point |
| An infrastructure attack with s > 200 address groups fills nearly every bucket in tried (55.5 of 64 buckets at s=32 groups; all but one bucket at s>67 groups) | Closed-form model (equation 9), group-to-bucket hashing with 4 independent hash functions |
| 448 real-world organizations (from CAIDA AS-to-organization and AS-to-prefix data, July 2014, supplemented by RIPE) hold at least 32 /16 groups and 256 addresses per group; such an organization eclipses a victim with over 80% probability by investing 5 hours at 27-minute rounds | Real-world IP-allocation measurement, not simulation |
| In the attacker's worst case for the smaller resource point specifically checked in Section 4.2.1: f=72% of tried with τ_a=27-minute rounds requires either 3,000 bots or an infrastructure attack of 20 groups × 256 addresses (5,120 addresses total) for 85% success; the same attack sustained for only 4 hours still exceeds 55% success | Closed-form model |
| Five live public-IP bitcoind nodes run continuously without restart for 43 days (12/23/2014-2/4/2015): new tables filled to 99% within 48 hours, but tried tables reached no more than 300/4,096 ≈ 8% full even after 43 days; 17% of tried addresses were more than 30 days old, 48% were more than 10 days old | Direct measurement of live nodes, supplemented by donated peers files from other operators (Table 1) |
| Live-experiment success rates (Table 2, 50 restarts per experiment, victim reverted to attack-end table state each time): worst-case infrastructure attack (32 groups × 256 addresses) 98% wins; worst-case botnet (2,300 addresses × 2 groups, 4,600 total) 100% wins; a transplanted-table botnet of 400 addresses run for 1 hour reached 88% wins; a live-node botnet attack of 400 addresses run for 1 hour reached 84% wins | Attacking machine forges TCP connections from reserved (240.0.0.0/8-249.0.0.0/8) IP ranges against victim bitcoind instances, either freshly initialized (worst case), loaded with a transplanted real node's tables, or attacking the paper's own live nodes directly |
| Countermeasures 1, 2, and 6 (deterministic random eviction, random address selection, quadrupling the number of tried/new buckets), once deployed, raise the botnet size needed for 50% eclipse success from thousands to 163,000 addresses, and to 284,000 addresses for 90% success | Closed-form model (equation 11) applied to the worst-case scenario, tried table fully legitimate before the attack begins |
| Countermeasure 3 (test-before-evict) bounds eclipse probability to f^8 < (1 − p·h/(64×64))^8 regardless of the number of addresses the attacker controls, where h is the number of legitimate addresses in tried and p is the fraction of those addresses that are live (accept incoming connections) during the attack | Closed-form derivation (equation 10), confirmed by Monte Carlo simulation (Figure 7) |
| With a measured live churn rate of p=28%, bounding eclipse success to 10% under test-before-evict requires about h=3,700 legitimate addresses in tried; the paper's own live nodes had h<400 | Combines the churn measurement from Table 1 with the equation-10 bound, showing test-before-evict alone is insufficient without also increasing h (motivating Countermeasure 4, feeler connections) |

### Parameters
- τ_a (attack round length): 27 minutes used throughout the closed-form model and most experiments.
- τ_ℓ (total time invested in the attack before the victim restarts): varied across experiments — 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 hours.
- f (fraction of tried controlled by the attacker) and f′ (fraction of tried still actively, freshly connected to the victim before restart): f′ = 8/(64×64) used as the standard "full table" assumption.
- s (number of distinct /16 address groups an infrastructure attacker controls) and t (addresses per group): tested at s=32, t=256 (8,192 total, the paper's primary worst-case infrastructure configuration) and s=20, t=256 (5,120 total).
- Botnet size (t, total distinct addresses, one group each): tested at 200, 400, 600, 2,300 (×2 groups = 4,600), with 400 identified as sufficient against the paper's own live nodes.
- p (per-address churn / liveness probability): measured at 28% on the paper's own live nodes (Table 1), used as the churn input for the test-before-evict bound.
- h (number of legitimate addresses in tried before the attack): the paper's own live nodes measured h<400 after 43 days of continuous uptime; the paper computes 3,700 as the h needed for 10% bounded eclipse probability at p=28% under test-before-evict.
- Number of outgoing connections: 8, the value bitcoind used at the time; the paper's own Countermeasure 7 proposes 12, reducing worst-case eclipse probability from f^8 to f^12.
- Table sizes: tried holds 64 buckets × 64 addresses (4,096 total); new holds 256 buckets × 64 addresses (16,384 total); Countermeasure 6 (deployed) scales both by a factor of four.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its attack applies only to nodes with public IP addresses; a private-IP node is affected only indirectly, if every one of its outgoing connections happens to be to an already-eclipsed public-IP node. The paper states its success-rate predictions from the closed-form model (Section 3.3) are a lower bound on the true success rate in practice, because the model assumes legitimate addresses are exactly τ_ℓ old at restart when in practice they are typically older — the paper's own experiments confirm this, with the actual success rate exceeding the model's prediction in almost every logged case (for example, one botnet configuration reached 88% actual success against a 34% prediction). The paper states Countermeasure 6 (more buckets) is effective only when tried already holds many legitimate addresses; if tried is mostly empty or stale, doubling the bucket count does not reduce the attacker's achieved fraction of tried, so this countermeasure is stated as requiring pairing with another (feeler connections) that actually populates tried with fresh legitimate entries. The paper states ensuring tried is kept full of legitimate addresses remains a challenge even after its proposed countermeasures, particularly because the live Bitcoin network may hold fewer than 16,384 public-IP nodes at a given time — fewer than the expanded table's total capacity. The paper explicitly limits its own scope by not studying Tor-connected nodes, citing separate prior work for that case.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The attack and its analysis assume the victim node eventually restarts; the paper argues this assumption is realistic (citing a measured 25% chance of a public-IP node going offline within 10 hours, forced software updates, and DDoS-inducible restarts) rather than treating it as a special case, so any system relying on connection-table integrity across the node's lifetime must account for restart as a normal, not exceptional, event. The paper's proposed test-before-evict countermeasure requires the node to attempt a live connection to the currently-stored older address before evicting it in favor of a new one, adding a network round-trip to every table-insertion decision, and its protection is bounded by the fraction of legitimate addresses actually online during the attack (parameter p) — a system deploying it still needs a separate mechanism (feeler connections, in this paper) to keep the legitimate-address count h in tried high enough for the resulting bound to be tight. The anchor-connections countermeasure requires the node to persist a small table of long-lived outgoing-connection addresses across restarts specifically so that at least one reconnection target is not subject to the tried/new selection process at all; this requires durable local storage that survives the same restart event the attack exploits. The paper's own diversify-incoming-connections and anomaly-detection suggestions both require the ability to observe and rate-limit by source IP address, which assumes the attacker cannot cheaply acquire many distinct source addresses — a assumption the paper's own infrastructure-attack analysis shows fails against any actor holding many IP address groups.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus.

## [HENZINGER-USENIXSEC-23] One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
**Citation:** Alexandra Henzinger, Matthew M. Hong, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Sarah Meiklejohn, Vinod Vaikuntanathan. "One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval." USENIX Security Symposium, 2023.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/949.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/949.pdf
**Domain:** G

### What it does
Private information retrieval (PIR) lets a client fetch one record from a server-held database
without the server learning which record was requested. The paper defines two single-server PIR
schemes — meaning the database lives on one server, with no non-colluding-server assumption — built
around a preprocessing step that shifts almost all server computation to a one-time offline phase,
independent of any client query.

Mechanism (SimplePIR): the server represents the N-record database as a square matrix D of
dimension roughly sqrt(N) by sqrt(N). Using Regev's learning-with-errors (LWE) based linearly
homomorphic encryption, the server precomputes, once per database and independent of any query, a
"hint" matrix that lets it later evaluate most of the matrix-vector product needed to answer a
query. This hint is not specific to any client; every client downloads and reuses the same hint
across an unbounded number of queries. To make one query, the client sends an encrypted
sqrt(N)-dimensional selection vector; the server computes the encrypted matrix-vector product using
its precomputed hint, needing per database byte fewer than one 32-bit multiplication and one 32-bit
addition at query time; the client decrypts to recover the requested column, then extracts its
desired record from that column using its own copy of the hint. The client holds no secret state
across queries (in contrast to schemes like SealPIR, whose clients keep persistent long-term
cryptographic secrets); the paper proves in an appendix that a malicious server can mount a
state-recovery attack against such stateful designs, breaking both past and future query privacy,
and states its stateless schemes are not vulnerable to that attack class.

Mechanism (DoublePIR): applies SimplePIR recursively to its own hint. In SimplePIR, of the
downloaded hint and the encrypted sqrt(N)-dimensional vector, the client actually needs only one
small part of the hint and one component of the vector to recover its record. DoublePIR runs
SimplePIR a second time over the hint matrix itself (using a non-black-box construction that saves a
factor equal to the lattice dimension — 1024 for the paper's chosen parameters — over a naive
recursive design), shrinking the client-downloaded hint to a size independent of the number of
records in the database, at the cost of higher per-query online communication and lower throughput
than SimplePIR.

Mechanism (private approximate set membership, applied to Certificate Transparency signed-certificate-timestamp
(SCT) auditing): the paper builds a new data structure for private set membership using either PIR
scheme, tolerant of a constant false-positive rate. Where a standard Bloom filter or PIR-by-keyword
approach requires the client to run PIR over a lambda*N-bit database (lambda approximately 128, the
security parameter, N the set size), this structure requires PIR over only 8N bits, a roughly
16x reduction in the size of the database the PIR is run over for this application.

### Measured results
All throughput measurements: single-threaded execution on an AWS c5n.metal instance running Ubuntu
22.04; each throughput figure is the average of five runs, with reported standard deviations under
10% of the measured throughput in all cases. Implementation: fewer than 1,200 lines of Go plus 200
lines of C for SimplePIR, plus 210 additional lines of Go for DoublePIR, no external library
dependencies, published under an MIT license.

| Scheme | Servers | Communication scaling | Max. measured throughput/core |
|---|---|---|---|
| DPF-based two-server PIR | 2 | O(log N) | 5,381 MB/s |
| XOR-based two-server PIR (constant-time) | 2 | O(sqrt N) | 6,067 MB/s |
| XOR-based two-server PIR (non-constant-time, side-channel-vulnerable) | 2 | O(sqrt N) | 11,797 MB/s |
| SealPIR | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 97 MB/s |
| MulPIR | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 69 MB/s (figure taken from the MulPIR paper; no public implementation available to these authors) |
| FastPIR | 1 | O(N) | 215 MB/s |
| OnionPIR | 1 | O(log N) | 104 MB/s |
| Spiral family | 1 | O(log N) | 1,314 MB/s |
| Kushilevitz-Ostrovsky + Paillier | 1 | O(N^epsilon) | 0.131 MB/s |
| XPIR | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 142 MB/s (figure taken from the SealPIR paper) |
| FrodoPIR (concurrent work) | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 1,256 MB/s |
| SimplePIR (this paper) | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 10,305 MB/s |
| DoublePIR (this paper) | 1 | O(sqrt N) | 7,622 MB/s |

Throughput figures normalized per core (two-server figures divided by two). Database and record
sizes underlying each figure are listed in the paper's Appendix A; for each competing scheme the
authors used the entry size that produced the highest reported throughput for that scheme.

Headline server-throughput comparison: SimplePIR reaches 10 GB/s/core (stated as 81% of the tested
machine's memory bandwidth), and DoublePIR reaches 7.4 GB/s/core, roughly 8x faster than the fastest
prior single-server PIR designed for the streaming setting (SpiralStreamPack) and roughly 30x faster
than the fastest prior single-server PIR designed for short entries (Spiral), both compared on the
same c5n.metal instance under the same methodology. SimplePIR/DoublePIR's per-core throughput
exceeds the per-server throughput of two-server PIR from distributed point functions (5.3 GB/s/core
cited). A hard upper bound for linear-work two-server PIR, measured by running only XOR operations
over the database, was 5.9 GB/s/core (full linear scan) and 11.5 GB/s/core (scan of a random half of
the database, non-constant-time).

| Quantity | SimplePIR | DoublePIR |
|---|---|---|
| Server compute per query, on a 1-byte-record database | fewer than one 32-bit multiplication and one 32-bit addition per database byte | same order, plus one additional SimplePIR-style recursive step |
| Hint size, general formula | roughly 4*sqrt(N) KB for a database of N bytes | roughly 16 MB for a database of one-byte records, independent of record count |
| Per-query online communication, 1 GB database | 242 KB | 345 KB |
| Hint size, 1 GB database | 121 MB | not separately stated at this size; the general 16 MB figure is for one-byte records |

Communication/throughput trade-off (Figure 6, database of 2^33 bits, entry sizes swept from 100 KB
to 10 MB, communication amortized over 100 queries): on databases with short entries, DoublePIR's
amortized communication is comparable to the most communication-efficient prior schemes (Spiral,
SpiralPack, SealPIR, OnionPIR); as entry size grows, DoublePIR's amortized communication rises
because the client downloads more hints. SpiralStream, SpiralStreamPack, and FastPIR — the schemes
with throughput closest to SimplePIR/DoublePIR — have much larger amortized communication than
either SimplePIR or DoublePIR on entry sizes below one kilobit.

Certificate Transparency SCT-auditing application: roughly five billion active SCTs exist in the web
today (cited to a third-party measurement source, not measured by this paper), with roughly six
million added or removed per day. Google Chrome's deployed approach provides k-anonymity for k=1000
and requires 24 bytes average client communication per TLS connection. This paper's PIR-based
construction, providing full cryptographic privacy rather than k-anonymity, requires 150 bytes and
0.0003 core-seconds of server compute per TLS connection on average, plus 16 MB of client download
and 150 KB of client storage per month to maintain the hint.

### Parameters
Security: plain learning-with-errors (LWE) assumption (Regev's encryption scheme), stated by the
authors as a weaker, more standard cryptographic assumption than the ring-LWE or NTRU-style
assumptions some prior lattice-based single-server PIR schemes use. Lattice dimension used for the
paper's concrete parameters: 1,024 (the value the DoublePIR construction's stated savings factor is
computed against). LWE parameters (n, q, chi) and plaintext modulus p are defined generically in the
construction (Section 4-5 formal descriptions) with p much less than q, delta = floor(q/p); the paper
does not give one single fixed numeric (n, q, chi, p) tuple as "the" deployment parameter set in the
text extracted here — parameters are chosen per database size via the paper's own selection
procedure, with database and record sizes for each comparison point tabulated in Appendix A. Security
notion: (T, epsilon)-security, indistinguishability of query distributions for any two indices i, j
against an adversary running in time at most T, with distinguishing advantage at most epsilon.
Certificate Transparency false-positive tolerance: the client's approximate-membership check is
correct in that a member string always returns "valid," but a non-member string returns "valid" with
probability at most 1/2 (a single check); correctness against a malicious auditor is explicitly not
required, since a malicious auditor could trivially misstate its own set of SCTs. Private
approximate-set-membership data-structure size: 8N bits for a set of size N, versus lambda*N bits
(lambda approximately 128) for a standard Bloom filter run under PIR, a stated 16x size reduction
driving a corresponding throughput speedup in the SCT application.

### Stated limitations
Two limitations are stated directly by the authors. First, the client must download a hint before
making any query; on databases of gigabyte scale the hint is tens of megabytes, and if a client makes
only a single query, hint download dominates total communication. Second, both schemes' online
per-query communication is on the order of hundreds of kilobytes, roughly 10x larger than some prior
single-server PIR schemes achieve. The authors state these as an intentional trade-off — large
computation savings and a small, simple codebase, at the cost of communication and storage overhead —
rather than as unresolved problems. Constructing a linearly homomorphic encryption scheme with
preprocessing that produces a smaller hint than sqrt(N) hints of sqrt(N) inputs each is stated as an
open direction for future work, which would reduce the offline communication in the resulting PIR
schemes. The Certificate Transparency auditing protocol does not require correctness to hold against
a malicious auditor (an auditor that lies about its own SCT set is not defended against), only privacy
for an honest client interacting with such an adversary; the paper explicitly limits its stated
security property to client privacy in that setting, not universal correctness. Extending the private
set-membership construction so that a malicious auditor cannot cause a legitimate website to be
flagged incorrectly is stated as an intriguing direction for future work, not solved in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A deployment must give every client an offline channel to download the per-database hint (121 MB for
a 1 GB database under SimplePIR, or 16 MB independent of record count under DoublePIR for one-byte
records) before that client's first query, and must re-distribute an updated hint whenever the
underlying database's content changes materially enough to invalidate the old hint's precomputed
structure; the paper does not analyze hint refresh cost under a continuously updating database, so a
system with frequent updates needs a separate accounting of that cost. Because clients hold no secret
state across queries, a system built on these schemes does not need the persistent per-client
key-management infrastructure that stateful schemes like SealPIR require, and is immune to the
state-recovery attack the paper describes against stateful designs — but the hint's non-client-specific,
reusable nature means the server must serve the identical hint to every client, so a design cannot
customize per-client database views through the hint mechanism. Security relies on the plain LWE
assumption; the throughput and communication figures reported here presuppose the AWS c5n.metal
single-threaded benchmarking environment the paper used, and porting the throughput number to a
different core or memory-bandwidth profile requires re-measurement, since SimplePIR's headline
throughput is explicitly reported relative to that machine's own memory bandwidth (81%). The
Certificate Transparency application requires the auditor (Certificate Transparency log server or
proxy) to hold the full SCT set the client will query against and to serve the same hint to all
clients; the paper's stated 16x speedup over Bloom-filter-based approaches for this application
assumes acceptance of a constant false-positive rate rather than exact membership.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper positions SimplePIR/DoublePIR as new points on a throughput-communication
trade-off curve, not as invalidating prior schemes' claims. Cross-paper in this corpus: this entry's
1,314 MB/s figure attributed to "the Spiral family" (their Table 1, sourced by these authors from the
Spiral paper or a related paper for the entry size that produced Spiral's own best reported
throughput) is not directly comparable, entry-size for entry-size, to the specific per-configuration
throughput numbers recorded in MENON-SP-22's own Table 2/3/4 in this corpus (which range from
159 MB/s to 1.94 GB/s across configurations); a reader combining the two entries should use each
paper's own reported configuration rather than treat the single 1,314 MB/s figure as Spiral's
throughput in general. MENON-USENIXSEC-24 (YPIR, this corpus) is the authors' own later paper
explicitly built to reach SimplePIR-class throughput while retaining Spiral-style small per-query
communication; a synthesis combining all three entries should check MENON-USENIXSEC-24's comparison
table against the SimplePIR/DoublePIR numbers recorded here rather than assume consistency.

### References worth retrieving
- Kushilevitz, Ostrovsky, "Replication is not needed: Single database, computationally-private
  information retrieval," FOCS 1997 — foundational (the paper's explicit starting-point construction;
  SimplePIR's server matrix representation and the DoublePIR recursion both descend from this).
- Regev, "On lattices, learning with errors, random linear codes, and cryptography," STOC 2005 —
  foundational (defines the LWE assumption and the Regev encryption scheme SimplePIR is built on).
- Chor, Goldreich, Kushilevitz, Sudan, "Private information retrieval," (journal version CHOR-JACM-98
  in this corpus) — foundational (defines PIR in the multi-server setting).
- Angel, Chen, Laine, Setty, "PIR with compressed queries and amortized query processing" (SealPIR) —
  competing (direct throughput comparison target; also the subject of the stateful-client

  corpus) — competing (direct throughput/communication comparison target across every table).
- Ahmad, Yang, Agrawal, El Abbadi, Gupta, "Addra" (FastPIR) — competing (direct comparison target).
- Mughees, Chen, Ren, "OnionPIR: Response efficient single-server PIR" — competing (direct comparison
  target).
- Ali, Lepoint, Patel, Raykova, Schoppmann, Seth, Yeo, "MulPIR" — competing (comparison target;
  throughput figure taken from the MulPIR paper directly, since no public implementation exists).
- Davidson, Pestana, Celi, "FrodoPIR" — competing (concurrent, near-identical throughput comparison
  target explicitly noted as concurrent work).
- Corrigan-Gibbs, Henzinger, Kogan, "Single-server private information retrieval with sublinear
  amortized time," EUROCRYPT 2022 — foundational (an earlier construction by an overlapping author
  set, a distinct paper from this one).
- Corrigan-Gibbs, Kogan, "Private information retrieval with sublinear online time," EUROCRYPT 2020 —
  foundational (predecessor sublinear-online-time PIR).
- Laurie, "Certificate transparency," Communications of the ACM — foundational (defines the

- DeBlasio, "Opt-out SCT auditing in Chrome" — foundational (describes Google Chrome's current

## [HERRMANN-P2P-14] Censorship-Resistant and Privacy-Preserving Distributed Web Search
**Citation:** Michael Herrmann, Ren Zhang, Kai-Chun Ning, Claudia Diaz, Bart Preneel. "Censorship-Resistant and Privacy-Preserving Distributed Web Search." IEEE P2P, 2014. DOI 10.1109/P2P.2014.6934312.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://cosicdatabase.esat.kuleuven.be/backend/publications/files/conferencepaper/2422
**Source URL:** https://cosicdatabase.esat.kuleuven.be/backend/publications/files/conferencepaper/2422
**Domain:** B

### What it does
The paper analyzes the three real-world distributed web search engines (DWSE) the authors identify as actually deployed — Faroo, Seeks, and YaCy — for resistance to censorship of search results and for protection of a searcher's identity, demonstrates working attacks against one of them (YaCy) on a live network, then proposes two new defense protocols (node density and webpage verification) and evaluates them by simulation.

Faroo runs a modified Kademlia distributed hash table (DHT); each crawled webpage generates reverse-word-index (RWI) entries of the form search-term to URL, each entry stored on the 20 nodes whose Kademlia IDs are closest to the hash of the search term, and a query is answered by the nodes closest to that hash, returning only the top 100 results. Node IDs are self-chosen (derived from the querying client's MAC address and other local information), which the paper identifies as the property an eclipse attack (placing malicious nodes to surround and intercept traffic to a target ID) exploits: an attacker computes the target ID of a keyword, generates 20 node IDs closer to it than any honest node, and deploys nodes with those IDs to become the sole index holders for that keyword.

Seeks runs on a Chord DHT but maps a query to other users who issued similar queries (via a locality-sensitive hash placing similar queries at the same index nodes), not to RWI entries, and re-ranks results already returned by centralized search engines rather than maintaining its own web index; the paper states this design already forgoes searcher anonymity by construction, since finding who is interested in a query only requires issuing that query.

YaCy addresses its full 63-bit ID space as a ring resembling Chord; every peer maintains a near-complete view of every other peer via principal (super-)peers that aggregate peer information and a periodic peer-ping gossip protocol. An RWI entry's address is 4 bits from the URL's hash and 59 bits from the word's hash, stored at the 3 closest successor peers; because all words on one URL share the same top 4 bits, all entries for one page fall in one "vertical partition" of the address ring. A single-term search builds a candidate set from the 2 closest successors of each of the 16 possible vertical positions for that term, plus (with 80% probability each) the 5 self-reported highest-RWI-count peers; the paper identifies that every value entering this candidate-set computation (RWI count, "root-mode" gossip-freshness flag, last-seen timestamp) is self-reported by the peer being described, with no verification by any other peer.

The paper's two proposed defenses: (1) the node density protocol flags a lookup target as likely eclipsed when the span (distance) covered by the r closest successor nodes to that target falls below a threshold p_n times the network-wide average span s, on the reasoning that an attacker inserting malicious nodes to surround a target compresses that span; it depends on a separately cited node-ID generation scheme (Zhang et al., reference [11]) to prevent an attacker from freely choosing IDs. (2) The webpage verification protocol distributes verification "tickets" for stored entries to random other peers, who periodically re-query the network for that entry and can detect a peer that is silently dropping or filtering it, using an anonymous lookup mechanism (Octopus) so the verifying peer's own identity and target are not exposed to the peer under test.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| YaCy live-network candidate-set composition, verified by direct experiment | Two closest successors to each vertical position: 100% inclusion; third closest successor: 0%; 5 highest-self-reported-RWI-count peers: mean 75.5% inclusion, std 4.79%; all other peers: 0% (RWI search). Solr search: root-mode peers, mean 79.23% inclusion, std 5.22%; the one Robinson peer with a matching search tag: 100%; the 9 plain Robinson peers: mean 26.07%, std 3.32% | private YaCy network of 149 PlanetLab nodes plus 1 lab-controlled principal/bootstrap peer (61 ordinary peers, 5 highest-RWI-count peers, 25 root-mode peers, 9 Robinson peers, 1 tagged Robinson peer, 3 peers placed after each vertical position for the term "Jediism"); 3 peers searched "Jediism" 50 times each at 200s/250s/300s intervals |
| YaCy keyword censorship, minimum attacker cost | 32 malicious peers suffice to receive/censor all search requests for one term, independent of network size, with 100% observed success rate in the experiment | live PlanetLab test network described above; cost derived from 2 successors x 16 vertical positions plus self-reported RWI-count manipulation, so the peer count does not scale with total network size |
| YaCy Solr-search route-capture attack (forcing honest peers to only peer-ping malicious peers) | 42, 36, and 28 minutes to complete, at 6.7%, 10%, and 20% malicious-peer fractions respectively; minimum 3 malicious peers required (each honest peer pings 3 peers per round) | same 150-peer test network |
| Snapshot-freshness improvement from active pinging | attacker learns 1% to 6% more peers than from the public principal-peer seedlist alone | queried freeworld's (YaCy's public network) principal peers at their 30-second seedlist-publication interval, then pinged the 50 most-recently-seen peers for their own seedlists |
| Node density protocol, detection vs. false-positive tradeoff | at p_n = 0.5: ~97% of attacks detected (3.0% false negative), 3.06% false positive; full curve: p_n=0.4 gives 0.82% FP/5.83% FN, p_n=0.45 gives 1.73%/4.08%, p_n=0.55 gives 5.0%/2.0%, p_n=0.6 gives 7.48%/1.36% | simulation of 1,000,000 honest nodes, 20,000 attacked (eclipsed) target IDs and 20,000 non-attacked targets, r=8 successor nodes required for censorship, 8 malicious nodes inserted per attacked target; results stated as quantitatively similar across other tested network sizes |
| Node density protocol under a Sybil attack shrinking the average span | at p_n=0.5 fixed: f=20% malicious gives 2.06% FP/3.68% FN; f=30% gives 0.91%/5.5%; f=40% gives 0.37%/8.37% (91.6% of attacks still detected); f=50% gives 0.11%/12.78% | same simulated network; f=50% corresponds to 1,000,000 malicious nodes added to the 1,000,000 honest nodes; 20,000 censored and 20,000 uncensored targets in each condition |
| Node density protocol, attack life expectancy | over 1,240 collected successful-attack lifetimes: longest = 2.2t, average = 0.35t (t = mean honest-node lifetime, exponentially distributed) | p_n=0.5 fixed; new nodes join at random ring positions replacing dead ones; an attack ends when a new node falls within the p_n x s region past the eclipsed target |
| Webpage verification protocol effectiveness | at verification probability p_v=1e-6, attacker censors most search requests before detection; at p_v=1e-4, detection efficiency rises significantly; at p_v=1e-3, attacker is "virtually not able to censor search results" | simulated networks of 1,000, 10,000, and 100,000 honest nodes (results stated as quantitatively the same across sizes; detailed figure given for 100,000); 20 search topics with Zipf(0.5) popularity, each node generating 1,000 entries and 2 tickets per entry, one-month simulated duration, per-minute per-honest-node query probability p_q=7%, 8 malicious successor nodes per attacked target |
| Webpage verification overhead | "negligible" — at p_v=1e-3 each node issues one verification request on average every 1,000 minutes, and the underlying anonymous-lookup primitive (Octopus, from a separately cited paper) is reported elsewhere to consume 4.3 Kbps at one secure lookup per 10 minutes | same simulation configuration; the 4.3 Kbps figure is attributed to Octopus's own paper [4], not independently measured here |

### Parameters
- Threat model: an internal, active, static (per Raymond's taxonomy) attacker controlling a set of colluding nodes with a modified client; the network is established by honest users and the attacker does not control bootstrap machines; a global (network-wide passive observer) attacker is explicitly excluded from scope.
- Node density protocol: r = 8 (successor nodes an attacker must control to censor a target — described by the authors as deliberately low, favoring the attacker, relative to Faroo's real value of 20); p_n swept over {0.4, 0.45, 0.5, 0.55, 0.6}; Sybil-fraction f swept over {20%, 30%, 40%, 50%}.
- Webpage verification protocol: p_q (per-minute query probability) = 7%; p_v (per-minute verification-request probability) swept over {1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-3}; 20 topics, Zipf exponent 0.5, 1,000 entries per node, 2 tickets per entry, one-month simulated run.
- YaCy live test network: 149 PlanetLab nodes plus 1 lab-controlled principal/bootstrap peer; unmodified YaCy client software on all honest peers.

### Stated limitations
The two proposed protocols provide only heuristic, not formally verified, guarantees; the authors state that formally verifying whether a DWSE satisfies censorship resistance and privacy protection is left to future work. The authors state explicitly that their countermeasures do not make a censorship attack impossible — they only raise its cost, so that an attacker with modest resources cannot inflict significant harm, while a sufficiently resourced attacker remains a known-hard, unsolved problem in peer-to-peer (P2P) systems generally. The threat model excludes a global (network-wide) passive adversary by construction. The Solr-search route-capture attack against YaCy could not fully control the random-Robinson-peer subset of the candidate set: an honest peer that already knows another peer stores RWI entries cannot be deceived into believing that peer is a Robinson peer, so this vector was identified as harder for the attacker than the root-mode and RWI-count vectors, though the authors state the attack can still partly succeed by spreading false Robinson-peer claims or via denial-of-service against Robinson peers. The node density protocol's underlying node-ID generation scheme is not evaluated in this paper; the authors explicitly defer to a separately cited paper [11] for that evaluation. No live-network experiment tests the two proposed defenses; both are evaluated only by simulation.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- The node density protocol requires an ID-generation scheme (cited separately, not built here) that prevents an attacker from freely choosing arbitrary node IDs; without it, an attacker can still place IDs precisely enough to defeat the density check, as demonstrated for YaCy and Faroo's current unrestricted self-chosen IDs.
- The node density protocol requires a network-wide consistent value for the reference span s that all honest nodes agree on; the paper states this needs a trusted certification authority (CA) known to all peers if a single fixed value is to be used network-wide, introducing a trust dependency the base DHT design does not otherwise have.
- The webpage verification protocol requires an underlying anonymous-lookup primitive (the paper specifies ShadowWalker or Octopus) so that a verifying peer's identity and target are not exposed to the peer being checked; without query anonymity, the peer under test could distinguish verification traffic from ordinary search traffic and pass every check while still censoring real users.
- The webpage verification protocol requires a routing-table update mechanism that removes a peer once flagged as malicious from every honest peer's local view; the paper assumes this removal is possible and effective but does not itself specify or evaluate that removal mechanism's own robustness against a peer rejoining under a new identity.
- Achieving searcher anonymity and query unlinkability (the two privacy properties the paper specifies) requires layering a separate anonymous-communication protocol (onion-routed paths via ShadowWalker or Octopus) beneath the DWSE; the DWSE mechanisms proposed here (node density, webpage verification) address only censorship resistance, not privacy, on their own.
- Recommendations are stated as built for a structured (DHT) overlay specifically, using Chord as the underlying routing substrate; the authors state this choice is made for scalability over unstructured networks and to avoid routing private information through a central server, so the proposed defenses are not stated to transfer to an unstructured overlay without further work.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Within its own related-work discussion, the paper states that a separately cited evaluation methodology for obfuscation-based private web search (OB-PWS, e.g. TrackMeNot-style dummy-query techniques) overestimates the privacy protection it provides, because that evaluation does not model a strategic adversary aware of the obfuscation mechanism — this is the authors' own attributed characterization of a different paper's [10] finding, not an independent measurement made in this paper.

### References worth retrieving
- **[2] Singh, Ngan, Druschel, Wallach, "Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses," IEEE INFOCOM 2006** — foundational: the eclipse attack this paper's central attack technique and its node density defense both target.
- **[3] Mittal, Borisov, "ShadowWalker: Peer-to-Peer Anonymous Communication Using Redundant Structured Topologies," ACM CCS 2009** — competing/foundational: one of the two anonymous-path primitives recommended for searcher anonymity; the paper notes ShadowWalker does not provide strong query unlinkability on its own.
- **[4] Wang, Borisov, "Octopus: A Secure and Anonymous DHT Lookup," IEEE ICDCS 2012** — foundational: the anonymous-lookup primitive the webpage verification protocol's overhead figure (4.3 Kbps per 10-minute lookup) is drawn from; also the source of the "attack life expectancy" simulation methodology this paper reuses.
- **[5] Liang, Naoumov, Ross, "The Index Poisoning Attack in P2P File Sharing Systems," IEEE INFOCOM 2006** — attack: the index poisoning attack this paper's threat model cites as one of the three well-known P2P attacks all three DWSE are shown vulnerable to.
- **[10] Balsa, Troncoso, Diaz, "OB-PWS: Obfuscation-Based Private Web Search," IEEE S&P 2012** — attack/critique: the source of the claim (adopted here) that OB-PWS evaluations overestimate protection against a strategic, obfuscation-aware adversary.
- **[11] Zhang, Zhang, Chen, Qin, Liu, Zhang, "Making Eclipse Attacks Computationally Infeasible in Large-Scale DHTs," IEEE PCCC or similar, cited as reference [11]** — foundational: the node-ID generation scheme the node density protocol depends on and explicitly does not itself evaluate.
- **[7] Maymounkov, Mazieres, "Kademlia," IPTPS 2002** — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF.md section 7): the DHT Faroo's design modifies.

## [HOFFMAN-CSUR-09] A Survey of Attack and Defense Techniques for Reputation Systems
**Citation:** Kevin Hoffman, David Zage, Cristina Nita-Rotaru. "A Survey of Attack and Defense Techniques for Reputation Systems." ACM Computing Surveys, 2009. DOI 10.1145/1592451.1592452.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://cnitarot.github.io/papers/p2p-reputation-survey.pdf
**Source URL:** https://cnitarot.github.io/papers/p2p-reputation-survey.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper provides a common vocabulary for comparing published reputation systems, so that a reader can identify which design choice in a given system permits which attack, without re-deriving the analysis for each new system independently. It decomposes every reputation system into three dimensions: formulation (the abstract specification of how raw observations turn into a reputation metric — its information sources, information type, and the metric itself), calculation (the concrete algorithm computing the metric value, characterized by structure, determinism, and computational efficiency), and dissemination (how computed values reach the parties that need them, characterized by structure, determinism, storage durability, and redundancy). Reputation-system input falls into four source types: manual feedback, automatic indirect observation, automatic direct observation, and inferred data propagated from other identities' observations.

The paper classifies attacks into five categories by which goal of the reputation system the attack defeats. Self-promoting attacks falsely raise the attacker's own reputation, exploiting formulation dimensions that accept positive feedback without verifying it corresponds to a real interaction. Whitewashing attacks let an attacker who has damaged its reputation escape the consequence and restart with a fresh or repaired reputation, exploiting the formulation's failure to distinguish newcomers from previously misbehaving identities. Slandering attacks report false negative feedback to lower another identity's reputation, exploiting formulation dimensions that lack feedback authentication or that weight negative feedback heavily. Orchestrated attacks combine several of the above strategies across a coalition of colluding identities that vary their behavior over time (the paper cites the oscillation attack, where colluders split into teams that alternate between honest and dishonest behavior to sustain average reputation while extracting the benefit of misbehavior). Denial-of-service attacks target the calculation or dissemination dimensions directly, for example by overloading a centralized calculation node or exploiting an underlying distributed hash table's own vulnerabilities.

For each attack category the paper pairs the exploited component with a corresponding defense family: mechanisms limiting the acquisition of multiple identities (centralized certificate issuance, IP-address-to-key binding, network coordinates, web-of-trust propagation, or social-network-based limits) address self-promoting and Sybil-enabled attacks; direct-observation verification and pre-trusted identity sets address formulation manipulation generally; redundancy and randomization in calculation and dissemination address denial of service; and irrefutable cryptographic proofs of interaction address slandering and fabricated feedback.

### Measured results
This is a survey; it reports no original experiments. Its factual content is a structured comparison of 24 published reputation systems (Beth 94, Zimmermann 95, eBay 96, Yu 00, P-Grid 01, CORE 02, XRep 02, EigenTrust 03, Lee 03, TrustMe 03, Xiong 03, Buchegger 04, Feldman 04, Guha 04, Marti 04, ARA 05, Scrivener 05, Song 05, TrustGuard 05, Xiong 05, Credence 06, PowerTrust 06, P2PRep 06, Li 07) along two paired tables: one recording each system's formulation, calculation, and dissemination design choices (including the asymptotic computational cost to calculate the reputation metric for a single identity — values ranging from O(1) for Buchegger 04 and Scrivener 05 to O(n^2) for Guha 04 and Xiong 05, where n is the number of nodes), and one recording, on an ordinal scale (none, minimal, partial, full), each system's susceptibility to each of the five attack categories against the defense mechanisms it employs. EigenTrust is stated to reduce its per-identity calculation cost from O(n) to O(log n) without loss of accuracy by relying on pre-trusted identities, a specific claim traced to its own source (Kamvar et al. 2003) rather than independently re-derived here.

### Parameters
Not applicable — the paper defines an analysis framework and taxonomy, not a mechanism with tunable parameters of its own. Individual systems' parameters (e.g., EigenTrust's pre-trusted identity set) are described qualitatively within the framework rather than with specific numeric values the survey itself sets or varies.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that none of the 24 surveyed reputation systems defends against all five attack categories, and that most existing techniques address selfish rational attackers plus only a limited subset of coalition-based malicious attacks. The attacker model adopted treats all attackers as insiders (entities with legitimate, authenticated access to the system) on the stated grounds that reputation systems push trust decisions to network edges, where end-node compromise is common, and this scoping choice is stated explicitly rather than derived — outsider (unauthenticated) attackers are outside the paper's classification. The paper states that identifying orchestrated attacks is difficult because colluders performing different roles at different times may show no direct observable interaction within any given time window, so clique-detection approaches over an identity-interaction graph can miss coordinated collusion that is only indirectly observable. On formulation sensitivity to negative feedback, the paper states an inherent trade-off it does not resolve: lower sensitivity resists slander from malicious collectives but tolerates prolonged bad behavior for the same reputation decrease, while higher sensitivity punishes bad behavior faster but exposes honest identities to more effective slander — stated as a property of the design space, without recommending a specific point on this trade-off. Reputation-based systems that compute trust exclusively from direct information limit exposure to slander but cannot function in systems with sparse pairwise interaction, where the paper states trust inference (using indirect, propagated observations) becomes necessary and must itself be made robust to attack.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A reputation system built using this framework requires an authentication mechanism external to the reputation logic itself to bind feedback to the identity that produced it; the paper states systems lacking data authentication and integrity checks cannot distinguish fabricated from legitimate feedback and are vulnerable to self-promotion and slandering as a direct consequence. Systems relying on direct-information-only formulations to resist slander require that interactions between identities be frequent enough to produce sufficient direct observations; below that density, the system must fall back to indirect, inferred trust data, which reintroduces exposure to propagated false information. Distributed calculation and dissemination approaches that use redundancy to resist denial of service require an underlying storage or routing layer (the paper cites DHT-based storage as one option) that itself is robust, since the paper explicitly notes DHTs carry their own vulnerabilities that an attacker can exploit to deny service to the reputation layer built on top. Systems using pre-trusted identity sets (the paper cites EigenTrust) require that this set be established and its members remain trustworthy externally to the reputation calculation itself, since the calculation's probabilistic convergence guarantee depends on treating pre-trusted identities as fixed anchors.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. This paper is repeatedly cited elsewhere in Sybil- and reputation-defense literature as the canonical component/attack taxonomy; nothing in its text claims a quantitative result that a target-corpus paper here disputes.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: J. R. Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 — the origin of the Sybil-attack framing the survey applies throughout its self-promoting and identity-multiplication attack discussion
- competing: S. D. Kamvar, M. T. Schlosser, H. Garcia-Molina, "The EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks," 2003 — one of the six systems analyzed in depth (Section 6.2), stated to rely on pre-trusted identities for convergence and reduces calculation cost from O(n) to O(log n)
- competing: P. Michiardi, R. Molva, "CORE: A Collaborative Reputation Mechanism to Enforce Node Cooperation in Mobile Ad Hoc Networks," 2002 — analyzed in depth (Section 6.1) as a heuristic-based defense
- competing: S. Marti, H. Garcia-Molina, [reputation/incentive work in P2P networks, 2004] — source of the "traitor" terminology for attackers exploiting slow reputation decay after gaining trust
- competing: M. Feldman, K. Lai, I. Stoica, J. Chuang, "Robust Incentive Techniques for Peer-to-Peer Networks," 2004 — source of the "mole" terminology for attackers interacting honestly with some identities while attacking via others
- competing: K. Walsh, E. G. Sirer, [Credence, cited in this survey's Section 6 analysis] — anonymous but semi-controlled certificate issuance requiring expensive client-side computation, proposed as a Sybil-attack mitigation
- attack: N. B. Douceur / related Sybil-attack literature on IP-address spoofing and network-coordinate manipulation defeating decentralized identity-binding defenses, cited via Zage and Nita-Rotaru 2007

### Verbatim extracts
"the formulation is a critical component since any weakness in the design of the formulation allows malicious manipulation" — on why formulation is the paper's primary analytical dimension.
"none of the existing systems provide defenses against all the attacks presented" — stated summary finding across the 24 surveyed systems.
"attackers can either work alone or in coalitions... we are primarily concerned with attacks caused by coalitions" — stated scope of the attacker model.
"identifying orchestrated attacks is difficult since instead of trying to identify cliques" — stated limitation of clique-based collusion detection.
"some distributed storage components such as DHTs may have their own vulnerabilities" — stated dependency of dissemination-layer defenses on an external storage layer's own security.

## [HU-SP-21] Merkle²: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System

**Citation:** Yuncong Hu, Kian Hooshmand, Harika Kalidhindi, Seung Jin Yang, Raluca Ada Popa. "Merkle²: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System." IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), 2021. DOI 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00088.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/453.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/453.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Merkle² lets a transparency log publish a new digest every second while keeping both the cost a data owner pays to check her own entries and the cost an auditor pays to check the whole log's integrity independent of how many digests have been published since the owner last checked, so a system does not have to trade short publication intervals (low latency for detecting a wrongly-served entry) against growing per-check cost as time passes. Prior designs split into two families: prefix trees (leaves ordered lexicographically by key, as in CONIKS), which support efficient lookup of a specific entry's current value but force a data owner to check every published digest because states in different epochs carry no defined relationship to each other; and chronological trees (leaves ordered by time of append, as in Certificate Transparency), which let an owner check only the newest digest against an old one via an efficient extension proof, but do not support efficient lookup by key. Merkle² nests the two: the outer structure is a chronological tree ordered by append time, and every internal node of that chronological tree — not just the leaves — is itself the root of an inner prefix tree covering all entries appended up to that point, so each data block ends up stored in O(log n) prefix trees, one per level on the path from its chronological leaf to the chronological root, where n is the number of entries. A lookup for a key locates it via the prefix trees, giving CONIKS-style key-indexed retrieval; monitoring compares only the latest chronological root against the last root the owner or auditor has already checked, using an extension proof over the chronological tree, and does not touch intervening epochs' prefix trees at all. Appending a new entry in the naive version of this structure would require rebuilding O(log n) prefix trees from scratch each time; the paper's "pre-build" technique instead maintains each prefix tree incrementally in the background before it becomes the append target, at the cost of fixing a maximum chronological tree height (and hence a maximum log capacity) in advance. A data owner needs to verify only two proofs ever, in the paper's design: a first-value proof at enrollment and, from then on, only the current-epoch monitoring proof — because monitoring proofs can be cached and skipped for prefix-tree branches already checked, an owner who has checked before does not have to re-download the intervening structure to catch up after being offline.

| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|

| Append time comparison to AAD (bilinear-accumulator-based log) | AAD "significantly slower" than both Merkle² and CONIKS even with 32-entry batching; AAD's own paper benchmarks only up to 2^13 = 8,192 ID-value pairs | AAD figures taken from AAD's own paper and repository, not independently re-run — the authors state their own EC2 setup could not run AAD (public-parameter generation alone reported to take over 20 hours), and AAD's original benchmarks used a more powerful r4.16xlarge instance |

### Parameters
- Hash function: SHA-3 (128-bit security level target).
- Signature scheme: Ed25519, stated as the only public-key operation in the system.
- Chronological tree height cap: 31, chosen to support the pre-build strategy; bounds total log capacity at 2^31 ID-value pairs and means each append touches 31 prefix trees.
- Persistent storage backend: LevelDB.
- VRFs (verifiable random functions) are explicitly not implemented, because the paper states privacy is not its focus — this is a deliberate scope exclusion, not a measured limitation.
- Baseline systems compared: CONIKS (both the original design and the authors' own persistent-data-structure-optimized "CONIKS*" variant), AAD (bilinear-accumulator-based transparency log), and ECT (chronological+prefix-tree hybrid for certificate transparency); AAD and ECT figures are taken from their own papers/repositories, not re-run on the authors' hardware.
- Asymptotic cost table (Table I) parameters: n = number of log entries, λ = AAD's security parameter, E = number of epochs elapsed, P = number of appends between epochs.
- Test-scale range: up to 2^20 ID-value pairs for microbenchmarks; up to 10⁶ ID-value pairs for end-to-end system evaluation and application scenarios.

### Stated limitations
The paper states directly, under "Limitations and future work," that Merkle² cannot outperform CONIKS when the epoch interval is long, because at long intervals append and lookup cost (which are more expensive in Merkle² than in CONIKS) dominate over monitoring cost (Merkle²'s comparative advantage); the crossover in the paper's own certificate/email-workload experiments occurs around a 1-hour epoch interval. The paper states it leaves improving append and lookup efficiency to future work, naming two unimplemented directions: a two-server split where one server pre-builds large future prefix trees while another serves current requests from smaller cached trees, and batching lookup proofs across users with a proxy layer to reduce server bandwidth. The paper states memory usage is a concern because data is replicated across the nested tree structure (Merkle² measured at ≈22 GiB vs. CONIKS's ≈6.3 GiB at the same 2^20-entry scale), and states an unimplemented optimization — skipping storage of prefix trees associated with chronological tree right children, which the paper says are not needed — is left to future work. The pre-build strategy requires fixing a maximum chronological tree height (31 in this implementation) in advance, which caps the total number of ID-value pairs the log can ever hold at 2^31; the paper does not describe a mechanism for extending capacity beyond a chosen height without redeployment. The paper explicitly declines to compare against Google Key Transparency's newer design because it is "still in its early stages" with "no protocol detail or implementation available for benchmarking" — this is a stated evidentiary gap, not a claim that the design underperforms.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The construction assumes the server picks the maximum chronological tree height (and thus maximum log capacity) before deployment, since the pre-build technique that keeps append cost bounded depends on the height being fixed in advance; a component needing unbounded future capacity must plan a height large enough in advance or accept a redeployment when the cap is reached. Concurrency control requires the server to serialize appends against each other (two concurrent appends may touch the same prefix tree), enforced in the prototype by having the server issue a position number to the user and reject the append if the corresponding signature is not returned within a short time bound; lookups and monitoring can run concurrently with appends because the hashes they need were already computed in past epochs. The soundness of an owner's monitoring shortcut (checking only the latest digest, skipping intervening epochs) depends on the owner having verified at least a first-value proof once at enrollment and having cached the resulting prefix-tree branch checks; a system that discards this cached state between sessions forces the owner back to a from-scratch check. Any external mechanism relying on Merkle²'s auditor cost advantage needs auditors who checked the log recently enough that the number of appends since their last check exceeds the paper's measured 28-append break-even point against CONIKS-style per-epoch digest fetching — below that append count, the paper's own data shows CONIKS's simpler per-epoch fetch is not meaningfully more expensive. The system assumes an Ed25519 key infrastructure for the one public-key operation it performs (append confirmation signing) and a SHA-3 hash function for all tree-node commitments; substituting either changes the paper's stated 128-bit security-level target and none of the reported performance numbers were measured under an alternative choice.

### Contradicts
This paper makes a specific claim about SEEMless (CHASE-CCS-19, same batch) worth flagging for cross-reference: it states SEEMless "relies on strong auditors to monitor the append-only property of the Persistent Patricia Trie, which still incurs a super-linear cost on the auditors" — an asymptotic-complexity characterization, not a disputed measured figure. This does not contradict SEEMless's own reported measured numbers (under 4.24 MB and under 0.3 s per adjacent-epoch audit at 10M users, per the CHASE-CCS-19 entry in this corpus) — a cost can be super-linear in an asymptotic sense while still being small in absolute terms at the specific scale SEEMless measured. A reader combining these two entries should treat the asymptotic classification and the absolute measured numbers as compatible, not conflicting, claims. No other paper in this corpus was found to directly contradict a measured figure in this entry.

## [HULSING-CCS-19] The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework

**Citation:** Daniel J. Bernstein, Andreas Hülsing, Stefan Kölbl, Ruben Niederhagen, Joost Rijneveld, Peter Schwabe. "The SPHINCS+ Signature Framework." ACM CCS, 2019. DOI 10.1145/3319535.3363229. (Note: the target registry's author field lists Hülsing, Butin, Gazdag, Rijneveld, Mohaisen — those are the authors of a different document, reference [31] in this paper's own bibliography, an IETF/RFC-track hash-based-signatures draft, not this CCS paper. Title, venue, year, and DOI in the retrieved text all match the target record exactly; only the author field in the registry entry is misattributed.)
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1086.pdf` (full version, dated September 23, 2019)
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/1086.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
SPHINCS+ produces a digital signature scheme that needs no persistent record of which keys it has already used (stateless), built entirely from hash-function security assumptions (no lattice or pairing assumption), so a signer can reuse the same long-term key pair on multiple machines or after restoring from backup without risking a forgery from key reuse — a failure mode that stateful hash-based schemes such as XMSS or LMS suffer if their usage counter is ever rolled back or duplicated. It generates a large virtual tree of one-time signing keys (a hypertree, split into d layers of Merkle trees, each of height h/d), addresses a leaf key pseudorandomly by hashing the message together with the signer's secret seed, and never needs to track which leaf was used before because a new message picks a fresh pseudorandom leaf with overwhelming odds of avoiding collision. Instead of a single-use one-time signature scheme signing the message digest directly, SPHINCS+ replaces it with a new few-time signature scheme the authors call FORS (forest of random subsets), which the authors state gives better size/speed trade-offs than the plain hash-to-obtain-a-leaf-index approach used by SPHINCS. The framework's second contribution is an abstraction called a tweakable hash function — a hash function parameterized by a public "tweak" value distinct per tree position — which lets the paper's security reduction treat every internal hash call generically and derive a single unified security bound, rather than re-deriving security for each hash-function instantiation choice from scratch. The framework offers two families of tweakable-hash-function instantiations, "robust" and "simple": robust achieves security in the standard model plus a quantum random oracle model (QROM) argument for compact public parameters, while simple gives up that formal guarantee for smaller code and faster execution. Signing is deterministic by default — the per-message randomizer R is derived from a secret PRF key and the message, with no external entropy source needed — but the framework supports an optional additional randomness input (OptRand) to counter side-channel attacks that exploit deterministic signing.

### Measured results
| Comparison | SPHINCS+ instantiation and parameters | Cycles: keypair / sign / verify | Bytes: sig / public key / secret key | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vs. SPHINCS-256 | Haraka, robust, n=192, h=51, d=17, b=7, k=45, w=16 | 1,254,968 / 29,015,002 / 2,739,770 | 30,696 / 48 / 96 | SPHINCS-256 baseline: 2,868,464 / 50,462,856 / 1,672,652 cycles, 41,000/1,056/1,088 bytes (SUPERCOP-reported, 3.5GHz Intel Xeon E3-1275 V3 Haswell); SPHINCS+ is stated as 25% shorter signatures and 1.7x faster signing than SPHINCS-256, both guaranteeing security for up to 2^50 signatures under the same key; SPHINCS+ figures are the median of 100 runs on the same Haswell CPU, gcc-5.4 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -flto |
| vs. Gravity-SPHINCS (robust) | Haraka, robust, n=192, h=66, d=22, b=8, k=33, w=16 | 1,257,826 / 38,840,268 / 3,467,192 | 35,664 / 48 / 96 | Gravity-SPHINCS baseline (parameter-set L): 30,729,044,392 / 32,564,796 / 625,752 cycles, max sig 35,168 bytes, pk 32, sk 1,048,608 bytes (SUPERCOP, 3.1GHz Intel Xeon E3-1220 V3); this SPHINCS+ instance has slightly larger signatures and slightly slower signing than Gravity-SPHINCS, attributed to a top-layer caching mechanism Gravity-SPHINCS uses that inflates its secret-key size and key-generation time |

| vs. Picnic2 (NIST level 5) | SHA-256, simple, n=256, h=63, d=9, b=12, k=29, w=16 | 43,317,320 / 527,413,100 / 5,463,884 | 33,408 / 64 / 128 | Picnic2-L5-FS baseline: 18,244 / 904,189,188 / 268,485,212 cycles, max sig 54,732 bytes (avg 46,282), pk 65, sk 97 bytes (SUPERCOP, 3.1GHz Haswell); SPHINCS+ signatures are 28% smaller than average Picnic2 and 39% smaller than worst-case Picnic2 signatures; signing over 70% faster; key generation much slower; verification almost 50x faster |

| SPHINCS-256's actual security (re-derived, not this paper's original claim) | n/a | n/a | n/a | The paper states SPHINCS-256's advertised 128-bit post-quantum security claim ignored a tightness gap in its proof; a later attack (cited as [33]) computing a preimage to one of many hashes in the SPHINCS-256 tree reduced its actual security to less than 190 bits classical and 95 bits post-quantum — this is a re-derivation from a cited external analysis, not a benchmark this paper ran itself |

### Parameters
- Hypertree height h and layer count d: search-selected per target instantiation (examples above range h=51 to h=66, d=9 to d=22); h is not free — the paper's parameter-search script iterates h from `s-8` to `s+20` where `s = log2(max signatures)`, and requires `h % d == 0`.
- FORS parameters b (height of each FORS tree) and k (number of FORS trees): search-selected together with the target forgery-probability bound; example values k=29 to k=49, b=7 to b=12.
- Winternitz parameter w: fixed to 16 or 256 in the exploration script; all reported benchmark instantiations use w=16, which the paper states is chosen for a "reasonable trade-off between signing time and signature size."
- Hash-function output length n: 192 or 256 bits in the reported comparisons (also 128-bit variants in the NIST table); larger n raises security level and signature size together.
- Tweakable hash function instantiation choice: robust (SHA-256, SHAKE256, or Haraka; needs a QROM argument for compact public parameters) or simple (same three hash-function choices, no such proof); Haraka-based instantiations cannot reach as high a security level as SHA-256/SHAKE256 because of a generic meet-in-the-middle collision attack on Haraka's internal state, with classical complexity 2^128.
- Maximum signatures per key pair: parameter sets are generated for a target maximum (e.g., 2^50 for the SPHINCS-256 comparison, 2^64 for all NIST-submitted instantiations) — the maximum is a design input to the parameter search, not a fixed constant of the framework.
- Message-randomization input R: derived deterministically as `R = PRF(SK.prf, OptRand, M)`; OptRand can be set to a fixed public value (fully deterministic signing) or to fresh randomness (probabilistic signing, stated as a side-channel countermeasure) — this is a configurable choice, not a fixed value.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that all its benchmarked schemes — SPHINCS+, SPHINCS-256, Gravity-SPHINCS, Picnic — "do not reach the performance of, e.g., lattice-based signature schemes like Dilithium, Falcon, or qTESLA," and states these symmetric-primitive-only schemes are "mainly interesting for applications without strong latency requirements, such as offline code signing or certificate signing," not applications with strict latency needs. The paper states a general rule of thumb for the whole hash-based-signature design space: "a linear decrease in signature size comes with an exponential decrease in signing speed" — smaller signatures cannot be obtained without an exponential signing-time cost within this framework. The robust tweakable-hash construction's proof of compact-public-parameter security depends on a quantum random oracle model (QROM) assumption; the paper characterizes this as "slightly stronger" than the assumptions needed for other constructions, and states this assumption is unneeded if one is willing to accept exponential-size public parameters instead. The "simple" instantiation drops that formal QROM guarantee for smaller code and higher speed, so choosing simple over robust is stated as an explicit security-versus-performance trade-off, not a strict improvement. Verification speed for SPHINCS+ is stated to be structurally slower than Gravity-SPHINCS because SPHINCS+ requires tweakable-hash calls at every node rather than plain hashing. LowMC v3, the symmetric primitive Picnic2's competitive performance relies on, is stated by the authors as "not [having] been intensively studied," with earlier LowMC versions shown by cited prior work not to meet their claimed security levels — the paper flags this as an open question about Picnic2's assumptions, not a property of SPHINCS+ itself.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A verifier must have access to and trust the public parameters (a public seed, or a larger public-parameter structure depending on the robust/simple construction choice) associated with a given public key; the security reduction is stated relative to those parameters being generated as specified, not arbitrarily. The deterministic default signing mode requires the signer to hold a secret PRF key (SK.prf) and secret seed (SK.seed) with confidentiality equivalent to the signing key itself — compromise of either breaks the unforgeability argument the same way a stolen private key would for a conventional scheme; no additional live entropy source is required to sign, which the paper's own design of `R = PRF(SK.prf, OptRand, M)` establishes as a difference from a nonce-based scheme like ECDSA that fails catastrophically on repeated or predictable per-signature randomness. A system embedding SPHINCS+ must pick a maximum-signature bound in advance (as a parameter-search input) — the paper's own search script takes `maxsigs` as a configuration constant, and instantiations are tuned to a chosen ceiling (2^50 in one comparison, 2^64 for the NIST submissions); a deployment issuing signatures indefinitely without such a planned ceiling is outside what this paper's parameter derivations cover. A system choosing a hash function for the tweakable-hash instantiation must independently trust that hash function's security (SHA-256, SHAKE256, or Haraka) at the target security level; Haraka-based instantiations are stated to be unable to reach the highest security levels reachable with SHA-256 or SHAKE256, because of the generic meet-in-the-middle attack noted above — a system requiring the highest formally provable security level should not select Haraka. Systems requiring fast verification at scale (e.g., verifying many signatures per second) should weigh SPHINCS+'s tweakable-hash-per-node verification cost against alternatives; the paper's own Picnic2 comparison shows SPHINCS+ verification nearly 50 times faster in that specific comparison, but the Gravity-SPHINCS comparison shows the opposite ordering, so verification speed is stated to depend on which competing scheme and parameter set is being compared, not a fixed universal ranking.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus — no other paper in this batch measures hash-based post-quantum signature performance. Note: the paper's own text corrects a claim commonly attributed to SPHINCS-256 (128-bit post-quantum security) — the paper states this figure ignored a tightness gap in the original proof and that a later attack reduced the actual figure to below 190 bits classical / 95 bits post-quantum; a reader citing "SPHINCS-256 achieves 128-bit post-quantum security" without this correction would be citing a claim this very paper says does not hold.

**Citation:** Ayae Ide, Tanusree Sharma. "Personhood Credentials: Human-Centered Design Recommendation Balancing Security, Usability, and Trust." arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.16375, 2025. DOI: 10.48550/ARXIV.2502.16375.
