## [KLEPPMANN-CONEXT-24] Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media

**Citation:** Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jake Gold, Jay Graber, Daniel Holmgren, Devin Ivy, Jeromy Johnson, Bryan Newbold, Jaz Volpert. "Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media." ACM DIN Workshop, CoNEXT, 2024. 9 pages. DOI 10.1145/3694809.3700740.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03239 (candidate URL list target; text on disk matches the DIN '24 extended version)
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1145/3694809.3700740
**Domain:** J+K

### What it does
The AT Protocol (Authenticated Transfer Protocol) separates social-media hosting into independently replaceable roles so a user can move between providers without losing their username, posts, or social graph. Each user account holds one repository: a signed, append-only collection of records (posts, likes, follows) encoded in DAG-CBOR (a restricted, compact form of the Concise Binary Object Representation). A Personal Data Server (PDS) hosts a set of repositories, exposes them over an HTTP API, and pushes a WebSocket stream of new and deleted records. A Relay crawls known PDSes, verifies the cryptographic proofs on each update, holds its own replica of every repository, and merges the per-PDS streams into one public stream called the firehose. An App View consumes the firehose and computes derived views specific to one social mode (like counts, reply threads, follower sets, timelines) that a client queries indirectly through the user's own PDS. Labelers and feed generators consume the firehose independently and produce, respectively, content-judgment labels and ranked post-ID lists that a client or App View applies as opt-in filters, so ranking and moderation policy are not fixed inside the App View. A repository's records form a Merkle Search Tree (a Merkle tree structure that stays balanced under arbitrary insertion and deletion order); the tree's root hash is signed after every change, which lets any party prove a record is or is not present in a given repository without holding the whole repository. Identity is a Decentralized Identifier (DID), an immutable URI that resolves to a DID document stating the user's current handle, PDS URL, and signing public key; a human-readable handle is a DNS name and is proved to correspond to a DID by a bidirectional link (a DNS TXT record or a `/.well-known/` HTTPS response naming the DID, plus the DID document naming the handle back). The paper defines two DID methods: `did:web`, which resolves via HTTPS to a domain the identity is permanently tied to, and `did:plc`, the protocol's own method, in which the DID is the truncated SHA-256 hash of the initial DID document and later versions are valid only if signed by the key authorized in the immediately preceding version, verified through a chain returned by a directory server.

### Measured results
| Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Over 10 million registered users | Growth from invite-only launch in February 2023 to the paper's writing, roughly 20 months, counted by Bluesky Social PBC's own registration records |
| Real-time single-server mirror of every user repository cost US$153/month | Measured in July 2024, when Bluesky had 6 million users; figure covers repository storage and inbound bandwidth for fetching records from PDSes; excludes compute for building and serving summary indexes; cited to a third-party operator's own report (Newbold, ref. [43]), not an experiment run by this paper's authors |
| "Tens of thousands" of custom feeds created | No date or measurement method given beyond this count; not usable as a precise figure |
| Farcaster per-user storage cost approximately $5 USD/year in Ethereum-equivalent currency | Stated as a comparison figure from Farcaster's own fee schedule (ref. [30]), at the time of writing, not independently measured by this paper |

No latency, throughput, or failure-rate experiment is run by the authors themselves; the paper is an architecture description with one third-party cost citation, not an evaluation study.

### Parameters
- Post length limit: 300 characters of text, up to four images, plus short-form video (Bluesky app-level lexicon parameter, not an AT Protocol parameter)
- DID hash truncation for `did:plc`: SHA-256 hash of the initial DID document, truncated to 120 bits, base32-encoded
- Scuttlebutt comparison parameter cited from related work: default follow-graph crawl depth of three hops

### Stated limitations
The protocol currently supports only public content; the authors state they are investigating mechanisms for private blocking actions but have not built them. Direct messages are handled by a centralized service operated by Bluesky Social PBC, with decentralization stated as a future plan, not a current property. The PLC directory server is a single point that can omit valid DID document versions or fail to respond, and can choose which fork to serve if two correctly signed successor DID documents exist for the same DID; the authors state a future version will use an append-only transparency log to mitigate this, which does not exist yet. Signing keys are held custodially by the PDS operator for ordinary users, so a compromised or malicious PDS operator holds the keys needed to forge repository updates on that user's behalf; the protocol places no requirement on how a PDS authenticates its users. `did:web` identity security depends on trusting the domain's web hosting provider and the certificate authorities that authenticate its HTTPS endpoint. The authors state that most of the indexing infrastructure is currently run by one company, though they argue this does not make the system centralized because repositories are public and re-indexable by anyone.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A Relay requires every PDS to serve a WebSocket stream of signed repository updates and to accept periodic re-crawl requests as a fallback when the stream is interrupted; without a re-crawl fallback, deletions and additions made during a network interruption are missed. An App View requires a Relay's firehose as its only input and does not itself crawl PDSes; a new social mode built on the protocol needs a new App View but can reuse the same PDSes and Relay. Handle verification requires DNS or HTTPS control over a domain and requires the App View performing verification to defend against DNS cache poisoning, optionally with DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions); the paper states this defense as a should, not as implemented. `did:plc` requires a directory server that returns the full version history for a DID so that clients can verify the unbroken signature chain themselves; the directory's honesty is not required for basic integrity, only for availability and fork-choice, per the paper's own analysis. Blocking enforcement requires block records to be public, because every App View must be able to read who blocks whom in order to drop disallowed interactions; a design that keeps blocks private would remove the App View's ability to enforce them under the mechanism this paper describes.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at the time of writing. Note for cross-paper checking: SECKIN-ARXIV-25 measures Bluesky's user and network growth through February 2025 and should be checked for growth-rate figures against this paper's "10 million users in 20 months" figure, since the two papers cover different measurement windows (this paper: through October 2024; SECKIN-ARXIV-25: through February 2025).

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Auvolat, Taïani, "Merkle Search Trees: Efficient State-Based CRDTs in Open Networks," SRDS 2019, DOI 10.1109/srds47363.2019.00032 — defines the Merkle Search Tree structure the repository uses
- foundational: Sporny, Longley, Sabadello, Reed, Steele, Allen, "Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) v1.0," W3C Recommendation, 2022 — the DID standard atproto's identity layer implements
- foundational: Laurie, "Certificate Transparency," ACM Queue 12(8), 2014, DOI 10.1145/2668152.2668154 — the append-only log design the authors cite as the intended future mitigation for PLC directory fork attacks
- competing: Henshaw-Plath (fiatjaf), "Pivoting Protocols, from SSB to Nostr," 2023 — Nostr's relay-based architecture, directly contrasted in this paper's related work
- competing: Srinivasan, "Farcaster: A Decentralized Social Network," 2023, and Farcaster Team, "Farcaster Architecture," 2024 — blockchain-anchored identity and storage-fee comparison system
- competing: Lemmer-Webber, Tallon, Shepherd, Guy, Prodromou, "ActivityPub," W3C Recommendation, 2018 — the Mastodon federation protocol this paper compares against on server lock-in and reply-thread consistency
- competing: "Scuttlebutt Protocol Guide," 2023, and Karlsson, "Launch of the PZP protocol and the future of Manyverse," 2024 — the peer-to-peer, key-on-device predecessor and its stated successor protocol addressing multi-device key loss
- attack/critique: Erin, "queer.af domain suspended without warning," 2024 — cited as a real instance of Mastodon-style server-loss risk to a user's social graph

- "it was possible to maintain a real-time copy of all user repositories on a single server for US$153 per month"
- "Any new version of the DID document is only valid if it has been signed by the key in the previous version"
- "there are no guarantees of anything [...] to use Nostr one must embrace the inherent chaos"
- "Fees are currently collected centrally by the Farcaster team"

## [KRISHNAN-ICIS-02] MISMATCH — NOT THE TARGET PAPER

**Target citation (registry/targets-deduped.json):** Ramayya Krishnan, Michael D. Smith, Zhulei Tang, Rahul Telang. "The Virtual Commons: Why Free-Riding Can Be Tolerated in File Sharing Networks." International Conference on Information Systems (ICIS), 2002.

## [KROL-EUROSP-24] DISC-NG: Robust Service Discovery in the Ethereum Global Network
**Citation:** Michał Król, Onur Ascigil, Sergi Rene, Alberto Sonnino, Matthieu Pigaglio, Ramin Sadre, Felix Lange, Etienne Rivière. "DISC-NG: Robust Service Discovery in the Ethereum Global Network." IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2024. DOI 10.1109/EUROSP60621.2024.00019.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/218598/3/main.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/218598/3/main.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
DISC-NG lets a node in the Ethereum Global Network (EGN — the set of decentralized services, including the Ethereum blockchain itself, that share one Kademlia-based distributed hash table, DHT, for peer discovery) find peers offering a given service, at a rate close to an undefended DHT lookup while resisting eclipse and censorship attacks a plain DHT lookup does not resist. An advertiser for service s builds an advertise table centered on the hash of s (rather than on the advertiser's own node identifier, as a normal Kademlia routing table is) and places a fixed number of ad copies (parameter K_register) into a random registrar in each bucket of that table. A discoverer builds the mirror search table and queries a bounded number of registrars per bucket (K_lookup), starting from the bucket farthest from the service hash and proceeding toward it, stopping once it has collected advertisements from a set number of distinct advertisers (F_lookup). Placement is randomized within each bucket but biased toward registrars close to the service hash, so that a popular service's ads are still reachable from far buckets — the buckets an attacker would need to control most of to build an eclipse are the largest fraction of the key space, since the farthest bucket alone covers roughly half of all possible registrar identifiers.

A registrar decides whether to admit an incoming ad using a waiting-time function rather than a fixed-size LRU (least-recently-used) or LFU (least-frequently-used) cache-replacement policy: on each registration attempt the registrar computes a waiting time from the ad cache's current occupancy, the number of ads already held for the same service, and a similarity score between the registering IP address and IP addresses already present in the cache, then returns a signed ticket recording how long the advertiser must still wait. The advertiser resubmits its ticket on a later attempt; the registrar recomputes a fresh waiting time against the ticket's accumulated wait and admits the ad once the remaining wait reaches zero. The registrar holds no per-advertiser state between requests — the ticket alone carries the accumulated wait — which the paper states denies an attacker the ability to exhaust registrar memory by abandoning in-progress registrations.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| DISC-NG discovers ten times more peers per time slot than DISCv5 (Ethereum's deployed discovery protocol) while reaching a similar or lower eclipse probability against a powerful attacker | Stated in the abstract; the concrete discovery-count comparison is Figures 19–20, network sizes 5,000/25,000/50,000 nodes and 100/300/600 services in the PeerSim-based simulator |
| DISC-NG reduces load on the busiest nodes by two orders of magnitude compared to vanilla DHT lookup, and eliminates the vulnerability of vanilla DHT lookup to resource-constrained attackers | Stated in the abstract, elaborated in the message-overhead measurements (Figures 17-18) comparing DISC-NG to the DHT baseline (16 closest nodes to the service-ID hash, LRU eviction) |
| Lookup eclipse rate at 20% / 33.33% / 50% Sybil (malicious) nodes: DHT baseline 21.4% / 37% / 59.7%; DHTTicket (DHT placement plus DISC-NG's admission control) 1.6% / 4.9% / 6.5%; DISCv5 0.3% / 0.3% / 0.3% up to moderate attacker fractions but rising with more resourceful attackers to 7.2% / 10.6% / 17.8% in a different plotted metric; DISC-NG stays under roughly 0.3-0.5% across the same range | Simulator, default 25,000-node network, service popularity following a Zipf distribution with exponent 1.0, target a moderately popular service with approximately 500 participating nodes, attacker identifiers uniformly distributed in the address space (worst case for the compared baselines, best case for DISC-NG per the paper's own statement), 5 attacker nodes reusing each IP address by default, malicious nodes register ads at 10 times the honest rate and return only malicious peers |
| With non-uniform Sybil placement (16 malicious nodes concentrated close to the target service ID), the DHT and DHTTicket baselines reach a 100% eclipse rate, versus 0% for DISCv5 and DISC-NG | Same simulator setup; the paper states these results are reported qualitatively, not plotted |
| Eclipse rate versus IP-pool size: DHT 39.5%/37%/37%, DHTTicket 2.8%/4.9%/11.4%, DISCv5 0.3%/0.3%/0.5%, DISC-NG 10.6%/10.6%/10.6%, for attacker IP pools of 50/5/1 IPs shared among attackers respectively — DISC-NG's worst case across this sweep stays under 0.5% per the paper's prose, meaning the 10.6% row is read from the DHTTicket line, not DISC-NG (see note below) | Same simulator setup, 33.33% malicious nodes fixed, IP-reuse pool size varied |
| PlanetLab-scale prototype: incoming/outgoing bandwidth and message counts cross-validated between a 50-server devp2p/Geth testbed (up to 1,000 nodes) and the PeerSim simulator | Testbed: 50 servers, 18-core Intel Xeon Gold 5220, 96 GB RAM, network sizes 200/500/1,000 nodes, tc-based network emulation reproducing round-trip latencies from an IPFS all-pairs latency dataset (8-91 ms, average 34 ms), each node's connection capped at 20 KB/s, 30 services with Zipf(α=1) popularity, F_lookup = 30 |
| Full ad-cache lookup: 66 µs local processing time; registration admission: 58 µs, largely independent of cache occupancy | Testbed prototype, per-request local processing time measurement (Figure 13) |
| Lookup latency remained on the order of a few hundred milliseconds across all tested network sizes | Testbed, 200/500/1,000-node configurations, cross-validated against the simulator |

Note on the IP-pool sweep: the text states DISC-NG's eclipse rate stays below 0.5% even in its worst tested configuration under increasing attacker IP diversity, and separately states DHT and DISCv5 show "significantly higher" rates that do not change much with IP count. The four percentage series printed together in the source text (39.5/37/37, 2.8/4.9/11.4, 0.3/0.3/0.5, 10.6/10.6/10.6) are not individually re-labeled by protocol in the extracted text at the point they appear; a reader needing the exact per-protocol assignment for this specific figure should consult Figure 22 in the original PDF rather than rely on this transcription's ordering.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Meaning | Default value |
|---|---|---|
| C | ad-cache capacity per registrar | 1,000 entries |
| K_register | ads placed per advertise-table bucket | 3 |
| K_lookup | parallel registrar queries per search-table bucket during lookup | 5 |
| E | ad expiry time (ad lifetime) | 15 minutes |
| F_lookup | number of distinct advertisers a discoverer tries to collect | 30 |
| F_return | maximum service-specific peers a single registrar returns per query | 10 |
| P_occ | occupancy exponent in the waiting-time formula | 10 |
| G | safety parameter scaling the influence of IP/service similarity on waiting time | 10^-7 |
| δ | registration-window during which a ticket is valid for reuse | 1 second |
| X_size | average advertisement request size | 1,000 bytes |
| m | number of buckets in the advertise/search table | 16 |
| T_max | assumed upper bound on traffic a single registrar can receive | under 1,125 (units as stated in Table 1; the paper states this is far above the reported real-world fiber speed record of about 10^14 bits per second, so it argues the bound is not restrictive in practice) |
| Simulation default network size | \|N\| | 25,000 nodes, extended up to 50,000 |
| Simulation default service count | \|S\| | 300 services |
| Service popularity distribution | Zipf exponent | 1.0 |
| Default malicious-node fraction | \|N_m\|/\|N\| | 33% |
| Default IP-reuse group size | attackers sharing one IP | 5 |

The paper states the waiting-time minimum formula as w_c = G·E / (1 − c/C)^P_occ, where c is current cache occupancy — the derivation for why larger P_occ deters cache overflow while smaller P_occ preserves usable cache space under normal traffic.

### Stated limitations
The paper's threat model assumes the underlying DHT already defends against DHT-level eclipse attacks — stated as Assumption 2, "at all times, all honest peers in the DHT overlay are connected through at least one other honest peer" — and DISC-NG's own security analysis holds only conditional on that assumption; DISC-NG defends against eclipse and censorship only at the service-discovery layer built on top of an already-uneclipsed DHT. The paper states it imposes no threshold on the fraction of malicious nodes to guarantee this discovery-layer protection, in contrast to schemes that require a bound on adversarial fraction. The paper assumes partial synchrony (bounded but unknown message-delivery delay ∆) and justifies this by citing that the Ethereum mainnet blockchain itself requires a strictly stronger synchrony assumption, so the paper is not proposing a weaker network model than what the deployment already needs. The conclusion states an explicit unsolved direction: "add Sybil identities detection mechanism" — DISC-NG does not itself detect or bound the number of Sybil identities an attacker registers, only limits their effect on ad-cache admission and placement. The paper states a single lookup query can still fail with a probability that increases with the number of malicious nodes and the diversity of attacker-controlled IP addresses, even though DISC-NG guarantees liveness across repeated queries (Theorems 2 and 3) — a discoverer needing certainty must retry, not rely on one query.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
DISC-NG requires an underlying Kademlia-style DHT whose own routing-table maintenance already resists eclipse attacks, and cites specific such mechanisms as preconditions rather than building one itself. It requires every advertisement to carry a verifiable digital signature — the lookup algorithm asserts `ad.hasValidSignature()` before accepting an advertisement — so a signing key-management scheme must exist elsewhere in the system. It requires partial synchrony: messages between honest nodes must be delivered within a bounded but not necessarily known delay ∆, and if the network partitions rather than delays, the paper's liveness proofs do not apply. It requires a per-node identifier space compatible with Kademlia-style bucket partitioning, since the advertise table and search table are both organized as buckets by XOR-distance-like proximity to the service hash. It requires a service-identification hash function to derive the service ID that both advertise and search tables center on. It requires no clock synchronization between advertisers and registrars, since a ticket only carries a duration to wait, not absolute timestamps — a property the design achieves rather than a requirement, worth noting for a synthesis step comparing this design's dependencies against a clock-dependent one.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Note for cross-paper synthesis: the brief's own registry entry for this paper flagged the search-snippet figures "17.8%" and "59.7%" as needing their exact conditions verified from the full text before use — the full text confirms 17.8% as DISCv5's eclipse rate at the higher end of the tested attacker-fraction sweep in the figure discussed in the text (not the 0.3% headline figure reported at lower attacker fractions in Figure 21) and 59.7% as the DHT baseline's eclipse rate at 50% malicious nodes; both figures are usable now that their conditions are attached, per the table above.

- Marcus, Heilman, Goldberg. "Low-Resource Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network." — attack-or-critique, cited as one of the DHT-level eclipse-prevention mechanisms DISC-NG's Assumption 2 relies on
- Henningsen, Teunis, Florian, [fourth author cut off in extraction]. Eclipse-attack-resistance paper for the Ethereum DHT, cited alongside Marcus et al. as a precondition mechanism. — attack-or-critique / foundational precondition

## [LACAVA-ANS-21] Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon
**Citation:** Lucio La Cava, Sergio Greco, Andrea Tagarelli. "Understanding the growth of the Fediverse through the lens of Mastodon." Applied Network Science 6, 2021. DOI 10.1007/S41109-021-00392-5.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15473
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15473
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper builds an up-to-date crawled dataset of the Mastodon instance-to-instance follow network and uses it to measure the topological structure of that network and how the structure changed over roughly three years, compared against an earlier published Mastodon dataset. It does not measure the distribution of user accounts across instances (how many users each instance hosts); the measured object throughout is a directed graph whose nodes are Mastodon server instances and whose edges are aggregated follow relationships between users of one instance and users of another.

Data was collected by a purpose-built crawler using only the public, authenticated Mastodon REST API, starting from a seed list of instances obtained from the instances.social tracker (approximately 900 of about 1,100 candidate instances granted the crawler an authentication token). From the timelines of these seed instances the crawler discovered approximately 81,000 seed users, then performed a breadth-first search over the user-follow graph, discovering new users and instances as it traversed. Collected edges were anonymized by hashing at collection time, so the raw dataset cannot be traced back to individual identities; no scraping outside the authenticated API was performed, so instances that declined to grant an authentication token contribute no data beyond what other instances' users reveal about them.

Three network models are derived from the same underlying crawled user-follow graph, all as directed graphs of instances rather than of individual users: the Instances network (edges exist between two instances if any user of one follows any user of the other, restricted to instances known to be Mastodon), the Online-Instances network (the subgraph restricted to instances currently reported online by the tracker sites), and the Expanded-Instances network (the same graph but including edges to and from instances belonging to other Fediverse platforms besides Mastodon, discovered incidentally because Mastodon's follow-listing API does not distinguish the platform of a followed or following account).

Instance status (Mastodon versus another platform, online versus offline) is determined by cross-referencing the crawled instance identifiers against two independent third-party tracker websites, instances.social and fediverse.party, rather than being inferred from the crawl itself.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Crawl produced 27,989,557 raw detected links; after de-duplication, approximately 1.4 million unique users and 18 million unique links, covering 16,282 instances of any Fediverse platform | Single crawl, November-December 2020, breadth-first search seeded from ~81,000 users across ~900 authenticated Mastodon instances |
| Merging the instances.social and fediverse.party trackers gives 9,433 known Mastodon instances total (online plus offline) and 1,193 known-online Mastodon instances | Third-party tracker data, cited "as reported in Table 1" of the paper, no date given beyond the crawl period |
| Restricting the census to instances shared between both tracker websites, rather than their union, reduces the online-instance count by 16.4% (to 997) and the overall count by 86.5% (to 1,276) | Same tracker-comparison dataset |
| The crawl intercepted (found data for) 6,960 of the 9,433 known Mastodon instances (73.8%), and 1,116 of the 1,193 known-online instances (93.5%) | Same crawl and tracker-comparison window |
| The dataset is stated to double the earlier state-of-the-art in currently-online instance count: this paper's 1,116 online instances found versus 548 reported by the earlier dataset (Zignani et al., mid-2017 to early-2018) | Direct comparison stated in the paper's own summary figure; the earlier dataset totaled 4,015 overall Mastodon instances versus 6,960 here |
| Instances network in-degree distribution: first quartile 91.5, median 202, mean 331, third quartile 413, non-outlier maximum 878; 21 instances have in-degree above 880, up to a maximum of 4,685 | Instances network, 6,960 nodes, crawled November-December 2020 |
| The top-5 instances by degree, in-degree, and out-degree are the same five in all three rankings: mastodon.social, pawoo.net, mastodon.xyz, octodon.social, and mstdn.io; mastodon.social is top-1 by every degree type | Same Instances network |
| In-degree CCDF: 50% of instances have in-degree at least 200; this drops to 20% around in-degree 600 and below 4% for the outlier instances | Same Instances network |
| Instances network structural summary: 6,960 nodes, 216,504 edges, reciprocity 65.1%, density 0.004, average degree 41.966 | Same crawl |
| Comparison against the earlier (Zignani et al.) network of 4,015 nodes and 95,221 edges: this paper's Instances network is +73% in node count and +127% in edge count; reciprocity is 8% lower, density is 33% lower, average degree is 37% higher, average path length and diameter are unchanged (2.340 and 5 respectively in both networks), degree assortativity is 5-13% more negative | Comparison of this paper's crawl (Nov-Dec 2020) against the previously published Zignani et al. dataset (2017-2018) |
| Restricting to online-only instances (Online-Instances network) versus the full Instances network: node count falls 84% (to 1,115 nodes), edge count falls 65% (to 75,046 edges), reciprocity rises 8% (to 70.6%), density rises roughly 14x (to 0.06), average degree more than doubles (to 87.074), average path length falls 13% and diameter falls 20% | Same crawl, subgraph restricted to instances reported online at collection time |
| Instance-ranking similarity across network variants, via Kendall's tau and Fagin's intersection metric on PageRank scores: Expanded-Instances vs. Instances, tau = 0.953; Online-Instances vs. Instances, tau = 0.899; Instances vs. the three-years-earlier network, tau = 0.626 (lower than the other comparisons, attributed to the temporal gap) | PageRank computed independently on each network variant, ranking correlation computed over the shared node set between each pair |

The paper reports negative degree assortativity (disassortative mixing, i.e., high-degree instances tend to connect to low-degree instances rather than to each other) as a consistent feature across every network variant tested (Instances: -0.253 to -0.274 depending on edge-direction treatment; Online-Instances: -0.284 to -0.290; the three-years-earlier network: -0.287 to -0.291), and states this distinguishes Mastodon's instance-level topology from well-known centralized social networks, which the paper states typically show positive assortativity, citing prior literature for that centralized-network baseline rather than measuring it directly in this paper.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| instances.social "dead" threshold | An instance is classed dead if inactive at least two weeks | Fixed value from the third-party tracker's own definition, not varied by the authors |
| instances.social "down" threshold | An instance is classed down if not currently reachable but was live within the preceding two weeks | Fixed value from the third-party tracker's own definition, not varied |
| Fagin's intersection metric top-k cutoff | Computed at k = 10, 50, 100, 500, 1,000 | These five values are the range tested; no single value is presented as the recommended default |
| Crawl duration / collection window | Approximately one month (November-December 2020 for the main crawl) | Not varied; single collection run |

### Stated limitations
The paper states the crawl's coverage of non-Mastodon Fediverse instances is necessarily partial, because such instances and users were discovered only incidentally through Mastodon-instance API responses, and the paper explicitly hedges its own Expanded-Instances findings on this basis: "although we detected non-Mastodon users and instances through Mastodon ones, and hence this knowledge of the Fediverse might be partial." It states it could not determine the online/offline status of instances in the earlier (Zignani et al.) comparison dataset at the time that dataset was itself created, so the paper's own claim of Mastodon reaching structural stability rests partly on a hypothesis ("we hypothesize that...Mastodon reached its stability") rather than on data available for both time points. It states explicitly that it does not analyze the content of posts or user-level social contents at all; only follow-relationship structure was collected and analyzed, and studying users' behavior and roles within and across instances is stated as the authors' planned next research stage, not something this paper addresses. The paper does not measure or report the number of user accounts hosted by each instance, or any resource-concentration metric (Gini coefficient, Nakamoto coefficient, HHI, or similar) over instance sizes; its concentration-adjacent findings (instance centrality via PageRank, core-decomposition inner-most-core sizes) measure structural position in the follow graph, not population share.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Reproducing or extending this paper's Instances-network measurements requires an authenticated Mastodon API token from each instance to be crawled, since the authors state they deliberately excluded any instance that declined to grant a token rather than scraping it by other means; a study that instead scrapes public HTML would collect a different, non-directly-comparable instance population. Comparing a new crawl's structural statistics against this paper's reported values requires matching the same graph granularity (instance-to-instance aggregated follow edges, not user-to-user edges), since the paper's own Table 3 versus Table 7 versus Table 8 comparisons show density, degree, and reciprocity shift substantially between the full Instances network, the Online-Instances subgraph, and the three-years-earlier dataset purely from differences in which instances are included, independent of any real change in the platform. Any downstream claim about "Mastodon's degree of centralization" sourced to this paper must specify whether it means the instance-level follow-graph topology (what this paper measures, e.g., disassortative mixing, PageRank concentration in a persistent small set of instances) or the distribution of user accounts across instances (what this paper does not measure); conflating the two would misattribute a user-population-concentration claim to this paper's evidence.

### Contradicts
The paper's own stated motivation for retrieval in this batch (per the target registry's why_needed field) was to determine whether Raman et al.'s 2019 instance-concentration figures held, worsened, or improved as the Fediverse grew. This paper does not perform that comparison: it cites Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case" (IMC 2019) only once, as reference [7] in a list of prior Mastodon-focused studies, and never discusses or reproduces any of that paper's specific findings or figures in its body text. The paper's own point of comparison throughout is Zignani, Gaito, Rossi's 2018 ICWSM dataset and findings, not Raman et al.'s. A claim that this paper confirms, refutes, or updates Raman et al.'s concentration figures is not supported by this paper's text and must not be attributed to it.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational (comparison baseline used throughout this paper): Zignani, Gaito, Rossi, "Follow the 'mastodon': Structure and evolution of a decentralized online social network," ICWSM 2018 — the paper this entry's every "earlier network" comparison figure is measured against; already implicitly retrieved in substance via this paper's Table 7/8 reproductions, but the original paper's own text was not separately read in this pass.
- competing/independent-measurement (named directly in the batch's retrieval rationale but not analyzed by this paper): Raman, Joglekar, De Cristofaro, Sastry, Tyson, "Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case," IMC 2019 — holds the instance-concentration figures this paper was expected, but found not, to update; still worth retrieving directly for those figures.
- competing: Zignani, Quadri, Gaito, Cherifi, Rossi, "The Footprints of a 'Mastodon': How a Decentralized Architecture Influences Online Social Relationships," IEEE INFOCOM Workshops 2019 — reports per-instance footprint statistics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient) for the top 10 Mastodon instances, a finer-grained companion result to this paper's top-5-by-degree finding.
- foundational: Zulli, Liu, Gehl, "Rethinking the 'Social' in 'Social Media': Insights into Topology, Abstraction, and Scale on the Mastodon Social Network," New Media & Society 22(7), 2020 — qualitative moderator-interview study cited as finding horizontal (inter-instance) rather than within-instance growth, a claim this paper's structural results are consistent with but did not directly test.
- foundational: Varol, Ferrara, Davis, Menczer, Flammini, "Online human-bot interactions: Detection, estimation, and characterization," ICWSM 2017 — source of the ~15% Twitter bot-prevalence figure this paper's related-work section contrasts against a cited ~5% Mastodon bot figure from Zignani et al.

## [LAS-EPRINT-26] De-SyRIS: A Decentralized Sybil-Resistant Identity System without a Trusted Credential Issuer
**Citation:** Michal Ľaš, Ivan Homoliak, Juraj Mariani. "De-SyRIS: A Decentralized Sybil-Resistant Identity System without a Trusted Credential Issuer." IACR ePrint Archive, 2026.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1723
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1723
**Domain:** F

### What it does
De-SyRIS assigns each human a single decentralized identity resistant to mass fake-account creation (Sybil attack) without any party centrally issuing or vouching for that identity. It combines two independent Sybil-resistance signals so that defeating one alone does not defeat the system: facial-biometric uniqueness checking, and zero-knowledge (a cryptographic proof that a statement is true without revealing the data that makes it true) social-graph analysis proving an entity is reachable from an externally reputable entity through a chain of privately-held connections.

Mechanism, registration: a user's device captures a facial scan, signs it with a Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) manifest (cryptographically signed metadata proving when, on what device, and by what application media was captured) to counter synthetic images, and sends scan plus manifest to a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE, a hardware-isolated region of a processor that keeps code and data confidential even from the machine's own operating system) running under Oasis ROFL (a stateless verifiable-compute layer producing an on-chain-verifiable attestation for each computed result). Inside the TEE the system verifies the manifest's freshness and originating application, runs liveness checks, extracts a biometric embedding, and matches it against an encrypted embedding database that only TEEs holding valid remote-attestation quotes can query. A first-time match produces "full" registration; a collision with an existing embedding produces "limited" registration, requiring the new account to collect community endorsements — each already-fully-registered user may issue exactly one endorsement — before it is promoted to full status. The signed TEE result is submitted to the Oasis Sapphire confidential smart-contract chain, which records the embedding hash and reputation state.

Mechanism, connection establishment: two users meeting in person photograph each other, sign the photos with C2PA manifests, and submit them to a TEE, which matches each fresh photo against the counterpart's stored embedding and, on success, computes a connection commitment CC_AB = H(min(ID_A,ID_B) || max(ID_A,ID_B)) so the commitment value is identical regardless of which party computed it. A relayer batches these commitments into an on-chain Merkle tree; users may bypass the relayer and submit directly if the relayer censors them.

Mechanism, social-graph verification (avoids ever exposing the graph itself, which the paper's own related-work section flags as the metadata-leakage failure of public-graph systems such as BrightID and Circles): an entity constructs a recursive zero-knowledge proof (ZK Random Walk) by proving its connection to the previous entity in a path and appending its own identity and reputation score, then forwarding the extended proof to the next hop. A valid path must have length O(log n) (n = number of entities in the network) and accumulate enough reputation along the way to include at least one externally-reputable entity. To prove a path has no repeated entity (a cycle) without revealing which entities are on it, each entity inserted into the path is added to a Bloom filter (a fixed-size bit array that support membership queries with possible false positives but never false negatives) carried forward with the proof; path-distinctness between multiple submitted paths is checked by a pairwise bitwise-AND of their Bloom filters — fewer than 2k set bits in the intersection (k = number of hash functions) indicates the paths are very likely fully disjoint. Once an entity has gathered the required O(log n) mutually disjoint paths, it aggregates them into a single ZK Proof of Paths, submitted to the smart contract, which verifies it and grants non-Sybil status plus an increment to the entity's own accumulated (intrinsic) reputation — letting entities who have proved themselves reduce dependence on externally-reputable anchors over time. State (reputation, connections) changes only at fixed epoch boundaries (3-7 days), requiring re-proof each epoch to stay verified.

### Measured results
| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Social-graph entity-verification simulation | 100 simulated entities, 30 epochs, three synthetic graph topologies (Holme-Kim, Watts-Strogatz, Kleinberg small-world), two trust-distribution modes (spread: reputation drawn from a normal distribution up to a capped maximum, applied to a percentage of entities; seeded: fewer entities set to the maximum reputation) | In the Holme-Kim model, spread mode needs 15%-30% of entities holding external reputation before verification propagates through the network; seeded mode needs 8%-10%. The paper states the Watts-Strogatz and Kleinberg models are "unsuitable due to weak connectivity" for this test, without a numeric propagation figure for them. |
| ZK Random Walk / ZK Proof of Paths circuit performance (proof-of-concept, Plonky2 scheme, "l" = path length) | Single-machine proof-of-concept implementation; the walk implementation used a simple nullifier array, not the Bloom-filter design described in the mechanism section | ZK Random Walk (linear circuit, per-recursion-depth): compile 1.56s, circuit size 8KB + l x 4.2MB, prove time 328.56ms, verify time 4.44ms, proof size 124KB. ZK Random Walk (cyclic, single self-referential circuit): compile 2.39s, size 8.4MB, prove 630.27ms, verify 4.68ms, proof 130KB. ZK Proof of Three Paths: compile 1.25s, size 16.9MB, prove 1.58s, verify 7.19ms, proof 143KB. ZK Proof of Six Paths: compile 2.65s, size 33.8MB, prove 2.82s, verify 12.41ms, proof 149KB. |
| Bloom filter sizing for path-distinctness checking (worked example, not a simulation sweep) | Path length 10, filter size 4096 bits, 3 hash functions | False-positive rate approximately 0.05%; false-negative rate approximately 0.01% |

The paper states explicitly that "a more detailed analysis is needed to evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness in preventing Sybil entities from obtaining verification" — the 100-entity simulation measures verification reachability under an honest population, not resistance to an adversarial one.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range tested |
|---|---|---|
| Path length for a valid ZK Random Walk / ZK Proof of Paths | O(log n) | not numerically fixed; scales with network size n |
| Epoch duration | between 3 and 7 days | stated as adjustable by "the system's intended strictness"; no specific value tested in the simulation |
| Endorsements required to promote a limited registration to full | "a specific endorsement threshold" | not numerically stated in the retrieved text |
| Endorsements one fully-registered user may issue | 1 | fixed, not varied |
| C2PA manifest freshness window, registration | example given: no older than one hour | not varied |
| C2PA manifest freshness window, connection establishment | example given: no older than 10 minutes | not varied |
| Bloom filter size / hash-function count (path-distinctness check) | 4096 bits, 3 hash functions, for path length 10 | not swept; one worked example only |
| Simulation network size | 100 entities | not varied |
| Simulation epoch count | 30 | not varied |

### Stated limitations
The system does not natively support key recovery or revocation; the authors propose, as unimplemented future work, routing recovery through trusted peers in the social graph instead of a centralized authority. The social-graph attack-resistance mechanism has no defense against an attacker who acquires k distinct attack edges (connections) into the honest region by using real, highly reputable identities as gateways to legitimize a large Sybil cluster; the paper states this outright as an open weakness, not merely a theoretical one. The system currently has no mechanism to penalize an entity for connecting indiscriminately with unknown (possibly Sybil) entities, which the authors say is "essential" future work. Entities can censor others by refusing to forward path proofs for them; the paper argues this has "statistically negligible impact" given the required multiplicity of paths but does not measure that claim numerically. Facial biometric registration depends on C2PA for anti-forgery, and the authors state that "since support for the C2PA standard in smartphones is not yet very widespread, it can theoretically be omitted," which the authors say reduces the registration-time defense to social-graph analysis alone. Merkle-proof persistence for zero-knowledge verification requires historical roots to remain available on-chain, and managing that root-availability buffer "without introducing centralized relayer dependencies remains a significant smart contract engineering challenge," per the authors. The reputation-threshold-for-a-valid-path setting is currently a fixed value derived from the maximum achievable intrinsic reputation with no external reputation; the authors state dynamic, network-adapting thresholds are future work. Community-endorsement-based correction of biometric false positives is stated by the authors to risk endorsements being "coerced" or otherwise obtained improperly, and the underlying facial-embedding quality and endorsement mechanism are called ongoing priorities, not solved problems.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires at least one operational TEE deployment (the paper specifies Oasis ROFL/Sapphire specifically) that can produce a remotely-attestable computation result; the paper's own discussion section states this is a live risk, not a design abstraction — it cites the 2025 SGX WireTap DRAM-bus-interposition attack (Seto et al., CCS 2025) as the reason the Integritee TEE-based project was discontinued, and states "Intel will not patch [it] as it assumes physical security," concluding that "the secure functioning of TEEs in decentralized environments remains an open question." Requires an encrypted, centrally-hosted (though TEE-gated) database of biometric embeddings reachable by every registering or connecting TEE instance — the paper labels this database "a centralized but encrypted repository," which is a centralization point in storage even though access is cryptographically gated. Requires at least a small externally-supplied reputation signal ("external reputation") injected into a minority of the entity population from outside the protocol, since the protocol's own intrinsic-reputation accumulation only functions once an entity has already completed at least one successful path proof — the system cannot bootstrap Sybil resistance from zero externally-supplied trust. Requires an on-chain relayer (or a fallback direct-submission path with degraded unlinkability) to batch connection commitments into the public Merkle tree; a permanently unavailable or fully compromised relayer forces users onto the direct-submission path, which the paper states "sacrifices some unlinkability." Requires that in-person meetings between connecting entities are not systematically fabricated at scale, since the whole social-graph Sybil-resistance claim rests on the assumption that establishing many mutual connections with honest entities is difficult for an attacker; the paper does not measure how difficult, only asserts it.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus regarding measured figures. On attribution: the target-registry's own description of this paper states its purpose is partly to determine "whether the trusted-execution-environment manufacturer becomes a new trusted party" — the retrieved text answers this only partially: it identifies Intel SGX and Oasis specifically as the deployed hardware/platform trust base and states outright that TEE security "remains an open question" in decentralized settings, but it does not analyze whether Intel or Oasis Labs becomes a systemic single point of trust comparable to World Network's Orb hardware manufacturer (which the paper's own related-work section criticizes on exactly that basis).

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: George Danezis, Prateek Mittal, "SybilInfer: Detecting sybil nodes using social networks," NDSS 2009 — cited as a social-graph analysis precedent.
- competing: BrightID, whitepaper, 2022 — public-graph proof-of-authority-blockchain social identity network; the paper states its public connection graph "risks metadata leakage," a criticism De-SyRIS's Bloom-filter/ZK design is built to avoid.
- competing: Circles ("money for a multipolar world"), whitepaper, 2024 — transitive-trust Universal Basic Income protocol with the same public-graph metadata-leakage property the paper criticizes.

## [LESNIEWSKI-LAAS-NSDI-10] Whanau: A Sybil-proof Distributed Hash Table
**Citation:** Chris Lesniewski-Laas, M. Frans Kaashoek. "Whanau: A Sybil-proof Distributed Hash Table." USENIX NSDI, 2010.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/whanau-nsdi10.pdf
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/whanau-nsdi10.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Whanau builds a one-hop distributed hash table (DHT) whose routing tables resist the Sybil
attack — an adversary creating an unlimited count of false identities to influence lookups. A
node's lookup correctness depends only on the count of social-graph edges connecting honest
users to adversary-controlled nodes ("attack edges"), not on how many false identities the
adversary creates behind those edges.

The mechanism runs in two phases. A SETUP phase runs periodically across all nodes and builds
each node's routing tables by sampling other nodes through random walks over the social graph:
each node's immediate social neighbors are the only edges it can walk, and no node holds a map
of the whole graph. Each node treats every sampled node as an equally likely candidate without
being able to tell honest samples from adversary samples, relying only on the fact that a large
fraction of samples land on honest nodes when the honest region of the graph is a fast-mixing
expander graph (a graph in which a random walk of length w = O(log n), for n honest nodes,
reaches close to the stationary distribution, so that the walk's endpoint is close to uniform
over graph edges). A LOOKUP phase then uses the constructed routing tables to find a
key-value record in O(1) messages and one network round trip, without further walks.

To counter an adversary that clusters its false identifiers immediately before a targeted key
(a clustering attack), Whanau introduces layered identifiers: honest node identifiers are placed
independently and uniformly at random within each of several layers, and a lookup tries each
layer in turn, so that a clustering attack concentrated in one layer's identifier space does not
help in the others. Each social-network edge is treated as a separate virtual node, so that
routing-table space and query load scale with a person's degree in the social graph (their count
of social connections) rather than being fixed per person — a policy choice the paper states,
not a measured property.

The instant-messaging (IM) application built on Whanau has each user publish one self-signed
(public key, IP address) tuple; a sender looks up the buddy's public key in the DHT, verifies the
returned tuple's signature, and sends to the returned address. Whanau supplies availability of
lookup (an honestly-inserted value is found), not integrity (the DHT also returns adversary-
inserted values for the same key); integrity is left to the application, which the IM example
handles by discarding records with invalid signatures.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Routing table size O(√(km log(km))) entries per node for aggregate system capacity of km keys, k = keys per node, m = honest edges | Analytic result, confirmed by simulation |
| Median LOOKUP: 2 messages at g=20,000 attack edges; 20 messages at g=2,000,000 attack edges, at table size 10,000 entries/link | Flickr social graph, n=1,624,992 nodes, m=15,476,835 edges (Table 2) |
| Minimum table size for fast lookups without attack: ≈1,000 ≈ √n entries/link; under g > n, requires ≈10,000 entries/link | Flickr graph |
| Performance transition point (LOOKUP messages grow exponentially) occurs at m/10 < g < m, not at the analytically predicted g > n/10 | Measured across all four datasets: Flickr (n=1.6M), LiveJournal (n=5.2M), YouTube (n=1.1M), DBLP (n=510K) |
| Layers become important (measurably reduce messages) above g=5,000 attack edges (0.3% of n) on Flickr; for g>20,000, ≈8 layers is best | Flickr, fixed resource budget of 100,000 table entries per link, clustering-attack adversary |
| Random-walk escape probability into Sybil region: 90% Sybil at walk length 40 when g=2,000,000 (1.35 attack-links/honest user on average); 60% honest at walk length 10 under the same attack | Flickr social graph |
| Random-walk mixing: CDF of per-edge landing probability approaches the ideal uniform (1/m) distribution as walk length increases from 10 to 80 steps | Sampled 100 random starting edges per network, computed over Flickr, LiveJournal, YouTube, DBLP |
| PlanetLab: median lookup latency ≈ one network round trip within PlanetLab, rising gradually with churn; percent of queries needing retry rises under churn and resets to baseline each time SETUP re-runs | 4,000 virtual Whanau nodes on 400 PlanetLab machines, routing-table size 200 entries/social link, node failure/recovery via Poisson process averaging 2 events/second, tested at 10% and 20% of virtual nodes offline plus a no-churn control |
| Table-size scaling matches the O(√m) prediction for a one-hop DHT; at m=10,000,000 edges, most lookups succeed in 1–2 messages at ≈2,000 entries/link | Synthetic preferential-attachment networks (power-law exponent ≈2) plus the four real datasets, no adversary simulated |

### Parameters
- Walk length w: fixed at 10 in the clustering-attack experiments (Section 9.2); the paper states w = O(log n) is required for fast mixing and that larger w costs more bandwidth and raises the chance a walk returns a Sybil node.
- Table size (entries per social-network edge): varied from 100 to 1,000,000 in experiments; minimum viable is ≈√m.
- Number of layers: varied from 1 to 10; optimal layer count rises with table-size budget and with attacker strength, determined empirically per network (Figures 10–11), no single fixed recommendation given.
- Retry limit: 120 messages, above which a lookup is counted as failed in the heat-map experiments (Figure 9 caption).
- Amplification: running 3·log2(n) independent protocol instances in parallel is stated to reduce lookup failure probability below 1/n³, given a base (g, ε, 1/2)-Sybil-proof instance.

### Stated limitations
The implementation is not aware of network locality (does not place routing-table entries by
network proximity). Routing tables require periodic full rebuilds (re-running SETUP) to react to
churn in the social graph and in the set of stored keys; the paper describes a bandwidth/latency
tradeoff for how often to rebuild but states this as future work, not solved. The protocol as
described handles 1 ≲ k ≲ m keys per node well; outside that range (k > m or k < 1) the paper
states specific modifications are required and analyzes them without simulating them. Integrity
of returned values is explicitly out of scope; an adversary can insert or overwrite key-value
pairs for the same key and Whanau will return them alongside honest values. The paper states
Whanau can be broken by social engineering attacks that persuade honest users to link to
Sybil identities, despite being provably Sybil-proof under its graph model. The PlanetLab
experiment's scale (4,000 virtual nodes) is stated by the authors as too small to test asymptotic
scaling behavior; it demonstrates functioning under churn only.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a pre-existing social graph of honest, mostly-symmetric trust edges in which the honest
region has no sparse cut internally and forms a fast-mixing expander graph; the paper's own
measurement of this property (Figure 6) is a prerequisite check that must be re-run on any graph
this is deployed against. Requires each node to know order-of-magnitude estimates of m (honest
edge count), w (mixing time), and k (keys per node) to size tables and walk lengths; does not
require nodes to know g (attack-edge count) or ε (fraction of loser nodes). Requires a mechanism
elsewhere in the system to supply per-record integrity (such as a signature scheme), because
Whanau's LOOKUP returns adversary-inserted records for a queried key without filtering them.
Requires periodic re-execution of the cooperative SETUP phase across the network to track churn;
this is a synchronized, network-wide operation, not an incremental per-node update.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving
- SybilGuard / SybilLimit — Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman, and Yu et al. follow-up (as cited: refs [27], [26]) — foundational (fast-mixing-graph random-walk Sybil defense that Whanau builds on)
- G. Danezis, C. Lesniewski-Laas, M. F. Kaashoek, R. Anderson. "Sybil-Resistant DHT Routing." ESORICS 2005 — foundational (the bootstrap-graph correctness criterion Whanau's authors state was left as an open problem)
- G. Danezis, P. Mittal. "SybilInfer: Detecting Sybil Nodes Using Social Networks." NDSS 2009 — competing (Bayesian inference over random walks for Sybil detection)
- I. Gupta, K. Birman, P. Linga, A. Demers, R. van Renesse. "Kelips: Building an Efficient and Stable P2P DHT through Increased Memory and Background Overhead." IPTPS 2003 — competing (the insecure one-hop DHT Whanau compares its non-adversarial scaling against)
- H. Rowaihy, W. Enck, P. McDaniel, T. La Porta. "Limiting Sybil Attacks in Structured P2P Networks." INFOCOM 2007 — competing
- A. Singh, T.-W. Ngan, P. Druschel, D. Wallach. "Eclipse Attacks on Overlay Networks: Threats and Defenses." INFOCOM 2006 — attack
- B. N. Levine, C. Shields, N. B. Margolin. "A Survey of Solutions to the Sybil Attack." UMass Amherst TR, 2006 — foundational (survey)
- A. Mislove, M. Marcon, P. Gummadi, P. Druschel, B. Bhattacharjee. "Measurement and Analysis of Online Social Networks." IMC 2007 — foundational (source of the social-graph datasets used in evaluation)
- C. Lesniewski-Laas, M. F. Kaashoek. "Whanaungatanga: Sybil-Proof Routing with Social Networks." MIT CSAIL TR-2009-045 — superseded-by (this NSDI paper is the published version of this technical report)

- "Whānau provides availability, but not integrity"
- "the number of Sybils in the social network does not affect the protocol's performance, but links between honest users and Sybils do"

## [LEVIEN-USS-98] Attack-Resistant Trust Metrics for Public Key Certification
**Citation:** Raph Levien, Alexander Aiken. "Attack-Resistant Trust Metrics for Public Key Certification." 7th USENIX Security Symposium, 1998.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/publications/library/proceedings/sec98/full_papers/levien/levien.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/publications/library/proceedings/sec98/full_papers/levien/levien.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper defines a trust metric as a function that decides, for a given client key (the source) and a target name/key binding, whether to accept that binding, computed from a graph of digitally signed certificates (a certificate is a signed statement binding a name to a key, made by one key about another). It gives an analytical framework for comparing trust metrics by how many keys or certificates an attacker must control to force acceptance of a false binding, proves a best-case theoretical limit no trust metric can beat, and presents a maximum-network-flow-based metric that meets that limit.

Mechanism, threat model: two attack types are distinguished. A node attack assumes the attacker fully compromises a key (equivalent to stealing its secret key), letting the attacker issue arbitrary certificates from it. An edge attack is weaker: the attacker cannot compromise a key but can trick its legitimate owner into signing one specific bad certificate (one edge in the certification graph), for instance by social-engineering a legitimate keyholder into vouching for an untrustworthy party. A trust metric can be tuned to resist one attack type more than the other; the paper's specific network-flow construction resists edge attacks far more than node attacks.

Mechanism, the theoretical limit (Section 5): define d as the minimum number of direct certifiers (predecessors) held by any key the trust metric is willing to widely accept. Because a node attack lets the attacker fabricate an entire subtree of certificates behind a single compromised key, no trust metric can be immune to an attack on d keys or more (the attacker simply compromises all d certifiers of some already-accepted key, then certifies an arbitrary target through them). For edge attacks, the paper shows the analogous best-case bound is beta*d/2, where beta (<=1, defined as the ratio between the actual number of second-degree predecessors of some widely-accepted key and d^2, the maximum possible) captures how much the certification graph's inbound paths overlap near any given widely-accepted node; beta is stated to be near 1 for random graphs and "hoped to be fairly high (greater than 0.5, say)" for realistic certification graphs, though the paper does not measure beta on any real certificate graph.

Mechanism, the network-flow trust metric that meets this bound (Section 6): treat the certificate graph as a flow network from source s (the client key) to target t (the key being verified), and accept the binding if the maximum flow between s and t is at least 1. Rather than giving every node a uniform capacity (which, for a target flow of 1, would require every node's capacity set to 0.5, meaning an attacker controlling any two well-placed nodes can already force acceptance), the metric assigns each node n a capacity C_(s,t)(n) = max(f_s(dist(s,n)), g_t(dist(n,t))), where dist(s,t) is the shortest-path hop count between source and target and f_s, g_t are functions of hop-distance from source and target respectively, tunable to weight nodes near the source (or target) with higher capacity than nodes farther away. One instantiation given in the paper (tuned to resist node attacks rather than edge attacks) sets f_s(1) = max(1/d, 1/|succ(s)|), f_s(l>=2) = 1/d, and g_t(l) = 1/d for all l, where succ(s) is the set of s's direct successors; these values are derived to make the network's maximum flow equal 1 for most (source, target) pairs while guaranteeing no more than d nodes anywhere in the graph carry capacity greater than 1/d. Raising capacities specifically near the source and target (rather than uniformly) is stated by the authors to have only a small effect on node-attack resistance (because the uniform-capacity metric is already close to the theoretical bound for node attacks) but to substantially improve edge-attack resistance, from requiring d edges to requiring beta*d/2.

### Measured results
This is a theoretical/analytical paper: its results are proved bounds and a comparison table of attacker resource requirements under different metrics, not measurements from an implemented system or a dataset. No experiment, simulation, testbed, node count, or runtime is reported anywhere in the retrieved text.

| Trust metric | Nodes needed for a successful node attack | Nodes needed for a successful edge attack | Edges needed for a successful edge attack |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shortest path (accept the target reachable by the shortest certificate chain) | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Maurer (probabilistic reachability metric, simplified to a single edge type) | 1 | 1 | d |
| Reiter & Stubblebine (bounded vertex-disjoint paths) | d | d | d |
| Maxflow (uniform node capacities) | d | d | d |
| Maxflow-edge (the paper's own capacity construction, weighted toward source/target) | d | beta*d/2 | beta*d/2 |
| Best case (proved bound; no metric can exceed this) | d | beta*d/2 | beta*d/2 |

The paper offers one concrete illustrative example, not a general experiment: for d=3 in a small hand-drawn graph (Figure 5), f_s(1)=0.5, f_s(l>=2)=0.333, g_t(l>=1)=0.333; the paper states that with uniform capacities set at 0.5 (the level needed for a maxflow of 1), "most attacks on two nodes succeed," whereas with source/target-weighted capacities in the same graph "the only successful two node attack is on {keyB, keyE}." For a numeric illustration of the theoretical bound's practical stakes, the paper states that for d=10 (each key certified by at least 10 others) and beta=0.5, an attacker needs 10 keys for a node attack but 50 keys for an edge attack under the maxflow-edge metric — this beta=0.5 figure is explicitly a plugged-in illustrative value, not a measured one (the paper elsewhere states "for realistic certification graphs" beta is merely "hoped to be" above 0.5).

The paper additionally reports a structural fact about one real certificate graph, cited from an external source rather than measured by the authors themselves: about 35% of the keys in the strongly-connected subgraph of the PGP web-of-trust key database (cited from N. McBurnett's "PGP web of trust statistics," 1996) have exactly one predecessor, meaning d=1 is the effective bound for that graph and no trust metric can offer any attack resistance advantage over a single-signature requirement there.

### Parameters
| Parameter | Definition | Value/notes |
|---|---|---|
| d | minimum number of direct certifiers of any key the metric is willing to accept widely | not fixed by the theory; the paper illustrates with d=10 (main worked example) and d=3 (Figure 5 example) |
| beta | ratio of the actual count of second-degree predecessors of a widely-accepted node to d^2 (the maximum possible); bounds edge-attack resistance | "very near one for random graphs"; "hoped to be fairly high (greater than 0.5, say)" for real certification graphs — explicitly not measured on a real graph in this paper |
| f_s(l), g_t(l) | capacity-assignment functions of hop-distance l from source/target | one instantiation given (f_s(1)=max(1/d, 1/|succ(s)|), f_s(l>=2)=1/d, g_t(l)=1/d); the paper states the metric is "parameterized by the exact definitions" of these functions, meaning other instantiations are possible and untested here |
| Maurer edge-probability parameter | probability assigned to each edge in Maurer's probabilistic reachability model | analyzed only at its two limits, probability -> 0 (becomes equivalent to shortest-path) and probability -> 1 (becomes equivalent to unit-capacity maxflow); proofs given in Appendix A, no intermediate value analyzed |

### Stated limitations
The framework's central assumption is that a good trust metric should accept most good name/key bindings; the authors state explicitly this assumption "is not always valid" — for high-security applications wanting a "very restricted guest list," a metric that rejects many good bindings may be preferable, and the paper's optimality results do not apply to that regime. The framework's second assumption is that the name space is opaque (no information can be extracted from the name string itself); the paper notes real names often have exploitable structure but states this is not modeled. The authors state a trust metric of any kind is "not particularly helpful" on certificate graphs like the PGP web of trust, where about 35% of keys have only one predecessor (d=1), because a source key must then choose between rejecting a large fraction of the graph or being highly vulnerable to a single-key forgery — the metric's protection scales with d, and low-d graphs give it almost nothing to work with. The paper explicitly leaves open a comparison between its maxflow-based metric and Reiter & Stubblebine's bounded-vertex-disjoint-paths metric on the question of whether a path-length bound improves resistance; it argues analytically (not empirically) that it does not, and states the argument's validity depends on the assumption that both compared metrics accept most good keys, which may not hold for metrics that intentionally accept only a fraction of good keys. The paper explicitly ends without validating the metric on any deployed or prototype certificate infrastructure, stating "only practical experience with a prototype system can determine whether this tradeoff is worthwhile," referring to the tradeoff between attack resistance and the increased certification burden the mechanism imposes on every key's owner.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires every key that will be widely accepted to be certified by at least d other keys, where d directly sets the minimum number of keys or certificates an attacker must control; the paper states this outright as a precondition ("for an attack-resistant key infrastructure based on trust metrics to be viable, the owner of every key must be willing and able to have a number of people to certify it") and states resisting attacks "increases the cost of certification" for every participant, not merely the operator. Requires a directed graph of signed certificates reachable from the verifying client's own key as the sole input to the flow computation; the mechanism itself supplies no way to discover, revoke, or freshness-check certificates, so an external certificate-distribution and revocation system must supply and maintain that graph. Requires the client (source) to already hold its own key as a fixed, trusted starting point (s in the flow formulation) — the metric evaluates trust in a target relative to one already-trusted source, and does not itself bootstrap that source's own trustworthiness. Requires whoever tunes f_s and g_t to know or estimate the graph's realistic d and beta, since the paper's own worked numeric comparisons (d=10, beta=0.5) are stated as illustrative choices rather than values derived from a specific measured deployment; deploying the metric without measuring these two figures on the target certificate population means the attacker-resource-requirement claims in the comparison table are unverified for that population.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. On attribution: the paper's own comparison table shows the Reiter & Stubblebine bounded-vertex-disjoint-paths metric requiring d nodes/edges for either attack type — identical to the paper's own uniform-capacity maxflow metric and strictly worse than the paper's own source/target-weighted maxflow-edge construction (beta*d/2) — which is a direct numeric disagreement with any claim that bounding path length improves attack resistance over unbounded maximum flow; the paper states this itself as its own analytical finding, not as a disagreement with an external source, since Reiter & Stubblebine's original paper is a comparison target here rather than a source of a rival measured figure.

### References worth retrieving
- competing: M. Reiter, S. Stubblebine, "Path Independence for Authentication in Large-Scale Systems," ACM CCS 1997 (cited as [RS97a]) — the bounded-vertex-disjoint-paths metric this paper argues is dominated by unbounded maxflow; holds Reiter and Stubblebine's own reported figures for direct comparison.
- competing: M. Reiter, S. Stubblebine, "Toward Acceptable Metrics of Authentication," IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 1997 (cited as [RS97b]) — a different network-flow-based trust metric from the same authors, distinct from the vertex-disjoint-paths metric in [RS97a].
- competing/foundational: U. Maurer, "Modelling a public-key infrastructure," ESORICS 1996 — origin of the probabilistic-edge trust metric this paper analyzes at its two probability limits and shows "succumbs to an attack on a single node" despite being edge-attack-resistant.
- foundational: T. Beth, M. Borcherding, B. Klein, "Valuation of trust in open networks," ESORICS 1994 (cited as [BBK94]) — the paper this work explicitly extends; BBK94 first demonstrated a single-node attack could arbitrarily manipulate their trust metric's output, motivating this paper's analytical framework.
- measurement (external, not a full paper retrieved here): N. McBurnett, "PGP web of trust statistics," http://bcn.boulder.co.us/~neal/pgpstat, 1996 — source of the cited 35%-single-predecessor figure for the real PGP web-of-trust graph; worth retrieving directly since the 1998 paper cites but does not reproduce the underlying measurement methodology.
- foundational (certificate-path metric predating this line): A. Tarah, C. Huitema, "Associating metrics to certification paths," ESORICS 1992 — an earlier certification-path metric, cited but not directly compared numerically in this paper's table.

- "there is an optimal trust metric based on maximum network flow."
- "the Reiter & Stubblebine trust metric is close to optimal, while the Maurer trust metric is easily attacked."
- "an attacker would require 10 keys in a node attack or 50 keys in a edge attack."
- "about 35% of the keys in the strongly connected subgraph have one predecessor."

## [LI-EPRINT-25] A Place for Everyone vs Everyone in its Place: Measuring and Attacking the Ethereum Global Network

**Citation:** Chenyu Li, Ren Zhang, Xiaorui Gong. "A Place for Everyone vs Everyone in its Place: Measuring and Attacking the Ethereum Global Network." Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2025/588.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/588.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/588.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper measures the Ethereum Global Network (EGN), the single Kademlia-based peer-to-peer overlay that Ethereum's node-discovery protocols Discv4 and Discv5 form, and shows that a design decision to let one overlay serve thousands of distinct blockchain services (Ethereum mainnet and its testnets, forks, and unrelated chains such as BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, and Gnosis) degrades both discovery efficiency and attack resistance for every one of those services. A Discv4 or Discv5 node's routing table (DHT) fills with peers regardless of which service those peers run, because neither protocol's node record carries reliable, mandatory service information: Discv4 servicing is inferred from four fields (protocolVersion, networkID, genesisHash, forkID) that only Ethereum-family services populate, and Discv5's node-record extension for service and topic information exists in the specification but the paper finds it implemented in no deployed client. A node therefore spends most of its discovery messages contacting peers of other services, which reject the resulting application-layer handshake, wasting bandwidth without narrowing the search. The same blending is then shown to weaken a standard node-discovery-table (DHT) pollution attack, described in section 5.1: an attacker who controls a small number of always-responsive nodes sends unsolicited Ping messages faster than the honest liveness-check interval, so its own node records occupy each victim's replacement slots and, once an existing entry fails its own liveness check, get promoted into the victim's bucket proper; the attacker also answers every Findnode request with Neighbors messages listing only its own entries, so its records propagate passively through the rest of the network. Because a blended DHT already holds mostly other-service peers before the attack starts, filling the remaining slots with attacker entries removes almost all of a victim's remaining same-service peers, producing far more nodes cut off from every honest same-service peer (a network partition) than the same attack causes in a hypothetical dedicated (single-service) overlay of the same size.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Discv4 network size | Fluctuated 94,180-113,524, averaging 103,432 nodes | 720 fifteen-day snapshots, December 12-27, 2024, via the Nebula crawler on a 32-core/128GB/4TB commercial VPS, 30-minute crawl duration per snapshot |
| Discv5 network size | Fluctuated 208,268-238,219, averaging 223,132 nodes | Same measurement period and crawler |
