### Parameters
- Crawler: Nebula, 30-minute crawl duration per iteration (chosen because the newly-discovered-node rate falls to about one per second beyond that duration, which the authors treat as ordinary churn rather than incomplete discovery); each Discv4 node queried with 15 Findnode messages against randomly selected target IDs (bucket-specific queries unsupported in Discv4); each Discv5 node queried with 17 Findnode messages, one per bucket.
- Discv4 liveness-check interval assumed by the attack: 10 seconds; attacker Ping interval: 1 second (chosen shorter than the liveness-check interval to win eviction races).
- Attack scale simulated: 1 to 330 attacker nodes, with the headline results reported at 300, representing under 0.3% of the measured network.
- Outgoing-connection targets in the efficiency experiment: 66 connections for BSC Mainnet and Polygon, 16 for the other four tested services, or a 12-hour timeout, whichever came first.

### Stated limitations
The threat model is explicitly described by the authors as weak: the attacker cannot remove long-term active honest peers from a victim's DHT, because those peers pass periodic liveness checks before eviction, so a node retains full isolation only if all its long-term peers already fall inside the attacker-controlled partition. A node the authors classify as partitioned by their DHT-based definition may still receive new blocks and transactions until its existing application-layer TCP connections close, including a connection that traverses a NAT (network address translator) the DHT-based analysis cannot observe. The DHT composition analysis in section 3.3 is stated to be infeasible for Discv5 for lack of service information; the authors substitute the Discv4 service distribution when calibrating the Discv5-adjacent simulation and state this as an assumption ("we use the service distribution of Discv4 as such information is not available in Discv5"), not a measured Discv5 fact. The simulation-based attack results are not measured on the live network; the paper states the choice to simulate is to avoid disrupting real-world services, and states the simulated environment was checked against the crawler's measurements but does not claim the simulation's absolute partition percentages would reproduce identically against the live network. The authors state they contacted the Ethereum Foundation about the findings and had not received a response at the time of writing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The attack requires that a node discovery protocol's passive-DHT-maintenance mechanism inserts any node record that pings it into a bucket or replacement slot without verifying the record's claimed service; removing that requirement (mandatory, verifiable service information at the record-insertion step, which is the paper's own section 6 proposal) would prevent the attack described here. The attack also requires that the liveness check interval a client uses (10 seconds in the deployed protocol) exceeds the interval an attacker can sustain a faster Ping rate at; a defense would need either a liveness check faster than any plausible attacker Ping rate or a bound on how quickly one source's record can occupy a replacement slot. Recovery from a network partition, in this paper's own model, depends entirely on some node in the partition retaining a link to a bootnode's DHT or receiving a new join from a node that bridges both sides; a component that manages bootnode routing tables independently of this design (for example, prioritizing same-service peers, the paper's second proposed fix) directly determines the partition-recovery probability this paper measures, so any redesign of bootnode peer selection changes the partition outcome measured here.

### Contradicts
DISC-NG (Krol, Ascigil, Rene, Sonnino, Pigaglio, Sadre, Lange, Riviere, EuroS&P 2024), described in this paper's related-work section as a parallel study addressing Discv5 inefficiency, is stated by this paper's authors to have identified the same low node-discovery-efficiency symptom but not the root cause (EGN's blended, multi-service overlay architecture); this paper states DISC-NG contains no comparison to dedicated single-service overlays and no security analysis. This is the paper's own characterization of DISC-NG, not independently verified against DISC-NG's own text in this entry, since DISC-NG was not part of this extraction batch.

### References worth retrieving

## [LI-INFOCOM-05] A Performance vs. Cost Framework for Evaluating DHT Design Tradeoffs Under Churn

**Citation:** Jinyang Li, Jeremy Stribling, Robert Morris, M. Frans Kaashoek, Thomer M. Gil. "A Performance vs. Cost Framework for Evaluating DHT Design Tradeoffs Under Churn." IEEE INFOCOM, 2005. DOI 10.1109/INFCOM.2005.1497894.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~strib/docs/dhtcomparison/dhtcomparison-infocom05.pdf
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~strib/docs/dhtcomparison/dhtcomparison-infocom05.pdf
**Domain:** A

Correction to the registry's why-needed note: the retrieved text does not mention Accordion anywhere. This paper simulates and compares Chord, Kademlia, Kelips, OneHop, and Tapestry using the performance-vs-cost (PVC) framework; it does not introduce Accordion's self-tuning bandwidth-budget routing table. Accordion is a distinct system by an overlapping author set (Jinyang Li, Jeremy Stribling, Thomer M. Gil, Robert Morris, M. Frans Kaashoek, "Bandwidth-efficient Management of DHT Routing Tables," NSDI 2005), not retrieved in this batch. This entry extracts only what the retrieved text supports.

### What it does
The performance-vs-cost (PVC) framework lets a person compare distributed-hash-table (DHT) protocol design choices by treating each protocol as trading network bandwidth for lookup performance under churn (continual node join and departure), rather than comparing protocols only on a static network. PVC records, for every simulation run of a protocol under one combination of parameter values, two numbers: the average bytes per second sent by a live node (the cost axis, counting lookup traffic, join traffic, and routing-table maintenance traffic together, with each message priced at 20 bytes of packet overhead plus 4 bytes per IP address or node identifier it carries) and either the median latency of successful lookups or the fraction of failed lookups (the performance axis). A lookup counts as failed if it returns the wrong node or times out entirely; PVC bounds total lookup retry time to four seconds before declaring failure, and reports failure rate and median successful-lookup latency as two separate statistics rather than folding failed lookups into the latency average, because a failed lookup would otherwise contribute a fixed four-second penalty that distorts the average. Plotting every simulated parameter combination as one point on the cost-performance plane and taking the lower convex hull (the curve of parameter combinations no other combination beats on both axes at once) yields the overall convex hull for a protocol: the best latency (or failure rate) achievable at each bandwidth level. To measure how important one specific parameter is, PVC fixes that parameter to one value, varies every other parameter, and takes the convex hull of just those runs; the area between that single-parameter hull and the overall hull, integrated over a fixed cost range, measures how much performance is lost by locking that parameter to a single value instead of tuning it — a large area means the parameter needs per-workload tuning, a near-zero area means one fixed value performs about as well as tuning it.

### Measured results
Simulator: p2psim, a discrete-event packet-level simulator that models message delay but not link transmission rate or queuing delay (because the experiments measure key lookups, not bulk data transfer).

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying network | Median round-trip delay 156 ms, average 178 ms | 1,024-node topology, pairwise latencies measured from 1,024 real DNS servers via the King method |
| Node churn model | Exponentially distributed session length, mean 1 hour per node; each rejoin uses a new IP address and DHT identifier | All experiments unless noted otherwise |
| Churn-intensive workload | Each node issues a lookup for a random key at intervals exponentially distributed with mean 600 s | Primary workload for most reported figures; 6 simulated hours per run, statistics collected only from the second half |
| Lookup-intensive workload | Mean lookup interval 9 s (about 67x the churn-intensive lookup rate) | Used for the workload-sensitivity comparison in section V.G |
| Best latency at fixed bandwidth, churn-intensive workload | At 10 bytes/node/s: OneHop achieves 160 ms median lookup latency; Kademlia achieves 450 ms, with best parameter settings for each | 1,024-node topology, churn-intensive workload, exhaustive parameter search |
| OneHop minimum bandwidth floor | 7.5 bytes/node/s at 1,024 nodes; about 21 bytes/node/s at 3,000 nodes | Because OneHop proactively notifies every node of every join/leave event, its minimum cost scales with churn rate times network size; 3,000-node topology latencies derived from Euclidean-square distance (no King-method data available at that scale), calibrated to the same 156 ms median latency as the 1,024-node topology |
| OneHop load imbalance | Slice and unit leader nodes use about 8x-10x the average node's bandwidth | 1,024-node topology; contrasted with Chord, Kelips, Tapestry, and Kademlia, whose 95th-percentile node uses no more than 2x the average node's bandwidth |
| Chord failure rate at low bandwidth | Chord shows a lower failure rate than the other four protocols when bandwidth is constrained | Churn-intensive workload, 1,024 nodes; attributed to Chord's lookup correctness depending only on successor pointers (tuned via tsucc), letting Chord stabilize only the successor list frequently rather than the whole routing table |
| Non-transitive network, failure rate | Chord's failure rate rises more than Tapestry's under non-transitivity | 1,024-node topology with 5% of node pairs having all packets between them dropped (calibrated to the measured 4% broken-pair rate reported for PlanetLab); standard join algorithms replaced with an oracle join for both protocols (this changes bandwidth consumption, so results are not directly comparable to the connected-network figures); at a fixed cost of 80 bytes/node/s, Tapestry's Table X best/worst failure rates range 0.013-0.075, Chord's range 0.029-0.048 |
| Chord base-parameter tuning | Changing Chord base b from 16 to 2 increases median lookup latency from 186 ms to 226 ms at a fixed cost of 40 bytes/node/s while other parameters are held at their individually-best values; base has little effect on failure rate at the same cost | Churn-intensive workload, 1,024 nodes |
| Kelips contact-count (ncontact) tuning | ncontact values above 16 approach the overall convex hull; maximizing ncontact=32 gives the best latency/cost tradeoff across the full measured cost range (1-100 bytes/node/s) | Same setup; Kelips minimum required per-node state is sqrt(n) + (sqrt(n)-1) contacts, below which lookups route through randomly chosen nodes and latency rises sharply |
| Kademlia parallelism vs. stabilization | ntell and alpha (lookup-parallelism parameters) rank as the most important parameters for latency; the best tstab value is always the maximum stabilization interval tested | Churn-intensive workload, 1,024 nodes |
| Kademlia learning-from-lookups vs. explicit stabilization, failure rate | With learning disabled, at a fixed 80 bytes/node/s: best/worst tstab failure rates are 0.036/0.122, versus normal (learning-enabled) Kademlia where tstab is also the least effective parameter for lowering failure rate | Churn-intensive workload, 1,024 nodes, Kademlia variant with the lookup-based neighbor-learning mechanism disabled |
| Lookup-intensive workload effect on Kademlia | Under the lookup-intensive workload, a smaller alpha=2 gives the best cost/latency tradeoff, versus the larger alpha=8 that is best under the churn-intensive workload; Kademlia's overall convex hull degrades more than the other four protocols under the lookup-intensive workload | 1,024 nodes, mean lookup interval 9 s |
| Lookup-intensive workload effect on Chord/Tapestry | A large base (32 or 64) becomes best across a wide cost range, reducing hop count to about 2.8 one-way hops; tstab (Chord) and the corresponding Tapestry stabilization parameter become the most important parameters to tune, replacing base's importance under the churn-intensive workload | Same 1,024-node topology, lookup-intensive workload |

### Parameters

| Protocol | Parameter | Range tested |

| Chord | Successor stabilization interval tsucc | 18 s - 4.8 min |
| Kelips | Gossip interval tgossip | 10 s - 19 min |
| Kelips | Group ration rgroup | 8, 16, 32 |
| Kelips | Contact ration rcontact | 8, 16, 32 |
| Kelips | Contacts per group ncontact | 2, 8, 16, 32 |
| Kelips | Routing entry timeout tout | 6, 18, 30 min |
| Kademlia | Nodes per bucket entry k | 2-32 |
| Kademlia | Parallel lookups alpha | 1-32 |
| Kademlia | Number of IDs returned per hop ntell | 2-32 |

Fixed experimental parameters (not varied): lookup message timeout = 3x round-trip time to the target node; maximum total lookup retry time before declaring failure = 4 seconds; node session length = exponential, mean 1 hour; Kelips group count g = sqrt(1000) = 32 for the 1,000-node Kelips runs.

### Stated limitations
The simulator does not model link transmission rate or queuing delay, only per-message propagation delay, because the paper's experiments measure key lookups rather than bulk data retrieval; the authors separately state, discussing Rhea et al.'s Bamboo comparison, that their own simulator does not model bandwidth congestion, which that other study found to be an important factor. The non-transitive-network experiment investigates only the effect of non-transitivity on lookups and explicitly defers investigating its effect on the join procedure to future work; the standard join algorithm was replaced with an oracle join for that experiment because nodes often failed to join at all in a non-transitive network under the normal algorithm. PVC's convex-hull search is described as an approximation: the paper states it is possible that better parameter combinations exist that PVC's grid search failed to find. PVC ignores per-node state-storage cost entirely (routing-table memory size), on the stated ground that communication cost is typically far larger than storage cost and that state's main expense is the communication needed to keep it correct — this is presented as a design decision of the framework, not a measured finding.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A protocol being compared under PVC must expose every tunable parameter that trades bandwidth for lookup performance (stabilization interval, routing-table size or base, lookup parallelism, gossip interval, or equivalent), because PVC's importance-ranking method depends on being able to fix one parameter and vary the rest; a protocol with an undocumented or hidden internal tuning knob cannot be fairly ranked by this method. Any two protocols compared on the same convex-hull plot must use the same lookup-timeout and lookup-retry-limit policy (3x round-trip time per message, 4-second total retry budget in this paper), since those thresholds directly set the failure-rate/latency tradeoff and differ from what a protocol's own default implementation might use. A workload used to drive a PVC comparison must specify both a churn rate (mean session length) and a lookup rate, because the paper shows protocol rankings reverse between the churn-intensive and lookup-intensive workloads for the same 1,024-node topology (Kademlia's best alpha value moves from 8 to 2, and Chord/Tapestry's stabilization parameter overtakes base in importance).

### Contradicts
The registry's why-needed note for this key states the paper "introduces Accordion's self-tuning bandwidth-budget DHT"; this is not supported by the retrieved text, which never mentions Accordion. That mechanism belongs to a separate paper (Li, Stribling, Gil, Morris, Kaashoek, "Bandwidth-efficient Management of DHT Routing Tables," NSDI 2005) not retrieved in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- Liben-Nowell, Balakrishnan, Karger, "Analysis of the evolution of peer-to-peer systems," cited as [2] — foundational (introduces the half-life metric for churn and an Omega(log n) stabilization-notification bound for Chord; the theoretical churn analysis this paper's empirical study is positioned against)
- Rhea, Geels, Roscoe, Kubiatowicz, "Handling churn in a DHT" (Bamboo), cited as [3] — competing (compared and contrasted directly in Related Work; the source of the finding that bandwidth congestion is an important factor this paper's simulator does not model)
- Castro, Costa, Rowstron, "Performance and dependability of structured peer-to-peer overlays" (MSPastry), cited as [4] — competing (Pastry implementation optimized for churn, discussed in Related Work)
- Lam, Liu, cited as [5] — competing (join/recovery algorithms for a hypercube-based DHT and the stronger "K-consistency" correctness notion, contrasted with this paper's focus on lookup latency/correctness)
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia," cited as [8] — foundational (already in corpus)
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord," cited as [7] — foundational
- Zhao, Kubiatowicz, Joseph, "Tapestry," cited as [11] — foundational
- Gupta, Linga, Birman, van Renesse, "Kelips" — foundational
- Gummadi, Gummadi, Gribble, Ratnasamy, Shenker, Stoica, on Proximity Neighbor Selection, cited as [1], [13], [18] — foundational

## [LIN-ICDEW-21] Measuring Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum using Multiple Metrics and Granularities

**Citation:** Qinwei Lin, Chao Li, Xifeng Zhao, Xianhai Chen. "Measuring Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum using Multiple Metrics and Granularities." IEEE ICDE Workshops, 2021. DOI 10.1109/ICDEW53142.2021.00022.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDEW53142.2021.00022 (also posted as arXiv:2101.10699)
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDEW53142.2021.00022
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper quantifies how concentrated block-production power is in Bitcoin and Ethereum over a full year, using three independent statistics computed at three time granularities, then adds a windowing method that avoids missing concentration spikes that fall across a fixed-interval boundary. Blocks are collected via Google BigQuery, a hosted service exposing an Application Programming Interface (a defined set of callable operations) over prebuilt blockchain datasets. The Gini coefficient (an inequality measure) is computed over the distribution of blocks produced by each distinct block producer within a window, giving a value from 0 (equal production) toward 1 (one producer dominates); the paper's own formula sums pairwise absolute differences in block counts across all producer pairs, divides by twice the number of producers times the total blocks produced. Shannon entropy (a measure of the unpredictability of a probability distribution) is computed over the same per-producer block-count distribution treated as a probability distribution, so a higher value means block production is spread more unpredictably across producers. The Nakamoto coefficient is the minimum number of distinct producers whose combined block share reaches 51% of all blocks in the window, so a higher value means more producers would need to combine to reach majority control. Two windowing methods are applied to each metric: fixed windows, which partition the year into non-overlapping day-, week-, or month-length intervals and compute one metric value per interval; and sliding windows, which use the same day/week/month length but advance the window by half its length each step, so consecutive windows overlap by half their length and a concentration event spanning a boundary between two fixed intervals appears fully within at least one sliding window instead of being split and diluted across two.

### Measured results
| Metric / chain | Fixed-window result | Sliding-window result |
|---|---|---|
| Gini coefficient, Bitcoin | Monthly values reach close to 0.90 in the first three months and are always higher than daily/weekly; daily values mostly 0.45-0.60, with extreme values near 0.25 in the first three months | Average of 0.523 (one-day windows), 0.667 (one-week), 0.760 (one-month) |
| Gini coefficient, Ethereum | Same ordering as Bitcoin (monthly > weekly > daily) but higher and more stable overall than Bitcoin's values | Average of 0.837 (one-day), 0.878 (one-week), 0.916 (one-month) |
| Shannon entropy, Bitcoin | Daily, weekly, monthly patterns are close to each other; daily entropy mostly in 3.5-4.0, with extreme values above 5.5, concentrated in the first two months | Average of 3.810 (one-day), 4.002 (one-week), 4.091 (one-month); more extreme values (>5.0) revealed than fixed-window results |
| Shannon entropy, Ethereum | Mostly within 3.3-3.5 across all granularities | Average of 3.420 (one-day), 3.433 (one-week), 3.445 (one-month) |
| Nakamoto coefficient, Bitcoin | Stable at 4 from day 100 to day 260; oscillates between 4 and 5 outside that range; daily values in the first 50 days reach above 35 at their highest | Mostly between 4 and 5; an abnormal spike at sliding-window position N=120 (approximately day 60) visible only in the sliding-window results, not the fixed-window results |
| Nakamoto coefficient, Ethereum | Fluctuates between 2 and 3 across all granularities | Majority of values between 2 and 3 |
| Data volume | 54,231 Bitcoin blocks collected, block numbers 556,459 to 610,690, all produced in 2019 | Sliding-window sizes: 144 blocks (approx. one day at Bitcoin's 10-minutes-per-block rate), 1,008 (one week), 4,320 (one month) |
| Data volume | 2,204,650 Ethereum blocks collected, block numbers 6,988,615 to 9,193,265, all produced in 2019 | Sliding-window sizes: 6,000 blocks (one day, at Ethereum's measured average of 6,000 blocks/day), 42,000 (one week), 180,000 (one month) |
| Named anomaly, Bitcoin day 14 (Jan. 14, 2019) | Daily Gini coefficient 0.34 and daily Shannon entropy 6.2, both extreme values, traced to two specific blocks (numbers 558,473 and 558,545) each containing more than 80-90 independent coinbase addresses, producing more than 80 distinct block producers on a day with only 148 total blocks | Not applicable to this entry (fixed-window observation) |

### Parameters
- Measurement year: 2019, for both chains
- Fixed-window granularities: day, week, month
- Sliding-window step length: half the window length, chosen "to simplify and clarify the main point of the sliding window based measurement approach" (the paper's own stated reason, not derived from any optimization)
- Bitcoin block production rate assumption: 10 minutes per block, used to derive the 144/1,008/4,320-block window sizes
- Ethereum block production rate: measured at 6,000 blocks/day average across the 2019 dataset, used to derive the 6,000/42,000/180,000-block window sizes
- Nakamoto-coefficient collusion threshold: 51% of overall mining power, cited from Srinivasan's original definition
- Formula for the number of sliding-window measurements: L = (S - N) / M + 1, where S is total blocks measured, N is window length, M is step length

### Stated limitations
The authors state that most prior decentralization measurement work used a single metric, a single granularity, or blocks from only one week, producing a snapshot rather than a continuous picture; this paper's stated contribution is multiple metrics, multiple granularities, and a full year of data, not a claim to have resolved every measurement question. The sliding-window approach is presented, by the authors' own description, as a response to a specific failure of short fixed windows: reducing fixed-window length to catch cross-interval events makes the metric overly sensitive to short-term fluctuations that do not reflect an actual change in mining-power distribution (their example: a miner with 10% of overall mining power that mines 30% of blocks within one particular day of an otherwise-normal week). The paper draws no causal conclusion about why Bitcoin is more decentralized than Ethereum in these measurements beyond noting the block-production-rate difference as a candidate explanation for part of the Gini-coefficient gap; the authors do not test that explanation directly. No admission-control, incentive, or attack analysis is offered; the paper measures only observed concentration, not why concentration arose or what would reduce it.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
This is a measurement study of two already-deployed Proof-of-Work blockchains and places no mechanical requirement on other system components; it is evidence about deployed decentralization outcomes, usable to compare against a design's own stated production-diversity target. A design that wants to reproduce or extend this measurement needs an equivalent block-producer identity signal; the paper computes its metrics over the distribution of blocks by producer address, so any comparable measurement of a different system requires a similarly reliable mapping from a produced block to the identity of its producer, which the paper obtains directly from each chain's own block-header data via Google BigQuery, not from a self-reported or inferred source.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper itself cites Wu, Peng, Xie, Huang (ICEIEC 2019, ref. [20]) as concluding "Bitcoin is usually more decentralized than Ethereum" using Shannon entropy alone, a conclusion this paper's multi-metric, multi-granularity results are stated to agree with rather than contradict. The paper also cites Gencer, Basu, Eyal, Van Renesse, Sirer (Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2018, ref. [5]) as finding "Bitcoin and Ethereum have fairly centralized mining processes," which this paper's Nakamoto-coefficient results (4-5 for Bitcoin, 2-3 for Ethereum) are consistent with, not contrary to.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Srinivasan, "Quantifying decentralization," 2017 (informal publication, cited as ref. [16]) — origin of the Nakamoto coefficient this paper uses as its third metric
- foundational: Eyal, Sirer, "Majority is not enough: Bitcoin mining is vulnerable," Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2014, pp. 436-454 — introduces selfish mining, cited as lowering the practical threshold for a 51% attack to 33% of mining power
- foundational: Kwon, Liu, Kim, Song, Kim, "Impossibility of full decentralization in permissionless blockchains," ACM Advances in Financial Technologies 2019, pp. 110-123 — cited as the source of the Gini-coefficient application to mining-power distribution
- competing: Wu, Peng, Xie, Huang, "An information entropy method to quantify the degrees of decentralization for blockchain systems," IEEE ICEIEC 2019, pp. 1-6 — prior single-metric (Shannon entropy only) Bitcoin/Ethereum comparison whose conclusion this paper extends with two additional metrics and three granularities
- competing: Gencer, Basu, Eyal, Van Renesse, Sirer, "Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum networks," Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2018, pp. 439-457 — application-layer/network-measurement comparison of the two chains, cited for finding Bitcoin has higher network capacity but more datacenter-clustered nodes than Ethereum
- competing: Li, Palanisamy, "Comparison of decentralization in DPoS and PoW blockchains," International Conference on Blockchain 2020, pp. 18-32 — prior work by an overlapping author comparing decentralization across a different consensus-mechanism boundary (Delegated Proof of Stake versus Proof of Work)
- foundational/attack: Eyal, "The miner's dilemma," IEEE S&P 2015, pp. 89-103 — game-theoretic analysis of mining-pool competition and block-withholding attacks, cited as motivation for why mining-power concentration matters for security
- independent-measurement: Wang, Chu, Yang, "Measurement and analysis of the Bitcoin networks: a view from mining pools," arXiv:1902.07549, 2019 — tracked over 1.56 million blocks and roughly 257 million historical transactions, cited as finding a few mining pools controlling and expected to keep controlling most Bitcoin computing resources
- attack/critique: Gervais, Karame, Capkun, Capkun, "Is Bitcoin a decentralized currency?", IEEE Security & Privacy 12(3), 2014, pp. 54-60 — analyzes Bitcoin centralization across web wallets, protocol maintenance, and blockchain forks

### Verbatim extracts
- "the degree of decentralization in Bitcoin is higher, while the degree of decentralization in Ethereum is more stable"
- "the use of sliding windows could reveal additional cross-interval information overlooked by the fixed window based measurements"
- "a lower Gini coefficient means that more miners need to collude to compromise a blockchain system"
- "Nakamoto coefficient is defined as the minimum number of entities required to collude for gathering over 51% of the overall mining power"
- "we found two abnormal blocks... containing more than 80 independent coinbase addresses"
- "Ethereum tends to be signiﬁcantly less decentralized in terms of the measurements of the Gini coefficient"

## [LOCHER-HOTNETS-06] Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap
**Citation:** Thomas Locher, Patrick Moor, Stefan Schmid, Roger Wattenhofer. "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap." Proc. 5th ACM Workshop on Hot Topics in Networks (HotNets-V), 2006. Pages 85-90.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://conferences.sigcomm.org/hotnets/2006/locher06free.pdf
**Source URL:** http://conferences.sigcomm.org/hotnets/2006/locher06free.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
BitThief is a BitTorrent client that completes downloads of complete files while uploading no data at all, defeating BitTorrent's tit-for-tat admission mechanism through the single non-reciprocal admission path that mechanism leaves open: optimistic unchoke. BitTorrent divides participants into seeders, who hold the complete file and upload to all requesters in round robin, and leechers, who upload only to peers that reciprocate, except that every leecher periodically unchokes one neighbor for free (optimistic unchoke) so that newly joined peers with nothing to share can start downloading. BitThief exploits this path three ways. First, it opens far more simultaneous connections than the reference client (up to 500, against a reference-client default of 80), which raises the number of seeder round robin slots and leecher optimistic-unchoke slots it can occupy at once; download rate rises linearly with the number of open connections because remote peers act independently of how many connections the requester holds, except that a second connection from the same IP address is refused by the reference client and by Azureus. Second, it re-announces to the tracker far more often than the reference client's roughly 1800-second interval, starting at a configurable short interval and backing off exponentially to once every 30 minutes, to acquire more peer addresses faster. Third, in place of the reference client's rarest-first piece selection, BitThief requests a random missing piece from whichever peer unchokes it, so no unchoke period goes unused. BitThief never announces any pieces to remote peers and never chokes or unchokes any remote peer, so every peer it contacts treats it as a peer that has just started downloading.

### Measured results
| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| 7 torrents (170 MB-798 MB; A-G), unrestricted BitThief (permitted to download from seeders and leechers), reference client v4.20.2 permitted up to 500 connections for fair comparison, 3 runs per client per torrent, over the public Internet | BitThief completed every torrent. On torrents A, B, F, BitThief was on average slightly faster than the reference client (reference client uploaded 232 MB on torrent A, 129 MB on torrent B in one run). On torrents E and G (few seeders, many leechers), BitThief took roughly 4x longer than the reference client, which itself uploaded over 3.5 GB. |
| Same 7 torrents, BitThief restricted to download only from leechers (seeders excluded), 3 runs, same conditions | All downloads finished. Average download time increased relative to the seeders-permitted case. On torrent C, where only 15% of peers were leechers (so BitThief could use less than one sixth of available peers), BitThief took roughly 5x longer than the reference client, which was permitted to use both seeders and leechers. |
| Controlled private-network testbed: one private tracker, a configurable number of reference clients as seeders/leechers, one BitThief instance, scenario with a single slow seeder | BitThief started 9 minutes after three reference clients but caught up, and all four clients finished at roughly the same time. |
| Same torrent (359 MB on TorrentLeech, a sharing community requiring a minimum upload ratio; 350 MB on Mininova, an open public tracker), 3 BitThief runs per site | Mininova runs (531 seeders, 303 leechers reported): 32, 32, 37 minutes. TorrentLeech runs (24 seeders, 1 leecher reported): 7:25, 7:08, 7:08 minutes -- more than 4x faster despite roughly 33x fewer reported peers, because community peers upload more broadly to protect their upload ratio. |
| Block-contribution distribution across peers for the same torrent, BitThief connected to 309 peers on Mininova and 349 on TorrentLeech | On TorrentLeech (community), contribution across peers was more balanced. On Mininova (open), only a small number of peers supplied a large fraction of all blocks. |
| Sharing-ratio manipulation on TorrentLeech, by sending fabricated upload totals in tracker announcements (the tracker does not verify announced upload/download totals) | BitThief attained a reported sharing ratio of 1.4 on TorrentLeech without uploading any data. |
| Garbage-piece exploit from a prior paper (Liogkas et al., IPTPS 2006), reimplemented and tested against the reference client and Azureus | Answering all subpiece requests for a piece with random data caused both clients to ban the sending IP address once hash verification failed. Withholding exactly one subpiece per piece (so blame could not be pinned on the sender alone) still fooled the reference client, but Azureus tracked which peer supplied the most subpieces of a failing piece, reserved the remaining requests for that peer, and banned the IP once requests went unanswered. The authors conclude uploading garbage in any tested form does not improve download performance. |

### Parameters
- Tracker-reported peer list size: default 50 addresses per announcement; protocol maximum requestable is 200, but most trackers observed trimmed the response to 50 regardless of the requested count.
- BitThief simultaneous connection limit used in experiments: up to 500 (reference client's is 80 by default; raised to 500 for the fair-comparison experiments via --min_peers 500 --max_initiate 500 --max_allow_in 500).
- Tracker re-announce interval: reference client follows the tracker-supplied interval (observed near 1800 s); BitThief starts at a configurable shorter interval and backs off exponentially to a ceiling of 1800 s (once every 30 minutes).
- Piece-availability announcement: BitThief announces an empty piece list at connection setup and never updates it; announcing any percentage below 100% did not change measured performance, but announcing 100% caused remote peers to treat BitThief as a seeder and refuse to send it any pieces.

### Stated limitations
The paper's controlled-testbed experiment illustrating recovery from a slow seeder is described by the authors as an idealized case because no additional leechers joined the swarm during the run. BitThief as built does not implement collusion among multiple free-riding instances, does not use the distributed (DHT-based) tracker protocol, and does not perform a Sybil attack of presenting multiple fake identities to the same remote peer, though the authors state this would be straightforward to add given multiple IP addresses and would plausibly double the achievable download rate. The authors state that faking whole pieces by finding SHA-1 hash collisions to defeat per-piece integrity checking is computationally infeasible with then-current techniques and storage. The authors state that a mechanism combining tit-for-tat with an efficient bootstrap allowance for newly joined peers (who have nothing to share yet) remains an open problem, which they name as future work rather than solved in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
For an incentive mechanism to withstand this attack, it cannot rely solely on a reciprocity check triggered only by past upload behavior, because BitThief supplies zero upload and still receives service through the optimistic-unchoke and seeder round robin paths, which are unconditional by design. Any defense that closes this path must either meter or price the optimistic-unchoke slot itself, or supply new peers with reciprocity credit from some other source, since the bootstrap problem (new peers have nothing to reciprocate with) is the reason the unconditional path exists in the first place. A tracker-side or community-side ratio-enforcement layer requires the tracker to verify announced upload/download totals against independent evidence (for example, corroboration from receiving peers), because self-reported totals in the announce message are accepted without verification in the deployed protocol and can be fabricated by a client that never transfers the claimed bytes. A per-peer integrity/ban mechanism such as Azureus's blame-single-supplier logic requires the receiving client to track, per remote peer, which subpieces of a not-yet-hash-verified piece it supplied, so that a failed hash check can be attributed to a specific peer rather than diffused across a piece's several suppliers.

### Contradicts
The paper's own framing distinguishes its finding from Jun and Ahamad [9], who define free riding as contributing considerably less than other peers and propose a tit-for-tat-oriented fix; this paper's authors state they instead demonstrate downloads with strictly zero upload, a stronger claim than reduced contribution. No other paper in the current evidence file's W3-5 batch reports free-riding numbers under the same connection-count and torrent-size conditions to compare directly; SIRIVIANOS-IPTPS-07 in this batch reports an independent free-riding construction and its completion-rate figures should be compared against BitThief's at the level of "peer-set size used" rather than at the level of a shared torrent, since the two papers use different torrents and swarm compositions.

### References worth retrieving
- Adar, Huberman, "Free Riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 -- foundational (earliest measurement of free riding in a P2P file-sharing network).
- Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 -- foundational (defines the multi-identity attack the paper explicitly notes BitThief could add).
- Liogkas, Nelson, Kohler, Zhang, "Exploiting BitTorrent For Fun (But Not Profit)," IPTPS 2006 -- competing/foundational (the closest prior work; implements three individual selfish exploits including the garbage-piece exploit this paper reimplements and extends by combining attacks).
- Jun, Ahamad, "Incentives in BitTorrent Induce Free Riding," P2PECON 2005 -- competing (argues BitTorrent's tit-for-tat is insufficient using a weaker definition of free riding; proposes an iterated-prisoner's-dilemma-based fix).
- Andrade, Mowbray, Lima, Wagner, Ripeanu, "Influences on Cooperation in BitTorrent Communities," P2PECON 2005 -- foundational (measures sharing-ratio enforcement effects in communities; this paper's community exploit builds directly on that measurement).
- Grolimund, Meisser, Schmid, Wattenhofer, "Havelaar: A Robust and Efficient Reputation System for Active Peer-to-Peer Systems," NetEcon 2006 -- competing (proposed reputation-based incentive mechanism for P2P systems).
- Vishnumurthy, Chandrakumar, Sirer, "KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for P2P Resource Sharing," P2PECON 2003 -- competing (currency-based incentive mechanism for P2P resource sharing).
- Tamilmani, Pai, Mohr, "SWIFT: A System with Incentives for Trading," P2PECON 2004 -- competing (alternative incentive mechanism for content trading).

### Verbatim extracts
- "we present BitThief, a free riding client that never contributes any real data"
- "opening more connections increases download speed linearly"
- "BitThief only requires roughly 5 times longer than the official client"
- "we now have a sharing ratio of 1.4 on TorrentLeech without ever uploading a single bit"
- "uploading random garbage, in any way, does not improve performance"

## [LUO-ARXIV-25] Unveiling Ethereum's P2P Network: The Role of Chain and Client Diversity

**Citation:** Jiahao Luo. "Unveiling Ethereum's P2P Network: The Role of Chain and Client Diversity." arXiv preprint, 2025. DOI 10.48550/ARXIV.2501.16236.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16236
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16236
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper measures how many peers discoverable in Ethereum's peer-to-peer overlay (devp2p, the protocol stack combining a node-discovery layer, the RLPx encrypted-transport layer, and application sub-protocols) are actually reachable and configuration-compatible with a mainnet full node, and separates that measurement from the underlying causes: node-discovery protocol non-compliance and multi-chain (fork and sidechain) fragmentation of the shared discovery table. The authors deploy five instrumented Geth (Go Ethereum, the reference full-node client) instances that log every discovery-protocol message (Ping, Pong, FindNode, Neighbors) and RLPx handshake (Hello, Status) they send or receive, store the decoded messages in a database, and classify every discovered peer into one of three categories: no sub-protocol exchange attempted, sub-protocol exchange attempted but incompatible, or fully compatible. The tool additionally tracks each peer's self-reported client software identifier and version string from the RLPx Hello message, which lets the authors attribute specific protocol deviations (message counts, disconnect reasons, IP-address bugs) to specific client implementations and versions rather than to the network as a whole.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 743,739 unique peers discovered, classified as 674,945 (90.8%) Class A (no sub-protocol exchange), 17,707 (2.4%) Class B (exchanged, incompatible), 51,087 (6.9%) Class C (fully compatible) | 5 instrumented Geth v1.14.0 full-node instances, Ubuntu 22.04, 1 Gb/s bandwidth, 256 GB RAM, 64 cores each; measurement window approximately May 2024 based on the reported daily message-rate chart |
| Over 8 billion messages collected; FindNode and its prerequisite Ping constitute ~91% of the total (3,735M Ping, 39M Pong, 3,996M FindNode, 172M Neighbors, 78M discovery-layer Disc, 366M RLPx Hello, 127M eth Status, all in millions) | Same deployment, full measurement period |
| ~2.64 million connection attempts/hour and ~16.9 million node-discovery attempts/hour | Same deployment; connection attempts capped at 10 per peer per minute to avoid overwhelming the network |
| 7,934 of 743,739 peers (1.07%) reported a private or fallback IP address in the discovery Ping message; 98.65% of those set it to 127.0.0.1, 0.44% to 0.0.0.0; only 156 of the 7,934 completed an RLPx sub-protocol exchange, predominantly running Besu (28.21%), Geth (23.72%), or OpenEthereum (18.59%) among that small reachable subset | Same deployment; attributed to a UPnP-NAT fallback bug, acknowledged and fixed by Besu (PRs #6225, #6439) and Reth developers during the study |
| 78.4 million Disconnect messages captured; reasons: Useless peer 41.58%, TCP sub-system error 31.39%, Disconnect requested 22.93%, Too many peers 2.84%, Breach of protocol 1.03%, all others under 0.3% each | Same deployment, "most recent measurement phase" |
| Compared to Kim et al. (2018): Useless-peer disconnects rose from under 1% to 41.58%, and Too-many-peers disconnects fell from 90% to 2.84% | Same dataset compared against the cited 2018 prior measurement (not independently re-verified by this author) |
| 92.12% of Breach-of-protocol disconnects were issued by Nethermind clients; the top 2 Nethermind builds (v1.25.4+20b10b35 and v1.26.0+0068729c) accounted for 41.7% and 26.8% of all breach disconnects respectively | Same dataset, Nethermind client-version breakdown of breach disconnects, 1,861 Nethermind peers examined |
| Of over 4 billion FindNode requests sent (>99.99% outbound), ~5% received a Neighbors response; 172.2 million Neighbors messages captured from 74,041 unique peers (average 2,285 replies/peer); 73.24% of individual Neighbors responses contained the specification-compliant 16 nodes, 26.01% contained fewer, and ~26% of requests timed out (Geth's default 1.5-second timeout when fewer than 16 nodes are received) | Same deployment |
| Node-count-per-response by client: Geth sends 12 then 16 nodes across two messages (spec-compliant, two-message split); Besu sends 13 nodes 71.89% of the time; Nethermind sends 12 nodes 16.64% of the time; Bor (Polygon's Geth fork) sends only 6, 9, or 10 nodes 87-90% of the time | Same deployment, per-client Neighbors-length distribution table across Geth, Erigon, Besu, Nethermind, bor, and reth |
| Sub-protocol prevalence: eth-68 on 78.05% of peers, snap-1 on 76.73%, eth-66 on 63.29%, eth-67 on 58.35%, older/other sub-protocols under 8% each | Same 74,041+ peer sample |
| Only 24.5% of all discovered peers run the correct current Ethereum mainnet configuration (network ID 1, specific genesis hash, specific fork ID); this is down from a previously reported 54.5% (Kim et al., not independently re-measured here); consequently only 19% of eth-68-supporting peers hold the proper mainnet configuration; 12.6% of mainnet-network-ID peers run pre-Cancun-upgrade (before 13 March 2024) fork identifiers | Same dataset, chain-parameter distribution measurement |
| Dial-attempt scaling: at 1,000,000 attempts, 53,685 unique peers found (29.51% unreachable, 57.42% incompatible, 13.07% fully compatible); at 500,000,000 attempts, 527,957 unique peers found (88.96% unreachable, 8.57% incompatible, 2.47% fully compatible); average of 947 connection attempts needed per successfully-reached live peer | Same deployment, 5-point dial-attempt sweep from 1 million to 500 million attempts |

### Parameters
- Node-discovery bucket size increased from the devp2p-specified 16 entries to 1,048,576 to widen the local routing table.
- Neighbors-message size capped at the specification's 16-node maximum to avoid amplification.
- Concurrent node-discovery tasks increased from Geth's default of 3 to 1,000, reducing time-to-connect-to-5,000-nodes from ~4 days to ~10 hours in the authors' own configuration.
- Dial-scheduler source count increased from 1 to 50, giving ~100 dials/second/node.
- Connection attempts throttled to a maximum of 10 per peer per minute network-wide.
- DHT (distributed hash table) refresh interval reduced from the default 5 minutes to 10 seconds.
- Geth's own default FindNode/Neighbors timeout: 1.5 seconds when fewer than 16 nodes are received (a Geth-internal parameter the paper measures the consequences of, not one the authors set).
- Measurement infrastructure: 5 Geth v1.14.0 instances, Ubuntu 22.04, 1 Gb/s bandwidth, 256 GB RAM, 64 cores per instance; MongoDB storage capped at 64 GB memory use; bandwidth usage self-limited to 1 Gbps and outbound transaction-request replies limited to half of received requests, stated as ethical/network-impact bounds rather than tuned experimental variables.

### Stated limitations
The paper does not report an aggregate, network-wide client-implementation market-share figure (e.g., "Geth holds X% of all Ethereum nodes"); every client-attribution figure in this paper is conditional on a specific narrow subpopulation — the 156 reachable peers with the private-IP bug, the 1,861 Nethermind peers examined for breach disconnects, or the per-client Neighbors-response-length table — and none of these subpopulations is presented as representative of the full peer population's client composition. Readers requiring an overall client-share concentration figure for Ethereum are not served by this paper; that number is not present in the retrieved text. The authors state "the full extent of these issues on overall network stability remains unclear" regarding the private-IP and peer-scoring bugs they identify. The paper's own comparison figures against Kim et al. (2018) are stated as taken from that prior study, not independently re-derived by this paper's own methodology on the earlier dataset, so the two measurements are not a controlled before/after comparison under identical instrumentation. The paper does not evaluate mobile or light-client peers, nor does it measure bandwidth or latency costs of the diversity-driven inefficiencies it identifies (it measures connection-success rates and disconnect/timeout counts, not throughput or user-facing latency).

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A shared node-discovery table (a single DHT serving Ethereum mainnet, Ethereum testnets, and unrelated EVM-compatible chains such as Polygon and BNB Smart Chain simultaneously, as measured here) requires an expensive per-candidate handshake (TCP connection, encryption, protocol Hello/Status exchange) before a peer's chain membership can be determined, so any design reusing a shared discovery layer across multiple independent chains or forks inherits a connection-success rate that falls as the number of incompatible chains sharing that layer grows — measured here at 2.47% fully compatible after 500 million dial attempts, down from 13.07% at 1 million attempts. A discovery protocol whose per-message size is capped by the underlying transport's datagram limit (UDP's 1,280-byte practical limit here, constraining Neighbors responses to 12-16 entries depending on IPv4 versus IPv6 addressing) requires every participating client implementation to agree on the exact node count per response, because this paper measures that implementations disagreeing on that count each other's messages does not error cleanly but instead produces timeouts (Geth waiting its full 1.5-second timeout for the fewer-than-16-node responses that Besu, Nethermind, and Bor send). A liveness/heartbeat message field used to populate address or scoring data (the discv4 Ping message's fromIP field feeding Geth's DHT bucket-ordering and Besu/Nethermind's peer-scoring) requires validation against the transport-layer source address, because this paper measures multiple client implementations (Geth via its UPnP-NAT fallback, CoreGeth, and its ETCMC fork) propagating unverified private/loopback addresses from that field into peer records.

### Contradicts
The paper's title and framing invite the expectation of an overall Ethereum client-market-share concentration figure, but no such aggregate figure appears in the retrieved text — a claim of "Ethereum node client concentration measured by Luo 2025" citing a specific percentage split across Geth/Nethermind/Besu/Erigon for the whole network would not be supported by this paper's own reported tables and must not be carried forward from this entry. No other paper in this batch measures Ethereum P2P network structure, so no cross-paper numeric contradiction exists in this batch.

## [MALKHI-PODC-02] Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly

**Citation:** Dahlia Malkhi, Moni Naor, David Ratajczak. "Viceroy: A Scalable and Dynamic Emulation of the Butterfly." ACM PODC, 2002. DOI 10.1145/571825.571857.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/viceroy.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~naor/PAPERS/viceroy.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
Viceroy locates data in a distributed hash table (DHT) while every server keeps a constant number of outbound links, so a server join or departure changes a constant number of links in expectation regardless of how many servers are in the network. It achieves this by having each server emulate one node of a butterfly network — a fixed interconnection pattern in which nodes are arranged in levels and each non-leaf node at level L connects down to two nodes at level L+1 and up to one node at level L-1.

Each server picks two values at join time: an identifier drawn independently and uniformly from the real interval [0,1), fixed for the server's lifetime, and a level, a positive integer chosen by a local estimation procedure (below). Three link sets connect servers: a general ring linking each server to its ring successor and predecessor by identifier order; a level ring linking servers that share the same level; and butterfly links — each server's "left down" link goes to the first level-L+1 server clockwise from its own identifier, its "right down" link goes to the first level-L+1 server clockwise from identifier + 1/2^L, and its "up" link goes to the first level-L-1 server clockwise from its own identifier.

A server estimates the network size n locally, without any global count, by taking the reciprocal of the ring distance to its immediate successor (1/d(s, succ(s))) as an estimate n0, then draws its level uniformly from [1, floor(log n0)]. This keeps level assignment self-adjusting to local density without communicating n to any server.

Lookup for target identifier x, starting at server y, runs in three phases: follow up-links to a level-1 root server; descend butterfly links, at each level-L server moving to the right-down link if the target is at ring distance >= 1/2^L and to the left-down link otherwise, until reaching a server with no further down link or one that overshoots the target; then traverse the general ring (clockwise or counter-clockwise) to the closest server to x. An improved third phase ("hopping," Section 7) interleaves level-ring links with ring links instead of stepping server-by-server, so the worst-case path length becomes logarithmic with high probability rather than only in expectation.

A background "bucket" mechanism (sketched, not fully specified) partitions the ring into contiguous groups of Theta(log n) servers each and reassigns levels within a bucket so every level from 1 to log n has at least one and at most a constant number of representatives per bucket, which bounds the largest number of incoming links any single server can receive.

### Measured results
None. The paper is a theoretical construction with worst-case and expected-case bounds proved as theorems; it contains no implementation, simulation, or empirical measurement. Every quantitative claim below is an asymptotic bound with a proof, not a measured figure, and is reported here as a stated bound, not a measurement, per Rule 1.

Stated asymptotic properties, each proved for a Viceroy network holding n servers, under the paper's own assumptions (see Requirements below):
- Out-degree of every server: 7 total (5 used in the simple, non-hopping lookup variant) (Theorem 6.6).
- Expected in-degree: O(1); largest in-degree: O(log n) with high probability, over the randomness of identifier and level choice (Theorem 6.6).
- Lookup path length (dilation): O(log n) in the worst case, with high probability, using the improved ("hopping") third-phase routing of Section 7 (Theorem 7.3). The simple lookup variant (Section 6) achieves O(log n) dilation only in expectation, not with high probability, because the ring-traversal third phase can pass through as many as O(log^2 n) servers in the worst case.
- Load per server (fraction of all-pairs lookups passing through a given server): expected O(log n / n); maximum over all servers, O(log^2 n / n) with high probability (Theorem 6.4).
- Join or leave cost: a constant number of link changes in expectation, and O(log n) link changes with high probability, per join or leave event.
- Bucket-mechanism overhead: a server leaving causes at most O(1) other servers to change level; a bucket reshuffle (triggered once every (c-1) log n steps for a paper-unspecified constant c) touches O(log n) servers, giving amortized O(1) per join/leave.

Table 1 (reproduced from the paper, comparing dilation / congestion / linkage cost against the schemes it cites): Chord — log n / (log n)/n / log n. Tapestry — log n / (log n)/n / log n. Content Addressable Network (CAN) with d dimensions — d*n^(1/d) / d*n^(1/d-1) / d. Kleinberg-style Small Worlds — log^2 n / (log^2 n)/n / O(1). Viceroy is the paper's proposed alternative to this table, trading Small Worlds' O(1) linkage cost for O(log n) dilation and O(log n) linkage cost at constant, not logarithmic, out-degree.

### Parameters
- Server identifier: drawn uniformly and independently from the continuous interval [0,1); in practice, a fixed number of random bits sufficient to make identifier collisions implausible (exact bit count not stated as a number, left to implementation).
- Level: integer in [1, floor(log n0)], n0 the server's local size estimate; redrawn only when floor(log n0) changes, per a footnote optimization, not on every join/leave elsewhere in the network.
- Bucket size: Theta(log n) servers; a bucket merges with a neighbor when its size drops below log n and splits when its size exceeds c*log n, for an unspecified constant c bounding the diversity property (at most c servers per level per bucket).
- Out-degree: fixed at 7 (2 down, 1 up, 2 ring — general successor/predecessor, 2 level-ring — next/prev on level); only 5 of the 7 links are used by the simple (non-hopping) lookup.

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly excludes concurrent joins and leaves and server failures from its model: it assumes multiple join and leave operations do not overlap and that servers never fail, and refers the reader to a separate paper (Lynch, Malkhi, Ratajczak, IPTPS 2002) for concurrency and failure handling. It does not address load hotspots — repeatedly requested identifiers overloading the servers along the corresponding lookup paths — though it states in a footnote that standard replica-placement mechanisms could be adapted to the DHT framework without demonstrating this. It assumes joins and leaves are independent of server identifiers, so the active server set stays randomly distributed on the ring; a correlated join/leave pattern is outside the analysis. It does not specify how a client or a joining server obtains the address of any already-active server (bootstrap discovery is out of scope). The bucket mechanism that bounds maximum in-degree is only sketched, not fully specified or analyzed to the same rigor as the base construction, by the authors' own statement.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- Requires that any server able to compute another server's identifier can open a connection to it; the paper treats connection establishment as a primitive and does not specify addressing, transport, or NAT traversal.
- Requires non-overlapping join/leave events (a serialization or locking discipline elsewhere in the system) for the join/leave algorithms and their O(1)-expected-link-change bound to apply as proved; concurrent joins/leaves are explicitly out of scope and left to a different mechanism.
- Requires a failure-free server population for the bounds as proved; crash tolerance is not part of this construction.
- Requires the level-selection procedure's local density estimate (1/d(s, succ(s))) to be accurate, which in turn requires identifiers to remain uniformly distributed on the ring — violated if join/leave is correlated with identifier choice (e.g., an adversary choosing identifiers to cluster in one region).
- Requires a separate bootstrap mechanism to supply a joining server or client with the address of one already-active server.
- Requires a separate mechanism (unspecified) to handle hotspots if uneven query popularity across identifiers is expected, since the load bound (Theorem 6.4) is an average over a uniform query distribution.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this corpus's current batch measures Viceroy independently.

- Foundational: B. Y. Zhao, J. D. Kubiatowicz, A. D. Joseph, "Tapestry: An infrastructure for fault-tolerant wide-area location and routing," UC Berkeley TR UCB/CSD-01-1141, 2001.
- Competing: S. Ratnasamy, P. Francis, M. Handley, R. Karp, S. Shenker, "A scalable content-addressable network," SIGCOMM 2001 — the constant-degree CAN alternative directly compared in Table 1.

## [MALVAI-NDSS-23] Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging

**Citation:** Harjasleen Malvai, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino, Esha Ghosh, Ercan Öztürk, Kevin Lewi, Sean Lawlor. "Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging." NDSS, 2023.
**Retrieved:** full text via candidate URL `https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/081.pdf`
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/081.pdf
**Domain:** E

### What it does
Parakeet lets a message provider prove it serves each user the one true public key it committed to, so a client can detect a provider that hands different keys to different people for the same username (server equivocation), without the client trusting the provider or a blockchain. The system separates two roles. A verifiable key directory (VKD) run by the identity provider (IdP) stores every username-to-public-key mapping and commits to it with a compact cryptographic digest each round (epoch); a client who queries it receives the current key plus a proof it belongs to the committed digest. Parakeet's VKD instantiates the ordered zero-knowledge set (oZKS) primitive over a compressed Merkle Patricia Trie, storing only the current state of each tree node rather than a new node copy at every epoch, which the paper states is what makes the storage cost bounded rather than growing with the number of epochs. Separately, a small committee of witness servers cross-checks the IdP's per-epoch digest through a consistency protocol: the IdP broadcasts a signed notification of the new digest, each witness verifies an append-only audit proof against the previous digest and signs a vote, and once a quorum of votes is collected they aggregate into a certificate that any client can check without contacting every witness. The consistency protocol runs without a leader and without an external blockchain, which the paper states is why its throughput does not degrade when witnesses crash. To bound storage growth from an always-appending tree, Parakeet adds a two-phase compaction mechanism: at a tombstone epoch, entries eligible for eventual deletion are marked (not removed); only after a further compaction epoch are tombstoned entries actually deleted; auditors check that only sufficiently old entries are tombstoned and only tombstoned entries are deleted, and a client that wants deletion-soundness must query its own key history at least once between a tombstone epoch and the following compaction epoch.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Verify notification (consistency protocol) | 68.70 ms mean, 1.50 ms std | Single core, witness machine (AWS t3.medium, 2 vCPU/1 physical core, 4 GB RAM, 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8259CL); committee of 4 witnesses; notification batch of 1,024 updates, 64 bytes each; mean/std over 10 runs |
| Create vote | 0.02 ms mean, 0.00 ms std | Same setup as above |
| Verify certificate | 0.16 ms mean, 0.01 ms std | Same setup as above; certificate = 3 votes combined (2f+1 with f=1 for a 4-witness committee) |
| Create notification (IdP side) | 47.12 ms mean, 9.30 ms std | AWS t3.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM), same 4-witness/1,024-batch/64-byte setup, 10-run mean/std; measured by subtracting server-side publish cost from total publish+notify cost |
| Verify vote | 0.07 ms mean, 0.00 ms std | Same IdP-side setup |
| Aggregate certificate | 0.00 ms mean (below measurable resolution), 0.00 ms std | Same IdP-side setup |
| VKD storage | ≈4.5 GB at 5 million users, linear growth | 100,000-user insertion batches, MySQL-backed storage, local Docker container |
| Projected VKD storage at 1 billion users | ≈850 GB | Extrapolated linearly from the 4.5 GB / 5-million-user measurement, not independently measured at that scale |

| First-year storage, Parakeet oZKS construction | ≈2.2 TB (1.1 TB base, doubled for concurrent-proof-generation node retention) | Same assumed WhatsApp-scale workload and node-state size; stated as roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the SEEMless-style projection |
| Five-year storage projection | SEEMless-style: growing to ≈110.9 TB; Parakeet: ≈3.4 TB | Same assumed workload, chart data (Figure 13) |
| Comparable throughput requirement for WhatsApp-scale deployment | ≈120 updates/s, derived from ≈2 billion monthly active users, ≈0.66 billion average downloads over five years, ≈3 devices/browsers per user | Authors' own derivation, not a measurement of an actual WhatsApp deployment; Parakeet's measured 800 updates/s is stated as exceeding this by "over 6x" |

### Parameters
- Byzantine fault model: 3f+1 total witnesses tolerate up to f Byzantine (arbitrary) failures; a quorum is any 2f+1 witnesses; network is assumed fully asynchronous (messages may be arbitrarily delayed and reordered but are eventually delivered).
- Benchmark baseline configuration: 10 honest witnesses, batch size 1,024 updates, update size 64 bytes (32-byte key + 32-byte value), committee size 4 for the microbenchmarks specifically.
- Tested batch-size range: 2^5 through 2^15 updates per batch.
- Tested witness-count range: 10, 20, 50 witnesses (throughput measured flat across this range).
- Tested crash-fault range: 0, 1, 3 crashed witnesses out of a 10-witness committee (3 stated as the maximum tolerable in that configuration).
- Node-state size for storage arithmetic: 64 bytes (32-byte hash output + 32 bytes of parent/child metadata).
- Signature scheme: ed25519-dalek, 32-byte public/private key pairs.
- Storage/transport implementation: Rust, tokio for async networking, RocksDB for persistence (unless otherwise specified), TCP for point-to-point channels.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that evaluating Byzantine (as opposed to crash) fault behavior for BFT-style protocols "is still an open question" and explicitly limits its crash-fault benchmark to crash faults only — no measurement of behavior under actively malicious (Byzantine) witnesses is reported. The compaction mechanism requires a client to come online and check its own key history at least once between each tombstone epoch and the following deletion epoch; a client that does not do so cannot detect a wrongful deletion, which the paper states as a minimal but real additional assumption compared to a pure append-only construction. The append-only base construction (before compaction) is stated to conflict with a right to full account-data deletion, which the paper mentions has relevance to "right to be forgotten" regulation. The 850 GB projected figure at 1 billion users is an extrapolation from a 5-million-user measurement, not a direct measurement at that scale. The throughput ceiling is attributed to the IdP being the system bottleneck (not the witness count), but the paper does not report the throughput ceiling of the IdP itself under further load, nor push witness count high enough to find where network overhead becomes the bottleneck — it states only that this crossover is "expected" to occur eventually.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every client of the directory must independently obtain a small server commitment for each epoch from an out-of-band source it trusts to be consistent across all clients — Parakeet supplies this itself via its witness quorum-certificate mechanism, but any component depending on Parakeet must be able to reach that witness quorum (a majority of 2f+1 out of 3f+1 witnesses) rather than trusting the IdP alone. At least one honest auditor must check each update for correctness every epoch for the non-equivocation soundness proof to hold; the paper's model assumes such an auditor exists (it can be any of the witnesses, executed as part of their normal protocol step) but the proof is void with zero honest auditors. Compaction's security depends on every client periodically running the KeyHistory check on its own key at least once per tombstone-to-deletion interval; a component that never re-queries an inactive user's key cannot detect that user's data being wrongly deleted. The protocol assumes bounded clock drift among witnesses is sufficient for f-fault tolerance deductions in the asynchronous model (the paper references bounded-clock-drift reasoning without giving a numeric bound). The system assumes the IdP and witnesses each hold a durable private signing key and that key compromise of the IdP is out of scope — Parakeet detects equivocation but does not itself prevent a compromised IdP from producing internally consistent but wrong data before compromise is discovered by another means. Deployment at the paper's benchmarked scale assumes access to persistent storage with fast random writes (RocksDB or MySQL in the reported configuration); the SEEMless-style comparison measurement shows that a naive append-only construction becomes storage-write-bound at a few hundred thousand users, so a system layering key transparency at billions-of-users scale needs the oZKS-style bounded-storage construction Parakeet supplies, not the plain append-only aZKS from SEEMless.

### Contradicts
None found against other entries in this corpus. Note for cross-reference: this paper positions itself as directly extending and superseding the storage and consistency limitations of SEEMless (CHASE-CCS-19 in this batch); see that entry's own reported figures for the comparison numbers this paper's Figure 5/6/12/13 measurements were built to contrast with. This paper also names Merkle² (HU-SP-21 in this batch) only in its bibliography — it does not benchmark against Merkle² directly and states no comparison figures against it in the retrieved text.
