## [OVEZIK-FC-24] SoK: A Stratified Approach to Blockchain Decentralization
**Citation:** Christina Ovezik, Dimitris Karakostas, Aggelos Kiayias. "SoK: A Stratified Approach to Blockchain Decentralization." Financial Cryptography and Data Security (FC), 2024. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-78676-1_8.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01291
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01291
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper gives a methodology for locating single points of failure in a blockchain system by decomposing the system into layers, and for each layer stating which resource, held by which kind of party, must stay distributed for the system's security properties to hold.

Four properties are defined as the things centralization can put at risk: safety (all honest participants hold the same settled view of the ledger), liveness (the settled view keeps being updated as new transactions arrive), privacy (a user's actions stay dissociated from their real-world identity and unlinkable to each other), and stability (the ledger's native asset's supply and market price stay predictable, operationalized as low short-term price volatility). A single point of failure is defined as one party whose compromise by an adversary would violate one or more of these properties.

The methodology decomposes a blockchain system into eight layers, modeled on the OSI network stack: hardware (physical machines and cloud capacity running consensus software), software (which client implementations run the protocol and which wallet software manages keys), network (peer-discovery bootstrapping and inter-instance topology), consensus (who holds the power that determines block production, both owned power and power delegated to pools), tokenomics (who owns tokens, from initial distribution onward), client API (which services applications and wallets depend on to read and submit to the ledger), governance (who decides protocol changes and who funds development), and geography (a cross-cutting dimension: physical concentration by country or jurisdiction, applicable to every other layer). For each layer, the paper's methodology asks the analyst to name the resource that is the layer's basic unit (for example, hashing power on the consensus layer), name the parties that control that resource (miners), and name which of the four properties are at risk if that resource distribution becomes concentrated.

Built on this decomposition, the paper defines the Minimum Decentralization Test (MDT): a system fails the MDT if there exists any one layer in which a single legal person (an individual or an organization, treated as a unit for legal-liability purposes rather than as a count of the human beings involved) controls enough of that layer's relevant parties to violate one of the four properties on its own. The MDT is deliberately a binary layer-by-layer test rather than a single continuous decentralization score; the paper does not propose a metric that aggregates across layers into one number, and states this as future work rather than as part of the current contribution.

### Measured results
The paper reports a case study applying the layer-by-layer methodology to Bitcoin, and a set of MDT applications to named systems. Figures below are quoted from the paper's own text, which in turn attributes each figure to a named third-party data source and an as-of date; the paper did not itself run the data-collection pipeline for most of these.

| Result | Conditions / attribution |
|---|---|
| The Bitcoin ASIC-manufacturer market is centralized around 4 manufacturers | As of 2022, cited to reference [185] in the paper's bibliography |
| 99.15% of Bitcoin full nodes run Bitcoin Core | Source cited as blockchair.com, date of measurement not stated beyond "as of writing" |
| 4 mining pools control more than 75% of Bitcoin's total mining power | Source cited as statista.com, "at the time of writing" |
| 53.3% of Bitcoin's nodes operate over Tor | Source: bitnodes, October 2022 |
| Approximately 43 million Bitcoin addresses hold a nonzero balance; the top 100 addresses control 14.01% of all Bitcoin wealth | Attributed to the paper's own Table 2 compilation, sourced from Blockchain ETL, Google BigQuery, and CoinCarp, dated April 2022 |
| Bitcoin's Gini coefficient of wealth is 0.5145 restricted to the 10,000 wealthiest addresses, and 0.956 over all addresses | Same source and date as above (Table 2) |
| Comparison figure: the income Gini coefficient of the 10 lowest-performing countries by that measure ranges 0.512-0.63 | Cited to World Bank Gini index data, reference [179] |
| Comparison figure: the richest 0.01% of individuals globally (approximately 520,000 people) hold 11% of all wealth | Cited to reference [85] |
| Bitcoin is traded on over 100 marketplaces at a combined transparent-plus-opaque volume of approximately $53 billion | Attributed to the paper's Table 3 compilation across 121 exchanges, sourced from CoinMarketCap, June 2022 |
| Binance accounts for 20% of total daily cryptocurrency trading volume | Source: CoinMarketCap, August 2022 |
| Bitcoin mining is geographically spread across 95 countries; over one-third is located in the USA, 18% in Kazakhstan, 11% in Russia | Source cited as reference [34], "at the time of writing" |
| Until 2021, China hosted up to 70.9% of Bitcoin mining power; following China's 2021 mining ban, Bitcoin's network-wide hashrate fell from 197 to 68 exahashes/second within one month | Source cited as reference [34] for the pre-ban share, bitinfocharts.com for the hashrate drop |
| 5-10% of all Ethereum nodes reportedly relied on the centralized Infura API service, as of 2018, with the reliance continuing in subsequent years | Cited to reference [138] |
| OpenSea handled approximately 98% of all NFT trading volume, as of 2021, charging a 2.5% commission on sales | Cited to reference [181] |

Case studies applying the binary MDT (not a continuous metric): fiat-backed stablecoins (Tether/USDT, USDC, Gemini Dollar, TrueUSD, Binance USD) are stated to fail the MDT at the governance layer, because in each a single legal entity is the sole party that can issue new tokens against escrowed currency and redeem them; wrapped-token bridges (Wrapped Bitcoin, custodied by BitGo; Huobi Bitcoin, custodied by Huobi) are stated to fail the MDT at the governance layer for the same reason, a single custodian being the sole party able to mint and burn the wrapped token.

### Parameters
The paper is a systematization and case-study methodology, not a parameterized experimental system; it defines no tunable protocol parameters. The one formal definition with an internal threshold is the Minimum Decentralization Test (Definition 1), whose only "parameter" is the existence quantifier over layers: the system fails if such a single controlling legal person exists in even one layer, with no numeric threshold stated for "a sufficient number of relevant parties" beyond "able to violate a property of interest" — left to case-by-case legal and technical judgment for each layer and system.

### Stated limitations
The paper states explicitly that its own contribution is a framework for analyzing decentralization, "not specific quantitative metrics," and states that identifying which specific metric to use per layer is left as future work. It states that it does not treat off-chain Layer-2 protocols (for example the Lightning Network) as a distinct layer of its own stratification, though it states the existing layers could in principle be applied to a Layer-1-plus-Layer-2 composite system, and that doing so is a promising but unexplored research direction. It states that analyzing decentralization of infrastructure the ledger stack depends on but does not itself define, such as physical network links, internet routing, or operating systems, is explicitly out of scope. It states that no aggregation methodology across layers into a single system-wide decentralization score is proposed, calling this a compelling direction for future work. It states that natural-disaster and similar exogenous physical hazards are outside the paper's scope, even though it notes such hazards could matter more when a resource is geographically concentrated. For several claims in the Bitcoin case study, the paper states explicitly that no concrete data could be found (for example, on the distribution of Bitcoin token ownership by wallet software type, and on the distribution of hashing power by specific hardware product), and reports the corresponding layer as inconclusive rather than filling the gap with an estimate.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A layer's decentralization analysis under this methodology requires that the resource being tracked at that layer be identifiable and attributable to a controlling party; the paper's own Bitcoin case study reports several layers (Bitcoin hardware-by-manufacturer share, token ownership by wallet-software type) as inconclusive precisely because no such attribution data exists, which means any later synthesis step drawing on this paper's Bitcoin figures for those specific sub-claims has no basis to cite. Applying the Minimum Decentralization Test to a component requires the analyst to first map that component's participants onto legal persons rather than technical identities or addresses, since the MDT's failure condition is specifically about legal-entity control, and the paper's own worked examples (stablecoin issuers, bridge custodians) are single named companies rather than technical roles. Any system aiming to pass the MDT at the governance layer specifically must avoid vesting sole minting, redemption, or protocol-upgrade authority in one legal entity, since every MDT-failure example the paper gives is a governance-layer single point of control. The paper's Gini-coefficient figures for token wealth are stated to be sensitive to whether multiple addresses controlled by one real-world entity are merged (which the paper's own Table 2 data does not do, since it counts by address); a synthesis step citing these figures as a measure of decentralization across people rather than across addresses would need that clustering step performed first, which this paper states was not done.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. No other entry in this batch measures Bitcoin's own hardware, wealth, or geography layers with figures that disagree with the ones reported here; OVEZIK-ACNS-25 (this batch) is a later paper by an overlapping author set that measures related quantities (Gini coefficient, Nakamoto coefficient, HHI) on Bitcoin's consensus and tokenomics layers using the authors' own five-year historical pipeline rather than the third-party point-in-time figures cited here, so the two papers' numbers are not directly comparable measurements of the same window and neither entry states the other's number is wrong.

### References worth retrieving
- competing/foundational: Zhang, Ma, Liu, "SoK: Blockchain decentralization," 2023 — a competing systematization of blockchain decentralization; cited in the companion OVEZIK-ACNS-25 bibliography (reference 70 there) as directly comparable prior SoK work.
- foundational: reference [34] in this paper's bibliography (the geographic mining-distribution and China-ban hashrate-drop source) — cited repeatedly for the Bitcoin geography case study; not independently retrieved or verified in this pass, only the paper's own citation of it was read.
- foundational: reference [185] (ASIC-manufacturer market concentration) and reference [138] (Infura centralization reliance figures) — both underlie specific numeric claims quoted above and were not independently retrieved.
- foundational: Platis, Sanderford, "Nakamoto coefficient," 2021 (cited as reference [144] in this paper) — the source the paper credits for introducing the Nakamoto coefficient metric, which the companion OVEZIK-ACNS-25 paper measures directly across five blockchains; worth retrieving to check the metric's original definition against the ACNS paper's stated variant (> 0.5 vs >= 0.51 threshold).
- foundational: Rosenthal, "Gini coefficients of cryptocurrencies," 2018 (reference [154]) — cited as the Gini-coefficient methodology source.
- foundational: Rhoades, "The Herfindahl-Hirschman index," Fed. Res. Bull., 1993 (reference [151]) — cited as the HHI methodology source, also used directly in OVEZIK-ACNS-25's empirical analysis.

### Verbatim extracts
- "A blockchain system fails the Minimum Decentralization Test (MDT) if and only if there exists a layer ... for which there is a single legal person that controls a sufficient number of relevant parties so that it is able to violate a property of interest."
- "our work offers a framework for analyzing blockchain decentralization, but not specific quantitative metrics"
- "4 pools control more than 75% of the whole network's mining power"
- "100 addresses controlling 14.01% of all wealth"
- "Bitcoin has a Gini coefficient of 0.514, considering only the 10,000 richest addresses, and a staggering 0.955 w.r.t. all addresses"

## [PERCIVAL-BSDCAN-09] Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions
**Citation:** Colin Percival. "Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions." BSDCan (self-published technical report; later standardized as RFC 7914), 2009. DOI: 10.17487/RFC7914 (registry-cited; this document itself carries no DOI).
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.tarsnap.com/scrypt/scrypt.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.tarsnap.com/scrypt/scrypt.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The scrypt key derivation function raises the cost of a brute-force password search performed on custom hardware, by forcing every evaluation to hold a large pseudorandom array in memory rather than only performing many arithmetic operations. The paper defines a memory-hard algorithm as one whose memory use S(n) grows almost as fast as its operation count T(n) (formally S(n) is Ω(T(n)^(1-e)) for arbitrarily small e), and a sequential memory-hard function as one where, in addition, no parallel machine with S*(n) processors and S*(n) memory can compute the function in expected time T*(n) such that S*(n) times T*(n) is asymptotically less than T(n) squared — meaning a parallel attacker gains nothing from adding processors unless it adds a matching amount of memory to each one. The construction, ROMix, builds an array of N pseudorandom blocks by repeated hashing, then makes a second pass reading blocks at positions selected by the current hash state, so that discarding the array to save memory forces recomputation from scratch; the paper proves ROMix is sequential memory-hard under the random oracle model. Because random hash-function calls waste real memory bandwidth on modern CPUs (cache lines and memory latency dominate a single hash call), the paper replaces the raw hash step with BlockMix, which mixes 2r blocks of state through repeated applications of the Salsa20/8 stream-cipher core, giving one sequential-memory-hard step that better matches real cache-line and memory-latency behavior; the combination is called SMix. The overall function, scrypt(P, S, N, r, p, dkLen), first derives p independent MFLen-sized blocks from the password P and salt S using one PBKDF2 (RFC 2898-family Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) call, mixes each of the p blocks independently through SMix with cost parameter N, and finally runs PBKDF2 once more over the concatenated mixed blocks to produce the derived key of length dkLen. Because the p independent mixing computations do not communicate, an implementor increases p to raise computational cost without increasing the memory footprint, which the paper states lets scrypt remain useful if CPU parallelism and memory capacity grow at different rates in the future.

### Measured results
The paper does not run a hardware implementation or a live-network deployment; its cost figures are derived estimates computed from published cryptographic-circuit design data and manufacturing-cost data for a stated process node, not from an executed experiment.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Circuit die area and throughput, per algorithm (source data for the cost model) | DES: about 4,000 logic gates, 2,000 Mbit/s; MD5: about 12,000 gates, 2,500 Mbit/s; SHA-256: about 20,000 gates, 2,500 Mbit/s; Blowfish: about 22,000 gates plus 4 KiB SRAM, 1,000 Mbit/s; Salsa20/8: about 24,000 gates, 2,000 Mbit/s | Figures drawn from published circuit datasheets and papers (cited: CAST, Helion, Good and Benaissa, Yan and Heys), all normalized to a 130 nm fabrication process because that was the node with the most published circuit data available |
| Manufacturing-cost assumptions used in the derivation | About 5 micrometer-squared per gate of random logic; about 2.5 micrometer-squared per bit of SRAM; about 0.1 micrometer-squared per bit of DRAM; about 0.1 USD per square millimeter of VLSI die | Estimated for a 130 nm process circa 2002; the paper states these together with the circuit figures above are the two derived inputs to every dollar-cost estimate in Table 1 |
| Estimated 1-year password-cracking hardware cost, interactive-login parameters (100 ms) | 6 lowercase letters: under 1 USD for every KDF; 8 chars from 95-symbol alphabet: DES-crypt under 1 USD, MD5 under 1 USD, MD5-crypt 130 USD, PBKDF2 18,000 USD, bcrypt (cost 95 ms) 130,000 USD, scrypt (64 ms) 4.8 million USD; 40-character English text: PBKDF2 200,000 USD, bcrypt 1.5 million USD, scrypt 52 million USD | Password-cracking hardware sized to find a password within an average 1-year search; parameters chosen so each KDF's per-guess time is under 100 ms on one core of a 2.5 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo; NIST SP 800-63 entropy estimation used for text-string passwords (4 bits for the first character, 2 bits each for the next 7, 1.5 bits each for the next 12, 1 bit each thereafter) |
| Estimated 1-year password-cracking hardware cost, file-encryption parameters (multi-second) | 8-char passwords: PBKDF2 (5.0 s) 920,000 USD, bcrypt (3.0 s) 4.3 million USD, scrypt (3.8 s) 19 billion USD; 40-character text: PBKDF2 10 million USD, bcrypt 47 million USD, scrypt 210 billion USD; 80-character text: bcrypt 1.5x10^12 USD, scrypt 2.3x10^23 USD | Same cost model; parameters chosen so each KDF's per-guess time is under 5 seconds on the same reference CPU, a duration the paper states is reasonable for encrypting or decrypting one sensitive file |
| Relative cost advantage of scrypt over alternatives, as stated by the authors | For interactive-login parameters, scrypt is 35 times more expensive to attack than bcrypt and 260 times more expensive than PBKDF2; for file-encryption parameters, scrypt's advantage grows to 4,000 times bcrypt and 20,000 times PBKDF2 | Same Table 1 dataset; the paper attributes the larger file-encryption-case advantage to scrypt increasing both computation time and required die area as N grows, whereas bcrypt and PBKDF2 only increase computation time |
| bcrypt passphrase-length ceiling effect | bcrypt's relative advantage over PBKDF2 falls for the longest text passwords in the table because bcrypt only uses the first 55 characters of a passphrase | Same Table 1 dataset, 80-character text-password column |

### Parameters
scrypt's tunable parameters: N (CPU/memory cost parameter, controlling array size and thus memory use and computation time), r (block-size parameter for BlockMix, set to 8 in the paper's worked examples), p (parallelization parameter, a positive integer at most (2^32-1)*hLen/MFLen, set to 1 in the paper's worked examples). The paper states r=8, p=1 "appears to yield good results" at the time of writing but expects the optimal r and p to rise as memory latency and CPU parallelism increase. Worked N values in the cost table: N=2^14 for the 100 ms (interactive-login) parameter set and N=2^20 for the 5 s (file-encryption) parameter set, both with r=8, p=1. ROMix's work parameter N must be less than 2^(k/8) for a k-bit hash output. SMix operates on 1024r-bit blocks and uses 4Nr applications of the Salsa20/8 core with 1024Nr + O(r) bits of storage (Theorem 2, proved in the paper, not measured). Conjecture 1 (unproven, stated as a conjecture) gives an expected minimum amortized area-time product per password of 1024*N^2*r^2*p*s*t for any circuit computing scrypt, where s is the minimum area to store one bit and t is the minimum time to evaluate one Salsa20/8 core — the basis for the paper's claim that doubling N is expected to roughly quadruple hardware attack cost, since both time and required space double.

### Stated limitations
The paper states that ROMix is proved sequential memory-hard only under the random oracle model, and that scrypt's own sequential-memory-hardness is a conjecture ("appears very likely"), not a proof, contingent on no new attack being found against scrypt or its Salsa20/8, BlockMix, or PBKDF2 components. The paper states its Table 1 dollar-cost figures are "very approximate" and reflect only cryptographic-circuit cost at circa-2002, 130 nm technology; the authors state the true cost including control circuitry, boards, power supplies, and operating costs could be 10 times higher, while future semiconductor and circuit-design improvements could make it 10 times lower. The paper states it could not obtain accurate real-world data on actual password-cracking hardware because organizations that build such hardware are described as "somewhat secretive," so all estimates rest on published cryptographic-circuit datasheets rather than measured attacker hardware. The paper documents a bug (an even-valued LCG multiplier arising 50% of the time on reinitialization) in the HEKS scheme by Reinhold, which it analyzes but states it does not believe meaningfully weakens HEKS; this is presented as an aside on a related prior scheme, not a limitation of scrypt. The paper proves HEKS itself is not sequential memory-hard (a parallel machine with O(L) processors computes it in O(N*K*L^0.5+e) time versus O(L^2 + N*K*L) sequentially), motivating scrypt's alternative construction rather than being a limitation of scrypt.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any deployment of scrypt requires a general-purpose machine with random-access memory on the order of 1024*N*r bytes available during key derivation, since the mixing step must hold the full pseudorandom array to avoid the intended recomputation cost; a memory-constrained device (embedded hardware, a low-memory mobile client) cannot use large N without paying the same time cost the scheme imposes on an attacker. Requires an underlying pseudorandom function for the two PBKDF2 calls that bracket the mixing step (the paper instantiates this with HMAC-SHA256); the security argument (Conjecture 1) is contingent on Salsa20/8 having no faster hardware evaluation and on BlockMix's shuffle step (unproven, only conjectured to hold) actually preventing partial-value pipelining attacks. Any system selecting scrypt as its key-derivation or proof-of-work-style memory-hard primitive must fix N, r, and p as a joint choice trading peak memory footprint against wall-clock latency; the paper does not give a formula deriving these from a target hardware-cost multiplier, only two worked example parameterizations (100 ms and 5 s targets on a specific 2.5 GHz CPU) that a later system must recompute against its own reference hardware and target latency.

### Contradicts
None found. No claim in this batch or corpus is described in the paper as being overturned, and no other entry in this batch reports a conflicting figure for scrypt's cost. This paper is itself the origin of the memory-hard-function cost argument that BIRYUKOV-FC-15 (also in this batch) references when noting that memory-hard proof-of-work functions such as scrypt (used in Litecoin) reduce GPU/ASIC advantage relative to CPU miners; BIRYUKOV-FC-15 states this consistently with this paper's own claim, not in contradiction to it.

### References worth retrieving
- Kelsey, Schneier, Hall, Wagner, "Secure applications of low-entropy keys," ISW 1997 — foundational: the paper that first formalized key stretching, cited as an early ancestor requiring "32-bit arithmetic and moderately large amounts of RAM."
- Provos, Mazieres, "A future-adaptable password scheme," USENIX ATC 1999 — competing: the paper defining bcrypt, this paper's direct comparison point throughout the cost table.
- Kaliski, "PKCS #5: Password-based cryptography specification version 2.0," RFC 2898, 2000 — foundational: defines PBKDF2, used both as a comparison KDF and as scrypt's own bracketing subroutine.
- Reinhold, "HEKS: A family of key stretching algorithms," 1999 (personal communication 2009 for confirmation) — foundational/superseded-by: the memory-hard-but-not-sequential-memory-hard predecessor this paper's Section 3 analyzes and whose parallel-attack weakness motivates ROMix.
- Florencio, Herley, "A large-scale study of web password habits," WWW 2007 — foundational: source of the cited 42.02-bit average password entropy figure for paypal.com used to motivate the need for key stretching.
- Bernstein, "The Salsa20 family of stream ciphers," 2007 — foundational: defines the Salsa20/8 core used as the underlying hash primitive in BlockMix and SMix.

"scrypt is a much more expensive key derivation function to attack than the alternatives"

## [PIATEK-NSDI-07] Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?
**Citation:** Michael Piatek, Tomas Isdal, Thomas E. Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Arun Venkataramani. "Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?" USENIX NSDI, 2007.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi07/tech/piatek/piatek.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi07/tech/piatek/piatek.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The paper measures how much of BitTorrent's observed cooperation comes from its tit-for-tat (TFT) reciprocity rule versus from unrewarded contribution by high-capacity peers, then builds BitTyrant, a client that raises download performance per unit of upload contribution without changing the wire protocol. BitTorrent divides a peer's upload capacity equally among the peers in its active set (the set of peers it is currently unchoking, sized by the reference client as floor(sqrt(0.6 * capacity)) minus the number of optimistic-unchoke slots); the paper terms this per-connection share the equal split rate. Standard TFT unchokes peers that reciprocated fastest in the recent past, plus a small number of randomly chosen optimistic unchokes that bootstrap new peers into the reciprocation game. The paper's model shows that a peer's chance of reciprocation from a candidate partner depends on that partner's active-set size, and that high-capacity peers therefore need hundreds of connections to fully reciprocate; because typical local-neighborhood sizes (50-100 peers in existing clients) are far smaller, most peers under-fill their upload capacity relative to what the model computes as their maximizing allocation, and the unused capacity is contributed without earning proportional download benefit — the paper's operational definition of altruism. BitTyrant exploits this gap with an alternative unchoke algorithm: for each candidate peer p, it tracks u_p (the upload rate needed to induce reciprocation from p, initialized from the measured equal-split-capacity distribution) and d_p (the observed or estimated download rate received from p), ranks connections by the ratio d_p/u_p, and greedily unchokes in ranked order until its own upload capacity is exhausted, so it maximizes total download rate per unit of upload spent rather than splitting capacity equally. After each round, u_p is decreased by a factor gamma if p reciprocated for r consecutive rounds (signaling u_p is set higher than necessary), and increased by a factor delta if p failed to reciprocate after being unchoked (signaling u_p is too low); for peers that have not yet sent data, BitTyrant estimates d_p from the rate at which the peer announces new blocks, then divides by the reference client's recommended active-set size for that implied capacity to approximate the peer's equal split rate. BitTyrant enlarges its own local neighborhood beyond the typical 50-100 peers by requesting more peers from both the centralized tracker and the DHT-based distributed tracker at the maximum allowed frequency, because the modeling shows high-capacity peers need a much larger candidate pool to find reciprocating partners. To avoid TCP throughput loss from splitting capacity across too many low-capacity connections, BitTyrant peers recognize one another via a Peer-ID hash advertised at connection time and switch between themselves to a block-based TFT variant that ramps send rates up to full capacity with fewer connections.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| BitTorrent client population sample | 301,595 unique BitTorrent IP addresses observed | 48-hour measurement period, April 2006, across 3,591 distinct autonomous systems and 160 countries; client-share breakdown: Azureus 47%, BitComet 20%, uTorrent 15%, BitLord 6%, Unknown 3%, Reference 2%, Remaining 7% |
| BitTyrant single-strategic-peer performance gain, real swarms | Median performance gain factor 1.72 (a 1 Mb/s-class client's stated headline figure is a median 70% gain); 25% of downloads finished at least twice as fast | 114 real-world swarms crawled from popular BitTorrent aggregation sites, swarms of 300-800 peers (up to 2,000), file size limited to under 1 GB; BitTyrant and an unmodified Azureus client joined simultaneously, both capped at 128 KB/s upload |
| Worst-case swarm behavior | BitTyrant's worst-performing swarm returned only 3 peers with equal-split capacity above 10 KB/s versus 8 for the unmodified client; total download time about 15 minutes (the tracker's minimum request interval) | Same 114-swarm study; attributed to the randomness of the tracker's returned peer subset, not a flaw in BitTyrant's ranking |
| Swarms with under 10% performance difference | 12 of 114 swarms | Attributed to data-availability limits (low seed capacity or newly available torrents) rather than upload-capacity distribution, meaning download rate was capped below any client's upload capacity regardless of strategy |
| Single strategic peer on synthetic swarm | BitTyrant produces lower variance and generally faster completion than unmodified Azureus, averaged over 6 trials | 350 PlanetLab nodes, upload capacities drawn from the measured distribution but scaled by 1/10 (along with file size, initial unchoke bandwidth, and block size) to fit PlanetLab's actual available bandwidth; 3 seeds with combined 128 KB/s capacity at University of Washington serving a 5 MB file; synthetic churn via immediate disconnect/reconnect on completion |
| Diminishing-returns point for high-capacity peers | BitTyrant identifies and stabilizes around 100 KB/s of upload as the point beyond which additional contribution does not yield proportionally faster download | Same 350-node PlanetLab experiment (Figure 11) |
| All-BitTyrant swarm performance (strategic, not selfish) | Overall completion-time performance improved and total swarm altruism increased relative to a swarm of unmodified Azureus clients | Same 350-node, 5 MB-file, 128 KB/s-seed-capacity PlanetLab setup, all 350 peers running BitTyrant simultaneously, departing immediately on completion |
| Selfish-BitTyrant degradation | Average completion time for a low-capacity peer rose from 314 to 733 seconds; for a 100 KB/s-capacity peer, from 108 to 190 seconds | Same PlanetLab setup, repeated with all high-capacity peers' upload capacity capped at 100 KB/s (the measured diminishing-returns point) to model selfish withholding of excess capacity |
| Reciprocation throughput scaling | Reciprocation throughput doubles between the 95th and 98th percentile of the capacity distribution | Derived from the paper's analytic model, parametrized by the measured upload-capacity distribution |
| Protocol overhead from enlarged neighborhood | Average protocol overhead as a share of total received file data rose from 0.9% (unmodified Azureus) to 1.9% (BitTyrant) | Measured across the same real-swarm and PlanetLab comparisons described above |

### Parameters
- Optimistic-unchoke slots omega: 2 simultaneous optimistic unchokes per peer (reference-client default, used in the model).
- Local neighborhood size lambda: 80 directly connected peers (reference-client default in the model); BitTyrant increases this beyond the reference client's default via more frequent tracker and DHT queries (no fixed target size stated as a single number).
- Active-set sizing function: active(r) = floor(sqrt(0.6r)) - omega, for upload-capacity rate r (reference BitTorrent client default formula).
- BitTyrant reciprocation-estimate update factors: gamma = 10% decrease in u_p if a peer reciprocates for r = 3 consecutive rounds; delta = 20% increase in u_p if a peer fails to reciprocate after being unchoked in the previous round.
- Optimistic-unchoke period T: 30 seconds (used in the convergence-time formula).
- Upload-capacity cap in the real-swarm evaluation: 128 KB/s for both BitTyrant and the comparison Azureus client.
- PlanetLab scaling factor: 1/10 applied to upload-capacity draws, file size, initial unchoke bandwidth, and block size, to fit available PlanetLab bandwidth while preserving the shape of the measured distribution.
- Selfish-cap experiment: high-capacity-peer upload capped at 100 KB/s, chosen as the empirically observed diminishing-returns point.
- File size in PlanetLab experiments: 5 MB, with 3 seeds totaling 128 KB/s combined capacity.

### Stated limitations
The authors state their analytic altruism model is not intended to be predictive: it rests on simplifying assumptions (a representative capacity distribution held constant across a swarm's lifetime, and uniform active-set sizing by all other peers) that the authors say are not realistic for every swarm, and its purpose is only to suggest where altruism originates and to guide BitTyrant's design. The paper states BitTyrant is not strategyproof, even when extended with the block-based TFT variant used between mutually recognizing BitTyrant peers, and explicitly leaves open for future work whether further strategic countermeasures against BitTyrant itself would be effective. Three additional cheating strategies (exploiting optimistic-unchoke weighting via identity churn, downloading-only-from-seeds exploits, and falsifying block availability) are described but explicitly not implemented in BitTyrant because the authors judge them fixable by simple client-side countermeasures; they are documented for completeness, not evaluated experimentally. The paper reports that when high-capacity peers behave strategically and selfishly (withholding capacity beyond the diminishing-returns point), aggregate swarm performance decreases and low-capacity peers are harmed the most, stated as a direct measured consequence of universal strategic adoption, not a hypothetical. The paper explicitly frames its own conclusion as an open question rather than a settled result: whether real-world adoption of BitTyrant-style selfishness will in practice degrade swarm performance, prompt a shift to centrally enforced incentives, or induce users to buy more bandwidth, is stated as unresolved and left for future observation following the client's public release.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
BitTyrant's unchoke-ranking mechanism requires an active set larger than the reference client's typical 50-100 peers to find enough high-value reciprocating partners; it achieves this by requesting more peers from the tracker and the DHT rather than needing any protocol change, so a system reusing this mechanism needs an underlying peer-discovery channel (centralized tracker, DHT, or both) capable of returning a larger and more frequently refreshed peer set on request. The reciprocation-rate estimator needs an initial estimate of a candidate peer's equal-split capacity before any direct data exchange with it, and the paper's method for that estimate (dividing an observed block-announcement rate by the reference client's recommended active-set size for the implied capacity) assumes the reference client's sqrt(0.6r) active-set-sizing formula remains the network's dominant convention — if the observed swarm's clients use a different active-set policy, this bootstrap estimate is stated by the authors to potentially misestimate capacity. The mechanism assumes the ability to observe, per connection, whether the remote peer reciprocated in each round (dp) and whether it reciprocated for the past r rounds, so it needs the underlying protocol to expose or allow inference of a peer-level reciprocation signal over time; a protocol that only reports a swarm-level or opaque aggregate result would not supply the per-connection signal this ranking algorithm consumes. The block-based TFT fallback between mutually recognizing BitTyrant clients requires each peer to reveal a stable, protocol-visible identifier (the Peer ID hash) at connection time, so any anonymity layer suppressing stable per-connection identifiers would remove the signal BitTyrant uses to switch into that faster-converging mode with other BitTyrant peers.

### Contradicts
The paper explicitly contradicts the "consensus" (its own characterization) that TFT alone makes BitTorrent robust to strategic behavior, attributed to Cohen's original 2003 IPTPS paper and repeated in subsequent work; it also contradicts the conclusion of Qiu and Srikant (SIGCOMM 2004) that BitTorrent's rate-based TFT converges to a Nash equilibrium in which all peers upload at full capacity — the paper states that result does not hold for typical file sizes under realistic bandwidth distributions and churn, which is precisely the gap BitTyrant exploits. No contradiction with another paper in this corpus was found.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: B. Cohen. "Incentives build robustness in BitTorrent." IPTPS, 2003. (Origin of the TFT design and the "incentives build robustness" claim this paper's title and conclusion directly dispute.)
- **Competing**: D. Qiu, R. Srikant. "Modeling and performance analysis of BitTorrent-like peer-to-peer networks." SIGCOMM, 2004. (Analytic Nash-equilibrium result for rate-based TFT that this paper's measured results contradict for realistic parameters.)
- **Competing**: A. Bharambe, C. Herley, V. Padmanabhan. "Analyzing and Improving a BitTorrent Network's Performance Mechanisms." INFOCOM, 2006. (Independent simulation finding significant altruism; proposes bandwidth-matched peer selection and block-level TFT as alternate mechanisms; the source paper judges its evolution path unconvincing without adoption incentive.)
- **Competing**: B. Fan, D.-M. Chiu, J. Liu. "The Delicate Tradeoffs in BitTorrent-like File Sharing Protocol Design." ICNP, 2006. (Proposes connection-rate-assignment strategies aimed at fairness and minimal altruism if universally adopted; robustness to strategic peers stated as unclear by this paper.)
- **Attack**: N. Liogkas, R. Nelson, E. Kohler, L. Zhang. "Exploiting BitTorrent for fun (but not profit)." IPTPS, 2006. (Identifies download-only-from-seeds and garbage-data-upload exploits; a third exploit, downloading only from fastest peers, is noted by this paper as not accounting for the upload contribution needed to induce reciprocation.)
- **Attack**: T. Locher, P. Moor, S. Schmid, R. Wattenhofer. "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap." HotNets, 2006. (Techniques including ignoring tracker rate limits and maximizing peer connections.)

## [PIETRZAK-ITCS-19] Simple Verifiable Delay Functions
**Citation:** Krzysztof Pietrzak. "Simple Verifiable Delay Functions." Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS), 2019. DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2019.60.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/627.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/627.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The construction makes the Rivest-Shamir-Wagner (RSW) time-lock puzzle publicly verifiable, producing a Verifiable Delay Function (VDF): a function whose output takes a fixed number of unavoidable sequential computation steps to produce, even with unlimited parallel hardware, but whose correctness any observer can check quickly. The RSW puzzle is a triple (N, x, T) where N = p*q is an RSA modulus, x is a random element, and T is a step count; its solution is y = x^(2^T) mod N, conjectured to require T sequential squarings by anyone who does not know the factorization of N (equivalently, the group order), while the party who set up N can compute the same y in two exponentiations. Pietrzak's protocol lets a prover convince a verifier that y was computed correctly without either party learning the factorization of N. The prover sends an intermediate value mu = x^(2^(T/2)); this splits verifying y = x^(2^T) into verifying mu = x^(2^(T/2)) and y = mu^(2^(T/2)), and the verifier combines these two half-size statements into one new statement (x', y') = (x^r * mu, mu^r * y), using a random challenge r, that holds with the same time parameter halved if the original statement was true, and almost certainly fails if it was false, regardless of what mu a cheating prover sent. Repeating this halving step log(T) times reduces the time parameter to 1, where the verifier checks the final statement directly. The interactive protocol becomes non-interactive (a proof the prover computes once and anyone can later check) by replacing each verifier challenge with a hash of the current transcript, an application of the Fiat-Shamir heuristic; the paper proves this transformation remains sound for its particular logarithmic-round protocol even though the standard Fiat-Shamir soundness argument covers only constant-round protocols. Computation runs over the group of signed quadratic residues (QR+_N, a group in which membership can be checked efficiently, unlike the plain quadratic residues) with N restricted to a product of two safe primes, which the paper states is what gives the protocol unconditional (information-theoretic) soundness rather than soundness resting on a computational hardness assumption.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Proof size | About 10 KB | log(T) <= 40 halving rounds, 2048-bit RSA modulus N, each proof element mu_i one 2048-bit group element (about 256 bytes), so t=40 elements give about 10,240 bytes |
| Verification cost | About 3*lambda*t = 12,000 modular multiplications, approximately 4 full RSA-style exponentiations | lambda = 100 (statistical security parameter), lambda_RSA = 2048, t = 40 halving rounds; the paper notes a standard RSA decryption or signature costs one full exponentiation for comparison |
| Proof-computation speedup over solving the puzzle | Over 2^13 (about 8,000-8,192) times faster than computing y itself, with no parallelism used | t = 40, lambda = 100; the paper's own example states that if computing y takes 1 hour, computing the accompanying proof pi takes about half a second on top |
| Memory required to compute the proof at this speed | About 2^27 bits, stated as about 8 MB | Same t=40, lambda=100 setting, using the paper's proof-computation strategy that stores 2^s intermediate group elements (s = t/2 - log(t*lambda)/2 in the worked single-core example) |
| Effect of truncating the halving protocol by Delta=10 rounds | Proof size falls about 25% (40 elements to 30); verification time falls about 15% | Trades 20 saved short exponentiations against 1,024 extra final squarings, for the same t=40, lambda=100 parameters |

These are the paper's own worked analytical estimates for stated parameter choices, not measurements from an executed implementation or benchmark run.

### Parameters
Statistical security parameter lambda: worked example lambda = 100. RSA modulus bit length lambda_RSA: worked example 2048 bits, required to satisfy lambda <= lambda_RSA/2 given that factoring is only subexponentially hard while the protocol's own soundness error is exponentially small in lambda. Time parameter T = 2^t: worked example t <= 40 (T <= 2^40), a power of two by construction; each unit increase in t doubles both the number of halving rounds and the size of the final proof. Truncation parameter Delta: worked example Delta = 10 out of t = 40 rounds, trading reduced proof size and verification cost against extra final squarings. Underlying group requirement: N must be a product of two safe primes (p and q where (p-1)/2 and (q-1)/2 are also prime), computation performed in the signed quadratic residue group QR+_N rather than plain Z*_N or QR_N.

### Stated limitations
The paper states the VDF's security requires that no party, including the prover, know the factorization of the public modulus N, so a real deployment needs either a trusted party to generate N or a multiparty-computation ("MPC ceremony") among participants of whom at least one is honest; the paper cites the Zcash parameter-generation ceremony as a precedent for the latter. This trusted-setup requirement is stated as absent from the earlier random-oracle-based Proof of Sequential Work constructions the paper builds on (Mahmoody-Moran-Vadhan; Cohen-Pietrzak), which need no such setup at all. The paper states that avoiding trusted setup by moving to class groups of an imaginary quadratic field (following Boneh-Bunz-Fisch and Wesolowski) converts the protocol's unconditional soundness into soundness resting on a computational hardness assumption (that finding a small-order group element is hard), a weaker guarantee than the RSA-safe-prime construction's own soundness. The paper states Dan Boneh raised the possibility of applying its proof technique to endomorphisms other than squaring, potentially toward post-quantum security, but states this remains unrealized: "currently we don't know of any such instantiations." The paper documents that its own Fiat-Shamir hashing must include the intermediate statement (x_i, T/2^(i-1), y_i) at every round, not only the prover's message mu_i, because Wesolowski privately communicated an attack on VDF uniqueness that succeeds if the y-values are omitted from the hash input; the paper's construction as specified includes them and the paper does not claim the omission-vulnerable variant is otherwise safe.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a setup procedure — a trusted party or an honest-majority multiparty-computation ceremony — to generate the RSA modulus N without any party retaining or reconstructing its factorization; any subsequent use of the VDF for repeated challenges reuses the same N, so a single compromised setup compromises every future instance built on that N. Requires a cryptographic hash function to instantiate the Fiat-Shamir transformation, with the protocol's soundness proof holding only in the random-oracle model when that hash is treated as ideal; a real implementation using a hash like SHA-256 gets soundness resting on the hash's computational security, not the protocol's stated unconditional guarantee. Requires the challenge x to be a generator of QR+_N, which a randomly sampled x satisfies almost certainly but which the paper states cannot itself be efficiently verified, so an adversary who can choose x adversarially cannot be prevented by this protocol alone from ever picking a non-generator, though the paper's proof shows this does not open a soundness gap in the proof system in the parameter regime described. Requires whatever consumes the VDF output (the paper's own example is the Chia blockchain's use of a VDF as a core ingredient) to be able to run the O(3*lambda*t) group-multiplication verification cost and store or transmit the roughly 10 KB proof for its chosen t; a consumer with tighter proof-size or verification-latency budgets faces the paper's own stated trade-off against Wesolowski's construction, which the paper states produces a single-group-element proof about a log(T) factor smaller with correspondingly faster verification, at the cost of a larger (O(T/log(T)) versus this paper's O(sqrt(T)*log(T))) proof-computation overhead and reliance on a computational hardness assumption rather than unconditional soundness.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper positions itself explicitly against a concurrent, not conflicting, construction: Wesolowski's VDF (cited as [Wes18], eprint 2018/623), described by this paper as having shorter proofs and faster verification at the cost of larger proof-computation overhead and a computational (rather than unconditional) soundness assumption. No numeric claim in this paper is stated by the paper itself to overturn a prior published figure, and no other entry in this batch reports a conflicting measurement for VDF construction cost.

### References worth retrieving
- Boneh, Bonneau, Bunz, Fisch, "Verifiable delay functions," CRYPTO 2018 — foundational: the paper defining VDFs formally, whose construction and security definitions this paper's §5 (completeness, sequentiality, soundness) instantiates.
- Wesolowski, "Efficient verifiable delay functions," Cryptology ePrint 2018/623 — competing: the concurrent VDF construction this paper compares against throughout, holding the alternative proof-size/verification-time/proof-computation-cost tradeoff point.
- Boneh, Bunz, Fisch, "A survey of two verifiable delay functions," Cryptology ePrint 2018/712 — foundational: the cited survey directly comparing this paper's construction against Wesolowski's, and the source for the class-group trusted-setup-avoidance discussion.
- Mahmoody, Moran, Vadhan, "Publicly verifiable proofs of sequential work," ITCS 2013 — foundational: introduces Proofs of Sequential Work, the concept this paper's VDF specializes, and is cited as not requiring trusted setup unlike this paper's RSA-group construction.
- Cohen, Pietrzak, "Simple proofs of sequential work," EUROCRYPT 2018 — foundational: the same author's prior random-oracle-based Proof of Sequential Work construction, cited as leaving open the problem this VDF paper addresses (public verifiability tied to a concrete puzzle) and as also not needing trusted setup.
- Rivest, Shamir, Wagner, "Time-lock puzzles and timed-release crypto," 1996 technical report — foundational: defines the underlying RSW time-lock puzzle this entire construction makes publicly verifiable.

## [POST-NSDI-11] Bazaar: Strengthening User Reputations in Online Marketplaces

**Citation:** Ansley Post, Vijit Shah, Alan Mislove. "Bazaar: Strengthening user reputations in online marketplaces." USENIX NSDI, 2011.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi11/tech/full_papers/Post.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
Bazaar bounds the amount of monetary fraud any user of an online marketplace can commit, regardless of how many identities that user controls, by computing a network flow value between buyer and seller instead of summing feedback counts. Every successful transaction between two identities creates or strengthens an undirected weighted link between them in a "risk network," where the weight equals the aggregate monetary value of past successful transactions between that pair. Before a transaction proceeds, the marketplace operator asks Bazaar for the maximum flow (the greatest total weight that can be routed via any combination of paths, limiting each edge to its own weight, the standard graph max-flow value) between the buyer and seller in the risk network; if that value is below the proposed transaction amount, the transaction is flagged as potentially fraudulent. If the transaction proceeds, Bazaar selects a set of paths between buyer and seller whose combined weight covers the transaction amount and temporarily lowers each path's weight by its assigned share of that amount, placing that credit "on hold" until feedback arrives. Positive buyer feedback restores the held weight and adds a new direct link (of the transaction's value) between buyer and seller; neutral feedback or a timeout restores the held weight without adding a link; negative feedback makes the reduction permanent, since a fraudulent seller's own risk-network links are what get depleted. Because the max-flow value across any network cut is bounded by that cut's total weight, a set of colluding or Sybil identities can defraud non-malicious users only up to the total weight of the links crossing the cut between the malicious identities and the rest of the network — a bound independent of how many identities the malicious party splits itself into or how much fictitious feedback it manufactures among its own identities. New users bootstrap by having real-world friends grant "virtual" starter links (at the friend's own reputational risk) or by depositing money in escrow with the marketplace operator, which then creates links of that value to random other users. To make max-flow computation tractable, Bazaar builds a "multi-graph": a series of nested subgraphs G_0 (the full risk network), G_1, G_2, ... where G_i keeps only edges of weight at least k^i for a configurable base k (suggested value 2); a flow query starts at the sparsest graph containing the needed weight and only descends to denser graphs as required, since Bazaar only needs to confirm the flow value exceeds a threshold, not compute its exact value.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Crawled dataset: 8,874,521 items of buyer-to-seller feedback across 3,168,455 distinct United-Kingdom users, spanning 5 eBay auction categories (Clothes, Collectibles, Computing, Electronics, Home/Garden), average prices £8.90-£21.31 | eBay.co.uk, 90-day feedback window (eBay's own retention limit), collected by breadth-first-search web scraping starting from one user, restricted to UK-located users and 5 named categories |
| Raising the link-weight threshold from £1 to £20 discards about 80% of risk-network links while the largest strongly connected component still contains most of the remaining nodes; for some categories the largest SCC does not fragment until the threshold passes £100 | Same eBay crawl, per-category risk networks built from positive-feedback transaction links |
| Multi-graph max-flow verification is 1.92x to 2.86x faster than single-graph max-flow, with per-category average query times of 6.29s (Clothes), 1.18s (Collectibles), 1.66s (Computing), 1.41s (Electronics), 5.34s (Home/Garden) versus 18.0s/2.53s/3.78s/2.71s/11.6s single-graph | 1,000 randomly selected user pairs per category, transaction amounts drawn from the observed auction-price trace, multi-graph base k=2, measured on a 2.83 GHz Intel Xeon machine |
| Multi-graph storage overhead is 221%-283% relative to a single graph, but 4.44-18.4 MB absolute, across 12-14 graph levels | Same 5 per-category risk networks, k=2 |
| At the Clothes category's average query time (6.29s), one server core completes 13,736 max-flow calculations per day; the trace's peak daily auction volume in that category was 80,846, implying a minimum 6-core server; concurrent-access conflicts on the same link occurred in 0.0165% of cases in that category | Same Clothes-category risk network and query set |
| No more than 5% (range 1.11%-4.68% across the 5 categories) of genuinely non-fraudulent transactions are incorrectly flagged as potentially fraudulent | Simulation using 80% of the crawled feedback to build the risk network, remaining 20% replayed as transactions, restricted to users with at least 5 observed transactions in the 90-day window, 10 runs per data point with different random seeds, no malicious users injected |
| Aggregate fraud a malicious user can conduct before all further transactions are flagged is empirically bounded by (and matches, within measurement noise) the total value of that user's prior non-fraudulent transactions (the y=x line) | Same simulation setup with 1% of users randomly designated malicious (following a cited prior study's methodology), each malicious user tested against randomly selected counterparties |
| Bazaar would have flagged 29.9%-42.6% (36.0% overall, £164,791.55) of all auctions that resulted in negative feedback in the 90-day trace as potentially fraudulent before they occurred | Same 90-day, 5-category eBay trace, computed from each seller's aggregate positive versus negative feedback value rather than from the live simulation |

### Parameters
- Multi-graph weight-threshold base k: suggested value 2 (each graph level keeps only edges of weight at least k^i)
- Feedback timeout T: configurable; used-value not stated as a specific number of days in the retrieved text
- Malicious-user fraction in the fraud-bound simulation: 1% of users, following a cited prior study's methodology
- Minimum observed-transaction count for a user to be included in the fraud-detection simulation: 5 transactions in the 90-day window
- Train/test split for simulation: 80% of feedback used to build the initial risk network, 20% replayed as simulated transactions
- Number of simulation runs per data point: 10, with different random seeds
- Purchase-time imputation: for the 45.4% of auctions lacking a recorded purchase time (fixed-price, multi-buyer auctions), a delay is subtracted from the feedback time, drawn from the observed delay distribution of auctions where both times are known
- Hardware for max-flow timing measurements: single machine, 2.83 GHz Intel Xeon processor

### Stated limitations
The paper states protecting sellers from fraudulent buyers is left to future work, noting this is partly mitigated because marketplace operators typically let sellers verify payment before shipping. It states that decentralizing the risk network (removing the requirement that the marketplace operator holds full knowledge of all transactions) is an open research question and future work, and that it does not know of any decentralized online marketplace to motivate a concrete design. It states a targeted-attack vector exists in which an attacker who has already accumulated legitimate transaction links can purchase a target seller's goods and give deliberately negative feedback to damage that seller's own outgoing links, though it argues Bazaar raises the cost of this attack relative to existing feedback systems because the attacker must first accumulate non-fraudulent transaction history. It states that a compromised user account lets an attacker conduct fraud up to that account's own Bazaar-bounded limit, an attack not unique to Bazaar but still bounded, unlike under unbounded feedback-based reputation. It states that if a malicious identity is the sole link between two otherwise-connected malicious identities and the rest of the network, the max-flow bound can be lower than the raw sum of that identity's prior successful transactions, because cut capacity, not link count, determines the bound. Multi-graph max-flow queries that fail (no sufficient-weight path set exists) must traverse every graph level and take longer on average than queries that succeed and can terminate early; the paper reports that treating queries running longer than 2 seconds as failures in the Computing category would misclassify only 5.5% of eventually-successful queries while lowering the average query time from 1.66s to 0.70s, an optimization not applied in the reported headline results.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Bazaar requires the marketplace operator to hold complete, authoritative knowledge of every transaction and its outcome (buyer identity, seller identity, monetary amount, and eventual feedback), because the risk network and its max-flow computation are built and queried centrally by that operator; the paper states explicitly that decentralizing this knowledge is unsolved. It requires a feedback channel from buyer to marketplace operator with three outcomes (positive, negative, neutral) plus a configurable timeout T that resolves silence to the neutral case. It requires the ability to place transaction weight "on hold" atomically at the time a transaction is authorized, meaning the operator's transaction-processing pipeline must call into Bazaar's flow computation before finalizing a sale, not asynchronously afterward. It assumes link weights are non-negative and that a transaction's value is fully known at authorization time, since the flow-reduction bookkeeping charges an exact monetary amount to specific paths. The bootstrapping mechanism assumes some new users have existing marketplace users willing to vouch for them via virtual links, or that the operator is willing to hold user funds in escrow; a system lacking either path leaves new users with zero max-flow to everyone and every one of their transactions flagged. It assumes rational-actor incentive alignment for honest feedback: the paper's own reasoning for why buyers report truthfully depends on the buyer's own links being at stake, meaning it does not defend against buyers who have no remaining stake in their own risk-network position.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch. Note for later composition checking: Bazaar's core guarantee (fraud bounded by cut value, not identity count) depends on the operator's full-network view; this composes poorly with any anonymity or partial-visibility tier that hides identities' transaction graphs from a shared computation point, since the max-flow computation cannot be run over information the operator does not hold.

### References worth retrieving
- Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002 — foundational (defines the Sybil attack that Bazaar's cut-based bound targets)
- Mislove, Post, Gummadi, Druschel. "Ostra: Leveraging trust to thwart unwanted communication" — foundational (the paper's own prior link-credit mechanism, applied here to marketplace transactions rather than message delivery, per the target-record's classification)
- Danezis, Mittal. "SybilInfer: Detecting Sybil Nodes using Social Networks" — competing
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao. "SybilLimit" — competing
- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman. "SybilGuard" — competing
- Tran, Min, Li, Subramanian. "Sybil-Resilient Online Content Voting" — competing (source of the 1% malicious-user-fraction methodology this paper reuses)
- Mislove, Marcon, Gummadi, Druschel, Bhattacharjee. "Measurement and Analysis of Online Social Networks" — foundational (source of the dense-core observation this paper's multi-graph design builds on)
- Chau, Pandit, Faloutsos. "Detecting fraudulent personalities in networks of online auctioneers" — competing (graph-based auction fraud detection)
- Pandit, Chau, Wang, Faloutsos. "NetProbe: a fast and scalable system for fraud detection in online auction networks" — competing
- DeFigueiredo, Barr. "TrustDavis: A Non-Exploitable Online Reputation System" — competing
- Ghosh, Mahdian, Reeves, Pennock, Fugger. (reputation/mechanism-design paper, full title not visible in the retrieved bibliography fragment) — competing
- Ford, Fulkerson. "Maximal flow through a network" — foundational (max-flow algorithm baseline)
- Goldberg, Rao. "Flows in Undirected Unit Capacity Networks" — foundational (alternative max-flow algorithm considered and rejected as too costly)
- Gomory, Hu. "Multi-Terminal Network Flows" — foundational (Gomory-Hu trees, considered and rejected for precomputing all-pairs max-flow)

## [REVUELTA-DLT-24] Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers
**Citation:** Alvaro Revuelta, Sergei Tikhomirov, Aaryamann Challani, Hanno Cornelius, Simon Pierre Vivier. "Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers." Distributed Ledger Technology Workshop (DLT), 2024. DOI: not recorded in registry.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper25.pdf
**Source URL:** https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3791/paper25.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The paper measures the message-propagation latency added by attaching a Rate Limiting Nullifier (RLN) zero-knowledge proof to every message gossiped over Waku Relay, a GossipSub-based publish-subscribe layer. RLN enforces a shared publishing rate limit without identifying publishers: a publisher registers a commitment c = H(sk) (H is the Poseidon hash) against an on-chain smart contract, paying a one-time on-chain registration fee that raises the cost of creating multiple identities; every relaying node maintains a local Merkle tree of all currently valid commitments, kept in sync through Ethereum RPC calls. To publish, a node computes an epoch value from the current time divided by the rate-limiting interval, an external nullifier from a hash of the epoch and an application-specific rln_identifier, an internal nullifier from a hash of its own secret key and the external nullifier, and a zero-knowledge proof that it holds a valid membership for the current epoch; it attaches the proof, both nullifiers, the epoch, and the Merkle root to the message. Each relaying node accepts a message only if the proof verifies, no other message relayed within the last g seconds (g = 20 s in the deployed configuration) carried the same internal nullifier, and the epoch is within g seconds of the node's own clock; a node that forwards an invalid message has its GossipSub peer score lowered until it is eventually isolated, which the paper states discourages a node from relaying on a spammer's behalf. The paper's own contribution is measurement, not the RLN mechanism: it builds an analytical latency model splitting end-to-end delay into proof-generation time at the publisher, per-hop transmission time, and per-hop validation (proof-verification plus decoding) time at each relay, then checks that model against a 1,000-node single-host simulation and a five-node real-world multi-host deployment.

### Measured results

| Measurement | Result | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| RLN proof generation / verification time, by hardware | MacBook M1 Pro 16GB: 85.7 ms / 2.7 ms; Bare Metal 256GB AMD EPYC 7502P 32-Core: 171.6 ms / 7.9 ms; Digital Ocean 8GB/4CPU: 276.3 ms / 4.5 ms; Digital Ocean 2GB/2CPU: 329.5 ms / 4.4 ms; Raspberry Pi 4B 4GB: 766.8 ms / 18.7 ms | nwaku reference implementation, Merkle tree depth 20, single-run-per-platform benchmark |
| Keccak256 hashing plus BN254 field-element conversion time | 2 KB message: 0.0055 ms; 25 KB: 0.061 ms; 100 KB: 0.244 ms; 500 KB: 1.222 ms | go-zerokit-rln library, darwin/arm64, cited as insignificant relative to overall latency |
| Multi-host end-to-end latency, 4-hop geographically distributed path | Average total latency across five runs: 2 KB message 477 ms, 25 KB 945 ms, 100 KB 1,689 ms, 500 KB 2,468 ms | 5 nwaku nodes on Digital Ocean (8 GB RAM, 4 vCPU), statically linked in order Singapore-Bangalore-San Francisco-New York-Frankfurt, degree 1 at the two endpoints and 2 at intermediaries, NTP-synchronized clocks, each figure averaged over 5 runs |
| Ping RTT between deployed node pairs | Ranged 59-236 ms across the 5x5 pair matrix (for example Bangalore-San Francisco 220 ms one direction, 218 ms the other) | Average of 5 ping requests within a 15-minute span, using the libp2p ping protocol and the wakucanary tool |
| Single-host simulation, 1,000 nodes, total latency distribution | Average total latency: 2 KB 497 ms, 25 KB 756 ms, 100 KB 900 ms, 500 KB 1,358 ms; 95th percentile: 2 KB 597 ms, 25 KB 930 ms, 100 KB 1,076 ms, 500 KB 1,665 ms; max: 2 KB 604 ms, 25 KB 993 ms, 100 KB 1,221 ms, 500 KB 2,468 ms | Shadow discrete-event simulator, 1,000 nwaku nodes, target mesh degree D=6 plus 25 gossip-only peers per node, 100 Mbps up/down bandwidth per node, 150 ms simulated network latency, 10 publisher nodes each sending 1 message, 9,990 total message-received events counted, first two messages excluded to avoid TCP-window-negotiation bias |
| Delivery-time headline claim | Messages of 25 KB or smaller delivered in under 1 second in both the simulation and the multi-host measurement; 95% of 500 KB messages delivered in under 1.7 seconds | Same simulation and multi-host datasets above |
| Path length (hop count) needed to reach all nodes | 4 hops sufficed in the 1,000-node simulation, versus 5 hops predicted by the paper's own closed-form best-topology formula for N=1000, D=6 | Attributed by the authors to variable node degree in the simulation versus the formula's fixed-degree assumption |
| Fraction of total latency attributable to RLN proof generation | About 10% of total latency for 500 KB messages, about 50% for 2 KB messages, in a 4-hop multi-host path | Derived from the same multi-host measurement (Table 3); proof generation is a one-time publisher-side cost independent of message size, so it forms a larger fraction of the (small) total latency for small messages |

### Parameters
Merkle tree depth for the RLN membership set: 20, fixed across all experiments per the RLN protocol specification the paper cites, described as a trade-off between anonymity-set size and proof-generation/verification cost. Maximum epoch gap g (rate-limit window and nullifier-collision window): 20 seconds, stated as the current deployed value. GossipSub mesh degree bounds in deployed Waku: D_low = 4, D_high = 12; typical target D = 6 (cited from libp2p documentation as "the ideal network peering degree"). Single-host simulation: N = 1,000 nodes, target mesh degree D = 6, 25 additional gossip-only peers per node, 100 Mbps upstream/downstream bandwidth per node, 150 ms simulated per-link latency, 10 publisher nodes. Multi-host deployment: N = 5 nodes, static linear topology (no peer discovery), Digital Ocean 8 GB RAM / 4 vCPU machines, path length h = 4 hops, message sizes tested 2, 25, 100, and 500 KB, 5 runs per message size.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its analytical model assumes a stable, regular-degree full-mesh topology and explicitly excludes node churn (nodes joining and leaving), naming investigation of churn's effect on propagation latency as future work. The paper states its measurements cover only low message-publishing rates and explicitly excludes the effect of higher rates, which the authors expect to increase GossipSub control-message overhead and processing load; this is stated as unexamined, not measured. The current nwaku implementation is stated not to support the economic slashing-of-deposit punishment for malicious publishers described in the original RLN proposal, so a misbehaving publisher whose messages are dropped for reused nullifiers faces no on-chain financial consequence in the deployed system, only network-level isolation via lowered GossipSub score. The paper states the RLN membership Merkle tree must currently be constructed and maintained locally by every publisher and verifier, which it states may be impractical for resource-restricted nodes, and reports the authors are investigating (not yet built) a design where the tree lives entirely on-chain to allow delegated proof generation. The paper states its 4-hop-suffices simulation finding used only 10 of 1,000 nodes as publishers and did not test adversarial conditions, node faults, network failures, or clock desynchronization, naming these as future work rather than tested cases. The simulation is stated to underestimate latency for 100 KB and 500 KB messages because the Shadow framework does not model CPU time for message decoding (only the benchmarked proof-verification time is injected), and conversely to overestimate latency for small (2 KB) messages, a discrepancy the authors attribute to this same CPU-time-modeling gap rather than to a flaw in the underlying RLN mechanism.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every relaying node must maintain a locally synchronized copy of the current RLN Merkle tree of valid commitments, which requires either an Ethereum RPC provider connection (the paper names Infura and Alchemy as examples) or the node running its own Ethereum execution client; a node lacking this synchronization cannot validate incoming proofs correctly. The rate-limit and replay-detection mechanism (the nullifier-collision check) requires every participating node's local clock to stay within the fixed epoch-gap window (20 s in the deployed system) of the network's shared time reference, which the paper's own multi-host experiment satisfies only by adding NTP synchronization; a node whose clock drifts beyond that gap will reject valid proofs or accept expired ones. The rate-limiting property depends on GossipSub's separate peer-scoring mechanism to enforce the consequence of relaying invalid messages (score reduction leading to eventual isolation); RLN itself only supplies the validity check; a network without a scoring/isolation layer underneath RLN gets proof verification but no consequence for relaying-node misbehavior. The measured latency figures assume TCP transport with an already-negotiated window and established handshake between neighboring nodes (the first two published messages were excluded from measurement to remove this effect); a system with a different transport or high per-hop connection churn would not inherit these latency figures unmodified. The underlying spam-resistance property depends on the on-chain registration step remaining an actual (non-zero) cost to acquire a membership commitment; the paper states this fee, not the zero-knowledge proof itself, is what deters an attacker from registering unlimited identities.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch measures Waku, RLN, or GossipSub latency, and this paper's central claim (RLN proof-related overhead is not the dominant cost, and is tolerable relative to end-to-end message latency) is not disputed by anything else here.

### References worth retrieving
- Whitehat, Taheri, Thoren, Kilic, Dimovski, "Rate Limit Nullifier," vacp2p RFC (rln-v1), cited [18] — foundational: the RLN protocol specification this paper's implementation follows and whose original economic-slashing design nwaku does not yet implement.
- Grassi, Khovratovich, Rechberger, Roy, Schofnegger, "Poseidon: A new hash function for zero-knowledge proof systems," USENIX Security 2021 — foundational: the hash function used for RLN's commitment and nullifier construction.
- Decker, Wattenhofer, "Information propagation in the bitcoin network," P2P 2013 — competing: prior latency-measurement methodology for a different gossip-based P2P network, cited as related work this paper's methodology follows.
- Neudecker, Andelfinger, Hartenstein, "Timing analysis for inferring the topology of the bitcoin peer-to-peer network," IEEE ATC 2016 — competing: independent latency/topology measurement on a comparable gossip network.
- Zhang, Lee, Ye, Qiao, "Evaluation of ethereum end-to-end transaction latency," NTMS 2021 — competing: comparable latency-measurement study on a related GossipSub-based network (Ethereum).
- Gluhovsky, "EIP-627: Whisper specification," 2017 — attack/superseded-by: prior proof-of-work-based spam-rate-limiting scheme for general-purpose messaging that the paper states "has not gained popularity," relevant as the direct predecessor mechanism RLN replaces.
- Unger, Dechand, Bonneau, Fahl, Perl, Goldberg, Smith, "SoK: Secure messaging," IEEE S&P 2015 — foundational: cited survey of decentralized/federated messaging protocol properties, relevant to comparing Waku's design goals against federated alternatives (ActivityPub, Matrix, Nostr, XMPP, AT Protocol, Farcaster) named in the same section.

"Currently, g is set to 20 s"
"Each registration incurs on-chain transaction fee"
"nwaku implementation does not yet support economic punishment"
