## [SHENG-NDSS-24] Proof of Backhaul: Trustfree Measurement of Broadband Bandwidth
**Citation:** Peiyao Sheng, Nikita Yadav, Vishal Sevani, Arun Babu, S. V. R. Anand, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath. "Proof of Backhaul: Trustfree Measurement of Broadband Bandwidth." NDSS, 2024.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2024-764-paper.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2024-764-paper.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Proof of Backhaul (PoB) lets a verifier that does not trust any single participant measure the backhaul bandwidth of an access point (the "prover") using a group of ordinary-bandwidth helper nodes ("challengers") instead of one dedicated high-bandwidth measurement server. A challenge coordinator selects n challengers, of which up to f = βn may be corrupted. Each selected challenger sends the prover a burst of UDP packets, each packet payload built only from Ed25519 digital signatures (so a corrupted party cannot omit plaintext content and still pass verification). The challenge duration is set long enough that the combined traffic from all challengers queues on the prover's single backhaul link, so the aggregate arrival rate at the prover reflects that link's capacity rather than any one challenger's own bandwidth. The prover hashes the packets it received from each challenger and builds a Merkle tree over those per-challenger hashes, then returns each challenger its own hash and the Merkle root; each challenger checks its Merkle proof and reports its measured round-trip time and packet count to the verifier. The verifier's bandwidth estimate uses the median of the reported round-trip times across challengers, which lowers the effect of individual challengers that report false round-trip times. Two participant attacks are named: a withholding attack, where a corrupted challenger sends fewer probe packets than instructed, and a rushing attack, where a corrupted challenger colludes with a corrupted prover to relay packets or acknowledgments outside the measured link to lower the apparent round-trip time and inflate the measured bandwidth. The protocol applies a correction factor α = (n − 2f)/(n − f) to the raw measured bandwidth to produce a "guaranteed bandwidth" that an honest prover is assured of, curtailing the inflation a rushing attack could otherwise produce. A deployed variant records challenge requests, participant selection, and results on the Ethereum blockchain, with a payer escrowing tokens that are distributed to the challengers used for that specific challenge.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Prover backhaul 250 Mbps, Linux `tc` rate limiter, 6 or more challengers, 100 ms challenge duration | Measured bandwidth error under 5% |
| Prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 4 challengers, 25 ms challenge duration | Measured 167 Mbps (33% low) |
| Prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 4 challengers, 200 ms challenge duration | Measured about 241 Mbps, about 4% error |
| Prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 100 ms challenge, 6+ challengers | About 3.5 MB of challenge data used, error under 5% |
| Single challenger, prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 10 ms challenge duration | Under 2% error, about 345 KB of data, but requires that one challenger to itself have 250 Mbps |
| 10 challengers, prover backhauls 500 / 750 / 1000 Mbps (honest, testbed) | Measured 474.7 / 705.4 / 921.4 Mbps; error 5.1% / 5.9% / 7.9%; Merkle-tree computation overhead 4.6 / 7.3 / 10.2 ms |
| n=10, f=2 corrupted challengers (20% Byzantine), prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 100 ms challenge | Honest median 251.5 Mbps; withholding-attack median 241.4 Mbps (raw error 3.6%), corrected guaranteed bandwidth ≈181 Mbps (28% below the true 250 Mbps, this is the intended conservative bound); rushing-attack median 331.5 Mbps, corrected guaranteed bandwidth ≈249 Mbps (close to true value) |
| Comparison at 500 Mbps backhaul: PoB vs. pathchar vs. MagicTrain vs. speedtest | Measured bandwidth 474.7 / 101.3 / 152.1 / 492.3 Mbps; data used 6.88 / 1.2 / 0.1 / 501 MB — pathchar and MagicTrain use less data but are far less accurate; speedtest is comparably accurate but uses about 73x more data than PoB |
| pathchar RTT-vs-packet-size fit, ping to prover, 15 packet sizes 100–1500 bytes, 500 measurements per size, 5 repeated experiments | Linear-fit intercepts vary by 50–100 ms across repeats of the same link, i.e. minimum-latency estimation is not reliable below 50–100 microsecond resolution, which the authors state makes pathchar infeasible for measuring links at 100 Mbps or higher |
| Real deployed system, ~25–30 active Ethereum-wallet challengers across US/Europe/Asia, 10 challenges per backhaul value at different times | Backhauls 500 / 700 / 1000 Mbps measured as 478.8 [stdev 11.9] / 671.5 [13.6] / 901.0 [16.0] Mbps; average error 4.2% / 4.1% / 9.9% |
| Available-bandwidth variant under synthetic cross-traffic, prover backhaul 250 Mbps, 10 challengers, base rate θ_P,0 = 40 Mbps, step δ = 20 Mbps | Available bandwidths 220 / 140 / 90 Mbps measured as 219.6 / 144.6 / 104.1 Mbps; the 90 Mbps case overestimates because challenge traffic itself displaces some of the injected cross-traffic |
| PoB-Shuffle variant, Byzantine fraction β = 1/3, target error probability ε = 0.5, challenger group sizes t = 2, 3, 4, 5, up to 500–1000 total challenger groups | Accuracy ratio rises with the number of challenger groups and with larger t, at the cost of higher per-group latency from the added shuffle round; for t = 3, 4, 5 no feasible parameters exist to reach the target error probability when the number of groups is small |

### Parameters
- Adversarial threshold: protocol proven for β < 1/3 corrupted challengers with no verifier timer; the authors state β up to 1/2 is achievable if the verifier has access to a timer.
- Guaranteed-bandwidth correction factor: α = (n − 2f)/(n − f), applied to the raw measured bandwidth (tested at n=10, f=2, i.e. β=0.2).
- Design-scope variants (Table II in the paper, not independently re-tabulated here): TCP-based variant with a fairness assumption reaches accuracy (1 − β); the no-signature variant drops accuracy to (1 − 3β)/(1 − β) because it loses non-deniability of packet delivery.
- Challenge packet size: 1514-byte UDP packets (1472-byte payload, 42-byte header), each carrying 23 distinct 64-byte Ed25519 signatures, chosen because bare 64-byte packets defeat WiFi's MAC-layer packet aggregation and lower measured throughput.
- Ed25519 signature generation: 50–60 microseconds per signature on a 1 GB RAM, 1-CPU-core Linux host; challengers precompute all needed signatures before the challenge starts because generation time (about 1.4 ms for 23 signatures) can exceed packet transmission time at low challenger bandwidths.
- Challenge duration tested: 25, 50, 100, 200 ms, with 10 repeated experiments per duration.
- Number of challengers tested: 4, 6, 8, 10 (testbed), 10 (security evaluation), up to 500–1000 challenger groups (PoB-Shuffle scaling experiment).
- Prover backhaul rate-limited with the Linux `tc` utility; per-challenger bandwidth set to θ_P / n.
- Packet drop compensation: each challenger sends 10% more data than the nominal requirement to compensate for an assumed maximum 10% packet drop rate.

### Stated limitations
The authors state that curtailing bandwidth inflation from a rushing attack necessarily lowers the guaranteed bandwidth even when all challengers report honestly (the 28% reduction at β=0.2 shown above). They state that a corrupted challenger with access to an external high-bandwidth "backdoor" link to the prover can still mount a rushing attack, and that eliminating this requires either limiting corrupted challengers' access to such links or adding a shuffle phase (PoB-Shuffle) that pairs challengers to jointly sign packets, at the cost of added communication overhead for verification; the authors state that "implementing an efficient system for such a shuffle protocol in practice is an active area of research." They state that designing a cross-traffic-aware available-bandwidth variant that is both data-efficient and holds a fixed accuracy guarantee "is an open problem." They state the protocol assumes the amount of cross traffic does not vary during a measurement's steps. The liveness of the system (whether a challenge terminates and produces a result at all) depends on a challenge coordinator behaving correctly; the authors state a poorly performing coordinator can compromise liveness, though not accuracy or soundness, and rely on economic incentives (commission fees) and a pool of redundant coordinators. The technique requires latency measurements accurate enough to overcome internet jitter, and the authors' own pathchar re-measurement (see the Measured results table above) documents 50–100 ms of jitter in minimum-RTT estimation on the same link across repeated experiments, which is the reason the authors give for why pathchar-family techniques cannot measure 100+ Mbps links but PoB's traffic-aggregation approach can.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The mechanism assumes digital signatures are available to every challenger and verifiable by the prover and verifier, and it names Ed25519 specifically for its low computational overhead relative to signature size. It requires the verifier or a challenge coordinator to be able to select a fresh, randomly drawn subset of challengers per measurement from a larger active pool, so that a corrupted prover cannot predict which parties will probe it. It requires all selected challengers to have a synchronized-enough view of time to compute round-trip times; the authors name NTP synchronization error (tens of milliseconds over the internet) as a source of measurement error the protocol must tolerate via the median-RTT step rather than eliminate. It requires the prover's backhaul to be modeled as a single bottleneck link, with the rest of the network core assumed effectively infinite-bandwidth (the paper states this as a modeling assumption, "we model the network core as a single point"). The on-chain deployment variant requires an underlying blockchain (Ethereum in the implementation) to record challenge requests and results and to hold escrowed payer tokens, plus a challenge coordinator role that is not itself Byzantine-fault-tolerant for liveness (only for correctness). The PoB-Shuffle extension requires pairwise coordination among challengers within a group before packet transmission, which raises per-measurement latency in proportion to group size t.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- Downey, A. B., "Using pathchar to estimate internet link characteristics." — competing (per-hop capacity estimation technique the paper directly benchmarks and finds infeasible above 100 Mbps due to timing jitter)
- Jain, M. and Dovrolis, C., "Pathload: A measurement tool for end-to-end available bandwidth." — competing (available-bandwidth measurement technique cited as related work)
- Zhou, P., Chang, R. K., Gu, X., Fei, M., Zhou, J., "Magic train: design of measurement..." — competing (MagicTrain, directly benchmarked against PoB in Table VI of the paper)
- Ghosh, M., Richardson, M., Ford, B., Jansen, R., "A torpath to..." — competing (Torpath, a proof system for Tor relay bandwidth remuneration, named as the closest prior decentralized-network telemetry proof system)
- Haleem, A., Allen, A., Thompson, A., Nijdam, M., Garg, R., "Helium..." — competing (deployed decentralized wireless network using proof-of-coverage tokenized incentives)
- Snader, R. and Borisov, N., "Eigenspeed: secure peer-to-peer bandwidth..." — attack/competing (secure bandwidth estimation against malicious peers using consensus vectors; the paper states this approach "doesn't fully appraise high-bandwidth nodes")
- Karame, G. O., Danev, B., Bannwart, C., Capkun, S., "On the security of..." — attack (bandwidth-inflation-attack analysis cited as related security work)
- Merkle, R. C., "A digital signature based on a conventional encryption..." — foundational (Merkle tree construction used directly in the protocol)

- "for β < 1/31, our protocol does not allow any prover to inflate the bandwidth"
- "previous work [26] reports errors over 20% for measuring bandwidths of 500 Mbps or more"

## [SHI-WWW-26] Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network

**Citation:** Ruisheng Shi, Yuxuan Liang, Zijun Guo, Qin Wang, Lina Lan, Chenfeng Wang, Zhuoyi Zheng. "Eclipse Attacks on Ethereum's Peer-to-Peer Network." ACM Web Conference (WWW), 2026. DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792231.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.16560
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16560
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper isolates an Ethereum execution-layer node from all benign peers after the node restarts, so an attacker controls every message the node sends and receives. The attack runs five stages against Ethereum's post-Merge peer-discovery stack (the discv4/discv5 Kademlia-style discovery table, the DNS-based peer list defined in EIP-1459, and libp2p-style outgoing/incoming connection slots). Stage one floods the target's discovery table with unsolicited Ping messages from attacker-controlled node records, evicting benign entries because Ethereum's discovery table applies no rate limit to incoming Ping messages. Stage two poisons the DNS-based peer list that Ethereum's official crawler publishes, by identifying the crawler's source IP from repeated log analysis and feeding it attacker node records that accumulate the crawler's maximum per-crawl score. Stage three occupies idle incoming-connection slots across the wider network before the target restarts, by running attacker nodes that continuously attempt connections to every reachable node with a free slot, so that when the target does reconnect fewer benign peers have a slot to offer. Stage four exploits the fact that a restarting node selects outgoing-connection targets by generating a random target ID and querying its own (now-poisoned) discovery table and DNS list for the closest match, so a discovery table and DNS list dominated by attacker entries causes outgoing connections to resolve to attacker nodes. Stage five races benign peers to fill the target's incoming-connection slots in the seconds after restart, using attacker nodes pre-registered as static peers so they reconnect immediately.

### Measured results

| Stage | Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discovery-table filling (single round) | Attacker occupancy of discovery table | 95% occupancy within 24 hours | Sepolia testnet, 272 attacker nodes continuously pinging one target node, IP-based admission limits disabled on the target |
| Discovery-table filling (repeated rounds) | Refill time after terminating a batch | Refilled to near 100% within about 1 hour, sustained over 6 rounds at 2-hour intervals | Same Sepolia setup, 272 attacker nodes per round |
| Discovery-table filling (per-round success) | Nodes inserted per 272 attempted | 91.5%-97.4% across 6 rounds, round 1; 93.4%-97.1%, round 2 | Sepolia testnet, 10 measured rounds |
| Bucket-targeted DB filling | Last-2-bucket / last-5-bucket occupancy at 66% overall DB fill rate, without attacker ID tuning | 76% / 44% | Sepolia testnet, 257 initial benign seed nodes, attacker node IDs not adapted |
| Bucket-targeted DB filling | Last-2-bucket / last-5-bucket occupancy at 66% overall DB fill rate, with attacker ID tuning | 83% / 51% | Same setup, attacker IDs adapted to target the last 8 buckets |
| DNS list poisoning feasibility | Attacker nodes reaching maximum crawler score | 5 of 10 experiments had at least one attacker node accepted; 1 of 10 had all 5 attacker nodes reach maximum score | Controlled 2-server testbed (not the live Ethereum crawler), 5 attacker nodes against one target, 10 trials |
| DNS list poisoning, estimated time to replace X% of entries | 0%/25%/50%/75%/100% -> 54/64/100/166/538 days | Derived from measured Sepolia DNS-list score distribution (275-2,688) as of July 17, 2025, assuming an attacker gains 3 points per crawl versus 1 point per crawl for a benign node (net daily score advantage of 5 points) |
| Available incoming slots, network-wide | 80.1% of Sepolia nodes with available slots, and 62.7% of mainnet nodes with available slots, have 10 or fewer slots free | 362 Sepolia nodes and 102 mainnet nodes found to have any available slots, out of node sets drawn from the public DNS list, over a 7-hour detection window |
| Available slots occupation attack | About 90% of nodes with available slots occupied, 34 nodes left with slots | Sepolia testnet, 200 attacker nodes launched from one public server against 1,268 static nodes drawn from the official DNS list, 2-hour attack window |
| Outgoing-connection hijacking, before network-wide slot occupation | 0% DNS-list poisoning -> 0/20 (0%); 25% -> 4/20 (20%); 50% -> 8/20 (40%); 75% -> 13/20 (65%); 100% -> 19/20 (95%) | Sepolia testnet, DB filling rate fixed at 50%, 20 trials per DNS-list poisoning rate |
| Outgoing-connection hijacking, after network-wide slot occupation | At 25% DNS-list poisoning / 50% DB filling: 4/20 (20%) -> 6/20 (30%); at 50% DNS-list poisoning / 50% DB filling: 8/20 (40%) -> 19/20 (95%) | Same setup, slot occupation from the stage-three attack applied first |
| Incoming-connection hijacking, Sepolia | 30/30 (100%) success within 30 seconds of target restart | 3 target full nodes on one server, 40 attacker nodes pre-registered as static peers on a second server, 30 trials, per-IP 30-second reconnection rate limit disabled on the target |
| Incoming-connection hijacking, mainnet | 24/40 (60%) success within 2 days of restart; 18/40 (45%) within 30 seconds; 23/40 (57%) within 1 day | Same attacker setup against mainnet full nodes, 40 trials |
| Public IP addresses required, full attack chain | 304 IP addresses for Sepolia; 720 for mainnet | Derived: 208 (or 624 for mainnet) for 50% DB pre-filling, 28 for DNS-list poisoning, 28 for outgoing-connection hijacking (shared /24-subnet limit of 10 discovery-table entries per subnet), 40 for incoming-connection hijacking; stages one and three reuse IP addresses |

The abstract states that "slots hijacking raises outgoing redirection success from 45% to 95%"; the closest matching table entry (Table 4, 50% DNS-list poisoning combined with 50% database filling) shows an increase from 40% (8/20) before slot occupation to 95% (19/20) after. The two abstract-and-table figures do not exactly agree on the starting value; this entry records both because the exact correspondence is not stated in the body text.

### Parameters
- Discovery table (Kademlia-style, XOR distance): 256 buckets by leading-zero-bit count; bucket k receives a randomly generated ID with probability P_k = 1/(2^(16-k)) - 1/(2^(16-(k-1))) = 1/2^(17-k).
- Attacker nodes per discovery-table-filling round: 272 (128 per targeted bucket across the last 8 buckets, since the paper reports each round inserts 8x16=128 nodes but uses 272 as the total attack-node count in the primary experiment).
- Per-/24-subnet discovery-table admission limit: 10 IP addresses.
- Per-IP incoming-connection rate limit: rejects repeated connection attempts from the same IP within 30 seconds.
- Default incoming-connection slot count per Ethereum node: up to 34 (default), the value used to size the incoming-hijacking attack at 40 attacker nodes.
- Geth client release cadence measured from the Merge (2022-09-15) to 2025-05-05: 56 versions over 32 months, about 1.75 releases per month, each release generally forcing a node restart.
- DB growth rate on an initially empty Sepolia full node: about 200 discovery-table entries per month.
- Sepolia network size (Ethereum official statistics, 2025-05-05): about 2,000 active nodes; mainnet: about 6,000 nodes (Appendix D).

### Stated limitations
The authors did not run the DNS-list poisoning attack against the live official devp2p crawler for ethical reasons; the feasibility figures for that stage come from a controlled 2-server testbed built to imitate the crawler's scoring logic, not from an attack on the production crawler. The paper reports no defense already deployed by Ethereum; the two countermeasures given (a ping-frequency blacklist and a DNS-node reporting/blacklist threshold) are proposed, not evaluated experimentally. The disclosure section states Ethereum's security team acknowledged the report but had not released a fix at the time of writing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A discovery-table implementation that rate-limits incoming Ping messages per source (the paper's own proposed countermeasure) removes the precondition stage one depends on: an attacker's ability to send unlimited unsolicited Ping messages without being dropped. A DNS-based peer list that caps the number of distinct node records permitted per source IP address or subnet removes the precondition stage two depends on. A node that retains a fixed reserve of incoming-connection slots exempt from network-wide occupation, or that rate-limits new incoming connections per unique remote IP at the network level rather than per pairwise IP, would raise the IP-resource cost the paper measures for stage three. Any component that relies on Ethereum's discovery table or DNS peer list as an honest source of peer identity (for example, a search or replication layer built on top of the same node-discovery stack) inherits the same restart-time exposure window this paper measures, because the underlying selection mechanism (closest-ID match against a table an attacker can dominate) is not specific to Ethereum's consensus logic.

### Contradicts
None found. LI-EPRINT-25 in this batch measures a related but distinct property (discv5 network size and connectivity on the broader Ethereum network) and does not report figures directly comparable to this paper's per-stage attack-success rates.

### References worth retrieving
- Marcus, Heilman, Goldberg, "Low-resource eclipse attacks on ethereum's peer-to-peer network," Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2018 — foundational (the two-attacker-host eclipse this paper's stage one and four build on and extend past the fixes made after that disclosure)
- Henningsen, Teunis, Florian, Scheuermann, "Eclipsing ethereum peers with false friends," EuroS&PW 2019 — foundational (prior Ethereum eclipse that did not require a restart)
- Heilman, Kendler, Zohar, Goldberg, "Eclipse attacks on Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network," USENIX Security 2015 — foundational (originating eclipse-attack technique)
- Tran, Shenoi, Kang, "On the Routing-Aware peering against Network-Eclipse attacks in bitcoin," USENIX Security 2021 — competing / attack (AS-level Erebus eclipse variant)
- Heo, Woo, Yoon, Kang, Shin, "Partitioning ethereum without eclipsing it," NDSS 2023 — competing (a partitioning attack on Ethereum that does not require full eclipse)
- Shi, Peng, Lan, Ge, Liu, Wang, Wang, "Eclipse attacks on monero's peer-to-peer network," NDSS 2025 — competing (same author group's prior eclipse work on a different network, the connection-reset technique referenced in Related Work)
- Li, Zhang, Gong, "A place for everyone vs everyone in its place: Measuring and attacking the ethereum global network," Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2025 — competing / independent measurement (LI-EPRINT-25 in this corpus)
- Kim, Ma, Murali, Mason, Miller, Bailey, "Measuring ethereum network peers," IMC 2018 — foundational (peer-measurement methodology)
- Wüst, Gervais, "Ethereum eclipse attacks," ETH Zurich technical report, 2016 — foundational

- "Slots hijacking raises outgoing redirection success from 45% to 95%" (abstract)

## [SIDDARTH-FRONTIERS-20] Who Watches the Watchmen? A Review of Subjective Approaches for Sybil-Resistance in Proof of Personhood Protocols

**Citation:** Divya Siddarth, Sergey Ivliev, Santiago Siri, Paula Berman. "Who Watches the Watchmen? A Review of Subjective Approaches for Sybil-Resistance in Proof of Personhood Protocols." Frontiers in Blockchain 3:590171, 2020. DOI: 10.3389/fbloc.2020.590171.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.3389/FBLOC.2020.590171
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.3389/FBLOC.2020.590171
**Domain:** E

### What it does
This is a review paper, not a single mechanism: it defines a taxonomy of proof-of-personhood (PoP) approaches — protocols that certify one human corresponds to one registered identity, so that a system built on top can prevent a Sybil attack (one actor registering many identities). It surveys seven deployed or prototype systems along that taxonomy and evaluates each on decentralization, privacy preservation, and scalability.

The taxonomy identifies two subjective-judgment primitives underlying every reviewed system. A reverse Turing test asks a human to complete a task easy for humans and hard for algorithms (the CAPTCHA family); the paper's cited example, Idena Network's FLIP test, asks the user to pick which of two orderings of images tells a coherent story, and this test alone stops automated bot registration but not one human passing the test multiple times to register multiple identities. A pseudonym party (or web-of-trust vouching, its asynchronous variant) certifies uniqueness by requiring one human to be physically or socially verifiable in only one place, either through synchronous group ceremonies or through existing members vouching for newcomers across a social graph.

Seven systems are classified by governance structure, size, blockchain, protocol, and substrate, then scored on decentralization, privacy, and scalability (Table 1): Idena Network (public network, ~4,012-4,012 users at time of writing, its own Idena chain, synchronous reverse-Turing-test ceremonies using FLIPs run roughly every two weeks, no personally identifying information required but node IP address observable); Humanity DAO (DAO governance, 640 approved members at peak, Ethereum, web-of-trust plus token-curated registry, required sharing a Twitter account, terminated January 2020 after a smart-contract change made joining prohibitively expensive for new applicants); Kleros / Proof of Humanity (DAO plus legal entity, Ethereum, web-of-trust plus token-curated registry with a distributed dispute-resolution court, requires photos, bios, and video selfies stored on IPFS, users vouch for each other with a financial stake forfeited if the vouched-for identity is later ruled duplicate or false); Upala (DAO, Ethereum, "price of forgery" identity model, verification groups assign each member a currency-denominated score that member can steal from the group's shared pool, an act that automatically deletes that member's identity); BrightID (DAO, 556 users with positive anti-Sybil rank at time of writing, Ethereum/IDChain, intersectional web of trust anchored to trusted seed identities, runs GroupSybilRank — a modification of the SybilRank algorithm — to score participants by graph affinity to seeds); Duniter (public network, 2,801 currency holders as of September 2020, its own Duniter chain, web of trust requiring five vouches from existing members and a maximum graph distance of five hops from designated referent members); Equality Protocol (DAO, 529 users, Ethereum, a meta-protocol scoring other DAOs' Sybil-resistance by combining a Quadratic-Voting-based subjective function with an objective Gini-coefficient measure of token distribution).

### Measured results

| Quantity | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Idena FLIP test human accuracy | 95% | Reported by the paper, citing Moritz 2020, for the Idena Network's AI-hard reverse Turing test |
| Idena FLIP test AI-team accuracy | 60-76% | Same source; best-performing AI teams attempting to solve the same FLIP test |
| WinoGrande NLP benchmark AUC, state-of-the-art model vs. human | 0.7-0.85 (model) vs. 0.94 (human) | Cited as evidence that text-based AI-hard tests (Winograd Schema Challenge variants) are vulnerable to advances like GPT-3, motivating image-based tests instead |
| Idena Network user count | 4,012 (Table 1) / "over 4,000" (body text) | As of the paper's writing (2020); network distributes mining and ceremony rewards reported around $1.5-2/day per participant |
| Duniter Ğ1 currency holders | 2,801 | As of September 2020 |
| BrightID users with positive anti-Sybil rank | 556 | As of the paper's writing (2020) |
| Equality Protocol users | 529 | As of the paper's writing (2020) |
| Humanity DAO peak membership | ~640 approved members | Launched May 2019, terminated January 2020 after repeated attacks including a smart-contract change that made joining prohibitively expensive |
| Facebook fake-account removal rate | on average 2 billion fake accounts per quarter | Cited from Facebook Research (SybilEdge detection method), used as evidence of the scale of Sybil-detection effort required even inside a fully centralized, non-anonymous social platform |

These are project self-reported adoption figures at a point in time (2020), not figures the paper's authors independently measured through an experiment; the paper conducts no controlled experiment of its own and reports no method or hardware for any of these counts.

### Parameters
Not applicable in the sense of a tunable mechanism parameter — this is a comparative review, not an implementation. Structural parameters reported per system: Duniter requires 5 vouches from existing members and a maximum graph distance of 5 hops from a referent member; Idena's validation ceremonies recur approximately every 2 weeks; BrightID's Minimal Anti-collusion Infrastructure (cited from Buterin 2019) lets a voter switch voting keys at any time, so a previously issued voting receipt can be invalidated at will by the voter, preventing verifiable vote-selling short of the voter also giving up the private key itself.

### Stated limitations
The paper states BrightID's GroupSybilRank algorithm's "effectiveness ... in the presence of multiple attack vectors remains to be proved," and separately states there is "no evidence of the Web of Trust schemes' effectiveness for Sybil-resistance in the presence of multiple attack vectors" for the four of seven reviewed systems built on a web of trust. It states a specific attack vector: a bad actor can forge multiple real relationships under different names across enough non-intersecting small groups to grow a significant Sybil presence over time, and that preventing this requires the kind of sophisticated behavioral- and content-classifier modeling Facebook uses (SybilEdge), not a property the web-of-trust protocols themselves guarantee. Reverse Turing tests are stated to stop automated bot attacks but not "human-generated attacks, in which one individual passes the test multiple times and creates multiple different identities" — a mechanical-turk-style marketplace for completing the test on another person's behalf is named as an open, unresolved incentive-model gap for Idena specifically. Kleros's mechanism compromises biometric information (video selfie, personal data) as a structural requirement, which the paper states "may de-incentivize potential users." Upala's score-proportional-to-stake design is stated to more easily benefit capital-rich users, and separately carries a named "avalanche user exit" risk: an event that triggers loss of trust in the system can cause many users to simultaneously destroy their own identities to seize the underlying pooled assets before others do, regardless of the reputation cost. BrightID is stated to not yet be a fully self-sovereign solution because, as of the paper's writing, no established path exists for individuals or groups outside its existing small seed network to self-authenticate, and its social graph is public, which the paper states may compromise user privacy if a participant's real-world identity is separately revealed. The Equality Protocol is stated to lack any verifiable mechanism within the protocol itself to confirm whether a user's subjective rating of another DAO's Sybil-resistance is accurate, creating a named conflict-of-interest and misaligned-incentive risk. Duniter's five-vouch, five-hop requirement is stated to significantly restrict network growth as a direct consequence of the same design that gives it its Sybil-resistance property, and its web of trust is stated to be geographically restricted (concentrated in France and nearby countries), limiting it to local rather than global use.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A reverse-Turing-test-based PoP mechanism (Idena's FLIP) requires a separate mechanism elsewhere in the system to stop one human from completing the test repeatedly under different identities, since the test by itself only distinguishes humans from machines, not one human from many. A web-of-trust vouching mechanism requires an existing social graph with enough density and diversity of connection sources that an attacker cannot cheaply construct many non-intersecting small groups of colluding accomplices; the paper states no reviewed system provides this as a proven property. A vouching-with-financial-stake mechanism (Kleros/Proof of Humanity) requires a functioning, sufficiently liquid financial-stake market and a dispute-resolution process (the paper cites Kleros Court or Aragon's courts) capable of adjudicating disputed identities faster than the incentive to submit false vouches accrues. A trusted-seed-based web of trust (BrightID) requires that seed selection itself be trustworthy and either centrally curated (reintroducing a point of centralization the paper explicitly notes) or subject to a scalable, decentralized seed-selection governance process that, as of the paper's writing, does not yet exist. A score-proportional-to-stake mechanism (Upala) requires that groups independently design and enforce their own admission and verification standards, since the base protocol supplies no floor against capital-rich actors buying higher scores. Any of the reviewed mechanisms used as an input to a downstream system (universal basic income distribution, quadratic voting, quadratic funding, decentralized-oracle witness sampling) requires that downstream system to tolerate the specific residual Sybil-penetration rate the chosen PoP mechanism leaves, since the paper explicitly notes democratic governance is possible under "bounded Sybil penetration" but does not itself quantify what bound each reviewed system achieves.

### Contradicts
None found. The paper does not measure any single figure that another paper in this corpus disputes.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational:** J. R. Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 — defines the Sybil attack itself, the failure every mechanism in this review addresses.
- **Foundational:** B. Ford, "Pseudonym Parties: An Offline Foundation for Online Accountability," 2012 — origin of the pseudonym-party primitive this paper's taxonomy builds on.
- **Attack-or-critique:** B. Viswanath, K. P. Gummadi, A. Post, A. Mislove, "An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses," SIGCOMM 2010 — analyzes exactly the web-of-trust Sybil-defense family four of the seven reviewed systems rely on; brief §8's known gap 3 in the governing brief cites this paper's finding that such defenses perform local community detection.
- **Attack-or-critique:** B. Viswanath, M. Mondal, K. P. Gummadi, A. Post, A. Mislove, "Canal: Scaling Social Network-Based Sybil Tolerance Schemes," EuroSys 2012 — follow-up scaling analysis of the same social-graph Sybil-defense family.
- **Competing:** M. Borge, E. Kokoris-Kogias, P. Jovanovic, L. Gasser, N. Gailly, B. Ford, "Proof-of-Personhood: Redemocratizing Permissionless Cryptocurrencies," IEEE EuroS&PW 2017 — an earlier, more formal proof-of-personhood proposal the paper's taxonomy descends from.
- **Competing:** N. Immorlica, M. O. Jackson, E. G. Weyl, "Verifying Identity as a Social Intersection," SSRN 2019 — theoretical extension of web-of-trust identity verification cited as a proposed but not fully deployed alternative (partially implemented by the closed-source Identiq network).
- **Attack-or-critique:** B. Adam, "Detecting Fake Accounts on Social Networks with SybilEdge," Facebook Research 2020 — the machine-learning-based detection method the paper cites as required in practice on top of any social-graph Sybil defense, given Facebook's reported quarterly fake-account removal rate.
- **Foundational:** L. von Ahn, M. Blum, N. J. Hopper, J. Langford, "CAPTCHA: Using Hard AI Problems for Security," EUROCRYPT 2003 — origin of the reverse-Turing-test primitive underlying Idena's FLIP mechanism.

- "Human accuracy in solving FLIPs is at 95%, while AI teams have been able to reach 60-76%."
- "there is still significant work to be done" regarding web-of-trust Sybil-resistance under multiple attack vectors.

- "there does not yet exist a verifiable mechanism within the protocol to confirm whether this perception of Sybil-resistance ... is true" (Equality Protocol).
- "democratic governance is possible even with bounded Sybil penetration."

## [SIRIVIANOS-IPTPS-07] Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit
**Citation:** Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Rex Chen, Xiaowei Yang. "Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit." Proc. 6th International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Systems (IPTPS), 2007.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://users.cs.duke.edu/~xwy/publications/largeview-iptps.pdf
**Source URL:** https://users.cs.duke.edu/~xwy/publications/largeview-iptps.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
The large view exploit lets a BitTorrent client achieve a high download rate while uploading no data, by obtaining a swarm view (the tracker's list of active peers for a torrent) far larger than the roughly 50-peer view a compliant client requests and connecting to every peer in that larger view. Connecting to more peers than the protocol specifies raises the probability of being one of the peers a remote leecher optimistically unchokes (BitTorrent's periodic, unconditional grant of upload bandwidth to one connected peer regardless of reciprocation, intended to let newly joined peers with nothing to share begin downloading) and raises the chance of discovering seeders (peers holding the complete file, who upload to requesters in round robin regardless of reciprocation). The authors built this exploit by modifying an existing BitTorrent client (Enhanced CTorrent) rather than writing one from scratch, changing only three behaviors: it never uploads any file chunk to any peer; it re-contacts the tracker every 15 seconds, mimicking a client that keeps rejoining the swarm, to keep requesting fresh partial swarm views; and it connects to every peer named in every view it receives, accumulating a view much larger than the tracker's per-request limit. A fourth, separately tested variant additionally disconnects from a leecher immediately after that leecher has unchoked it, uploaded data, and choked it again, then reconnects to the same leecher under a fresh connection, erasing that leecher's record of past reciprocation with this client (the authors term this whitewashing). The paper proposes, but does not implement or measure, a countermeasure: synchronize all clients and the tracker to a shared time interval T, give every newly joined client the complete swarm membership as of the end of the prior interval, and have each client use a pseudorandom function seeded by its own IP address and the current interval to compute which N peers it is entitled to connect to; a peer receiving a connection request recomputes this function for the requester's claimed IP and refuses the connection if the requester's IP does not appear among its own valid N targets, with N set larger than the standard 50-peer view specifically so that multiple compliant clients behind one NAT (Network Address Translator, a device that lets several devices share one public IP address) can still be assigned disjoint peer sets.

### Measured results
| Setting | Result |
|---|---|
| PlanetLab-hosted private swarm, one initial seeder, approximately 300 leechers (mix of compliant Enhanced CTorrent clients and large-view free-riders) on distinct PlanetLab nodes, 12 MB file, every client (compliant and free-rider) rate-limited to 30 KB/s upload and download, 8-10 completion-time measurements collected per PlanetLab node, no whitewashing, free-riders reaching an average view of approximately 250 clients after approximately 150 seconds | 10% free-riders: mean completion time 823 s (free-rider) vs 872 s (compliant); free-riders faster. 40% free-riders: 1299 s (free-rider) vs 1290 s (compliant); nearly equal, with compliant clients showing higher variance. 60% free-riders: 1720 s (free-rider) vs 1581 s (compliant); compliant clients faster. A baseline swarm with no free-riders under the same setup had mean completion time 741 s, below all three mixed-population cases. |
| Same PlanetLab setup, approximately 300 leechers, 12 MB file, 30 KB/s rate limit, 10% free-riders, this time performing whitewashing (disconnect/reconnect to leechers after being unchoked) | Mean completion time 852 s (free-rider) vs 903 s (compliant); free-rider still faster than compliant, but both slower than the corresponding non-whitewashing 10% case (823 s / 872 s above). At a separately noted 1% free-rider fraction (figure not plotted), large-view-only free-riders reached 644 s mean completion versus 680 s for free-riders that additionally whitewashed, so whitewashing degraded the free-rider's own performance at that population level too. |
| 15 public BitTorrent torrents (drawn from torrentportal.com, file sizes approximately 500 MB-2 GB, swarm sizes roughly 50-650 peers, average seeder counts ranging 8.48-242.18 and average leecher counts ranging 41.21-492.01 per torrent per Table I), one compliant and one free-riding CTorrent client per torrent on separate machines in the same LAN, joining simultaneously, not rate-limited, one run per torrent | The free-riding client completed faster than the compliant client in 12 of 15 torrents. In the 3 torrents where it did not win (torrents 2, 3, 13), those had among the smallest average seeder counts (9.88, 14.19, 8.48) and comparatively small swarms, which the authors attribute to the larger view providing little benefit when the tracker's standard 50-peer response already covers most of a small swarm. Torrent 7 had a small overall swarm (51.89 average leechers) but a comparatively high seeder count (30.83 average, with the authors noting approximately 31 seeders total discoverable), and the free-rider won there specifically because its larger view let it discover nearly all available seeders. |

### Parameters
- Rate limit applied to all PlanetLab clients (compliant and free-rider), both directions: 30 KB/s, chosen to give all clients equal resources.
- File size for PlanetLab experiments: 12 MB, shared across all PlanetLab trials (Figures 1 and 3).
- Free-rider tracker re-announce interval: every 15 seconds.
- Free-rider average acquired swarm view: approximately 250 clients, reached after approximately 150 seconds into the download, against a compliant client's standard limit of connecting to at most 50 peers.
- Measurements per PlanetLab node: 8 to 10, varying with node availability.
- Countermeasure design parameters T (interval duration), a (post-interval connection delay, stated only as "much less than T"), and N (per-client allowed peer-connection count, stated only as "greater than 50"): none given numeric values; the paper states determining good values for T, a, and N empirically is future work.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the proposed countermeasure (synchronized interval-based pseudorandom peer assignment) is unimplemented and unmeasured: assessing its added load on the tracker, and empirically determining working values for its T, a, and N parameters, are both named explicitly as future work. The authors state their technique for identifying a peer by IP address is undermined by clients sharing one IP behind a NAT, and their proposed fix (setting N above the standard 50-peer view so NAT-sharing compliant clients can still receive disjoint peer assignments) is a design sketch, not a validated solution with a chosen N. The paper explicitly separates its own single-run, unaveraged public-torrent measurements (one run per torrent, 15 torrents) from its averaged PlanetLab measurements (8-10 runs per node), so its 12-of-15 public-torrent win count for the free-rider does not carry the same statistical confidence as the PlanetLab means. The authors state they observed no correlation between file size and the exploit's effectiveness, without further quantifying that null finding. The authors state whitewashing (disconnect/reconnect to erase reciprocation history) reduces overall swarm throughput and degrades even the whitewashing free-rider's own completion time relative to a free-rider that does not whitewash, concluding a rational free-rider has no incentive to whitewash, a conclusion the authors state follows directly from their own measured 1% and 10% comparisons above.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The exploit as measured requires only the standard tracker announce protocol and the standard practice, which the authors note is already implemented in mainstream compliant clients for tracker-failure resilience, of accepting and merging additional peer lists from other peers, so no protocol change or credential is required to mount it. The authors' proposed countermeasure requires every client and the tracker to share a synchronized time reference (interval boundaries of duration T) and requires the tracker to actively push membership-change updates (joins and departures) to all currently connected clients at each interval boundary, which the paper states may be assessed for tracker load but is not measured in this paper. The countermeasure requires clients to authenticate connection requests by IP address as the sole identifier, so it provides no defense, and the paper does not claim one, against a client that can present multiple distinct IP addresses. The countermeasure's disjoint-peer-set guarantee for NAT-sharing compliant clients depends on the tracker choosing N larger than the standard 50-peer view; the paper does not state a lower bound relating N to the number of clients expected behind a single NAT.

### Contradicts
None found in this paper's own claims. Cross-reference within this batch: LOCHER-HOTNETS-06 (BitThief) and this paper both report free-riding constructions against BitTorrent's tit-for-tat mechanism using materially different swarm compositions and metrics (BitThief reports relative download-time multiples against a reference client across 7 named public torrents and one controlled testbed; this paper reports absolute mean completion times across a controlled PlanetLab population sweep and a 15-torrent public sample with a win-count metric), so the two papers' numbers are not directly comparable as a single figure, though both independently conclude that a client that uploads nothing can match or beat a tit-for-tat-compliant client under common conditions. This paper explicitly distinguishes its own free-rider definition (zero upload) from Jun and Ahamad's cited PlanetLab study (approximately 150 leechers, 75 free-riders capped at 4 KB/s upload against a 100 KB/s cap for others, so a "free-rider" there still uploads at reduced rate), so a synthesis must not merge the two papers' free-rider population figures as measuring the same condition.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohen, "Incentives build robustness in BitTorrent," P2PEcon 2003 -- foundational (the original description of BitTorrent's tit-for-tat mechanism this exploit targets).
- Axelrod, "The Evolution of Cooperation," Basic Books, 1984 -- foundational (the iterated-prisoner's-dilemma game-theoretic framework the paper uses to explain why tit-for-tat is exploitable when the game has a finite, client-controlled number of rounds).
- Jun, Ahamad, "Incentives in BitTorrent induce free riding," P2PEcon 2005 -- competing (an independent PlanetLab measurement of BitTorrent free-riding under a weaker, reduced-upload-rate definition of free-rider, explicitly contrasted against this paper's zero-upload definition).
- Liogkas, R., Kohler, Zhang, "Exploiting BitTorrent for fun (but not profit)," IPTPS 2006 -- competing/foundational (shows peers that connect only to discovered seeders can raise download rate without contributing bandwidth; cited as related prior evidence for this paper's design rationale).
- Locher, Moor, Schmid, Wattenhofer, "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap," HotNets 2006 -- competing (the near-concurrent BitThief paper, retrieved in this same batch as LOCHER-HOTNETS-06; this paper explicitly enumerates four ways its own experiments differ from and complement BitThief's).
- Piatek, Isdal, Anderson, Krishnamurthy, Venkataramani, "Do incentives build robustness in BitTorrent?," NSDI 2006 -- competing (shows careful peer and per-peer-upload-rate selection can raise download rate while substantially cutting uplink use, a related but distinct exploit from the large-view technique).
- Andrade, Mowbray, Lima, Wagner, Ripeanu, "Influences on cooperation in BitTorrent communities," P2PEcon 2005 -- competing (shows free-riders can attain better sharing ratios than compliant peers in seeder-heavy swarms).
- Shneidman, Parkes, Massoulie, "Faithfulness in internet algorithms," PINS 2004 -- attack (conjectures a Sybil-based optimistic-unchoke-frequency attack via multiple presented identities, explicitly distinguished by this paper from the large-view exploit, which requires no multiple identities).
- Douceur, "The Sybil Attack," IPTPS 2002 -- foundational (cited for the multiple-identity attack the paper explicitly notes its own exploit does not require).
- Li, Clement, Wong, Napper, Roy, Alvisi, Dahlin, "BAR Gossip," OSDI 2006 -- foundational (source of the verifiable pseudorandom peer-selection technique this paper's proposed countermeasure adapts, originally assuming certifiable per-client key pairs and a leave-only churn model this paper explicitly relaxes).
- Feldman, Papadimitriou, Chuang, Stoica, "Free-riding and whitewashing in peer-to-peer systems," IEEE JSAC 2006 -- foundational (source of the term "whitewashing" this paper adopts for its disconnect-and-reconnect technique).

## [SIRIVIANOS-USENIXATC-07] Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives
**Citation:** Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Xiaowei Yang, Stanislaw Jarecki. "Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives." USENIX Annual Technical Conference, 2007. Pages 157-170.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix07/tech/full_papers/sirivianos/sirivianos.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix07/tech/full_papers/sirivianos/sirivianos.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
Dandelion incentivizes peer-to-peer clients to upload content to each other by withholding the decryption key for a content chunk from a downloading client until that client's upload activity has been credited by a central server, so that a client gains no benefit from downloading without also uploading, regardless of whether its peers hold content it wants in return. A file is split into fixed-size chunks; each chunk is distributed encrypted, and a client must obtain the corresponding decryption key from the server to use it. The server maintains a per-client credit balance: a downloading client B spends delta_c credit units to acquire a chunk from an uploading client A, and A earns delta_r credit units for correctly serving that chunk, with delta_c set equal to delta_r so two colluding clients cannot inflate their combined credit by falsely claiming to have exchanged chunks with each other. The protocol runs as a three-party fair exchange for every chunk transaction: client A encrypts the chunk fresh for each request and sends it to client B along with a signed ticket; B, upon receiving the encrypted chunk, immediately requests the decryption key from the server rather than waiting to verify the chunk's integrity itself; the server authenticates the request (HMAC), verifies the ticket (HMAC), decrypts the server-held copy of the decryption key (symmetric encryption), updates both clients' credit, signs the decryption key response, and returns it. Because the server is a mandatory party to every single-chunk exchange, and because the server can check a client's credit balance before releasing a decryption key, the paper proves (Lemmas 4.1-4.4 in the paper, proofs deferred to a companion technical report [51]) that a selfish client cannot claim credit for chunks it never delivered, cannot claim credit for corrupted chunks it delivered, cannot impersonate another client's ID, and cannot replay old signed messages to fraudulently charge or blacklist another client. If a client cannot retrieve a chunk from peers in time, it falls back to requesting the plaintext chunk directly from the server for a higher, delta_s > delta_c credit charge, or receives an error if the server is overloaded, so the pipeline degrades gracefully rather than stalling.

### Measured results

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| Per-chunk server cryptographic operation timings, dual Pentium D 2.8 GHz / 1 MB CPU, 1 GB RAM, 250 GB/7200 RPM HDD, Linux 2.6.5, getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) over 10,000 executions, HMAC-SHA1 (128-bit key) for auth/ticket/signing, 8-byte-block Blowfish-CBC (128-bit key, 128-bit IV) for chunk/key encryption, SHA-1 for chunk hashing | Authenticate decryption key request (98 bytes): 0.018 ms; generate ticket (78 bytes): 0.018 ms; encrypt/decrypt decryption key (32 bytes): 0.056 ms; sign decryption key response (46 bytes): 0.017 ms — total CPU-centric cost for operations 1-4: 109 microseconds. Encrypt/decrypt a 128 KB chunk: 0.715 ms; hash a 128 KB encrypted chunk: 0.487 ms |
| Credit-file operations, gettimeofday() over 10,000 executions, 10,000-entry file with 44-byte entries | Query credit file: ~0.004 ms; update without forcing disk commit: ~0.02 ms; update with fsync() disk commit (HDD caching disabled): ~9.25 ms; update with disk commit every 100 updates (amortized): ~0.27 ms |
| Server-side decryption-key-request throughput, ~200 clients on distinct PlanetLab hosts, server rate-limited at the application layer to 1-5 Mb/s, per-client request rate swept 1-14 req/sec, 10-minute runs averaged over 10 repetitions | At 1-3 Mb/s, throughput scales with bandwidth (bandwidth-bound); at 4-5 Mb/s, throughput plateaus at approximately 1,200 decryption-key responses per second (CPU-bound, server CPU utilization approaches ~100%); with 128 KB chunks, this supports approximately 1,200 simultaneous clients each downloading at 128 KB/s from each other; memory utilization stays low throughout |
| Chunk-size sensitivity, ~40 leechers, one initial seeder, PlanetLab, file sizes 10/100/250 MB, chunk sizes 64/128/256/512/1024/2048 KB | For a 10 MB file, 64 KB chunks give the best mean download completion time, with performance degrading as chunk size grows; for a 250 MB file, 128 KB chunks outperform 64 KB chunks; the paper adopts 128 KB chunks for the rest of its evaluation based on this tradeoff |
| Seeder-probability impact, ~200 leechers, one initial seeder, PlanetLab, seed-after-completion probability a in {25%, 100%}, file sizes from 0.5 to 250 MB, 10 repetitions per configuration, 95% confidence intervals reported | For a 250 MB file, mean swarm-wide download completion time was 674 seconds at a=100% versus 837 seconds at a=25%; the relative benefit of full seeding shrinks as file size grows, because larger files keep leechers online (and thus contributing uplink) longer regardless of a |
| Comparison against BitTorrent, ~200 CTorrent 1.3.4 tit-for-tat-compliant leechers with all leechers remaining online after completion (a=100%), same PlanetLab conditions and file-size sweep | Dandelion (a=100%) achieves download completion times comparable to, and for some file sizes better than, BitTorrent; the paper states it does not claim general superiority, since both protocols' performance depends on numerous unexplored parameters |
| Credit distribution, single 250 MB file, ~200 leechers, one initial seeder, all clients start with 100% of the credit needed and all become seeders on completion | Product-moment correlation coefficient between a client's average download rate and its final credit ratio: 0.72 (the fastest downloaders/uploaders accumulate the most credit); 25.8% of clients ended with less than 70% of their initial credit, i.e. they uploaded substantially less than they downloaded |
| Prior free-riding measurement cited from the authors' own earlier work [50] | A modified "large view" free-riding CTorrent client downloaded faster than a tit-for-tat-compliant client in 12 of 15 randomly selected public torrents, file sizes 500 MB-2 GB, swarm sizes 50-1,000 peers; in a PlanetLab swarm of ~300 leechers rate-limited to 30 KB/sec plus one seeder at 120 KB/sec, when compliant clients made up 90% of the swarm, free-riders downloaded faster than compliant clients in the same (mixed) swarm and only slightly worse than compliant clients in a swarm with no free-riders |

### Parameters
- Credit unit values: delta_c (cost to download a chunk) set equal to delta_r (reward for uploading a chunk), specifically to prevent two colluding clients from inflating their combined credit through mutual false claims.
- Server fallback charge for direct plaintext-chunk delivery when the server is moderately busy: delta_s, set greater than delta_c to discourage clients from preferring the server over peers.
- Chunk size: swept at 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 KB; 128 KB adopted for the main evaluation.
- Cryptography: HMAC-SHA1 with 128-bit keys for authentication, ticket verification, and response signing; 8-byte-block Blowfish-CBC with 128-bit key and 128-bit IV for chunk and key encryption; SHA-1 for chunk hashing.
- Test hardware for profiling: dual Pentium D 2.8 GHz/1 MB CPU, 1 GB RAM, 250 GB/7200 RPM HDD, Linux 2.6.5-1.358smp.
- Test hardware for the system-performance (Section 6.3) experiments: Xeon 3 GHz/2 MB CPU, 2 GB RAM PlanetLab VServer, server rate-limited to 2 Mb/s; TCP sender/receiver buffer size set to 120 KB to cover PlanetLab's bandwidth-delay product.
- Deployment scale evaluated: up to ~200-300 PlanetLab-hosted clients (leechers) per experiment; the profiling-based projection (not a direct load test at this scale) states a server on the tested commodity hardware with a 4-5 Mb/s access link can support "a few thousand clients."

### Stated limitations
The paper states its threat model explicitly excludes bandwidth or connection-flooding denial-of-service attacks ("we consider bandwidth or connection flooding attacks outside the scope of this work"); the non-manipulability proofs cover only protocol-message-level attacks. Observation 4.8 states a malicious client can always abandon a protocol run partway through, denying the counterparty resources already spent, and the paper's only mitigation is that this costs the attacker resources roughly proportional to the victim's, calling the attack "not particularly practical" rather than prevented; a further, partial mitigation (short-lived tickets issued only to accounts in good standing, and an option for the server to charge for ticket issuance) is described as deterrence, not elimination. The security proofs for Lemmas 4.1-4.4 are stated but not proved in this paper; the paper states the proofs are deferred to the Appendix of a companion technical report. The paper explicitly declines to claim general superiority over BitTorrent, stating performance of both protocols depends on unexplored parameters. The design assumes "weak security of the IP network": clients can eavesdrop but the paper assumes they cannot corrupt or interfere with routing/forwarding at the network layer, and separately assumes communication errors may occur during message transmission; a network model departing from this (active tampering with routing, not just message content) is outside what the paper's guarantees cover. The 1,200-clients-per-server figure and the "few thousand clients" scalability projection are extrapolated from a 200-client PlanetLab throughput measurement and single-machine CPU/bandwidth profiling, not from a load test actually run at thousands of concurrent clients; the paper's own Section 6.1 states the per-operation profiling "does not consider the parallel processing of I/O and CPU operations" and "does not include the cost of system calls and the cost of TCP/IP stack processing," and explicitly states "we refrain from deriving conclusions on the throughput of the server" from that profiling data alone. The scheme's non-manipulability rests on centralizing every single-chunk exchange through one server that checks credit balances synchronously; the paper's own Section 5.1 states this server, though logically separable from the credit base, is combined into a single machine in the actual prototype, and single-server involvement in every chunk exchange is the design choice the paper explicitly trades for scalability ("we trade scalability for the ability to provide robust incentives").

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The provable non-manipulability property depends on each client holding one authenticated, paid account with the content provider; the paper states explicitly that "a user cannot boost its credit by presenting multiple IDs (Sybil attack) and claiming to have uploaded to some of its registered IDs" precisely because "each user maintains an authenticated paid account with the provider" and "essentially purchases its initial credit." This means the fair-exchange proof depends on a centralized, identity-verifying, paid-registration process external to the peer-to-peer protocol itself; the paper does not analyze or claim the proof holds for clients that can obtain fresh, unauthenticated identities at low or zero cost. The mechanism requires a single server (or a server cluster acting with a shared, consistent credit ledger) to be reachable and responsive for every chunk exchange between any two clients, since decryption keys are withheld until the server processes and settles a credit transaction for that specific chunk; a design in which client pairs can complete a chunk exchange without contacting a shared arbiter is incompatible with this proof structure. It requires clients to encrypt each served chunk freshly per request (stated in Lemma 4.2's precondition) rather than caching one encrypted copy, so that credit crediting and content delivery stay bound to the exact request being served. It requires the server to issue short-lived, per-transaction tickets to prevent abandoned-protocol-run denial-of-service attacks from unauthorized or blacklisted clients, meaning ticket-issuance state (validity windows, per-account status) must be tracked centrally alongside the credit ledger. The design assumes the content provider can price accumulated virtual credit such that "the benefit that a selfish client gains from acquiring virtual currency for content it uploads exceeds the cost of utilizing its uplink to upload it" — an external pricing decision the protocol itself does not make or verify, and without which the stated incentive-compatibility (Nash equilibrium of cooperation) argument does not follow.

### Contradicts
None found. No other paper in this batch reports a conflicting measurement of the same quantity.

### References worth retrieving
- Cohen, B., "Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent." P2P Econ, 2003. — foundational (defines BitTorrent's rate-based tit-for-tat incentive mechanism that this paper's incentive design is built to improve on)
- Douceur, J. R., "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS, 2002. — foundational (defines the Sybil attack the paper's centralized-paid-account requirement is stated to prevent)
- Locher, T., Moor, P., Schmid, S., Wattenhofer, R., "Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap." — competing (near-concurrent independent experimental demonstration of the same BitTorrent free-riding weakness this paper's own prior work also measured)
- Liogkas, N., Nelson, R., Kohler, E., Zhang, L., "Exploiting BitTorrent For Fun (But Not Profit)." — attack (prior BitTorrent-exploitation work the paper's own "large view" free-riding client builds on)
- Jun, S., Ahamad, M., "Incentives in BitTorrent Induce Free Riding." — attack/critique (prior critique of BitTorrent's tit-for-tat incentive scheme cited among the sources motivating this paper's design)
- Li, J., Kang, X., "Proof of Service in a Hybrid P2P Environment." ISPA. — competing (a proof-of-service fair-exchange scheme the paper directly contrasts its own design against, noting the prior scheme did not provide an experimental evaluation and is vulnerable to selfish clients obtaining content from other selfish peers without sufficient credit)
- Vishnumurthy, V., Chandrakumar, S., Sirer, E. G., "KARMA: A Secure Economy for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing." — competing (a distributed, non-centralized virtual-currency incentive scheme, part of the design space this paper's centralized-server approach is positioned against)
- Yang, B., Garcia-Molina, H., "PPay: Micropayments for Peer-to-peer Systems." — competing (a peer-to-peer micropayment scheme relevant to the paper's virtual-currency incentive design)

## [SIT-IPTPS-02] Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables

**Citation:** Emil Sit, Robert Morris. "Security Considerations for Peer-to-Peer Distributed Hash Tables." IPTPS, 2002. DOI 10.1007/3-540-45748-8_25.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:security02/chord:security02.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title/authors/abstract)
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:security02/chord:security02.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
The paper classifies liveness attacks against distributed hash table (DHT) lookup systems — attacks that prevent participants from finding data, as distinct from data-authenticity attacks, which the authors state are already addressed by cryptographic techniques such as self-certifying path names. It defines the adversary model, enumerates attack classes against routing and against storage, and derives six design principles from the defenses discussed for each class. The paper contains no implementation and no experiment; it is an analytical taxonomy applied to three published DHT designs, Chord, Pastry, and CAN (content-addressable network).

The adversary model: a malicious node can generate packets with arbitrary content, including forged source IP addresses, but can only receive packets addressed to its own IP address. This lets a node use IP address as a weak identity check: a node receiving a packet from address X can confirm the sender controls X by sending a confirmation request to X. Malicious nodes may conspire, each individually bound by this same constraint. Malicious nodes cannot overhear or modify traffic between other nodes.

The six design principles the paper derives: (1) define verifiable system invariants and verify them; (2) let the querier observe lookup progress hop by hop, so it can detect a lookup that fails to converge toward the target key; (3) assign node identifiers to nodes in a verifiable way, for example by deriving the identifier from a cryptographic hash of the node's IP address and port, so another node can check a claimed identifier against the claimant's network address; (4) treat routing-table entries chosen by a latency- or performance-based server-selection rule as attacker-influenceable, since an adversary can offer itself as the lowest-latency or best-ratio option and thereby bias which nodes get chosen; (5) cross-check a node's own routing table by issuing random queries through previously-trusted nodes and comparing results, to detect that a node has been diverted into a parallel, internally-consistent malicious network (a partition attack); (6) avoid single points of responsibility in the storage layer — replication must be organized so that no single node governs whether a client obtains a replica, and clients must independently determine the correct replica set rather than asking one node for it.

Attack-specific mechanisms discussed: incorrect lookup forwarding (a node forwards a query to a wrong or non-existent node) is detected when the querier can verify that each hop's identifier distance to the key strictly decreases, which requires an iterative-lookup design where each hop reports back to the querier — this check is stated to be impossible under CAN's proposed recursive-forwarding round-trip-time (RTT) optimization, where a node forwards to whichever neighbor has the best progress-to-RTT ratio without involving the querier. Incorrect routing-table updates (a node injects false entries into another node's routing table) are mitigated by requiring each update to satisfy a checkable structural rule (Pastry requires each table entry to share the correct address-prefix length) and by requiring reachability verification before an update is incorporated. Partition attacks (an adversary builds a self-consistent parallel network and diverts a joining or rejoining node into it) are mitigated by bootstrapping new nodes only from an out-of-band trusted source, and by an already-joined node periodically cross-checking against previously-used nodes with random queries. Storage-denial (a node claims not to hold data it is responsible for, or claims to hold data but refuses to serve it) is mitigated only by replication combined with the single-point-of-responsibility principle: querying clients must consult at least two independent replica sites before concluding data is truly missing, because consulting only the node structurally responsible for replication (as DHash does) leaves the client unable to distinguish "data missing" from "the one node that controls replica lookup is lying." Inconsistent behavior (a node behaves correctly toward nearby-in-identifier-space nodes and incorrectly toward distant ones) is stated to be undetectable by distant nodes reporting the bad behavior to near ones unless responses are signed, because an unsigned complaint cannot be distinguished from a false complaint meant to discredit a benign node. Node overload (packet flooding against a targeted node or its replicas) is mitigated by assigning node identifiers independently of network topology and by physically dispersing replicas, so a topologically localized attack cannot take out an entire portion of the key space. Unsolicited/forged responses (a node that referred a querier to a next hop forges a reply purporting to come from that next hop) are mitigated with a per-query random nonce that the genuine respondent must echo back.

### Measured results
None. This is an analytical/taxonomic paper; it contains no experiment, no simulation, and no reported numeric result of any kind. No figure in this paper may be cited as measured evidence.

### Parameters
None stated. The paper introduces no tunable parameter of its own; it discusses design choices made by the systems it analyzes (Chord's successor-list replication, Pastry's prefix-verification rule, CAN's RTT-ratio neighbor selection) without stating specific numeric configurations for any of them.

### Stated limitations
The paper explicitly scopes itself to liveness attacks only, stating that data-correctness and data-authenticity attacks are considered already addressed by existing cryptographic techniques (citing self-certifying path names) and are out of scope. The adversary model explicitly excludes a node's ability to overhear or modify traffic between two other nodes; an adversary with that capability is not analyzed. The paper states that trust metrics built on IP address are dangerous in a network with high churn and weak identity, because a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)-assigned address can belong to a malicious node one day and a benign node the next. For the inconsistent-behavior attack, the paper states plainly that without public-key signatures on responses, "each node must make its own determination as to whether another node is malicious," i.e., no cross-node verification mechanism is offered. For the verifiable-node-identifier defense, the paper states that deriving a node's identifier from a hash of its IP address, port, and virtual-node number (as Chord does) still leaves a single physical host able to run many virtual nodes and thereby exercise some choice over which keys it becomes responsible for, so Chord's approach only partially closes the attack DHash remains exposed to. The rapid-join/-leave rebalancing attack is stated to be unavoidable in general: any DHT, with or without adversaries, must already handle rebalancing triggered by ordinary churn, so the paper offers no defense beyond noting that the adversary's model here (no ability to fake liveness of a node cheaply, and rebalancing requiring acknowledged data transfer) limits how cheaply an adversary can trigger excess rebalancing.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
For principle 2 (observable lookup progress) to be enforceable, the lookup protocol must be iterative (each hop reports the next hop back to the querier) rather than fully recursive/relayed, because the paper states this check is impossible under CAN's proposed RTT-optimized recursive forwarding. For principle 3 (verifiable node identifiers) to be enforceable, the identifier-derivation function must bind the identifier to something the querier can independently check against the network, such as the claimant's IP address and port; a system letting a node choose its own identifier arbitrarily (as the paper states CAN allows) cannot support this check. For principle 5 (cross-checking via random queries) to work, a node must maintain a set of other nodes it has successfully used in the past, obtained through an out-of-band trusted bootstrap the first time, and query randomness must be preserved so a malicious partition cannot distinguish a verification probe from a real query it wants to intercept. For the storage/replication defenses (principle 6) to work, the system must let a client independently compute or discover the full replica set for a key rather than obtaining it through one designated node, and must support the client querying at least two replica sites per lookup. For the inconsistent-behavior and unsolicited-response defenses, the system needs either digital signatures on all node responses (to let a third party verify a complaint about a node, and to let a querier verify a reply's claimed origin) or, absent that, a per-query random nonce that a legitimate respondent echoes back, which defends only against response forgery, not against a node lying about its own state.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this batch (W1-5). This paper predates and is foundational to later disjoint-path and puzzle-based Sybil-resistance work (e.g., S/Kademlia, already in the corpus per BRIEF.md section 7); it does not itself measure a lookup-success rate under attack, so it cannot be checked against S/Kademlia's 99%-success figure for disagreement — the two papers operate at different levels: this one is a taxonomy, S/Kademlia is a measured defense.

- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area Cooperative Storage with CFS," SOSP 2001 — foundational (DHash storage layer analyzed throughout Section 4).
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, "A Scalable Content-Addressable Network," SIGCOMM 2001 — foundational/competing structured overlay (CAN, analyzed as a specific case throughout).
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, Distributed Object Location and Routing for Large-scale Peer-to-peer Systems," Middleware 2001 — foundational/competing structured overlay (Pastry, analyzed as a specific case).
- Stoica, Morris, Karger, Kaashoek, Balakrishnan, "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications," SIGCOMM 2001 — foundational/competing structured overlay (Chord, analyzed as a specific case).
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Storage Management and Caching in PAST, a Large-scale, Persistent Peer-to-peer Storage Utility," SOSP 2001 — foundational storage-layer design cited alongside DHash.
- Fu, Kaashoek, Mazières, "Fast and Secure Distributed Read-only File System," OSDI 2000 — foundational (source of the self-certifying-pathname technique the paper cites as solving the data-authenticity problem it excludes from scope).
- Freedman, Sit, Cates, Morris, "Tarzan: A Peer-to-peer Anonymizing Network Layer," IPTPS 2002 — application example cited for the server-selection-abuse attack (Tarzan uses Chord to pick random relay nodes).
- Rowstron, Kermarrec, Castro, Druschel, "SCRIBE: The Design of a Large-scale Event Notification Infrastructure," Networked Group Communication Workshop 2001 — foundational application built on a structured overlay, cited as a DHT-based system.

- Krishnamurthy, Wang, Xie, "Early Measurements of a Cluster-based Architecture for P2P Systems," SIGCOMM Internet Measurement Workshop 2001 — cited as evidence that peer-to-peer file-sharing populations churn rapidly; independent measurement.
