## [STEINER-CCR-07] Exploiting KAD: Possible Uses and Misuses

**Citation:** Moritz Steiner, Taoufik En-Najjary, Ernst W. Biersack. "Exploiting KAD: Possible Uses and Misuses." ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, 2007. DOI 10.1145/1290168.1290176.
**Retrieved:** full text via http://www.moritzsteiner.de/papers/ExploitingKAD.pdf
**Source URL:** http://www.moritzsteiner.de/papers/ExploitingKAD.pdf
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
The paper states and measures three attacks executed against the live, deployed KAD network — the Kademlia-based distributed hash table (DHT) protocol used by eMule, aMule, and formerly Overnet, with several million simultaneous users at the time of writing — each built from the same underlying Sybil attack (introducing many peer identities controlled by one entity, following Douceur's original definition of the Sybil attack as "the forging of multiple identities").

KAD identifies each node by a 128-bit Kad ID and routes by prefix matching: node A forwards a query for node B to whichever routing-table entry has the smallest bitwise exclusive-or (XOR) distance to B, iteratively, with three parallel routing lookups per query for churn robustness. A key is published redundantly on ten peers whose Kad ID agrees with the key in its first 8 bits (the "tolerance zone"), republished every 5 or 24 hours depending on content type; a search launches three parallel routing lookups toward the key.

Spying attack (Section 3.1): the authors' "spy" tool creates thousands of stateless Sybil identities on a single physical machine, crawls a target 8-bit zone of the Kad ID space to discover currently active peers, sends "hello" messages to those peers so the peers insert the Sybil identities into their own routing-table buckets ("poisoning" the tables), then answers subsequent route requests destined for that zone with further Sybil identities so the requester's routing lookup is steered entirely through Sybils; the follow-up publish or search request from the victim then also lands on a Sybil, and its content is logged.

Eclipsing attack (Section 3.2): to make a specific keyword K unfindable by anyone using KAD's search algorithm (though the underlying content remains stored, unreachable, on the original regular peers), the authors position a small number of Sybil identities with Kad IDs closer to K's hash than any real peer's, then poison regular peers' routing tables the same way as the spying attack, so every search request for K terminates on a Sybil, which simply drops it instead of answering.

DDOS-enlistment attack (Section 3.3): identical Sybil placement to the eclipse attack, except each Sybil, instead of dropping the intercepted search request, replies with the IP address of a third-party "target" host, causing the querying peer to contact that target — enlisting ordinary KAD peers as an amplification/reflection mechanism against a machine they were never trying to reach.

### Measured results

| Attack | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Full-network crawl speed | Authors' own breadth-first crawler, issuing route requests, run over "the last 18 months" of study | Full Kad-ID-space crawl completed in about 8 minutes; found between 3 and 4.3 million distinct peers per full crawl, of which 1.5 to 2 million were directly reachable (not behind NAT/firewall) |
| Zone crawl speed | 8-bit zone (1/256th of the full Kad ID space) | Under 2.5 seconds per zone crawl; the same zone was crawled every 5 minutes for slightly less than 6 months |
| Spying attack, traffic volume | Spy tool running 2^16 (65,536) Sybil identities in one 8-bit zone, on a single physical machine, for one day | Observed 1.4 million distinct files published, 42,000 distinct keyword hashes, 1.5 million distinct users; approximately 1,000 search requests, 10,000 publish requests, and 25,000 route requests per minute reaching the Sybils; approximately 400 KB/sec incoming and 200 KB/sec outgoing traffic load on the spying machine |
| Publish vs. search traffic ratio | Same spying-attack measurement | Publish traffic exceeds search traffic by one order of magnitude in message count and two orders of magnitude in total bytes transmitted |
| Eclipsing attack, minimum Sybil count | Live KAD network | As few as 8 Sybil identities positioned around a keyword's hash were sufficient to make all search requests for that keyword terminate on a Sybil |
| Eclipsing attack, resource cost by keyword popularity | 32 Sybils running on one physical machine, eclipsing two specific keywords, "the" (popular) and "dreirad" (German for "tricycle," less popular) | For "the": 41,801 route messages/min, 1,091 hello messages/min, 12,360 publish messages/min, 704 search messages/min, 186 KB/sec total incoming bandwidth. For "dreirad": 818 route messages/min, 433 hello messages/min, 290 publish messages/min, 49 search messages/min, 32 KB/sec total incoming bandwidth |
| DDOS-enlistment attack | Attack directed by the authors against their own machines, using KAD peers redirected by Sybils | Incoming traffic on the order of several Mbit/sec observed on the targeted machines; no fixed Sybil count or duration stated for this specific run |
| Independently reported real-world DDOS scale | Cited third-party report (Prolexic, May 2007), not measured by the authors | More than 300,000 peers observed participating in a peer-to-peer-based DDOS attack in the wild |

### Parameters
- Kad ID length: 128 bits.
- Publish redundancy: 10 peers per key, selected by 8-bit prefix agreement with the key (the "tolerance zone"), not by strict numeric closeness.
- Republish interval: 5 or 24 hours, depending on content type.
- Parallel routing lookups per query: 3 (both publish and search use this).
- Spying-attack zone size used in the reported measurement: 8-bit zone (yielding 2^16 = 65,536 Sybil identities placed).
- Eclipsing-attack Sybil count: as low as 8 sufficient in principle; 32 used in the reported resource-consumption measurement (Table 1).
- Crawl frequency for the 6-month zone study: every 5 minutes.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its proposed defense — a centralized agent binding each Kad ID to a cell-phone number via SMS verification, or alternatively a CAPTCHA-based Reverse Turing Test — cannot prevent a peer from giving away or having stolen a validly obtained Kad ID, and requires re-issuing a new Kad ID whenever the peer's IP address changes, since IP address is bound into the encrypted ID. It states the scheme cannot prevent a well-resourced attacker from obtaining multiple valid Kad IDs by controlling multiple phone numbers or solving multiple CAPTCHAs, and states plainly that it will never be possible to prevent an attacker with sufficient resources from obtaining multiple Kad IDs. It states that, given KAD's scale (several million simultaneous peers), a disruptive attack would probably require an attacker to introduce thousands of Sybils, without deriving that count from a model or measurement, so this is a bound of the authors' judgment, not a derived figure. The paper explicitly states the article is an editorial note submitted to Computer Communication Review (CCR) and was not peer-reviewed.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
- The spying and eclipsing attacks both require the ability to have Sybil identities' presence inserted into victim peers' routing tables (via unsolicited "hello" messages accepted by KAD's own protocol); a routing-table admission policy that verifies a peer's identifier through means other than the peer's self-reported claim would remove this precondition.
- The eclipsing attack requires the victim's routing lookup to be steerable entirely through attacker-controlled nodes before it reaches any honest node; a lookup mechanism guaranteeing at least one disjoint, attacker-independent path (the property S/Kademlia's disjoint-path lookup targets, per the already-verified S/Kademlia entry) would change this precondition, though this paper does not measure disjoint-path lookup itself.
- The DDOS-enlistment attack requires ordinary KAD peers to accept and act on a search response's supplied IP address without independently verifying that the responding node is authoritative for the requested content; a verification step at the requesting peer (e.g., confirming the response against a second independent path) would remove the precondition this attack exploits.
- The paper's own proposed centralized-identity defense requires a trusted central agent (CA) to hold the CA's private key securely and to keep a list of (phone number, expiration) and (IP address, expiration) pairs, and requires every participating peer to know the CA's public key to verify Kad ID validity — reintroducing a single point of trust into an otherwise decentralized system, a value tradeoff the paper states but does not resolve.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch against other current entries. This paper's Table 1 and Section 3 findings are themselves a directly measured cost figure that BRIEF.md's registry `why_needed` field frames as a check against Sybil/eclipse cost claims made only in simulation elsewhere (e.g., Pitch Black, already verified per BRIEF.md section 7, which used a simulated/testbed adversary rather than a live-network Sybil deployment); no simulated figure from another entry in this batch directly measures the same live-network cost, so no direct numeric contradiction is recorded.

### References worth retrieving
- Attack/critique: N. Naoumov, K. Ross, "Exploiting p2p systems for ddos attacks," International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Information Management, May 2006 — index-poisoning and routing-poisoning attack taxonomy for the related Overnet system, cited as directly relevant to KAD given their similar routing.
- Competing (Sybil defense): H. Rowaihy, W. Enck, P. McDaniel, T. La Porta, "Limiting sybil attacks in structured p2p networks," IEEE INFOCOM 2007 — hierarchical hash-puzzle admission-control defense, critiqued by this paper as still vulnerable to a resourceful attacker.
- Competing (Sybil defense): H. Yu, M. Kaminsky, P. B. Gibbons, A. Flaxman, "Sybilguard: Defending against sybil attacks via social networks," ACM SIGCOMM 2006 — social-graph-based Sybil defense, critiqued here as requiring a well-connected social network not present in deployed DHT-based p2p systems.
- Competing (eclipse defense): M. Castro, P. Druschel, A. Ganesh, A. Rowstron, D. Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," OSDI 2002 — Constrained Routing Tables defense, critiqued here as preventing proximity neighbor selection because it leaves no flexibility in neighbor choice.
- Attack/critique: A. Singh, M. Castro, P. Druschel, A. Rowstron, "Defending against eclipse attacks on overlay networks," ACM SIGOPS 2004 — the workshop-length predecessor paper; note this is the paper mistakenly retrieved under key SINGH-INFOCOM-06 in this batch (see that key's mismatch record).
- Foundational: A. Singh et al., "Eclipse attacks on overlay networks: Threats and defenses," Proc. INFOCOM 2006 — cited here by exact venue/year, confirming the correct citation for the SINGH-INFOCOM-06 target that this batch's retrieval fetched the wrong document for.
- Foundational: J. R. Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — origin of the Sybil-attack concept this entire paper builds on.
- Foundational (measurement): D. Stutzbach, R. Rejaie, "Improving lookup performance over a widely-deployed DHT," INFOCOM 2006 — cited for KAD implementation detail; a churn/lookup-performance measurement paper on the same live network.

## [STEINER-IMC-07] A Global View of KAD

**Citation:** Moritz Steiner, Taoufik En-Najjary, Ernst W. Biersack. "A Global View of KAD." ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC), 2007. DOI 10.1145/1298306.1298323.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.moritzsteiner.de/papers/KADsteiner.pdf (candidate URL from registry; local file matches title/authors/abstract)
**Source URL:** https://www.moritzsteiner.de/papers/KADsteiner.pdf
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
The paper measures the deployed population and churn behavior of KAD, a Kademlia-derived distributed hash table (DHT) that forms the publishing and search network inside the eDonkey2000 peer-to-peer file-sharing system. The authors build a crawler, Blizzard, that discovers KAD peers by iterative breadth-first queries starting from several hundred known contacts, logging each peer's crawl timestamp, IP address, and KAD ID (KAD's node identifier). Blizzard runs two independent instances, one at the University of Mannheim and one at Institut Eurecom, to cross-check against crawler crashes or local network loss. Two crawl types are run: a full crawl of the entire KAD identifier space, and a zone crawl restricted to one 256th of the identifier space (all IDs sharing the same 8 high-order bits), which is far cheaper and lets the authors sample at short time intervals. KAD's routing structure follows Kademlia: peers are stored in buckets ordered by XOR distance to the local node, each bucket holding up to 10 contacts, with iterative forwarding to the contact whose ID shares the longest common prefix with the destination. KAD publishes two key types on the 10 peers whose ID matches the key in the first 8 bits (the "tolerance zone"): source keys (hash of file content), republished every 5 hours, and keyword keys (hash of filename tokens), republished every 24 hours.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| 3 to 4.3 million distinct peers found per full crawl | Full crawl of the entire KAD ID space; peers not behind NAT/firewall (1.5-2 million) are the directly contactable subset used for the rest of the paper's statistics |
| A full crawl completes in about 8 minutes and generates about 3 GB of inbound and outbound traffic each | Single crawler machine, 100 Mbit/s bidirectional bandwidth-limited; first million peers found in ~10 s, second million in ~50 s, after which discovery rate drops sharply |
| Full crawls run 3 times/day, 2006-08-18 to 2006-08-26 and 2006-10-03 to 2006-10-12; one full crawl/day from 2007-03-20 onward | Crawl schedule used for full-crawl statistics |
| Zone crawl of 8-bit zone 0x5b run once every 5 minutes for 179 days (2006-09-23 to 2007-03-21), totaling 51,552 crawls | Basis for essentially all churn and demographic statistics in the paper |
| 12,000 to 20,000 peers observed per 8-bit zone, versus a theoretical maximum of 2^120 addresses per zone | Full crawl; near-uniform distribution across the 256 zones except outlier zones caused by modified clients reusing one KAD ID across >10,000 instances (observed in zone 0xe1) |
| Weekend peer population about 10% higher than weekday | Full crawl population over roughly two weeks, diurnal/weekly pattern |
| Europe (Spain, France, Italy, Germany) is the highest-population continent; China is the single highest-population country; under 15% of peers are in the Americas | Country distribution from Maxmind IP geolocation, full crawl and 8-bit zone crawls, corroborating each other |
| Zone crawl over 179 days: 400,278 distinct KAD IDs, 3,228,890 distinct IP addresses, peers from 168 countries and 2,384 ISPs; 174,318 KAD IDs seen for only a single session; 242,487 KAD IDs with lifetime <= 1 day | 8-bit zone 0x5b, 51,552 crawls over 179 days; more than half of Chinese-origin KAD IDs were seen for only one session |
| Peer arrival/departure counts between consecutive 5-minute crawls follow a Negative Binomial distribution with parameters r=16.81, p=0.127; arrival and departure CDFs are statistically the same | First week of the 179-day zone crawl |
| Approximately 2,000 new KAD IDs per day in the sampled zone, extrapolated to about 500,000 new KAD IDs/day and about 180 million new KAD IDs/year system-wide | Zone crawl, 8-bit zone extrapolated to the full 256-zone ID space; more than 50% of new KAD IDs originate in China, over one order of magnitude more than any other single country |
| Rate of KAD-ID change ("KAD ID aliasing") after one month: about 35% for Chinese-origin peers, about 20% for Spanish-origin peers, about 10% average across all countries | Pivot-set method: peers holding the same IP address and same KAD ID across full crawls of 2007-03-20 and 2007-03-30 (160,641 peers, the "pivot set"), tracked in daily full crawls from 2007-04-01 onward for subsequent KAD ID changes on the same IP |
| Session lengths show a long tail, with sessions as long as 78 days, and are best fit by a Weibull distribution with shape parameter k < 1 | Stated in the conclusion as a summary finding; detailed data referred to the authors' companion technical report, not presented in this paper |

### Parameters
KAD bucket size: 10 contacts. Tolerance zone for key publication: 8 bits (10 peers per key). Source-key republish interval: 5 hours. Keyword-key republish interval: 24 hours. Zone-crawl granularity: 8-bit zone (1/256th of the ID space). Zone-crawl sampling interval: every 5 minutes. Crawler bandwidth: 100 Mbit/s bidirectional (a measurement-infrastructure parameter, not a KAD protocol parameter). Pivot-set qualification window: same IP address and same KAD ID held across a 10-day interval (2007-03-20 to 2007-03-30).

### Stated limitations
The paper states that KAD ID aliasing (peers changing their KAD ID, sometimes every session) makes it impossible to characterize true end-user lifetime from crawl data alone; the measured peer lifetime is only a lower bound on end-user lifetime. The authors state they have no explanation for why end-users change their KAD ID, and state this as an open problem, with a suspicion (explicitly unconfirmed) that Chinese clients run a modified implementation that assigns a new KAD ID per session. The paper reports finding modified KAD clients that reuse a single KAD ID across more than 10,000 simultaneous instances in some zones, which the authors state functions as free-riding because publishing and forwarding load meant for one peer is spread across all instances sharing that ID; they note that if the number of such modified clients grew large enough, the peers sharing an ID would be unable to see or download from one another, degrading application performance for those peers specifically. Detailed per-peer session-length and connected-time-per-day results are stated to exist but were not presented in this paper for space reasons, and the authors refer the reader to a separate technical report (Steiner, En-Najjary, Biersack, "Analyzing Peer Behavior in KAD," Institut Eurecom TR, 2007) for that data.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A crawler-based measurement of a deployed Kademlia-family DHT requires the crawler to hold several hundred initial contacts to bootstrap discovery. Any protocol or client claiming persistent per-peer identity across sessions must be checked against measured behavior rather than assumed, because this paper finds that assumption false for a substantial and geographically concentrated minority of the deployed population (up to 35% KAD-ID churn per month in one country). A system that infers peer lifetime, availability, or reputation from a node identifier must account for identifier churn independent of peer departure, or it will conflate identifier turnover with population turnover. A system relying on tolerance-zone or bucket-based key replication (10 peers per key here) must also handle the same key-holder set being partly composed of NAT/firewalled peers that publish and search but do not store or forward for others, which this paper measures as roughly 50-60% of the observed population (1.5-2 million of 3-4.3 million).

### Contradicts
This paper contradicts the assumption, stated by the authors to be present in all prior KAD publications, that KAD IDs are persistent across sessions; the measured KAD-ID aliasing rate (up to 35%/month for Chinese peers) directly disproves that assumption for the deployed system. No other entry in this batch measures KAD or contradicts this paper's figures. None found among W1-5.

## [STOICA-SIGCOMM-01] Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications
**Citation:** Ion Stoica, Robert Morris, David R. Karger, M. Frans Kaashoek, Hari Balakrishnan. "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-peer Lookup Service for Internet Applications." ACM SIGCOMM, 2001. DOI 10.1145/383059.383071.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:sigcomm01/chord_sigcomm.pdf
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/papers/chord:sigcomm01/chord_sigcomm.pdf
**Domain:** A

### Extraction note
The text on disk is a PDF-to-text conversion in which mathematical notation (variable names, exponents, and most numeric parameters embedded in equations and theorem statements, in Sections 4 through 6.5 and the Conclusion) was rendered as unprintable control characters rather than as readable digits or symbols. Section 6.6 (the deployed-prototype latency measurements) and isolated numeric values elsewhere in running prose (e.g., "457", "32 virtual nodes", "160-bit keys") survived intact. Per the governing rule that a figure without its stated conditions is not usable, the entries below include only the results whose numeric values are legible in the retrieved text; qualitative claims that do not depend on a garbled number (e.g., "the mean path length increases logarithmically with the number of nodes") are included because the paper states them in plain prose independent of the missing figures.

### What it does
Chord answers one question for a peer-to-peer system: given a key, which node in the network is responsible for storing that key's associated value. It provides only this one operation, `lookup(key) -> node`, and leaves data storage, replication, and caching to the application built on top of it.

Chord assigns every node and every key an identifier by hashing (the paper uses SHA-1) the node's IP address or the key's content into the same fixed-length identifier space, arranged as a circle (the identifier ring) that wraps from the highest value back to zero. A key is assigned to its successor: the first node whose identifier is equal to or follows the key's identifier when moving clockwise around the ring. This assignment is a form of consistent hashing, chosen because when a node joins or leaves, only the keys assigned to that node's immediate ring neighbors need to move, not the whole key space.

Every node maintains a successor pointer (the next node clockwise on the ring) and a finger table: a routing table whose i-th entry points to the first node succeeding the current node's identifier plus 2^(i-1) (using a fixed identifier length in bits, so the finger table has one entry per bit). A lookup is resolved by forwarding the query to the finger-table entry with the largest identifier that still precedes the target key, repeatedly halving the remaining identifier-space distance to the key at each hop until the query reaches the key's successor.

Because only the successor pointer is required for correctness (a node with an empty or wrong finger table can still find the right key eventually by walking successor pointers, just more slowly), Chord separates a fast path (the finger table, an optimization) from a correctness-critical path (successor-pointer maintenance). New-node joins and node departures are handled by a periodic background "stabilization" protocol: each node periodically asks its successor for the successor's own predecessor, and updates its own successor pointer if that predecessor turns out to be a more accurate (or newly joined) node; each node also notifies its successor of its own existence, letting the successor update its predecessor pointer. Finger-table entries are corrected by the same periodic process, run independently by each node, without requiring any global coordination or synchronized round.

Consistent hashing alone can allocate keys unevenly if node identifiers do not cover the identifier space uniformly. Chord addresses this by allowing each physical node to run multiple independent "virtual nodes," each with its own independently hashed identifier and its own slice of keys and finger-table entries; the paper's discussion of an a-priori-bounded network (at most one Chord server per IPv4 address) recommends 32 virtual nodes per physical node in that case to achieve good load balance.

### Measured results
| Metric | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Median lookup latency on a deployed Internet prototype | Ranges from 180 ms to 285 ms depending on the number of running Chord node instances | 10 physical sites on a subset of the RON (Resilient Overlay Networks) testbed in California, Colorado, Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania; nodes run UNIX, use 160-bit SHA-1-derived keys, communicate over TCP, run in iterative-lookup style; multiple independent Chord software copies run per physical site to test scaling beyond 10 nodes; each site issues 16 lookups for randomly chosen keys, one at a time, per node-count data point |
| Lookup latency components at 180 nodes | A typical lookup involves 5 two-way message exchanges (4 for the Chord lookup itself, 1 final message to the successor node); measured typical round-trip delay between sites was 60 ms (via ping); the resulting expected lookup time (5 x 60 ms = 300 ms) is close to the measured median of 285 ms | Same 10-site, 180-instance experiment |
| Effect of network size on lookup latency | "Lookup latency grows slowly with the total number of nodes," corroborating the simulation's logarithmic-scaling result | Same deployment, latency measured across the tested range of node counts (5th, 50th, 95th percentiles plotted) |
| Effect of virtual nodes on load balance | The 99th percentile of keys-per-node decreases and the 1st percentile increases as the number of virtual nodes per real node grows (paper tests values including 1, an unspecified middle value, and 20 virtual nodes per node); one worked example without virtual nodes reports a maximum of 457 keys stored at the single most heavily loaded node | Simulated network; the specific node count and total key count for this experiment are not legible in the retrieved text (see Extraction note) |
| Effect of simultaneous node failures | The mean fraction of lookups that fail after a simultaneous failure of a fraction of nodes is "almost exactly" equal to that failed fraction, which the paper states means failures produce no additional (super-proportional) lookup-failure amplification; the paper explicitly contrasts this with the fraction that would fail (one-half) if the Chord ring had instead partitioned into two equal halves, and states its results do not show that pattern | Simulated network, nodes failed simultaneously without replication of stored values, lookup considered failed only if it does not reach the pre-failure-responsible node, network allowed to finish stabilizing before failure rate is measured; specific node/key counts not legible in the retrieved text |
| Effect of continuous node join/leave churn on lookups during stabilization | Lookup failure rate increases with the join/leave (Poisson) rate relative to the stabilization interval; the paper's own approximate explanation (failure probability roughly proportional to path length times number of concurrently failed nodes) matches the simulated curve's shape but the simulated failure rate runs "slightly worse" than that approximation, attributed to a failed node sometimes needing more than one stabilization round to be fully cleared from finger tables | Simulated network of 500 nodes; lookups generated by a Poisson process at 1/second; joins/leaves generated by a Poisson process at rates from a low value up to roughly 3 failures per stabilization interval; each node runs stabilization at randomized intervals averaging 30 seconds and updates all finger-table entries on every invocation (a simulator-only simplification, not matching the paper's own pseudocode in Figure 7); results averaged over approximately 2 hours of simulated time, confidence intervals from 10 independent runs |

### Parameters
- Identifier length used in the deployed prototype: 160 bits, derived from SHA-1.
- Deployed-prototype lookup count per data point: 16 lookups per physical site per node-count value tested.
- Deployed testbed: 10 physical sites (RON testbed subset), located in California, Colorado, Massachusetts, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania.
- Measured typical inter-site round-trip time: 60 ms (via ping), used to explain the 285 ms median lookup latency at 180 node instances.
- Recommended virtual-node count under an a-priori bound of one Chord server per IPv4 address: 32 virtual nodes per physical node.
- Stabilization interval in the churn simulation: randomized, averaging 30 seconds per node, independently scheduled per node (no global synchronization).
- Simulated churn-experiment network size: 500 nodes (this specific figure is legible; the corresponding key-population and churn-rate axis values referenced in the same section are not legible in the retrieved text).
- Finger-table structure: one entry per bit of the identifier space, entry i covering identifiers starting at the node's own identifier plus 2^(i-1) (the exact per-experiment identifier-space size used in the simulations is not legible in the retrieved text).

### Stated limitations
The authors state Chord "currently has no specific mechanism to heal partitioned rings," and that such rings could appear locally consistent to the stabilization procedure even while globally split; they propose (without implementing) two mitigations — periodic lookups for a node's own identifier to detect whether the ring reports it as absent, and each node maintaining a long-term memory of a random set of previously encountered nodes to increase overlap across a partition — and note the first only detects partitions among nodes that already know of each other. They state a malicious or buggy set of participants "could present an incorrect view of the Chord ring," calling this a threat to data availability rather than authenticity, conditional on the data itself being cryptographically authenticated. They state an attacker could target one data item by inserting a node with an identifier immediately preceding that item's key and returning errors when queried for it, and that requiring (and checking) SHA-1-derived node identifiers from IP addresses "makes this attack harder" without eliminating it. They state that although the number of routing messages per lookup may already be too many for some applications, especially when each message crosses the wide-area Internet to a random host, no implemented fix is offered — only an unimplemented sketch (placing fingers at higher-radix intervals or measuring delay across multiple equivalent finger candidates via server selection, most effective under recursive rather than iterative routing). For the simulator itself, the paper states its lookup-failure-during-churn experiment does not retry failed queries, calling the reported failure rates "the worst-case scenario for the query failures induced by state inconsistency," and that its correctness criterion (reaching the current successor of a key) is "slightly optimistic" because it ignores whether the higher-layer application has actually migrated the associated data to that successor yet.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Chord resolves only to the responsible node for a key; the paper states explicitly that the correctness of a lookup under concurrent joins, leaves, and failures depends on maintaining accurate successor pointers via the periodic stabilization protocol, so any deployment needs that background process running continuously and needs to tolerate a bounded self-correction delay (governed by the stabilization interval, 30 seconds average in the paper's experiments) before newly joined or newly failed nodes are reflected network-wide. Because Chord itself provides no data replication or value storage, an application built on Chord (the paper names a "cooperative file sharing," "time-shared available storage," and "distributed indices for document and service discovery" as intended uses) must independently replicate or otherwise recover values stored under a key before that node fails, since the paper's own failure experiment explicitly modeled "a system that stores values with keys but does not replicate the values or recover them after failures," and states this design choice, not Chord's routing correctness, as the reason a node failure can still lose a key's stored value even though the ring self-heals its routing structure. Any component built on Chord's identifier assignment needs node identifiers to be derived by a hash function whose preimages are hard to construct (SHA-1, in the deployed prototype); the future-work section states this specifically as the defense against an attacker inserting an identifier chosen to sit immediately before a target key.

### Contradicts
None found regarding a claim commonly attributed to this paper.
No numeric conflict with another entry in this corpus was found in the reviewed text; RHEA-USENIXATC-04 (Bamboo) measures MIT Chord as a comparison baseline under churn on a different (ModelNet-emulated, 1,000-node) testbed and reports Chord completing and returning consistent lookups but with mean latency growing faster under high churn than Bamboo's — this is a different experimental setting (emulated churn-focused benchmark vs. this paper's own 10-site low-churn Internet deployment and its own churn simulation) and is not a direct contradiction of any figure in this entry, since RHEA-USENIXATC-04 does not report the same metric (mean lookup latency vs. churn rate) that this paper measures (lookup failure rate vs. churn rate).

### References worth retrieving
- Karger, Lehman, Leighton, Levine, Lewin, Panigrahy, consistent hashing paper (cited as [11]) — foundational, the load-balancing theory (including the virtual-node/multiple-hashes-per-node technique) Chord's key-assignment scheme is built on.
- Plaxton, Rajaraman, Richa, "Accessing nearby copies of replicated objects in a distributed environment" (cited as [19]) — foundational, cited as the source of the prefix-based routing approach a variant of which underlies related systems including OceanStore.
- Ratnasamy, Francis, Handley, Karp, Shenker, CAN (cited as [20]) — competing, a contemporaneous DHT design in the related-work comparison.
- Druschel, Rowstron, "PAST: Persistent and anonymous storage in a peer-to-peer networking environment" (cited as [8]) — competing/foundational, a DHT-based storage system built on similar routing principles.
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, Stoica, "Wide-area cooperative storage with CFS" (cited as [7]) — foundational/self-citation, the distributed file system whose Chord component is the source of the deployed-prototype measurements in Section 6.6.
- Clarke, Sandberg, Wiley, Hong, Freenet (cited as [5]) — foundational, an earlier decentralized information-storage system in the related-work discussion.

- Li, Jannotti, De Couto, Karger, Morris (cited as [14]) — foundational, cited in the related-work section (a Grid location system).

## [STRIBLING-IPTPS-05] OverCite: A Cooperative Digital Research Library
**Citation:** Jeremy Stribling, Isaac G. Councill, Jinyang Li, M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger, Robert Morris, Scott Shenker. "OverCite: A Cooperative Digital Research Library." IPTPS, 2005. DOI 10.1007/11558989_7.
**Retrieved:** full text via Jeremy Stribling's MIT Master's thesis (same title, September 2005), https://dspace.mit.edu (MIT DSpace) — see note below
**Source URL:** https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/~strib/docs/overcite/overcite_meng.pdf (thesis; the IPTPS conference paper itself was not the document on disk)
**Domain:** B

Note on source document: the file on disk (`sources/text/STRIBLING-IPTPS-05.txt`) is Jeremy Stribling's Master of Science thesis at MIT, titled identically ("OverCite: A Cooperative Digital Research Library"), submitted September 2005, single-authored. It is not the seven-author IPTPS conference paper the registry record cites. The thesis itself states explicitly, in its acknowledgments: "Portions of this thesis were previously published in Jeremy Stribling, Isaac G. Councill, Jinyang Li, M. Frans Kaashoek, David R. Karger, Robert Morris and Scott Shenker. OverCite: A Cooperative Digital Research Library. In Proceedings of the 3rd IPTPS, February 2005" — an exact match to the registry's cited title, venue, and full author list. Per this repository's own retrieval guidance (a thesis by the lead author frequently contains a conference paper's content in expanded form), this entry is built from the thesis as the authoritative, more detailed superset of the IPTPS paper's content, not treated as a wrong-document mismatch. Every fact below is attributed to the thesis; where the thesis presents material as evaluation of a system built after the IPTPS submission (e.g., the Chapter 6 prototype measurements), that is noted, since the thesis is dated seven months after the IPTPS paper and may include work done after the conference version was finalized.

### What it does
OverCite distributes CiteSeer, a centralized computer-science research-paper search and citation index, across many volunteer-donated nodes using a distributed hash table (DHT) — peer-to-peer software that lets a set of nodes jointly store and retrieve data without a central coordinator, remaining available under node churn (nodes joining, leaving, or failing). The goal is to let institutions donate spare storage and bandwidth instead of running the whole service on one organization's hardware, while keeping search quality comparable to the centralized system.

Each OverCite node runs up to four components: a DHT process, an index server, a Web crawler, and a Web front-end. The DHT process (the paper uses DHash, a Chord-based DHT) stores every document file, every piece of meta-data, and the full citation graph as key/value pairs in a shared table, so any node can retrieve any object without contacting a specific owning node directly; because OverCite is designed to run on at most a few hundred relatively stable nodes, each DHT node keeps a full routing table and achieves one-hop lookups rather than the O(log n) multi-hop lookups typical of larger DHT deployments. The inverted search index (the data structure mapping search terms to matching documents) is partitioned by document rather than by keyword, into k partitions, so that each document is indexed in exactly one partition; a query is sent in parallel to one server in each of the k partitions, so each server searches only about 1/k of the full index, and the k servers' top-ranked results (by a specified ranking criterion such as citation count) are merged and sorted at the node that received the query from the client. Document-based partitioning is chosen specifically to avoid the expensive join operation a keyword-partitioned index would need to combine multiple keyword's posting lists for a multi-keyword query, and to limit the communication needed when inserting a new document (an insertion only needs to reach the one partition holding that document, rather than every partition holding one of its keywords). The Web crawler coordinates via a shared to-be-crawled URL list stored in the DHT: each crawler process picks a random pending URL, fetches the page, extracts text and citations from any new document found, stores the document, its extracted words, and its meta-data in the DHT, and notifies the other nodes in its own index partition to fetch and index the new document's words. A subset of nodes run the Web front-end, which accepts a query, forwards it to the appropriate partition servers, merges and ranks the returned results, retrieves requested document files from the DHT (optionally converting file formats), and serves them to the user; round-robin DNS spreads client load across the front-end nodes.

### Measured results
Two distinct classes of figures appear: analytical (calculated) projections in Chapter 4, and empirical prototype measurements in Chapter 6, deployed on real machines rather than simulated.

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| CiteSeer baseline scale (as of measurement date) | 715,000 papers indexed; 750 new documents per week; 767 GB total document storage; 44 GB meta-data storage; 18 GB inverted index; over 1,000,000 hits/day; 250,000 searches/day; 34.4 GB total daily traffic (21 GB of it document downloads); average CPU load 66% | Production PSU (Pennsylvania State University) CiteSeer deployment, statistics current as of November 2004, running on two servers each with two 2.8 GHz processors |
| Calculated crawling/insertion bandwidth overhead | OverCite requires roughly 3x more total bandwidth than CiteSeer for crawling and inserting new documents, spread across all nodes; with n=100 nodes, k=20 partitions, and DHT replication factor f=2, per-document overhead is calculated at 1.84 MB above CiteSeer's current 0.735 MB per document, and per-node storage is calculated at 25 GB | Analytical calculation (not measured), using the PSU CiteSeer statistics above as inputs and the stated parameter choices (n=100 approximating PlanetLab's then-available donated nodes, k=20, f=2, the DHash default) |
| Calculated query-traffic overhead | About 8.5 GB/day of additional network traffic (85 MB per node) for query forwarding and results, versus CiteSeer's 34.4 GB/day total traffic | Calculated from k=20 partitions, m=10 results returned per node per query, 250,000 searches/day, 170 bytes per per-node response (20-byte document ID + 150 bytes of context/meta-data/rank value) |
| Calculated theoretical storage-scaling benefit | An n-node OverCite network is calculated to provide a performance benefit "of n/3 times the current centralized system"; the paper's own worked example states 100 nodes gives approximately 30x the storage of a single CiteSeer node | Analytical calculation in Chapter 4, derived from the roughly 3x aggregate bandwidth/storage overhead figure above, not from a deployed measurement |
| CiteSeer query performance (baseline for comparison) | Query throughput holds roughly constant at about 5 queries/second as concurrency increases from 0 to 140 concurrent clients; latency increases linearly with concurrency | Measured on an unloaded production CiteSeer mirror at PSU, full repository (over 700,000 documents), 1,000 total queries issued at each concurrency level; the paper states this result is not directly comparable to the OverCite prototype figures below because of the different document-set size and different hardware |
| OverCite single-node ("centralized baseline") throughput | Query throughput levels off around 14 queries/second as concurrency rises to 140 concurrent clients; latency rises linearly with concurrency | Single OverCite node indexing the full loaded document set with one partition (k=1) and a full in-memory meta-data cache, no DHT or remote-index communication involved |
| OverCite distributed (2-partition) throughput vs. single-node | Multi-partition (k=2) deployment achieves higher query throughput than the single-node case, despite added DHT lookup and inter-node communication latency, because each of the two servers searches only half the index | 11-node deployment (5 geographically spread North American nodes plus 3 local MIT nodes running full components, plus 3 additional MIT nodes participating only in the DHT), k=2 index partitions, 14,755 documents loaded from the CiteSeer repository, DHash spawning 3 virtual nodes per physical node for load balancing, results averaged over 5 experimental runs (except two latency/throughput figures limited by time constraints to a single run) |
| Effect of adding more Web-server front-ends | Adding more Web servers as query entry points generally increases aggregate query throughput, though the trend fluctuates across the range tested because of variation in DHT lookup times between experiments and nodes | 128 concurrent queries issued across 0 to 8 Web servers, each configured to use a different neighboring node for its remote index-partition forwarding |
| File-serving throughput ceiling | Throughput plateaus at about 1.2 MB/s regardless of concurrent-request count once request throttling is enabled; without throttling, throughput drops toward zero due to RPC timeouts and disk-bound livelock | Single Web server serving PostScript/PDF files from the DHT, varying concurrent file requests from 0 to 140; DHash reconstructs each block from 7 of 11 available fragment-holding nodes in this small deployment; the paper's own back-of-envelope calculation (2 disk seeks per lookup at 10 ms each, 50 fetches/sec/node capacity, 7/11 fraction of fetches touching each node in an 11-node DHT, 16 KB blocks) predicts a theoretical ceiling of about 1.22 MB/s, matching the observed 1.2 MB/s plateau |
| Storage cost comparison | Centralized single-node storage cost for 14,755 documents: 4.5 GB document storage + 0.15 GB meta-data + 0.40 GB index = 5.05 GB total. Distributed per-node average: 1.15 GB document + 0.35 GB meta-data + 0.21 GB index = 1.71 GB total per node, against a calculated prediction of 1.09 GB per node (using f=2 for content-hash data and f=5 for other data, DHash's own defaults) | 11-node, k=2-partition OverCite deployment storing the same 14,755-document set; the paper attributes the gap between the 1.71 GB measured and 1.09 GB predicted per-node figures to (a) file-system overhead from inode and indirect blocks in OverCite's storage format, (b) extra non-content-hash replicas created by an imperfect DHash replication implementation, and (c) a small amount of test-only data |
| Measured storage-scaling factor | Total system storage (11 x 1.71 GB = 18.81 GB) is stated as "less than a factor of four more" than the 5.05 GB centralized total; per-node storage dropped by "nearly a factor of three" when going from 1 node to 11 nodes; extrapolating this scaling factor, the paper projects an n-node OverCite network can store n/4 times as much data as a single CiteSeer node | Same 11-node, 14,755-document deployment as above; the n/4 extrapolation is stated as an assumption ("assuming this scaling factor holds indefinitely"), not itself a measurement at larger n |
| Implementation size | OverCite's own code is about 10,000 lines; the DHash and Chord libraries it depends on are about 40,000 lines combined | Stated code-size comparison, not a performance measurement |
| Query-type distribution (motivating a proposed optimization, not evaluated) | 40% of "answerable" queries in an October 2004 CiteSeer query trace match only a paper's title or author list; a complete title/author meta-data index for the full CiteSeer corpus is calculated at only 50 MB | Analysis of a real CiteSeer query trace (October 2004); used to motivate (not to evaluate) a proposed optimization of replicating a small title/author index on every node |

### Parameters
- n: total number of participating OverCite nodes; illustrative value 100 used in Chapter 4's calculations (approximating PlanetLab's then-available donated capacity); the Chapter 6 prototype used 11 nodes.
- k: number of inverted-index partitions; illustrative value 20 used in Chapter 4's bandwidth/storage calculations (chosen so only a few nodes index the full text of each new document); the Chapter 6 prototype used k=2.
- f: DHT replication factor (number of redundant fragments/copies DHash stores per block); the paper's calculations use f=2 for content-hash data and separately note f=5 as the DHash default for non-content-hash (mutable) data.
- m: number of top-ranked results each per-partition index server returns per query; b: number of top results the front-end ultimately displays to the user; both set to 30 in the Chapter 6 experiments (m = b = 30), though Chapter 4's bandwidth calculation illustratively uses m=10.
- Document ID (DID) size: 20 bytes, used in the per-query traffic calculation.
- Per-result context/meta-data/rank payload: about 150 bytes, used in the same calculation.
- DHT virtual nodes per physical node: 3 (for load balancing in the Chapter 6 deployment).
- File-download throttling: the deployment throttles outstanding DHash fetch operations; the paper reports both the throttled (stable, 1.2 MB/s plateau) and unthrottled (livelock, throughput collapse) behavior as a direct comparison.

### Stated limitations
The thesis states directly that "a well-funded, professionally-maintained, centralized library service will always have more available resources ... and obtain better performance, than a distributed approach constructed from volunteer resources," framing OverCite's contribution as feasibility, not superiority, at matched resource levels. The implementation described has no working crawler module: the thesis states "the current implementation does not yet include a Crawler module; we have populated OverCite with existing CiteSeer data, and plan to implement a distributed crawler in the future," so every reported measurement operates on data loaded from the existing centralized CiteSeer corpus, not on data OverCite itself discovered and indexed. The evaluation is stated by the authors to be preliminary and small-scale relative to the system's design target: "the scale of the following preliminary experiments is smaller than the expected size of an OverCite system, and the code is currently an early prototype." The CiteSeer-versus-OverCite throughput comparison is explicitly flagged as not a fair or direct comparison, because the CiteSeer mirror served the full repository (over 700,000 documents) on different hardware than the OverCite prototype's 14,755-document, 11-node deployment; the paper states "a more direct comparison is an objective for future work." The file-serving throughput ceiling (1.2 MB/s) and the unthrottled livelock behavior are both stated to be artifacts of running on a small (11-node) DHT specifically, where a large fraction of nodes participates in every block fetch; the paper states this behavior is not expected to persist "once we deploy OverCite on a larger DHT." The thesis lists an unimplemented feature required before full operation: "there remain many ways to improve the system," specifically an automatic document-set reconciliation algorithm between nodes sharing an index partition (proposed future use of Merkle trees for gossip-based synchronization, not implemented), and states the DHT does not natively support storing mutable data under an arbitrary application-chosen key, a feature the authors state they found "essential" and had to work around, and which they recommend future DHT designs include. The one-hop DHT routing design is stated to depend on OverCite running on "a relatively small number of nodes"; the paper notes the underlying Chord lookup protocol it uses is optimized for much larger deployments than OverCite targets, and states a plan (not yet executed) to move to a different lookup protocol, Accordion, designed to perform well at both small and large scale.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Document-based (rather than keyword-based) index partitioning requires every query to be broadcast to all k partition-holding servers in parallel, so query cost scales with the number of partitions regardless of how few keywords the query contains; this is an explicit design tradeoff the paper makes to avoid keyword-partitioning's join cost, not a free choice. The DHT layer must support one-hop lookup for the system's latency assumptions to hold, which the paper states requires every participating node to maintain a full routing table — a requirement that in turn assumes network size stays in "the few hundred volunteer servers" range the design targets, not the scale of a general-purpose global DHT deployment. The system assumes participating nodes are relatively stable and that failed nodes typically return with their disks intact, which the paper uses to justify making the DHT layer "lazy about re-replicating data stored on failed nodes" — a churn model different from one where failed nodes are assumed to be permanently gone or to return with data loss. The meta-data and content tables are stored as generic key/value pairs in one shared DHT keyspace, interpreted by context rather than by an explicit schema, which requires every component reading a given key to already know, out of band, what type of value it should decode there. The crawler's deduplication logic (checking a new document's title, authors, and shingle-level text similarity against existing entries) requires the Titles and Files tables to already be populated and consistent at the time of a new insertion, so insertion order and DHT read consistency directly affect whether duplicate documents are correctly detected. The file-serving throughput result demonstrates that DHT block-reconstruction cost (fetching a threshold number of fragments per block, here 7 of 11 fragment-holding nodes) is not independent of total DHT size: the same erasure-coding-style redundancy parameter that provides fault tolerance on a large DHT concentrates load onto nearly every node when the DHT is small, so a deployment's minimum viable node count is constrained jointly by the replication/reconstruction parameters and by the target per-node fetch rate, not by storage capacity alone.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch.

### References worth retrieving
- Li, Loo, Hellerstein, Kaashoek, Karger, Morris, "On the Feasibility of Peer-to-Peer Web Indexing and Search," IPTPS 2003 — foundational/competing (keyword-partitioned peer-to-peer indexing approach; OverCite's document-based partitioning is chosen specifically as an alternative to this and similar keyword-partitioning designs).
- Reynolds and Vahdat, "Efficient Peer-to-Peer Keyword Searching," Middleware 2003 — competing (another keyword-partitioned peer-to-peer search design cited alongside the above as the alternative OverCite's partitioning choice avoids).
- Suel, Mathur, Wu, Zhang, Delis, Kharrazi, Long, Shanmugasundaram, "ODISSEA: A Peer-to-Peer Architecture for Scalable Web Search and Information Retrieval," WebDB 2003 — competing (another distributed web-search architecture in the same design space).
- Shi, Yang, Wang, Yu, Qu, Chen, "Making Peer-to-Peer Keyword Searching Feasible Using Multi-Level Partitioning," IPTPS 2004 — competing (keyword-partitioning alternative).
- Loo, Huebsch, Stoica, Hellerstein, "The Case for a Hybrid P2P Search Infrastructure," IPTPS 2004 — competing (alternative hybrid design for distributed search).
- Huebsch, Hellerstein, Lanham, Loo, Shenker, Stoica, "Querying the Internet with PIER," VLDB 2003 — competing (declarative query processing over a DHT, an alternative approach to distributed search coordination).
- Fagin, Lotem, Naor, "Optimal Aggregation Algorithms for Middleware," JCSS 66, 2003 — foundational (already in this corpus as FAGIN-PODS-01; cited here as a proposed future-work optimization for combining per-partition ranked result lists, "threshold aggregation algorithms").
- Dabek, Kaashoek, Li, Morris, Robertson, Sit, "Designing a DHT for Low Latency and High Throughput," NSDI 2004 — foundational (DHash, the specific DHT implementation OverCite is built on).
- Gupta, Liskov, Rodrigues, "Efficient Routing for Peer-to-Peer Overlays," NSDI 2004 — foundational (one-hop DHT lookup design OverCite's routing-table assumption is built on).
- Li, Stribling, Kaashoek, Morris, "Bandwidth-Efficient Management of DHT Routing Tables," NSDI 2005 — foundational (Accordion, the lookup protocol the thesis states it plans to migrate to for better small-and-large-scale performance).
- Maymounkov and Mazieres, "Kademlia: A Peer-to-Peer Information System Based on the XOR Metric," IPTPS 2002 — foundational (already a verified seed in this corpus; cited as an alternative DHT design).
- Stoica, Morris, Liben-Nowell, Karger, Kaashoek, Dabek, Balakrishnan, "Chord: A Scalable Peer-to-Peer Lookup Protocol for Internet Applications," IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 2002 — foundational (the lookup layer underlying DHash, which OverCite's implementation directly depends on).

## [SUN-USENIXSEC-15] RAPTOR: Routing Attacks on Privacy in Tor

**Citation:** Yixin Sun, Anne Edmundson, Laurent Vanbever, Oscar Li, Jennifer Rexford, Mung Chiang, Prateek Mittal. "RAPTOR: Routing Attacks on Privacy in Tor." 24th USENIX Security Symposium, 2015. Pages 271-286.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-sun.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-sun.pdf
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper deanonymizes Tor users through routing manipulation at the level of BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol autonomous systems use to exchange reachability routes across the Internet), rather than by running a Tor relay. Three related attacks: first, an autonomous system (AS) that already sees the forward-direction path from a client to its guard relay can independently examine whether it also sees the return path from the exit relay to the destination, or vice versa — asymmetric routing on the Internet means the two directions of a single connection frequently take different AS-level paths, so any single AS observing either direction on both segments of the same Tor circuit already possesses a correlation opportunity that whole-flow-symmetric adversary models miss. Second, routine BGP route changes over time (churn) cause a growing set of ASes to have appeared, cumulatively, on both segments of a given (client, destination) pair's circuit at different moments, so the compromising AS set for a fixed pair of endpoints only grows as time passes. Third, an AS can actively manipulate BGP itself: a hijack (announcing a route to a prefix the announcing AS does not own, causing traffic to be misdirected) reveals which clients use a targeted guard relay, and an interception (announcing a more specific prefix so that traffic is drawn to the attacker but still forwarded on to the legitimate destination, keeping the connection alive) lets the attacker perform traffic analysis on live Tor circuits without the client or relay detecting an outage. The paper's traffic-correlation technique (used to confirm a suspected client-server pairing) computes the Spearman rank correlation between the time series of transmitted-byte counts derived from TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers captured at each end, and needs only one direction's data, not the full duplex stream — that is what makes the asymmetric-routing observation exploitable.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Asymmetric traffic-analysis correlation attack: average 95% detection accuracy after 300 seconds, all errors false negatives, 0% false positives | 100 PlanetLab machines (50 as Tor clients via Privoxy-tunneled wget, 50 as web servers each hosting a 100 MB file), simultaneous downloads over the live Tor network, tcpdump capture for 300 s, tested in all 4 combinations of ACK-only vs. data-carrying observation at client and server |
| 80% accuracy reached within 1 minute, 95% within 5 minutes | Same experiment, accuracy measured as a function of elapsed capture time |
| Without considering churn, at least 0.75% of all Tor circuits are compromised by one AS for 50% of (client, destination) pairs, rising to 6% at the 75th percentile and 13% at the 95th percentile | Static baseline from 612+ million BGP updates across 550,000 IP prefixes, collected by 6 RIPE Looking Glass routers (rrc00, rrc01, rrc03, rrc04, rrc11, rrc14) over 250+ BGP sessions, January 2015; 6,755 Tor relays in the same period (1,459 guards, 1,182 exits, 338 both) |
| BGP churn increases compromised circuits for 60% of (client, destination) pairs over one month, by up to 50% (ratio 1.5) in 20% of cases; compromisable pairs rose from 5,593 to 5,754 (~3% increase) | Same BGP dataset, one-month observation window, a circuit counted as compromised only if the compromising AS was on-path for at least 30 seconds |
| 10 named ASes (e.g. NTT, IIJ, BroadbandONE, Inet7, Level3) each simultaneously see traffic for up to 90-91% of all (guard, exit) relay pairs | Same BGP dataset |
| Data-plane confirmation: 12.8% of Tor circuits vulnerable to a same-AS-on-both-forward-paths adversary on day 1, rising to 21.3% considering asymmetric paths on day 1, and to 31.8% by day 21 | 70 RIPE Atlas probes across 4 AS sets (10 ASes with the most Tor clients, 25 ASes holding ~50% of guard bandwidth, 25 ASes holding ~50% of exit bandwidth, 10 ASes with the most Tor destinations), daily traceroutes over 3 weeks, 10×25×25×10 = 62,500 possible circuits measured |
| 6 ASes and 70 IP prefixes host ~30% of all Tor guard and exit relays and ~40% of total Tor network bandwidth | Computed from the same 6,755-relay dataset; named hosts include OVH, Hetzner, Online.net, Wedos, Leaseweb, PlusServer |
| 2 real-world Indosat BGP hijacks affected Tor relays: 2011 event hijacked 5 relays (1 guard, 4 exit); 2014 event hijacked 44 relays (38 guards, 17 exits, 11 both) | Historical Routeviews BGP data matched against Tor relay prefix lists for known hijack events |
| A 2014 Canadian Bitcoin-theft hijack (2 prefixes, ~USD 83,000 stolen) incidentally hijacked one Tor guard relay | Same historical BGP data cross-reference |
| Live BGP interception attack against the authors' own Tor guard relay achieved 90% traffic-analysis accuracy (8% false negative, 2% false positive), with the connection staying alive throughout | Transit Portal deployments at Georgia Tech (legitimate path) and ISI (attacker path) connected via VPN tunnels to one relay; 50 PlanetLab clients configured to use that relay as sole guard; more-specific /24 prefix announced by ISI 20 s after traffic start, drained the legitimate path within ~35 s, withdrawn at 300 s with recovery in ~22 s |
| Over 90% of BGP prefixes hosting Tor relays are shorter than /24, the maximum length still globally routable and therefore hijackable | Prefix-length distribution computed over the same relay dataset |

### Parameters
- Circuit compromise definition for churn analysis: an AS counted as compromising a circuit only if it remained on-path for at least 30 seconds, "as it is unlikely that a time-correlation attack can be performed in shorter timescale" (the paper does not derive this threshold from a separate measurement; it is stated as an assumption).
- Traceroute measurement: daily over a 3-week period, 4 AS sets of size 10, 25, 25, 10, giving 62,500 possible circuit combinations.
- BGP dataset: January 2015, 6 RIPE-maintained Looking Glass collection points, 250+ BGP sessions, 612+ million updates over 550,000 prefixes.
- Interception-attack timing: traffic drain after more-specific announcement took ~35 seconds to propagate; traffic recovery after withdrawal took ~22 seconds; attack window was 300 seconds of a 100 MB download per client.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the interception-attack accuracy (90%) is lower than the static asymmetric-analysis accuracy (95%) because all 50 test clients shared one guard relay and started requests simultaneously, artificially compressing the achievable bandwidths of different client-server pairs toward similarity — a condition the authors describe as "an extreme and very unlikely case in real Tor connections," expecting higher accuracy with fewer clients sharing a guard. The authors state they consider only individual, non-colluding autonomous systems as adversaries, and note in discussion that colluding ASes, such as those "within the same legal jurisdiction," would increase attack capability beyond what is measured. The authors state their proposed "select closer guards" countermeasure (favoring guards with a shorter AS-level path from the client) has an unresolved trade-off, because it makes the guard's identity more informative about the client's likely location, and explicitly leave this trade-off for future work. The authors state their real-world hijack and interception experiments used only their own generated traffic and their own controlled relay, with a firewall dropping real user traffic from the experimental relay, so no live Tor user was exposed to the interception experiment.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A privacy tier that assumes symmetric routing observation is required to defeat a traffic-correlation attack is broken by any network topology exhibiting routing asymmetry, because an adversary needs only one direction of one of the two path segments (client-to-guard, exit-to-destination) to run the correlation attack described here, which halves the on-path coverage an adversary needs relative to a full-duplex observation model. A relay-selection mechanism that keeps a client's guard fixed for a long tenure (also measured, from the network-adversary angle, in JOHNSON-CCS-13) accumulates additional exposure over that tenure purely from BGP route churn, independent of any adversary action, because the set of ASes that have appeared on-path for a fixed (client, destination) pair only grows monotonically as routing updates accrue. A design that concentrates a large share of relay bandwidth or relay count within a small number of network prefixes (measured here at 6 ASes and 70 prefixes for ~30% of Tor relays and ~40% of bandwidth) creates a small set of maximally attractive BGP hijack and interception targets, so any capacity-ordered overlay reusing a similarly concentrated hosting pattern inherits the same vulnerability without additional relay-diversity requirements on physical network placement. A design relying on route-security protocols (secure BGP variants, cited by the authors as a mitigation) to close this attack requires deployment across multiple independent network operators simultaneously, which the authors state has been slow to happen in practice.

### Contradicts
None found within this batch. This paper's asymmetric-routing and churn-based attack results are additive to, and build on, the AS-level and IXP-level adversary analysis in JOHNSON-CCS-13, which the RAPTOR authors cite directly as related work analyzing "the security of the Tor network against AS-level adversaries in terms of user understandable metrics"; the two papers measure different adversary capabilities (route manipulation here versus passive fixed-position observation there) and do not report conflicting figures for the same quantity.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Feamster, Dingledine. First to analyze AS-level adversaries against Tor (cited as reference [28], not independently retrieved here).
- foundational: Syverson, Tsudik, Reed, Landwehr. "Towards an analysis of onion routing security." Designing Privacy Enhancing Technologies, 2001.
- competing/foundational: Edman, Syverson. Impact of Tor path-selection strategies on network security (cited as reference [26]).
- foundational (this paper's own preliminary version): Vanbever, Li, Rexford, Mittal. "Anonymity on quicksand: Using BGP to compromise Tor." ACM HotNets-XIII, 2014.
- attack/related: Murdoch, Zieliński. Internet-exchange-level adversary analysis (cited as reference [40], same paper as PET 2007 in JOHNSON-CCS-13's bibliography).
- competing: Akhoondi et al. LASTor — path-selection algorithm minimizing AS-level correlation opportunity (cited as reference [13]).
- attack (BGP defenses, superseded-by candidates): Zhang, Zhang, Hu, Mao, Bush. "iSPY: Detecting IP prefix hijacking on my own." IEEE/ACM ToN 18(6), 2010.
- attack detection: Zheng, Ji, Pei, Wang, Francis. "A light-weight distributed scheme for detecting IP prefix hijacks in real-time." SIGCOMM 2007.
