## [TAHERIBOSHROOYEH-ARXIV-22] WAKU-RLN-RELAY: Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Economic Spam Protection
**Citation:** Sanaz Taheri-Boshrooyeh, Oskar Thorén, Barry Whitehat, Wei Jie Koh, Onur Kilic, Kobi Gurkan. "WAKU-RLN-RELAY: Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Economic Spam Protection." arXiv:2207.00117, 2022. DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2207.00117.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.00117
**Source URL:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.00117
**Domain:** I

### What it does
WAKU-RLN-RELAY limits each participant of a gossip-based publish-subscribe network to one message per fixed time interval (an epoch) without requiring any per-message computational cost or a central rate-limiting authority, and it turns a second message in the same epoch into cryptographic proof of the sender's identity key that any observer can extract and use to forfeit that sender's deposited stake. Each participant registers by generating a private identity key sk and a public commitment pk = H(sk) (H a cryptographic hash function), submitting pk plus a deposit of Ether to a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, and having pk added as a leaf of a Merkle tree (a binary tree in which each internal node is the hash of its two children, so a leaf's presence can be proven by a path of hashes to the root) called the identity commitment tree; unlike the base Semaphore protocol on which this construction extends, the contract itself stores only an ordered list of registered public keys, not the Merkle tree, and each peer builds and maintains the tree locally by listening to the contract's insertion and deletion events, which the paper states avoids the gas cost of on-chain tree updates that scales logarithmically in group size and, for deletion, cannot be batched. An epoch is a public, universally computable value: the current Unix time divided by a configured epoch length T and rounded up. To publish a message m in epoch e, a sender computes a two-point Shamir secret share of its own identity key using (2,n)-Shamir secret sharing (a scheme by which a degree-1 polynomial is uniquely determined by any two of its points, so one point alone reveals nothing about the polynomial while two points reconstruct it): the sender sets x = H(m) and y = sk + H(sk, e) * x, so distinct messages in the same epoch produce distinct (x, y) points lying on the sender's own secret line, while two messages sharing an epoch value give two points on the same line. The sender also computes an internal nullifier phi = H(H(sk, e)), a value that any two messages from the same sender in the same epoch will share, and attaches (x, y), phi, e, the identity-commitment-tree root, and a zkSNARK (a zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge, a proof system letting a prover convince a verifier a computation was performed correctly without revealing its private inputs) proving membership in the tree, correctness of the share, and correctness of phi, all without revealing sk or the sender's position in the tree. A routing peer relaying the message bundle keeps, for the last Thr epochs, a local table (the nullifier map) of every internal nullifier phi and share (x,y) it has seen; on receiving a new bundle it verifies the zkSNARK, checks whether phi already appears in the table for a different (x,y) pair, and if so uses the two (x,y) points from the same line to solve for sk directly (evaluating the reconstructed line at x=0), publishes that recovered sk to the contract, and collects the offending sender's deposit as a reward, after which the sender's identity commitment is removed from the group. A message whose attached epoch differs from the routing peer's own current epoch by more than a threshold Thr is dropped outright, bounding both the memory a peer must retain in the nullifier map and the exposure of newly joined peers replaying stale epochs.

### Measured results
| Measurement | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Membership-proof generation time: approximately 0.5 s | Group size 2^32 (approximately 4 billion peers); measured on an iPhone 8; figure attributed to the RLN library the authors used [17], not independently re-measured in this paper. |
| Proof verification time: approximately 30 ms, constant regardless of group size | Same RLN library and proof-of-concept implementation; hardware for the verification-side measurement not separately stated. |
| Per-peer persistent storage: 32 bytes each for the identity public and secret keys, plus a prover key of approximately 3.89 MB | Figure attributed to the RLN library [17]. |
| Identity-commitment-tree storage: 67 MB per peer for a tree of depth 20 (up to 2^20, approximately 1,048,576, members) | Stated as reducible to 0.128 KB using a separate storage-efficient tree-update proposal [18] not implemented in this paper's proof of concept. |
| Ethereum gas cost of one membership insertion or deletion: 40,000 gas, stated to exceed 20 USD at the time of writing | Stated as reducible to 20,000 gas using batch insertion; batching does not apply to deletion because deletions touch non-adjacent leaves. This figure depends on Ethereum gas-price and Ether-price conditions specific to the time of writing and is not a property of the RLN mechanism itself. |

The paper labels its own performance section a proof-of-concept implementation with a "rough performance evaluation" and states that Merkle-tree computation overhead specifically was not benchmarked ("the concrete benchmarking result in this regard is not available").

### Parameters
- Epoch length T: the time interval in seconds over which one message is permitted per identity; application-set, with the paper giving 1 second as an example acceptable rate for a chat application and stating that same rate would be too low for communication among Ethereum network validators, without giving a numeric alternative for that case.
- Maximum epoch gap Thr: the number of epochs of drift a routing peer tolerates between its own current epoch and a received message's attached epoch before dropping the message; the paper gives the formula Thr = ceil((NetworkDelay + ClockAsynchrony) / T), where NetworkDelay is the maximum time for a message to fully propagate through the network and ClockAsynchrony is the maximum clock drift observed across peers, both in seconds; no numeric value for NetworkDelay or ClockAsynchrony is measured or given in this paper.
- Merkle tree depth used in the storage measurement above: 20 (supports up to roughly 1,048,576 registered identities without resizing).
- Deposit amount v (the Ether quantity locked per registration): described only as "some amount of Ether"; no numeric value given.
- Proof system: Groth16 (a specific zkSNARK construction), with parameter generation via a multi-party trusted setup ceremony citing prior implementations.

### Stated limitations
The authors state Merkle-tree computation overhead was an unknown discovered only during the proof-of-concept build and remains unbenchmarked. The design leaves the identity commitment tree stored in full by every publishing peer, which the authors state produces storage cost linear in the size of the group, and list as future work a partial-view tree construction giving O(log N) storage instead. The authors state registration and slashing transactions are subject to Ethereum block-mining delay before taking effect, so a peer must wait after registering before it can publish, and list off-chain group-management alternatives (state channels, optimistic rollups, a distributed-hash-table-based scheme) as unimplemented future directions to remove this delay. The authors state a race condition exists when two peers simultaneously attempt to submit a recovered spammer identity key to claim the reward, since submitting the key in plaintext lets an observer copy and resubmit it first; their proposed fix (commit to the key, then later reveal it) is presented as a mitigation, not as implemented and measured. The authors identify two open problems with no known solution stated in the paper: an attacker who registers k identities and spends k times the membership fee obtains k messages per epoch rather than one, a limitation the authors say can only be raised in cost, not eliminated, by increasing the membership fee; and a spammer can withdraw its deposited stake before a routing peer catches and reports a double-signaling attempt, forfeiting only the initial registration fee rather than the full deposit a slasher would otherwise have claimed.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every routing peer must independently reconstruct and keep synchronized an identity commitment tree by observing the registration/removal event stream from the same smart contract, because the contract itself no longer stores the tree; a peer that falls behind risks proving membership against a stale root, which the paper states can expose that peer's leaf index and compromise its own anonymity. The mechanism requires loosely synchronized clocks across peers (bounded by the ClockAsynchrony term in the Thr formula) and a bound on network propagation delay, since both terms are inputs the deploying application must estimate to set the epoch-gap threshold; setting Thr too low drops legitimate recently-published messages arriving after a slow propagation path, and setting it too high extends how far back a newly registered peer could replay stale epochs. The mechanism assumes participant honesty only in the negative sense that spam is defined purely by messaging rate (more than one message per epoch), not by content, so a downstream component relying on this mechanism for content moderation gets none: a single properly rate-limited message can carry arbitrary content and passes unmodified. The scheme requires an underlying transport that delivers the full message bundle (message, identity-key share, internal nullifier, epoch, tree root, and zkSNARK proof) to every peer that must run the routing/slashing check, and it requires every such peer to hold a verifier for the specific zkSNARK proof system (Groth16) and, if trust in a single-party setup is unacceptable, requires the identity commitment tree's proving/verifying parameters to have come from a multi-party trusted-setup ceremony trusted by that peer.

### Contradicts
None found within this paper's own claims. Cross-reference for later composition: this mechanism and BACK-HASHCASH-02's non-interactive hashcash rate limiter are not measurements of the same mechanism and do not disagree numerically, but they differ in what a rate-limited peer must possess: hashcash requires only local compute and no registration, while WAKU-RLN-RELAY requires a funded on-chain registration and a live view of a specific smart contract's state, a materially different requirement on the rest of the system that a synthesis comparing the two must state explicitly rather than comparing on cost alone.

### References worth retrieving
- Dwork, Naor, "Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail," CRYPTO 1992 -- foundational (cited directly as the origin of the proof-of-work spam-prevention alternative this paper argues against on computational-cost grounds; retrieved in this batch as DWORK-CRYPTO-92).
- Vyzovitis, Napora, McCormick, Dias, Psaras, "GossipSub: Attack-resilient message propagation in the Filecoin and Eth2.0 networks," arXiv:2007.02754, 2020 -- foundational (the underlying gossip routing protocol, WAKU-RELAY, is described as a thin layer over GossipSub; also cited as the source of the peer-scoring spam defense this paper argues against on censorship-susceptibility and Sybil-cost grounds).
- Gurkan, Koh, Whitehat, "Semaphore: Zero-knowledge signaling on Ethereum," community proposal, 2020 -- foundational (the base zero-knowledge signaling framework this paper extends with Shamir secret sharing).
- "RLN original proposal," ethresear.ch forum post, cited as [9] -- foundational (the original Rate-Limiting Nullifier proposal this paper implements and adapts for peer-to-peer resource-restricted settings).
- Shamir, "How to share a secret," Communications of the ACM 22(11), 1979 -- foundational (the (2,n)-secret-sharing scheme used to derive the identity-key share published with each message).
- Groth, "On the size of pairing-based non-interactive arguments," EUROCRYPT 2016 -- foundational (Groth16, the zkSNARK proof system used for the membership/share/nullifier proof).
- Unger, Dechand, Bonneau, Fahl, Perl, Goldberg, Smith, "SoK: Secure Messaging," IEEE S&P 2015 -- foundational (systematization-of-knowledge survey cited for the messaging-system anonymity requirements this design targets).
- Kate, Zaverucha, Goldberg, "Polynomial commitments," technical report, 2010 -- competing (cited as an alternative path for lowering per-peer Merkle-tree storage overhead, not adopted in this paper's construction).
- Kuszmaul, "Verkle trees," 2019 -- competing (cited as an alternative tree structure for lowering storage overhead, not adopted in this paper's construction).

- "reveals its identity/private key by which it has registered to the group"
- "Generating membership proof to a group size of 2^32 ... takes ~0.5s on an iPhone 8"

## [TANG-CCR-03] pSearch: Information Retrieval in Structured Overlays
**Citation:** Chunqiang Tang, Zhichen Xu, Mallik Mahalingam. "pSearch: Information Retrieval in Structured Overlays." ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 33(1), 2003. DOI 10.1145/774763.774777.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall02/cs597C/P2P/Applications/pSearch.pdf (PDF re-extracted with PyMuPDF after the committed .txt copy proved unusable — see note below)
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall02/cs597C/P2P/Applications/pSearch.pdf
**Domain:** B

Note on source text: the committed file `sources/text/TANG-CCR-03.txt` renders every body-text character as a literal glyph-name token (for example the word "search" appears as `/D7/CT/CP/D6/CR/D0`), which is not readable text — the extractor that produced it failed on this PDF's embedded font. The title, author names, and affiliations at the top of that file are plain and confirm this is the correct paper. This entry was built by re-extracting `sources/pdf/TANG-CCR-03.pdf` locally with PyMuPDF, which renders readable (if letter-spaced) text; that re-extraction is the full-text source used for every claim below, not the committed .txt file.

### What it does
pSearch answers full-text and semantic queries in a peer-to-peer network by placing document representations at network locations chosen so that a query only has to contact nodes near the query's own representation, instead of contacting every node (query broadcast) or maintaining one global inverted index. It runs on eCAN, a hierarchical version of the CAN (Content-Addressable Network) distributed hash table (DHT) that the paper states routes in O(log n) hops and follows paths approximating the underlying Internet topology (this bound and the topology claim are attributed to the eCAN report, Xu and Zhang, HPL-2002-41, and not re-derived inside this paper). CAN organizes a logical address space as a d-dimensional Cartesian space (a d-torus) partitioned into zones, each owned by one or more nodes; an object's key is a point in this space, and the object is stored at the node owning the zone containing that point, so locating an object reduces to routing to the zone containing its key.

Two algorithms are defined, both keying eCAN storage locations off information-retrieval (IR) representations of documents. Peer-to-peer Vector Space Model (pVSM) computes each document's Vector Space Model (VSM) term vector — each vector element weighted by term frequency times inverse document frequency (TF*IDF) — takes the m most heavily weighted terms, hashes each term with a hash function h into a point in the CAN space, and stores (h(term), document-index) pairs at the nodes owning those points. A query hashes each of its own terms the same way, routes to the corresponding nodes, and each contacted node ranks locally using VSM before returning candidates to the querying node, which merges and re-ranks them globally.

Peer-to-peer Latent Semantic Indexing (pLSI) instead computes each document's semantic vector using Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI, a term-document matrix decomposition that maps documents into a lower-dimensional semantic space), and uses that vector directly as coordinates in a CAN space of matching dimensionality (l = k, where l is the LSI space's dimensionality and k is CAN's). A document's (semantic-vector, index) pair is stored via eCAN routing on that key; a query's semantic vector is computed the same way and routed to the corresponding zone, then the query is flooded outward to nodes within a radius r (set by a similarity threshold or a target result count) so that documents whose semantic vectors are close but not identical to the query's are still found. Because LSI semantic vectors are normalized to unit length and therefore lie on the surface of a hypersphere, a naive placement onto CAN coordinates is unbalanced; pLSI first transforms an l-dimensional semantic vector S = (s1, ..., sl) into an (l-1)-dimensional parameter vector using the polar-coordinate transform theta_j = arctan(s_(j+1) / sqrt(sum_{i=1}^{j} s_i^2)) for j = 1, ..., l-1 (the paper's Equation 1), and routes using the parameter vector instead of the raw semantic vector, because points on the unit hypersphere have only l-1 degrees of freedom.

Because LSI's semantic space typically has 100-300 dimensions and nearest-neighbor search degrades in that many dimensions (attributed to Weber, Schek, and Blott, VLDB 1998), pLSI reduces dimensionality with a multi-plane scheme: the lower elements of a parameter vector (which the paper states carry decreasing importance as a consequence of the underlying singular value decomposition, so earlier elements matter more) are partitioned into several low-dimensional subvectors, one per plane, and CAN's own dimensionality is set to that of a single plane. Each subvector is used as the DHT key for routing and flooding on its plane independently; each plane returns its own locally best-matching documents into a combined pre-selection set, which the query's originating node then re-ranks using the full semantic vector.

Node bootstrap for both algorithms is modified from plain CAN: a joining node picks a random document it is about to publish and routes its join request toward that document's own key (term vector position for pVSM, parameter vector position for pLSI) rather than to a uniformly random point. This ties a node's zone location to the content it is about to host, producing three effects the paper attributes to this choice: load balancing (each node ends up storing roughly the same number of index entries, because node density in the space tracks index density), index locality (a node's other published content tends to land in its own or neighboring zones), and query locality (a user's queries tend to be searched in zones near where that user's own content already lives, because a user's queries reflect the user's own interests).

### Measured results
| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| pVSM index-completeness on MEDLINE | Storing a document's index under its 30 most important terms achieves a result "as good as" full VSM: with high probability, at least one query term is among a document's top-30 stored terms whenever VSM itself would have returned that document | MEDLINE corpus, 1,033 documents; no node count, hardware, or run count stated for this specific experiment |
| pLSI accuracy vs. nodes visited (Figure 5) | Visiting about 0.4%-1.0% of nodes achieves approximately 95% accuracy (percentage overlap between documents returned by pLSI and by non-distributed LSI); accuracy improves further when more nodes are allowed to be visited | Text Retrieval Conference (TREC) corpus, 528,543 documents; network sizes of 1,000, 5,000, and 10,000 nodes plotted on the x-axis; parameters were tuned via what the paper calls "a large number of configurations in search of the right system parameters," with no run count or hardware stated |
| Multi-plane configuration found effective | 4-6 planes, each holding about 10-12 dimensions (elements) of the reduced parameter vector | Same TREC-corpus experiment as above; stated as the configuration the authors found effective after their parameter search, not as a bound with a stated confidence interval |
| Multi-plane pre-selection example | For a top-15-document query, the first three planes return 30, 20, and 10 documents respectively, for 60 documents total in the pre-selection set before final re-ranking | Illustrative parameterization given in the multi-plane description, not tied to a specific corpus run in the text extracted |

No message-count, bandwidth, or latency figures are given for pVSM; its only stated quantitative property is that the number of nodes it must visit for a query "is bounded by the number of terms in the query, which is usually small," a structural claim rather than a measured count.

### Parameters
- m (pVSM): number of most-heavily-weighted terms under which a document's index is stored; the paper states 30 achieves near-full-VSM recall on the MEDLINE experiment, and separately states m can vary per document (Section 3.4).
- l, k (pLSI): dimensionality of the LSI semantic space (l) and of the CAN Cartesian space (k); the paper sets l = k so the LSI vector can serve directly as CAN coordinates before the polar transform reduces it to l-1.
- LSI semantic-space dimensionality in practice: stated as 100-300 dimensions ("medium dimensionality"), the range that triggers the curse-of-dimensionality problem the multi-plane scheme addresses.
- Number of planes: 4-6, found effective by parameter search on the TREC/pLSI experiment.
- Dimensions (parameter-vector elements) per plane: about 10-12, found effective in the same search.
- Flooding radius r (pLSI): set per query by either a similarity threshold or the number of documents the user wants; no default numeric value is given.
- Per-plane result counts in the worked example: 30, 20, 10 for the first three planes when the user wants the top 15 documents (a fixed illustrative choice, not a derived or swept parameter).

### Stated limitations
The paper states outright that, "due to the space limit," further results and the authors' own suggestions for configuring the system are deferred to a later, separate publication — the evaluation in this paper is explicitly partial by the authors' own statement. Four problems are listed as needing solutions for pLSI (sphere distribution of semantic vectors producing unbalanced load, uneven distribution of semantic vectors on the hypersphere producing hot spots, the curse of dimensionality at 100-300 dimensions, and a global-statistics dependency), and the paper addresses each one but does not claim to have measured the residual hot-spot skew after its fixes are applied. A "global state problem" is stated for both pVSM and pLSI: both need global information (the term dictionary and inverse document frequency values for pVSM; comparable global statistics for pLSI) computed from a representative document sample and merged periodically over a combining tree that approximates the network topology; the paper states it expects this global state to change slowly, "at the rate of weeks or even months," an assumption rather than a measured update rate. Coarse-granularity indexing (clustering many documents at one node into fewer index entries via hierarchical k-means) and relevance feedback (both the conventional query-refinement use and an index-migration use, where a popular document's index is stored under more terms or moved closer to the queries that successfully retrieve it) are both listed under "Advanced Issues" as left for future work, with no evaluation given for either in this paper.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
pSearch requires eCAN as its routing substrate specifically, not a generic DHT: the load-balancing, index-locality, and query-locality properties described above all depend on eCAN's bootstrap process being modified so a joining node's position is chosen from a document it is about to publish, which is a change to the DHT's join protocol, not an add-on above an unmodified DHT. Both pVSM and pLSI require every participating node to compute IR representations locally (VSM term vectors with TF*IDF weights, or LSI semantic vectors via singular value decomposition) using a shared global dictionary and shared inverse-document-frequency statistics; producing and maintaining that shared global state requires a combining-tree mechanism sampling documents across the network, which the paper assumes changes slowly enough (weeks to months) that its own staleness is not a documented problem. pLSI's flooding step requires every node within a query's flooding radius r to receive and answer the query, so the radius, not just the destination node, determines message cost per query; the paper gives no formula relating r to node density or query accuracy beyond the empirical 0.4%-1.0%-of-nodes-for-95%-accuracy point in Figure 5. The multi-plane dimensionality reduction requires a document's index to be published independently to a node on every plane (4-6 separate publications per document in the effective configuration found), so storage and publication cost scale with plane count. Nothing in the extracted text states an assumption about participant honesty; the mechanism as described assumes every node that receives a routed or flooded query answers it correctly and returns its true local ranking.

### Contradicts
None found against another entry in this batch. The paper's own related-work section states that systems relying on heuristic forwarding without control over content placement — routing indices (Crespo and Garcia-Molina) and attenuated Bloom filters (Rhea and Kubiatowicz) — "may fail to retrieve important documents," an attributed comparison claim rather than a measurement pSearch itself ran against those systems.

### References worth retrieving
- Bergman, "The Deep Web: Surfacing Hidden Value," BrightPlanet, 2000 — foundational (motivating scale statistic, not a system).
- Berry, Drmac, Jessup, "Matrices, Vector Spaces, and Information Retrieval," SIAM Review 41(2), 1999 — foundational (VSM/LSI mathematical basis).
- Crespo and Garcia-Molina, "Routing Indices for Peer-to-Peer Systems," ICDCS, July 2002 — competing (heuristic query-forwarding alternative).
- Cuenca-Acuna and Nguyen, "Text-Based Content Search and Retrieval in Ad Hoc P2P Communities," International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Computing, May 2002 — competing (Bloom-filter-plus-flooding alternative; also the source pSearch cites for the naive-VSM-in-DHT term-storage cost problem).

- "JXTA Search," http://search.jxta.org — competing (centralized-hub query broker).
- Lv, Cao, Cohen, Li, Shenker, "Search and Replication in Unstructured Peer-to-Peer Networks," ICS '02 — already held in this corpus (foundational/competing; cited here for the claim that expanding-ring search and random walk outperform Gnutella query flooding).
- Milojicic, Kalogeraki, Lukose, Nagaraja, Pruyne, Richard, Rollins, Xu, "Peer-to-Peer Computing," HP Labs Technical Report HPL-2002-57, 2002 — foundational (survey).

## [TRAN-NSDI-09] Sybil-Resilient Online Content Voting
**Citation:** Dinh Nguyen Tran, Bonan Min, Jinyang Li, Lakshminarayanan Subramanian. "Sybil-Resilient Online Content Voting." USENIX NSDI, 2009.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi09/tech/full_papers/tran/tran.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi09/tech/full_papers/tran/tran.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SumUp aggregates votes on a piece of online content (a positive/negative or scalar-valued opinion
cast by a user, such as a "digg" on a news site) so that the count of bogus votes a Sybil attacker
can inject is bounded by the count of attack edges (edges in the trust network connecting an
honest user to an adversary-controlled node), independent of how many Sybil identities the
adversary creates behind those edges.

The mechanism computes an approximate max-flow (maximum flow, the largest amount of a
commodity that can be pushed through a capacitated network from a source to a set of sinks)
from a designated vote collector node to every voter on a given object, over the trust network,
with each trust link's capacity capped at one vote-carrying unit. Because a small number of
attack edges forms a narrow passage between the honest and Sybil regions of the trust graph
(the same sparse-cut assumption used in SybilGuard/SybilLimit-family defenses), a Sybil vote's
flow path is congested at that narrow passage regardless of how many further Sybil identities
exist downstream of it, capping the flow — and thus the vote count — that can pass. SumUp caps
the total votes collectible per object at a value Cmax, and assigns per-link capacity through
ticket distribution: the collector distributes Cmax tickets outward via breadth-first search, and
each link's capacity equals the number of tickets it carries. SumUp sets Cmax adaptively per
object, starting from an initial value (100 in the evaluation) and doubling it whenever collected
votes exceed a fraction ρ of the current Cmax, so Cmax tracks the true number of honest voters nv
without requiring nv to be known in advance; the paper derives that the resulting Cmax converges
to (2/ρ)(nv + eA), so an attacker's influence on the chosen Cmax is bounded by the additive term
eA (eA = attack-edge count), not by the number of Sybil identities. A fast greedy approximation
(not exact max-flow computation, which the paper measures as far slower) computes the vote-flow
paths in practice.

The paper proves two average-case bounds for a bounded-degree expander graph (a graph in which
every node has bounded degree and any two node subsets are connected by a number of edges close
to what random chance would predict): the expected attack capacity per attack edge is
1 + O((Cmax/n)·log(Cmax)), which becomes 1+o(1) when Cmax = O(n^α) for α<1 (n = node count in
the trust network); and the expected fraction of Cmax honest voters whose votes are collected is
(d−λ₂)/d · (1 − Cmax/n), where d is the graph's regular degree and λ₂ is the second-largest
eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix (a standard expander-quality measure — a graph mixes better,
and this fraction rises, as λ₂ moves further below d).

Link pruning caps each node's incoming-link count at a threshold d_in_thres (default 3) to bound
how many attack edges a single adversarial node close to the collector can exploit, while
preserving a spanning structure so no honest node is disconnected. A separate feedback mechanism
(Section 6, modeled on Ostra's credit-penalty design cited by the authors) lets the vote collector
mark specific votes as malicious; SumUp then raises a penalty value on every link along the path
to that voter (not just the final link, because the voter itself might be a re-used Sybil identity
rather than the actual attacker), reduces that link's future ticket allocation by an exponential
weighting function w(p_i) = 0.2^(p_i), and eliminates a link outright once its penalty exceeds a
threshold (default 5), re-admitting a previously pruned link to keep every honest node connected
to some path. Eliminated links are re-added at a slow rate over time to recover from a temporary
misclassification.

### Measured results

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Average attack capacity per attack edge stays close to 1 even as honest voters approach 10% of total nodes; SumUp collects >90% of honest votes across all three test networks with link pruning disabled | YouTube (446K nodes, 3.458M edges in the strongly connected component), Flickr (1.530M nodes, 21.399M edges), and a 3,000-node synthetic network (24.248K edges); eA=100 attack edges injected via 10 adversarial nodes each with 10 random honest-node links; Cmax adapted from initial 100 with ρ=0.5; averaged over 5 runs per data point |
| Pruning at d_in_thres=3 does not reduce the fraction of honest votes collected (still >90%) versus no pruning, while pruning above 3 attack edges per adversary sharply reduces average attack capacity per attack edge | YouTube network, same eA=100 attack setup |
| With greedy-search threshold of 20 non-greedy steps, SumUp collects >80% of honest votes; with non-greedy steps disabled entirely, SumUp still collects >40% of votes | Pruned YouTube graph |
| SumUp takes ~5ms to collect 1,000 votes from one vote collector on YouTube and Flickr; the exact Ford-Fulkerson max-flow algorithm takes 50 seconds to collect the same 1,000 votes on YouTube | Single AMD Opteron 2.5GHz CPU, 8GB memory |
| SumUp's average attack capacity is ≈1 vote per attack edge at <10% honest-voter fraction, versus SybilLimit's ≈30 bogus votes per attack edge under the same conditions, though both carry the same O(log n) asymptotic bound per attack edge | Un-pruned YouTube network; SybilLimit implemented with manually-determined parameters w=15, r=3000 |
| Under continuous adversarial vote casting with feedback enabled (worst case: 1 of the collector's 4 outgoing links is an attack edge, 400 honest voters per timestep), attack capacity drops from an initial CA=800 (=Cmax/4, Cmax=3200) to 97 after one feedback round, 90% of attack edges eliminated after 12 timesteps, all attack edges eliminated after 22 timesteps total, while honest votes collected stay above 80% throughout | YouTube graph |
| Deployed on a crawled Digg dataset: 3,002,907 nodes / 5,063,244 edges in the full "follow" network, 466,326 nodes / 4,908,958 edges in the strongly connected component (SCC); SCC holds 15% of nodes but 88% of votes | Digg voting trace 2004/12/01–2008/09/21 for diggs (6,494,987 submitted articles, 137,480 marked popular), and a separate bury-vote stream from 2008/08/13–2008/09/15 (38,033 articles, 5,794 with bury data) |
| For 0.5% of popular articles, SumUp (run with Digg's founder as vote collector) collects less than 50% of the votes an article received before being marked popular, versus the >90% collection rate the paper's synthetic-network experiments predict | Digg dataset, popular articles only |
| Manual classification of 30 randomly sampled suspicious articles per threshold (20%/30%/40%/50% of expected diggs collected) found: advertisements (5,4,2,1 respectively), phishing (1,0,0,0), obscure political articles (2,2,0,0), articles with >30% newly-registered voters (11,7,8,10), articles with fewer than 50 total diggs (1,3,6,4), and no obvious attack evidence in roughly half the samples (10,14,14,15) | Digg dataset; article counts behind each threshold were 41, 131, 300, 800 respectively |
| Lower fraction of diggs collected by SumUp before popularity correlates with a higher average bury-vote count after popularity | 5,794 popular articles with bury data available |
| 5 suspicious articles found where a single voter's actions correlate with ~30 other identities voting on the same article, all created the same day as the article's submission, with similar usernames | Digg dataset, manual follow-up inspection |

### Parameters
- Cmax (maximum votes collectible per object): initial value 100, doubled whenever collected votes exceed ρ·Cmax; converges to (2/ρ)(nv+eA) where nv is the true honest-voter count.
- ρ (Cmax doubling threshold fraction): default 0.5, derived to stay above the worst-case adversary flow fraction x (defined as CA=x·Cmax) so that Cmax cannot be driven to infinity; the paper states this requires ρ>x and that no vote-aggregation scheme can defend when x≥0.5 (adversary controls a majority of the collector's immediate links).
- d_in_thres (incoming-link cap under pruning): default 3; tested against no pruning and against 1 in the sensitivity experiment (Figure 6).
- Non-greedy-step threshold t (for the greedy max-flow approximation): tested at 0, 10, 20, and full (exact) max-flow.
- Link-elimination penalty threshold: default 5 (link removed once accumulated penalty exceeds this).
- Weight function for capacity adjustment under feedback: w(p_i) = 0.2^(p_i), chosen because it satisfies both a monotonicity requirement (higher penalty → lower weight) and a ratio-invariance requirement under equal additional penalties.
- eA (attack edges injected in synthetic evaluation): fixed at 100, via 10 adversarial nodes each with 10 random honest-node links.
- SybilLimit comparison parameters: w=15 (random-walk length), r=3000 (number of walks), stated as manually determined, not derived by a documented search procedure.

### Stated limitations
The paper states its formal security analysis (Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.2) assumes the trust
network is a bounded-degree expander graph with randomly placed attack edges, and explicitly
separates this from the worst case where the vote collector is directly adjacent to adversarial
nodes, which it states can raise attack capacity to "a significant fraction of Cmax" — addressed
only by the separate feedback mechanism (Section 6), not by the base max-flow design. It states
the base design (Section 5) "does not address the worst case scenario" and also does not, by
itself, prevent an adversary from casting up to eA bogus votes on every object in the system
simultaneously — feedback-driven link elimination reduces this over time but only for objects on
which feedback is actually given, described as available for "a very small subset of objects."
For the Digg deployment, the paper states there is no ground truth for which Digg users are
Sybils, so its attack-detection results rest on manual sampling and correlation with independently
collected bury-vote data, not on verified ground truth. It states bury-vote data does not reveal
the identity of the user who cast the bury, preventing evaluation of SumUp's feedback mechanism on
real Digg data. It states link pruning assumes a well-connected node is a signal an adversary can
exploit, but that pruning is a heuristic — "we speculate that the more honest neighbors an
adversarial node has, the easier for it to trick an honest node into trusting it" — not a proven
property. It states a distributed peer-to-peer implementation of SumUp requires each node to
obtain a complete view of the trust network (via gossip or crawling), which the paper explicitly
distinguishes as an easier problem than the decentralized-routing designs used by Ostra and
SybilLimit, where each node knows only a local neighborhood; SumUp's decentralized design is
described only as a sketch ("we outline one such distributed design"), not evaluated.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a pre-existing trust network in which an attacker cannot easily obtain many attack edges;
the paper states this as the sole requirement on the network's source (social graph, follow graph,
etc.), without requiring a specific mixing-time bound beyond what its expander-graph proofs assume.
Requires the vote collector to hold or be able to traverse the trust network to compute max-flow
paths from itself to voters — this is inherently a centralized-per-collector computation in the
base design, with the decentralized variant requiring every node to hold a full crawled or
gossip-assembled copy of the trust graph. Requires an object-ranking system elsewhere in the
stack to consume SumUp's aggregated vote counts and values; the paper states final ranking-
algorithm design is explicitly out of scope. Requires feedback (a collector's after-the-fact
negative marking of specific votes as malicious) to bound worst-case attack capacity below eA and
to defend against an adversary adjacent to the collector; without feedback, the system's guarantee
is only the average-case bound from Theorem 5.1, not a worst-case one. A distributed peer-to-peer
deployment additionally requires a Sybil-resilient distributed hash table if votes are retrieved
from one rather than gathered by flooding, which the paper states as an unaddressed dependency
resolved by citing separate prior Sybil-resilient DHT work.

### Contradicts
None found among the papers in this corpus.

### References worth retrieving

- H. Yu, P. Gibbons, M. Kaminsky, F. Xiao. "SybilLimit: A Near-Optimal Social Network Defense against Sybil Attacks." IEEE S&P 2008 — competing (directly compared in Figure 10; SumUp measures roughly 30x lower attack capacity per attack edge under equal asymptotic bounds)

## [TRAUDT-ICDCS-21] FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor
**Citation:** Matthew Traudt, Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson. "FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor." IEEE ICDCS, 2021. DOI 10.1109/ICDCS51616.2021.00044.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.robgjansen.com/publications/flashflow-icdcs2021.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.robgjansen.com/publications/flashflow-icdcs2021.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
FlashFlow measures the true forwarding capacity of a Tor relay so the Tor network can assign load-balancing weights that a relay cannot inflate by lying about its own bandwidth. Tor relays currently self-report bandwidth to Bandwidth Authorities (BW Auths), which combine the self-report with a small active download test (TorFlow); a relay controls the self-reported number and prior work showed this self-report can be forged to inflate a relay's assigned traffic share. FlashFlow replaces the self-report with a load test large enough to force the relay to carry all the traffic it claims to be able to carry. A FlashFlow team, which constitutes one BW Auth, has a coordinator and one or more measurers. The coordinator opens an authenticated connection (keyed by a public key distributed in the Tor consensus) to each measurer and to the target relay, then divides the total measurement traffic across m measurers, each running k_i = max(1, c_i/p_i) modified Tor processes, where c_i is the measurer's CPU-core count and p_i is its expected number of parallel measurements that period. Each measurer sends and receives normal-looking Tor cells to and from the target over measurement circuits; sent cell contents are randomly generated and a fraction p of returned cells are checked byte-for-byte, so a relay that forges a response (skips decryption, or replies before receiving) is caught with probability approaching 1 as more responses are checked, and a relay forging k responses evades detection with probability only (1−p)^k. The team measures a candidate capacity z; if z is small enough relative to the team's allocated capacity a_i (specifically z < Σ_i a_i (1−ε1)/g), the measurement is accepted as accurate because the true capacity x must then lie in the interval ((1−ε1)x, (1+ε2)x); otherwise the allocated capacity is at least doubled (z0 = max(z, 2z0)) and the relay is remeasured. New relays without a prior estimate start from the 75th-percentile capacity observed across the network in the preceding month. Because the target relay also carries its normal client traffic during the load test, the design caps the relay's self-reported normal traffic at a ratio r of the total measured traffic during the measurement window, so a relay cannot claim high capacity by counting client traffic it never actually forwarded beyond that ratio. Measurement timing per relay is drawn from a schedule known only to the BW Auths and generated from a shared random seed each 24-hour measurement period, so a relay cannot predict when it will be tested and inflate capacity only during that window; results from a majority of BW Auths are aggregated by taking the median, following Tor's existing directory-authority trust model.

### Measured results
| Metric | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Malicious-relay capacity inflation bound (analytic) | At most 1.33x true capacity, versus a demonstrated 177x for TorFlow | Derived from the traffic-ratio cap 1/(1−r) with recommended r = 0.25; the 177x figure is cited from the PeerFlow paper's demonstrated attack against TorFlow |
| Measurement accuracy, Internet experiments | Within 11% of ground truth (0.89-1.11x capacity) in 95% of experiments; within 20% in 99.8% of experiments | Real Internet hosts in Fremont CA, Santa Rosa CA, Washington DC, Bangalore, and Amsterdam; target relay throughput limits of 10, 250, 500, 750 Mbit/s and unlimited; each configuration run 7 times over 24 hours, 30-second measurement slots, multiplier g = 2.25 |
| Ground-truth capacity, single relay | 890 Mbit/s maximum median throughput, consuming 95-100% of one CPU core | Lab-controlled relay on the US-SW host measured by supporting Tor processes on the remaining lab machines |
| Tor single-relay processing ceiling | 1.25 Gbit/s maximum, using 20 TCP sockets, Tor reaching 100% CPU on one core | 120-second lab measurement designed to minimize network, TCP, and Tor flow-control limits; consistent with the fastest publicly claimed relay capacity, 998 Mbit/s in July 2019 |
| Background-traffic ratio cap behavior | When r <= 50/250 = 0.2, background traffic during measurement is consistently held to 250r; above that ratio background traffic stays at its unconstrained rate of ~50 Mbit/s | Real Tor relay run for 60 days to earn the Guard flag and attract genuine client traffic, capacity-limited to 250 Mbit/s, measured by one FlashFlow measurer in Amsterdam, ratios r tested between 0.1 and 0.5 |
| Full-network measurement speed (simulation) | Median 5 hours (599 30-second slots; min 4.9, max 5.1 hours) to measure the entire network, median 6,419 relays (min 6,355, max 6,528), median total capacity 608 Gbit/s (min 592, max 621) | Simulated using archived Tor consensuses/descriptors for each day of July 2019, greedy scheduler, one team of 3 measurers at 1 Gbit/s each, excess factor f = 2.84 |
| New-relay measurement speed (simulation) | Median 30 seconds to measure new relays in a consensus (min 0 minutes, max 13 minutes); median of 3 new relays per consensus (min 0, max 98) | Same July 2019 consensus replay; new-relay capacity estimate set to the 75th-percentile advertised bandwidth from June 2019 descriptors, 51 Mbit/s |
| Added network load | 5.89 TiB/day per FlashFlow team, about 0.3% of the ~1,965 TiB/day the Tor network forwarded in June-August 2019 | Computed as f * C * t with f = 2.84, C = 608 Gbit/s network capacity, t = 30 s measurement duration |
| Network capacity/weight error (Shadow simulation) | FlashFlow: 14% network capacity error, 4% network weight error; TorFlow: 29% network weight error (86% relative reduction by FlashFlow); median and interquartile relay capacity error for FlashFlow both 16% | Shadow discrete-event simulator, private test network 5% the size of the public Tor network: 3 Directory Authorities, 328 relays sampled from January 2019 consensus, 397 TGen clients modeling 40k Tor users' traffic, plus 40 benchmark clients |
| Transfer-time improvement | Median transfer time decreases by 15% (50 KiB), 29% (1 MiB), 37% (5 MiB) versus TorFlow at 100% traffic load; standard deviation decreases by 55%, 61%, 41% respectively | Same Shadow simulation, three load levels tested (100%, 115%, 130% of normal client traffic), timeouts set to 15/60/120 seconds for the three file sizes |
| Transfer timeout rate | Median rate of transfer timeouts decreases by 100% (effectively eliminated) for FlashFlow at all three load levels, versus 5%, 10%, 23% timeout rates for TorFlow at 100%, 115%, 130% load | Same Shadow simulation |
| Throughput scaling under added load | Increasing client load by 15%/30% increases median Tor network throughput by 15%/29% under FlashFlow weights but only 12%/18% under TorFlow weights | Same Shadow simulation |

### Parameters
- Excess capacity factor f = g(1+ε2)/(1−ε1); used value f = 2.84 for the July 2019 simulation, derived from g = 2.25, ε1 = 0.20, ε2 = 0.05.
- Number of measurement sockets s = 160 (value that maximized throughput on the slowest lab host; determined empirically, range not stated).
- Capacity-estimate multiplier g = 2.25 (smallest g found sufficient for accuracy in the paper's own tuning experiments).
- Measurement duration t = 30 seconds (chosen as, in the authors' words, a reasonable balance of time-to-result versus accuracy).
- Error-bound parameters ε1 = 0.20, ε2 = 0.05.
- Background-traffic ratio r: recommended value 0.25; range tested 0.1-0.5 in the client-background-traffic experiment.
- Measurement period p = 24 hours.
- Response-check probability p (fraction of returned cells verified byte-for-byte): a design variable, no single numeric default stated in the extracted text.
- Measurement team capacity in the simulation study: 3 measurers, 1 Gbit/s each (3 Gbit/s total).
- New-relay initial capacity estimate: 75th-percentile advertised bandwidth among all relays over the preceding month (51 Mbit/s in the July 2019 dataset).

### Stated limitations
The authors state a malicious relay controlling multiple IP addresses on one physical machine can be measured separately at different times and obtain a capacity estimate equal to the shared machine's full capacity for each of its aliases, a Sybil-style limitation FlashFlow shares with TorFlow; their proposed mitigation is to measure suspected co-resident relays simultaneously and average the result, not yet built into the described system. A second stated limitation: because measurement slots are short (30 seconds), FlashFlow may capture a host's burst throughput rather than its sustainable capacity where an ISP or hosting provider throttles sustained rates below burst rates; the authors argue the median of separately scheduled measurements from different BW Auths mitigates this when the burst is due to shared-resource congestion, and that a rate limit applied faster than 15 seconds would still be caught. The threat model explicitly excludes an adversary that controls an autonomous-system-level network position, an adversary that runs a Sybil attack, and an adversary that can change its relay's capacity quickly; the security analysis is stated to hold only under an honest majority of BW Auths (and, transitively, of Directory Authorities that each trust their own BW Auth). The authors state FlashFlow measures capacity, not whether a relay actually forwards real client traffic, and note a relay could send little to no client traffic on non-measurement circuits while reporting accurate self-measured capacity; they call this an additional limitation shared with TorFlow and leave detecting such misbehavior as future work. Future work sections list the unresolved problem of detecting co-resident relays automatically (by IP address or autonomous-system-number heuristics) and combining FlashFlow's secure capacity floor with additional, insecure dynamic measurements (per-relay CPU or network utilization) to further refine weights without reopening the inflation vulnerability.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
FlashFlow requires the same Directory Authority (DirAuth) and Bandwidth Authority (BW Auth) infrastructure Tor already runs: DirAuths distribute the coordinator's public key in the network consensus, and a majority of DirAuths (and, in the paper's recommended configuration, their associated BW Auths) must be honest for the security bound to hold. It requires the BW Auths to hold sufficiently synchronized clocks to coordinate a shared, secret measurement schedule generated from a jointly produced random seed (the paper points to Tor's existing secure-randomness protocol as the source of that seed). It requires the measurement team's aggregate bandwidth capacity to exceed the highest capacity among target relays by the factor f = g(1+ε2)/(1−ε1), meaning the rest of the system must provision and fund measurer bandwidth (3 Gbit/s per team in the deployed-scale simulation) as an ongoing operational cost, separate from relay bandwidth. It requires the target relay to run modified Tor software able to accept authenticated measurement connections and to be reachable simultaneously by the number of measurers a given test allocates. It requires an existing weight-consumption mechanism — Tor's v3bw file format and consensus-voting process — to accept FlashFlow's capacity and weight outputs unchanged, since FlashFlow only replaces how a BW Auth produces those numbers, not how DirAuths use them.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. Against the specific claim it is designed to supersede: the paper's own related-work section cites PeerFlow's demonstrated 177x weight-inflation attack against TorFlow and PeerFlow's own analytic self-inflation bound of 4.5x for its recommended parameters, both of which FlashFlow's inflation bound of 1.33x is measured against directly in Table II of the source; this is the authors' own comparison, not a disagreement between independent measurements of the same system.

### References worth retrieving
- **Foundational**: Tor project. "TorFlow" [28] — the currently deployed system FlashFlow replaces; described in the paper's Background section rather than cited as a separate retrievable paper.
- **Competing**: PeerFlow, cited as reference [23] — reports the 177x TorFlow weight-inflation attack and its own analytic inflation bound of 4.5x under recommended parameters and 2/τ in general (τ = trusted relay-weight fraction); produces capacity lower bounds via peer-reported byte counts, needs 14+ days to measure the largest 96.8% of relays.
- **Competing**: Snader, Borisov. EigenSpeed peer-measurement system, cited as reference [32], plus a demonstrated attack achieving 21.5x weight inflation with 20% trusted relays (by number or weight), and separately a "targeted liar attack" reaching 7.4-28.1x depending on trusted-relay fraction.
- **Competing**: Reference [33], Snader and Borisov — a simpler median-of-pairwise-speed variant of EigenSpeed, stated to be vulnerable to a Sybil attack because it uses an unweighted median.
- **Competing**: Reference [9], "SmarTor" — decentralizes BW Auth operation via blockchain and trusted execution environments but keeps TorFlow's file-download measurement technique, so it is stated to remain vulnerable to the same bandwidth-inflation attacks as TorFlow.
- **Competing**: Reference [25], "Simple Bandwidth Scanner" — an easier-to-maintain reimplementation producing the same results as TorFlow, addressing none of its security weaknesses.
- **Competing**: Reference [13], "TightRope" — assumes capacity weights already exist and instead optimizes path selection for load balancing using differential privacy over current relay load.
- **Competing**: Reference [36], Wang et al. — client-side lightweight active latency measurement to detect and avoid congested relays, an alternative mechanism to server-side capacity measurement.
- **Attack**: References [10, 12, 23, 34] — collectively cited as prior work demonstrating TorFlow's self-report and weight-inflation vulnerabilities; [34] and [23] specifically demonstrate 89x and 177x inflation attacks respectively.

## [TRAUTWEIN-INFOCOM-24] IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide

**Citation:** Dennis Trautwein, Yiluo Wei, Yiannis Psaras, Moritz Schubotz, Ignacio Castro, Bela Gipp, Gareth Tyson. "IPFS in the Fast Lane: Accelerating Record Storage with Optimistic Provide." IEEE INFOCOM, 2024. DOI 10.1109/INFOCOM52122.2024.10621404.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://gipplab.uni-goettingen.de/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/trautwein2024.pdf
**Source URL:** https://gipplab.uni-goettingen.de/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/trautwein2024.pdf
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
Optimistic Provide shortens the time a Kademlia-based InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) node takes to store a provider record (a PUT operation: publishing that this node holds a given piece of content) by ending the record-placement process as soon as it is statistically confident it has found the right peers, instead of waiting for every peer contacted to confirm. The unmodified (classic) PUT operation runs in two phases: a DHT walk that queries progressively closer peers until the three currently-closest-known peers have all responded, and a follow-up phase that pushes the record to the 20 peers closest to the target key found during the walk. The paper's own measurement (section III) finds the DHT walk consumes over 90% of total PUT latency in most cases, because the walk's own termination rule waits for confirmation from the three closest known peers even after the eventual 20 recipients have already been discovered; an unreachable peer among those three stalls the whole walk while the algorithm backtracks to more distant peers (a behavior the paper calls DHT Walk backtracking). Optimistic Provide replaces this rule with three changes. First, it computes, using an estimate of the total DHT population size, a maximum XOR distance from the target key such that any peer discovered inside that distance is a member of the true closest-20 set with probability p_individual; a peer discovered within that distance is stored to immediately, without waiting for the walk to finish. Second, it computes a second maximum average distance for the currently-known set of 20 closest peers such that, with probability p_set, that set already equals the true closest-20 set; once the known set's average distance falls under that threshold, the walk terminates early instead of waiting for the three-closest-peer confirmation. Third, since ending the walk early skips backtracking and can leave a slow or unreachable peer among the 20 recipients in the follow-up phase, the follow-up phase itself returns control to the caller once k' of the 20 contacted peers have responded (k'=5 chosen in this paper's evaluation, tunable), while the remaining queries continue asynchronously in the background rather than being canceled. The distance thresholds behind steps one and two require a live estimate of the total number of peers in the DHT; the paper derives this from Kademlia's own XOR-distance order statistics (the expected distance to the i-th-closest peer among N total peers is 1/(N+1) times i, so measuring several order-statistic distances and fitting a line through the origin yields an estimate of N), sampled for free from the routing-table-refresh lookups every node already performs, corrected for a keyspace-density bias that would otherwise skew the estimate.

### Measured results

| Result | Value | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline PUT latency percentiles, IPFS, classic algorithm (done strategy: wait for all 20 follow-up responses) | 50th 6.3 s, 90th 20.6 s, 95th 49.8 s | Two servers in central Europe, two-day measurement window; classic sample size 8,502 |
| Baseline PUT latency, first measurement (walk + follow-up breakdown) | 8,503 measurements | One host in eu-central-1 AWS region, 2023-06-06 to 2023-06-07; DHT walk accounts for over 90% of total latency in the majority of cases |
| Optimal (theoretical minimum) DHT walk termination | Terminates several seconds earlier than the actual walk in most cases; only 4.3% of PUT operations experience no delay at all between discovering all 20 closest peers and the follow-up phase | Same eu-central-1 measurement |
| Median time to discover final PUT recipients (before follow-up phase begins) | 1.3 s | Same measurement, cited as motivation for the design in section IV |
| PUT latency, IPFS, Optimistic Provide vs. classic (done strategy) | 50th: 5.1 s (vs 6.3 s classic), 90th: 8.7 s (vs 20.6 s), 95th: 15.4 s (vs 49.8 s); speed-ups 1.2x/2.3x/3.2x | Two servers in central Europe, two-day window; optimistic sample size 11,964, classic 8,502 |
| PUT latency, IPFS, Optimistic Provide (return strategy, k'=5) vs. classic (return strategy, 15th of 20 responses) | 50th: 0.51 s (vs 5.8 s classic), 90th: 0.80 s (vs 15.8 s), 95th: 0.92 s (vs 43.0 s); speed-ups 11.3x/19.7x/46.7x | Same setup |

### Parameters
- p_individual (probability threshold for immediately accepting a single discovered peer as a member of the closest-20 set): chosen as 0.9 in evaluation; stated as freely tunable.
- p_set (probability threshold for accepting the current known 20-closest-peer set as the true closest-20 set, computed via the expected distance of the hypothetical 10.5th-closest peer): chosen as 0.9 in evaluation; stated as tunable.
- k' (number of the 20 follow-up-phase peers whose responses are awaited before returning control to the caller, remaining queries continuing asynchronously): chosen as 5, based on a cited prior study finding that lowering k to 15 in classic IPFS record replication has negligible impact on availability; stated as configurable.
- Network size estimation rolling window t_window: 2 hours.
- Network size estimation minimum/maximum sample counts S_min / S_max: 16 / 192 lookups (S_min corresponds to one full routing-table refresh; S_max corresponds to one full refresh every 10 minutes for 2 hours); both stated as tunable and affecting estimation accuracy.
- Kademlia identifier length L: 256 bits (used in the order-statistic-based network-size derivation).
- Maximum bucket level k_max for the bias-correction weighting function: 20 for IPFS.
- Routing-table refresh depth in the deployed Kubo and Lotus clients: the first 16 of 256 possible buckets, each refresh issuing 16 lookups.
- DHT walk timeout (both approaches, regional experiment): 3 minutes.
- Kubo (IPFS reference implementation) version supporting Optimistic Provide: v0.20.0 and later.

### Stated limitations
The authors state as future work an investigation of how severe network conditions — network partitioning, high churn, and Sybil attacks — affect Optimistic Provide and its component mechanisms; none of these conditions are evaluated in this paper. They state as future work a deeper investigation into the cause of the observed difference in RPC success-rate variation between the IPFS and Filecoin networks, which this paper does not explain. The network-size estimation method systematically underestimates true network size (6.0% for IPFS, 13.5% for Filecoin, both relative to a full-crawl baseline) because it reuses routing-table-refresh lookups that are biased toward the requesting peer's local keyspace neighborhood and excludes peers made undialable by the same backtracking behavior the paper's mechanism is designed around; the authors state this underestimate does not measurably harm PUT performance in their results but note that a deployment needing more accurate absolute counts would need a separately-derived scaling factor, since the underestimate is consistent across measurement points rather than fully corrected. The full network-size crawl used as the accuracy baseline is itself described only as covering the peers the crawler could find and dial, not as a verified ground truth; the paper treats it as the best available comparison rather than an exact count.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Every participating peer must implement the same threshold-based termination logic to be optimistically stored to during another peer's DHT walk, which the paper achieves by upstreaming the change into the shared go-libp2p-kad-dht implementation used by both the IPFS reference client Kubo and the Filecoin reference client Lotus; the paper states full backward compatibility is maintained, meaning a peer without the update still participates correctly in a walk initiated by an updated peer, but does not state what performance a walk initiated by an updated peer against entirely non-updated peers would achieve. Every peer must independently estimate the live network size to compute the distance thresholds; this estimate is derived only from data the peer's own routing-table-refresh queries already produce, so a peer skipping refreshes or refreshing fewer than the S_min=16 lookups per rolling 2-hour window operates on state accuracy the paper does not evaluate. Both the p_individual and p_set thresholds assume DHT peer identifiers are uniformly randomly distributed across the identifier space (stated explicitly in section IV-B); a system where identifiers cluster non-uniformly (through adversarial identifier selection or a non-uniform assignment scheme) would compute unreliable proximity thresholds, and the paper's stated future work on Sybil-attack impact has not yet examined this. Reducing k' below 20 in the follow-up phase requires accepting that a record's full 20-way replication is asynchronous rather than confirmed at return time; a caller that needs the paper's own PUT operation to guarantee replication before returning must use the done strategy, whose latency the paper measures separately and which is markedly slower.

### Contradicts
None found. This paper's own comparison to Trautwein et al.'s earlier IPFS measurement study (cited as reference [5], "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web") is presented as complementary, not contradictory: this paper describes that earlier study as reporting GET performance as "already satisfactory" while this paper's contribution addresses PUT latency specifically. That earlier paper is the source of the 112-second 90th-percentile content-storing latency figure cited secondhand in ZHANG-FC-23 in this corpus; ZHANG-FC-23 should be checked against the original IPFS measurement paper directly rather than against this Optimistic Provide paper, which measures a modified protocol and different latency figures (6.3-49.8 s baseline).

### References worth retrieving
- Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web," cited as [5] — foundational (the prior IPFS measurement study this paper's PUT-performance motivation and network-size-estimation baseline build on; the likely source of the 90th-percentile content-storing latency figure cited secondhand elsewhere in this corpus, and it should be retrieved and checked directly rather than assumed identical to this paper)
- Stutzbach, Rejaie — competing (cited as [34], a Kademlia performance model with proposed enhancements including lookup parallelization)
- Falkner, Piatek, John, Krishnamurthy, Anderson — cited as [36], network-aware peer selection for DHT performance — competing
- Binzenhofer, Staehle, Henjes or similar — cited as [37]/[38]/[39]/[40]/[41]/[42], network-size-estimation methods (custom protocol, explicit keyspace sampling, Sample & Collide, HopsSampling, Gossip-based Aggregation) — competing (alternative network-size-estimation approaches this paper's own method is built against and improves on for per-peer overhead)
- The proximity-model source cited as [17], the order-statistic-based network-size-estimation technique this paper's own derivation builds directly on — foundational

### Verbatim extracts
- "PUT latencies of 6.3 s, 20.6 s, and 49.8 s for the 50th, 90th and 95th percentile" (section III)
- "the DHT walk is the primary contributor to the overall latency, making up over 90% of the total time" (section III)
- "Only 4.3% of PUT operations do not experience any delay" (section III)
- "we choose k' = 5 based on previous studies" (section IV-A)
- "Individual peers, on average, estimate the network size to be 6.0% and 13.5% lower" (section V-B)
- "Our approach uses at most 56% the networking resources than the baseline" (section V)
- "we plan to investigate the impact of severe network conditions such as network partitioning, high churn, or Sybil attacks" (Conclusion)

## [TYAGI-EUROCRYPT-22] A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications
**Citation:** Nirvan Tyagi, Sofía Celi, Thomas Ristenpart, Nick Sullivan, Stefano Tessaro, Christopher A. Wood. "A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications." EUROCRYPT, 2022. DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-07085-3_23.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/864.pdf
**Source URL:** https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/864.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
A partially oblivious pseudorandom function (POPRF) lets a client obtain a keyed function output on a private input `x` bound to a public input `t` (called a tag), while the server that holds the key learns neither `x` nor which output resulted from which request. "Partially oblivious" distinguishes the tag `t`, visible to both parties, from `x`, hidden from the server. The paper's construction, 3HashSDHI, computes `Ev(sk, t, x) = H2(x, H1(x)^(1/(sk+H2'(t))))`, combining the 2HashDH oblivious pseudorandom function (OPRF) of Jarecki, Kiayias, and Krawczyk (JARECKI-ASIACRYPT-14) with the Dodis-Yampolskiy pseudorandom function. To request an evaluation, the client blinds its input as `B = H1(x)^r` for random `r`, sends `B` and the public tag `t`; the server returns `B' = B^(1/(sk+H2'(t)))`; the client unblinds by computing `(B')^(1/r)` and finishing with `H2`. The server additionally produces a Chaum-Pedersen non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proof of discrete-log equality so the client can verify the response was computed under the claimed public key, without which a malicious server could return arbitrary values undetected. Security is proved in the random oracle model by reduction to a new assumption, one-more gap strong Diffie-Hellman inversion, itself shown implied by the q-discrete-log assumption in the algebraic group model.

Applied to Privacy Pass token issuance, binding a token to a public tag `t` (for example a coarse timestamp such as the current day, or a client autonomous system number) lets a server enforce that a client's tokens are scoped to that tag without needing per-scope secret keys or client-verified key rotation.

### Measured results
All measurements from a Go implementation using the CIRCL cryptographic library, ristretto255 group (bn256 curve for the pairing-based Pythia baseline), on a 2.6 GHz 6-core Intel Core i7 with 32 GB RAM, macOS 10.15.7, averaged over 1000 measurements per operation, input size L fixed at 16 bytes, tag size T varied at 1, 8, and 64 bytes.

| Scheme | T (bytes) | KeyGen (µs) | KeyVerify (µs) | Req (µs) | BlindEv (µs) | Finalize (µs) | Full Ev (µs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2HashDH | 1 | 0 | 0 | 73 | 222 | 392 | 77 |
| 2HashDH | 64 | 0 | 0 | 84 | 256 | 447 | 89 |
| 3HashSDHI | 1 | 0 | 0 | 85 | 369 | 527 | 125 |
| 3HashSDHI | 64 | 0 | 0 | 75 | 328 | 471 | 110 |
| Pythia | 1 | 168 | 0 | 849 | 4068 | 6070 | 2871 |
| Pythia | 64 | 171 | 0 | 809 | 3922 | 5849 | 2768 |
| ABVOPRF | 1 | 294 | 292 | 74 | 517 | 684 | 370 |
| ABVOPRF | 64 | 15053 | 19196 | 80 | 15305 | 19702 | 15163 |

Excluding precomputable operations (the KeyGen/KeyVerify columns above), 3HashSDHI Finalize cost at T=64 bytes is 472 µs against 447 µs for 2HashDH (approximately 25% relative overhead, per the paper's own framing including all operations), 5843 µs for Pythia, and 19721 µs for ABVOPRF — an order of magnitude above 3HashSDHI at large tag size, attributed by the authors to ABVOPRF's tag-length-linear proof cost.

### Parameters
- Group: ristretto255 for 2HashDH, 3HashSDHI, ABVOPRF; bn256 pairing-friendly curve for Pythia.
- Input size L: fixed at 16 bytes across all measurements.
- Tag size T: 1, 8, 64 bytes, the tested range.
- Averaging: 1000 measurements per operation, on the stated single-machine hardware.

### Stated limitations
3HashSDHI does not support key rotation: distributing per-tag rotation tokens analogous to Pythia's compact rotation token trivially reveals both the old and new secret keys, because the tag hashes are publicly computable. The authors state finding a pairing-free POPRF that also supports key rotation is an open problem. The one-more gap strong Diffie-Hellman inversion assumption's tightness under the algebraic group model reduction is stated as open to further tightening. Binding a token to a public tag reduces the anonymity set of redemption to only the clients issued tokens under that same tag value, a property the authors state holds for the key-rotation alternative as well; the authors state that choosing how to use the tag "requires care and further work to identify best practices." Extending the construction to also carry a private metadata bit (indistinguishable-but-server-decodable, as in Kreuter et al., KREUTER-FC-22's antecedent construction) is left to future work; the authors state a randomized variant would likely be needed, since a deterministic pseudorandom function cannot achieve indistinguishability between private-metadata values.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Verification of a POPRF response requires the client to have the server's public key `pk` in advance and to run the Chaum-Pedersen zero-knowledge proof check on every response; without this check a malicious server can return an arbitrary value. Any protocol using tag-scoped tokens (for example a rate-limiting scheme selecting `t` as an autonomous-system number or time window) needs a mechanism, external to the POPRF itself, for client and server to agree on the tag value before the request — the POPRF does not negotiate or authenticate the tag. Because binding to a tag narrows the anonymity set to clients sharing that tag, any system composing this primitive with an unlinkability requirement must independently bound how coarse-grained the tag partition is; the paper does not supply that bound. The random-oracle-model proof requires hash functions `H1`, `H2` in the construction to be modeled as random oracles; a real deployment must instantiate them with cryptographic hash functions believed to behave as such.

### Contradicts
None found.

### References worth retrieving
- **JARECKI-ASIACRYPT-14** [JKK14] — already in this corpus; 2HashDH OPRF, foundational.
- **[JKX18]** Jarecki, Krawczyk, Xu, "OPAQUE: an asymmetric PAKE protocol secure against pre-computation attacks," EUROCRYPT 2018 — foundational, one of this paper's three target applications.
- **[DGS+18]** Davidson, Goldberg, Sullivan, Tankersley, Valsorda, "Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously," PoPETs 2018(3) — foundational, defines Privacy Pass and the hoarding/farming attack this paper addresses.
- **[ECS+15]** Everspaugh, Chatterjee, Scott, Juels, Ristenpart, "The Pythia PRF Service," USENIX Security 2015 — competing pairing-based construction, directly benchmarked against.
- **[HIJ+21]** Huang et al. (Facebook), "PrivateStats: De-Identified Authenticated Logging at Scale," 2021 — competing attribute-based VOPRF (ABVOPRF), directly benchmarked against.
- **KREUTER-FC-22** [KLOR20 in this bibliography, listed as CRYPTO 2020 "Anonymous tokens with private metadata bit"] — already in this corpus; competing construction for private-metadata tokens.
- **[SS21]** Silde, Strand, "Anonymous tokens with public metadata and applications to private contact tracing," ePrint 2021/203 — concurrent independent work describing the same 3HashSDHI-equivalent construction with an incomplete security analysis; superseded-by relationship is the reverse (this paper's proof supersedes SS21's incomplete one for the same construction).
- **[JKX21]** Jarecki, Krawczyk, Xu, "On the (in)security of the Diffie-Hellman oblivious PRF with multiplicative blinding," Public Key Cryptography 2021 — attack/critique, on multiplicative-blinding variants of 2HashDH-style OPRFs.
- **[TPY+19]** Thomas et al., "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting," USENIX Security 2019 — foundational for the breach-alerting application discussed.
- **[CMZ14]** Chase, Meiklejohn, Zaverucha, "Algebraic MACs and keyed-verification anonymous credentials," CCS 2014 — foundational, algebraic-MAC line that KREUTER-FC-22 builds on.

- "the POPRF introduces approximately a 25% overhead (in terms of µs to compute)"
- "the 3HashSDHI construction does not support key rotations even if one omits the final H2 evaluation"
- "Some loss of privacy is fundamental to restricted token use, and choosing how to make use of t requires care"
- "a deterministic primitive (like a PRF) is insufficient to achieve indistinguishability between private metadata bits"
