## [URDANETA-CSUR-11] A Survey of DHT Security Techniques
**Citation:** Guido Urdaneta, Guillaume Pierre, Maarten van Steen. "A Survey of DHT Security Techniques." ACM Computing Surveys 43(2), 2011. DOI 10.1145/1883612.1883615.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.distributed-systems.net/my-data/papers/2011.acm-cs.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.distributed-systems.net/my-data/papers/2011.acm-cs.pdf
**Domain:** A

### What it does
This paper classifies published defenses for distributed hash tables (DHTs — overlay networks in which each node holds a small routing table and a lookup for key k is routed hop by hop toward the node responsible for k) against three attack categories and states each defense's mechanism and disadvantage. It runs no experiments of its own; every quantitative figure below is a figure the survey reports from the paper it discusses, not a measurement performed by Urdaneta, Pierre, and van Steen. The three categories: the Sybil attack (one physical attacker creates many logical identities), the Eclipse attack (an attacker occupies enough of a correct node's routing-table entries to isolate that node from the honest network, also called routing-table poisoning), and routing/storage attacks (a poisoned routing table or a colluding storage-set causes a lookup to fail or return forged data).

Sybil defenses fall into six mechanism families: centralized certification (a trusted authority signs one certificate per identity), distributed registration (nodes vet each other's join requests without a central authority), physical-network-characteristic fingerprinting (network coordinates or measured latency distinguish physical hosts), social-network-based verification (SybilGuard, SybilLimit — described below), computational puzzles (a node must solve a proof-of-work puzzle to obtain or keep an identity), and game-theoretic mechanisms (an economic penalty for operating Sybil identities).

Eclipse defenses fall into two families: constrained routing tables, where the only entries a node may hold are determined by a public function of node identifiers (defeats Eclipse by construction but forecloses proximity-based neighbor selection), and defenses that keep a proximity-optimized table alongside a constrained fallback table, switching to the fallback when a routing-failure test signals that the optimized table has been poisoned.

Routing/storage defenses combine redundant storage (replication or erasure coding across multiple nodes so that no single compromised node controls a key) with redundant routing (sending a lookup along multiple paths or through multiple candidate next-hops per step, so a single malicious node on one path does not block the lookup). Replicas placed at numerically close identifiers ease consistency maintenance for mutable data; replicas spread across the identifier space are harder for a spatially concentrated attacker to capture, but the paper argues this is not a large improvement because placement functions are public and an attacker can target all relevant locations for a given key. Redundant routing takes one of three forms: wide paths (each routing hop attempts several candidate next-hops in parallel; the hop advances if any one candidate is honest), multiple disjoint paths (independent full paths from source to destination; success requires a majority of paths to be entirely honest), or multiple wide paths (successive attempts at a full wide-path route).

### Measured results
All figures below are as reported by this survey about other authors' experiments; none is this survey's own measurement. Retrieve the cited primary source before using a figure in a selection.

| Reported finding | Conditions (as stated in survey text) | Source discussed |
|---|---|---|
| 15% malicious nodes produces approximately 80% malicious entries in standard Pastry routing tables | Pastry proximity-based routing table, no defense | Condie et al. 2006, cited by Urdaneta section 4.6 |
| Probability of successful single-path routing ≈ 0.24 | f = 0.25 fraction malicious, path length 5, formula (1−f)^5 | Worked example in the survey's own text, section 4 |
| Redundant-routing false-positive probability 0.77 under a node-suppression attack vs. 0.12 without attack | Fraction of colluders f = 0.3, γ = 1.23, 256 samples for the distance test, target false-negative rate 0.001 | Castro et al. 2002, section 5.2 |
| Checked iterative routing adds 2.7 extra hops on average | Castro et al.'s simulation, exact node count and topology not given in this survey's text | Castro et al. 2002, section 5.2 |
| Probability of reaching all correct replicas ≈ (1−f)^(1+log_b N) | f = fraction malicious, b = identifier base, N = expected node count | Castro et al. 2002 formula, section 5.2 |
| SybilGuard: 99.96% of nodes have at least 10 route intersections at group size w=300 (no malicious nodes) | Kleinberg synthetic social-network model, up to 1,000,000 nodes, degree 24 | Yu et al. 2006, section 3.7 |
| SybilGuard: probability that all routes remain in the honest region stays near 100% for attack edges g ≤ 2,000, dropping to 99.8% at g = 2,500 | 1,000,000-node network, w=300 (route length parameter reported elsewhere in the text as needing to be as large as 2,000 for a million-node network) | Yu et al. 2006, section 3.7 |
| SybilLimit accepts between 10 and 20 Sybil nodes per attack edge | Synthetic Kleinberg network of 1,000,000 nodes / 10.9 million edges (w=10, r=10,000); Friendster 932,000 nodes / 7.8 million edges (w=10, r=8,000); LiveJournal 900,000 nodes / 8.7 million edges (w=10, r=12,000); DBLP 106,000 nodes / 626,000 edges (w=15, r=3,000) | Yu et al. 2008, section 3.8 |
| Myrmic: 97th/90th percentile lookup times 346 ms / 281 ms; 93% of lookups solved within 6 hops plus verification | PlanetLab testbed, 120 nodes, all correct, certificate size l=3, 500 lookups per node at 1 request per 3 seconds | Section 5.7 (referenced from surrounding text; source paper not separately keyed here) |
| Myrmic: 0.0122% of lookups fail | LAN environment, 1,000 nodes, 30% malicious, verification procedure assumed infallible | Same as above |
| KAD DHT estimated size: 1.5 million nodes (Steiner et al. 2007) vs. 4 million nodes (Crosby and Wallach 2007) | Two independent measurement studies of the same deployed network, methodology not detailed in this survey | Section 6 |

### Parameters
No parameters are this survey's own; each value above belongs to the cited primary paper and is listed under Measured results with its source.

### Stated limitations
The survey states that none of the reviewed Eclipse or Sybil defenses is evaluated against an adversary that attacks a small subset of nodes, a specific key, or specific routing-table rows, or that poisons slowly by behaving correctly most of the time — these are called more subtle attacks left unaddressed by every proposal it reviews. Singh et al. 2006 (cited within) explicitly states that defending against localized attacks, where an honest node is geographically surrounded by malicious nodes, remains an open problem. The survey states that no reviewed transactional DHT design tolerates malicious nodes. The survey states that Rodrigues and Liskov's study of erasure coding versus replication does not model mutable data or malicious nodes, so its bandwidth-parity finding may not hold once both are considered. The survey concludes that current deployed DHTs (KAD, BitTorrent, LimeWire, the Storm botnet, OpenDHT) are not designed to tolerate malicious nodes, and that Kademlia (used by all of them) remains vulnerable to Sybil and Eclipse attacks because nodes generate their own identifiers.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
The survey's own conclusion (section 7) states four preconditions the reviewed literature treats as jointly necessary for a secure DHT: secure assignment of node identifiers (an identifier a node cannot freely choose), a bound on the fraction of malicious nodes, malicious nodes spread across the identifier space rather than concentrated, and data replication combined with a routing mechanism that reaches a correct replica set with high probability. Centralized-certification Sybil defenses require an online or offline certification authority trusted by all participants and a certificate-revocation mechanism. Social-network Sybil defenses (SybilGuard, SybilLimit) require every participant to hold a genuine social relationship with some other participants, offline distribution of a symmetric key per social edge, and low churn in the social graph, since registry and witness tables update only on social-graph change. Computational-puzzle Sybil defenses require every honest node to continuously spend computing resources on puzzle solutions and require the puzzle difficulty to be set low enough for the least-capable honest node to keep solving puzzles while retaining spare capacity for other work; the survey cites a measurement (Anderson and Fedak 2006) that the most powerful nodes in a real peer-to-peer system have several orders of magnitude more CPU capacity than the least powerful, which bounds how high that difficulty can be set. Redundant-routing schemes based on multiple disjoint paths require paths to actually be disjoint for the stated success probability to hold; the survey states this disjointness is not guaranteed in practice. Eclipse defenses based on constrained routing tables require stable, randomly assigned node identifiers and foreclose proximity-based neighbor selection as a performance optimization.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus. The paper is itself a secondary source over the papers it discusses (Castro et al. 2002 [CASTRO-OSDI-02 in this corpus], Yu et al., Singh et al., and others); a downstream synthesis step should prefer the primary source's own reported conditions over this survey's paraphrase where the two differ.

### References worth retrieving
- Castro, Druschel, Ganesh, Rowstron, Wallach. "Secure Routing for Structured Peer-to-Peer Overlay Networks." OSDI 2002. — foundational (already in corpus as CASTRO-OSDI-02)
- Douceur. "The Sybil Attack." IPTPS 2002. — foundational, defines the Sybil attack this entire literature responds to
- Baumgart, Mies. "S/Kademlia: A Practicable Approach Towards Secure Key-Based Routing." ICPADS 2007. — competing / already read per brief section 7
- Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman. "SybilGuard." (venue not given in this excerpt) 2006. — foundational for social-graph Sybil defense
- Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao. "SybilLimit." 2008. — foundational, supersedes SybilGuard on the same social-graph mechanism
- Singh, Castro, Druschel, Rowstron. "Defending against Eclipse attacks on overlay networks." 2006. — competing, in-degree/out-degree control approach
- Awerbuch, Scheideler. "Towards a Scalable and Robust DHT." SPAA 2006. — competing, de Bruijn-graph-based theoretical defense
- Condie, Kacholia, Sankararaman, Hellerstein, Maniatis. "Induced Churn as Shelter from Routing Table Poisoning." NDSS 2006. — competing, augments Castro et al.'s two-table defense
- Fiat, Saia, Young. S-Chord swarm-based erasure-coded defense, 2005. — competing, theoretical

## [VISHNUMURTHY-P2PECON-03] KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing
**Citation:** Vivek Vishnumurthy, Sangeeth Chandrakumar, Emin Gün Sirer. "KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing." Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PEcon), 2003.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.cornell.edu/people/egs/papers/karma.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.cornell.edu/people/egs/papers/karma.pdf
**Domain:** I

### What it does
KARMA discourages participants in a peer-to-peer system from consuming more resources than they contribute, without a central accounting server. Each participant holds a single scalar balance, called karma, that rises when the participant contributes a resource (a file, a message, a computation result) and falls when the participant consumes one. A resource-consuming operation is refused if the consumer's karma balance is below the price of the operation.

The balance for a node A is not held by A itself. It is held redundantly by a bank-set: the k nodes whose node identifiers are closest, in a circular identifier space, to the hash of A's own identifier. A distributed hash table (the paper builds on Pastry) maps A's identifier to this set of k closest nodes, so the bank-set assignment is a deterministic function of A's identifier rather than a choice A or anyone else makes. Each bank-set member independently stores A's signed balance, the last transaction sequence number, and a recent transaction log.

A karma transfer from consumer A to provider B proceeds as follows. A sends B a message, signed with A's private key, stating the balance A would hold after the transfer and a sequence number that prevents replay. B forwards this to its own bank-set, whose members query BankA. BankA members check that the signed balance A supplied matches their stored balance; if so, they acknowledge, deduct the amount from A's account, and inform A. BankB members that receive a majority of positive acknowledgements from BankA credit B's account and inform B, at which point B transfers the resource to A. Bank-set members act independently and do not run a Byzantine agreement protocol among themselves: commutativity of addition guarantees that once a node stops issuing new transactions, the members of its bank-set converge on the same balance regardless of the order in which they observed credits and debits. A balance may dip transiently negative at one member if that member sees a debit before a credit that a majority of the bank-set saw in the opposite order; the balance is corrected once the credit propagates, so this transient underflow is contained to less than half the bank-set.

A new node obtains its identifier through a cryptographic puzzle: it selects a public/private key pair and a value x such that MD5(public key) matches MD5(x) in the low n digits, then sets its identifier to MD5(public key, x). This ties identifier assignment to a proof of computation the node cannot precompute for a chosen identifier, and n controls the difficulty of that computation. On joining, a node's prospective bank-set members exchange signed account records for it; if more than k/2 of them agree on a balance and sequence number, that balance is adopted, otherwise the node is initialized with a fixed system-wide starting balance and sequence number zero.

To bound long-run inflation or deflation of the total karma supply, the system recomputes a correction factor rho at the end of each epoch (a period the paper describes as typically spanning several months): rho equals (karma_total_at_epoch_start times nodes_active_now) divided by (karma_total_now times nodes_active_at_epoch_start). Each bank-set node broadcasts, at epoch end, the count and unused balances of nodes that went inactive and the count of nodes that joined; every node then computes the new totals and applies rho to the accounts for which it is a bank-set member.

For a file-sharing application built on KARMA, a file is hashed to a rendezvous node, which providers advertise to and seekers query; the seeker runs an auction over the karma bid providers submit and picks the lowest bidder. File delivery itself uses a Certified Mail scheme: the provider sends the file encrypted with a symmetric key, and the consumer receives the decryption key only in exchange for a signed receipt, so a karma transfer completes if and only if the file transfer completes, and vice versa.

### Measured results
The paper is a design paper with one analytic (not experimental) probability computation, no implementation or simulation is reported.

| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Probability that an attacker who has compromised 10% of the nodes in a 1,000,000-node network controls a majority of some single 64-member bank-set is under 5.6 × 10^-12 | Closed-form calculation, not measured: attacker controls 10% of 1,000,000 nodes; expected attacker-controlled members of a given 64-member bank-set is 6.4 (10% of 64); bound derived via a Chernoff-style tail bound P(X > 32) = P(X > (1+4)·6.4) < (e^4/5^5)^6.4 |
| Probability that the attacker controls a majority in at least one bank-set across the whole network is under 5.6 × 10^-6 | Same setting, multiplied by the total number of bank-sets in a 1,000,000-node network at k=64 |
| Simply having peers announce their held content produces "less than a tenth of a percent" bandwidth overhead | This figure appears in the companion BitTorrent paper (COHEN-IPTPS-03), not in KARMA; do not attribute it to this paper |
| Currency-correction protocol requires O(N^2) messages per epoch, where N is the number of nodes in the system | Stated as an asymptotic message-count bound, not measured; the paper argues the cost is acceptable because an epoch spans several months, without stating what "several months" is derived from |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used in the paper | Tested range |
|---|---|---|
| Bank-set size k | Used symbolically throughout; the one worked numeric example uses k=64 | No range tested; the paper states only that the system needs "at least k nodes in the system at all times" |
| Node-identifier puzzle difficulty n | Left as "a parameter that can be used to limit the difficulty of the puzzle" | Not specified numerically |
| Epoch length | Described as "typically several months" | Not derived or measured; stated as a design assumption used to argue the O(N^2) correction cost is acceptable |
| Fraction of malicious nodes tolerated by the underlying secure-routing layer | Cited from Castro et al.'s secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlays as tolerating up to 25% of nodes not adhering to the routing protocol | This bound is imported from the cited secure-routing paper, not derived within KARMA |
| Adversarial fraction in the worked bank-set-corruption example | 10% of a 1,000,000-node network | Single point example, not a range |
| Compensation dampening threshold for bank-node service karma | Example given: award extra karma only after a bank node has performed 10^4 transactions on behalf of others | Presented as an example fix, not a derived or tested value |

### Stated limitations
The paper states that KARMA relies on the identifier-to-bank-set mapping remaining secure, and its own tamper-resilience bound is conditioned entirely on the security of that underlying DHT routing layer: the authors write that "the limiting factor to KARMA's tamper-resilience lies in the p2p routing substrate, and not in the higher level protocols." It leaves the resource-pricing mechanism (how many units of karma a given resource in a given application costs) entirely to the application built on top of KARMA. It states that KARMA cannot prevent Sybil attacks in a peer-to-peer setting without external identifiers, and only limits the rate at which new identifiers can be manufactured through the cryptographic-puzzle join procedure; the authors write they "permit Sybil attacks but limit the rate at which they can be launched." The paper also identifies, without resolving beyond a sketch, a second-order incentive problem: bank-set members themselves have no built-in incentive to perform bank-node work honestly and consistently for other nodes, and the paper's proposed compensation (awarding karma for bank-node service) is presented with the caveat that it risks a runaway chain reaction of compensatory transactions unless a dampening rule is added, and risks violating the zero-sum property of the currency, which the paper says a taxation-based alternative might address instead, without specifying the tax mechanism.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
KARMA requires an underlying secure-routing DHT (the paper builds on Pastry with the Castro et al. secure-routing extension) that tolerates a bounded fraction of adversarial nodes and can map a node's hashed identifier to the k nodes closest to that hash; KARMA's own security bound against bank-set corruption holds only conditional on that routing layer's own bound holding. It requires every participant to hold a persistent public/private key pair, established once at join time through the identifier-generation puzzle, and requires all subsequent balance and transaction messages to be signed by that key. It requires the DHT to notify a newly joined or newly failed bank-set member of which accounts now fall under its responsibility, so that node can retrieve those accounts' balances by majority vote from the account's other current bank-set members. It requires an application layer to supply the actual exchange semantics (what resource a transaction concerns, and how many karma units it costs); KARMA supplies only the balance-transfer and file-delivery-atomicity primitives, not pricing. It requires that the fraction of malicious members within any single node's bank-set stay below one-half at the moment of a transaction decision, since the transfer protocol resolves consumer-side and provider-side approval by majority vote within each bank-set. It requires application-level periodic delivery of epoch-boundary join/leave counts and balances between all bank-set members to keep the inflation-correction factor consistent, and tolerates temporary inconsistency between nodes in different epochs only by rescaling in-flight payments with the correction factor.

### Contradicts
None found. No other entry in this batch measures or discusses the karma/bank-set credit-scheme mechanism.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: A. Rowstron, P. Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, distributed object location and routing for large-scale peer-to-peer systems," IFIP/ACM Middleware 2001 — the DHT KARMA layers its bank-set assignment on top of.
- foundational: M. Castro, P. Druschel, A. Ganesh, A. Rowstron, D. Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," OSDI 2002 — supplies the 25%-adversarial-node routing-resilience bound KARMA's own security argument depends on.
- attack: J. Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — the attack KARMA states it does not prevent, only rate-limits.
- competing: T. Ngan, D. S. Wallach, P. Druschel, "Enforcing Fair Sharing of Peer-to-Peer Resources," IPTPS 2003 — a fairness mechanism for spatial (storage) resources verified by random audit, which the KARMA authors argue does not extend to temporal resources like bandwidth.
- competing: J. Shneidman, D. Parkes, "Rationality and Self-Interest in Peer to Peer Networks," IPTPS 2003 — mechanism-design framing for incentivizing globally beneficial peer behavior, cited as a parallel approach to KARMA's accounting approach.
- foundational: S. Saroiu, P. K. Gummadi, S. D. Gribble, "A measurement study of peer-to-peer file sharing systems," MMCN 2002 — source of the cited 20-40% Napster / ~70% Gnutella freeloading figures that motivate KARMA.
- foundational: E. Adar, B. Huberman, "Free riding on Gnutella," First Monday 5(10), 2000 — the other cited source for the freeloading motivation, also cited directly by COHEN-IPTPS-03 in this batch.

## [VISWANATH-SIGCOMM-10] An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses

**Citation:** Bimal Viswanath, Ansley Post, P. Krishna Gummadi, Alan Mislove. "An Analysis of Social Network-Based Sybil Defenses." ACM SIGCOMM, 2010. DOI 10.1145/1851182.1851226.
**Retrieved:** full text
**Source URL:** http://ccr.sigcomm.org/online/files/p363.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
The paper shows that four published social-graph Sybil-defense schemes (SybilGuard, SybilLimit, SybilInfer, SumUp) all reduce to the same underlying graph operation despite differing algorithms and stated goals: each, given a trusted node, produces a ranking of every other node by trustworthiness, and each scheme's tunable parameters only move a cutoff point along that fixed ranking rather than changing which nodes rank near the top. The paper establishes this by running every scheme's algorithm at many parameter settings and observing that partitions grow or shrink monotonically (nodes added to the Sybil set are never later removed as a parameter is swept in one direction), which lets the authors convert every partitioning-based scheme into a single ranking for direct comparison. The paper then measures mutual information between pairs of schemes' rankings at every cutoff position and conductance (the ratio of edges leaving a candidate set to edges inside it) of each candidate partition, and finds the rankings agree most strongly exactly where conductance has a local minimum — the boundary of a locally tightly connected node cluster around the trusted node, i.e., a local community. It substitutes an explicit off-the-shelf local community-detection algorithm (Mislove's greedy conductance-minimization method) for each scheme's own ranking procedure and finds it performs comparably. It then shows the negative consequence of that structural equivalence: a network whose honest population is itself split into multiple tightly-knit sub-communities is harder for every one of these schemes to defend, and an adversary who chooses which specific honest nodes to attach Sybils to (rather than attaching uniformly at random) is far more effective than the schemes' own published evaluations assumed.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| All four schemes' rankings agree most strongly (highest pairwise mutual information) at the same cutoff point, which coincides with a local minimum (trough) in conductance | Synthetic network from a cited prior study (rewired to have controllable community structure), and repeated on real-world Facebook (Rice University graduate-student network) and Astrophysics co-authorship networks (dataset sizes in Table 2: Facebook 514 nodes/3,313 links avg. degree 13; Astrophysicists 14,845 nodes/119,652 links avg. degree 16; also YouTube 446,181/1,728,938 avg. degree 7.7; Advogato 5,264/43,027 avg. degree 16) |
| An off-the-shelf local community-detection algorithm (Mislove's, minimizing conductance) achieves accuracy comparable to SybilInfer and higher than SybilGuard/SybilLimit, all improving as more Sybils are added, on a synthetic scale-free topology | 1,000-node scale-free non-Sybil network (Barabasi-Albert), 10% (100 nodes) compromised uniformly at random into Sybils, additional Sybil identities added in a matching scale-free topology, swept 30 to 1,000 additional Sybils, averaged over 100 runs, mean 789 attack edges connecting Sybil and non-Sybil regions; SybilGuard and SybilLimit under-detect because they cap accepted Sybils at O(log N) per attack edge and the injected Sybil count stays below that bound |
| The same four schemes plus community detection all achieve markedly lower absolute accuracy on a real social graph than on the synthetic topology of similar density, though community detection remains comparable to or better than the explicit schemes | Facebook graduate-student network (514 nodes, half the size of the synthetic test), additional Sybils swept 0-400 |
| Community detection substituted for SumUp's voting-envelope construction produces more stable vote accuracy (fraction of counted votes that are genuinely non-Sybil) across three real networks than SumUp's original envelope method, whose accuracy varies widely by network | Advogato, Astrophysics, YouTube networks; 100 attack edges injected via 10 Sybil nodes each linked to 10 random non-Sybil nodes, each Sybil further attached to many additional Sybil identities by single links, non-Sybil voter fraction swept from 0.001 to 1 of total non-Sybil nodes, averaged over 5 runs, methodology matching SumUp's original evaluation |
| Detection accuracy (AUC/A', probability a random Sybil ranks below a random non-Sybil) of all four schemes falls from near 1.0 toward 0.5 (random) as the non-Sybil region's community structure increases, holding node count, link count, and degree distribution fixed | Synthetic Barabasi-Albert network of 512 nodes rewired in 5-link increments from no community structure to two 256-node communities joined by 5 links; a 256-node Sybil region attached by 40 links at each rewiring step |
| The same degradation pattern holds on real networks: a correlation coefficient of -0.81 is measured between network modularity (a community-structure metric, range -1 to 1) and detection accuracy (A') | 8 real datasets (Table 3: Facebook undergrad 1,208 nodes/43,043 links modularity 0.278; Advogato 5,264/43,027 modularity 0.318; Wikipedia votes 7,066/100,736 modularity 0.350; email 1,133/5,451 modularity 0.504; Astrophysicists 14,845/119,652 modularity 0.621; Facebook grad 514/3,313 modularity 0.644; High-energy physics 8,638/24,806 modularity 0.690; Relativity 4,158/13,422 modularity 0.790), each given a power-law Sybil region sized to one-quarter its non-Sybil node count, attached with random links equal to 5% of non-Sybil-internal link count |
| Restricting Sybil attack edges to target only the k nodes closest (by community-detection ranking) to the trusted node, instead of placing them uniformly at random, monotonically decreases detection accuracy as k shrinks, for a fixed total number of Sybil-to-non-Sybil links | Synthetic network from the community-structure experiment (rewired to 40 inter-community links), k swept 0 to 500 |
| On the Facebook graduate-student network, the same targeted-attachment experiment drives accuracy first to 0.5 (random) and then below 0.5, meaning Sybils are ranked higher than non-Sybils | Facebook graduate-student network (514 nodes), k swept 0 to 500 |

### Parameters
- Synthetic scale-free non-Sybil network for the community-detection comparison (Section 4): 1,000 nodes, Barabasi-Albert generator, 10% (100 nodes) turned Sybil uniformly at random, additional Sybils added in matching scale-free topology, swept 30-1,000, 100 runs averaged, mean 789 attack edges
- Synthetic network for community-structure sensitivity (Section 5.1): Barabasi-Albert, 512 nodes, initial degree parameter m=8 (about 3,900 links), rewired in increments of 5 links down to 5 remaining inter-community links between two 256-node halves; attached Sybil region of 256 nodes via 40 links
- Real-network community-structure experiment (Section 5.1): Sybil region sized to one-quarter of non-Sybil node count per network, attached with links equal to 5% of non-Sybil-internal link count
- Targeted-attack experiment (Section 5.2): same rewired synthetic network fixed at 40 inter-community links; k (number of nodes nearest the trusted node, by community-detection ranking, among which Sybil links are randomly placed) swept 0-500 on both synthetic and Facebook (514-node) networks
- SumUp-comparison attack model: 100 attack edges via 10 Sybil nodes each linked to 10 randomly chosen non-Sybil nodes, each Sybil further attached to additional Sybil identities via single links, 5 runs averaged
- SybilGuard/SybilLimit theoretical acceptance bound cited: O(log N) accepted Sybils per attack edge, where N is total non-Sybil network size

### Stated limitations
The paper states its own analysis deliberately strips each scheme of its application-specific optimizations (e.g., SybilGuard/SybilLimit's decentralization-specific design features, SumUp's voting-specific mechanisms) to compare the shared graph-partitioning core, meaning results describe that core algorithm and not necessarily every deployed variant's full behavior. It states it did not formally prove that every parameter of every Sybil-defense scheme induces a monotonic node ordering, only that this held for every scheme, environment, and parameter setting the authors tested. It states its focus on local (as opposed to global) community-detection algorithms was a deliberate choice justified by a cited prior finding that global and local algorithms share similar properties, and explicitly leaves verifying this equivalence for community detection under Sybil attack to future work. It states, as an open question, whether the core assumption every examined scheme makes — that Sybils can only form a bounded number of links to non-Sybils — holds in any of today's real online social networks, citing evidence that in at least one real network it does not. It states that identifying communities reliably across a wide range of real-world networks is itself a difficult, unsolved problem in the community-detection literature, an additional limitation beyond the ones the paper directly measures. The paper's discussion section raises, as unresolved value questions rather than measured findings, whether the mere existence of Sybil (multiple) identities should be treated as evidence of misbehavior at all, and whether Sybil-tolerance (limiting a Sybil's effect, as SumUp does) is preferable in principle to explicit Sybil identification — the paper does not claim these are settled.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any system built on one of these four schemes, or on community detection as a substitute, needs a designated trusted node (or trusted-node set) from which the ranking is computed, since every measured ranking here is defined relative to that node's position in the graph. It requires the input social graph to be undirected or convertible to an undirected weighted graph, since the paper's own conductance and modularity computations, and the schemes they analyze, operate on undirected graphs (Table 3 states this explicitly for the real-world datasets used). The paper's finding that accuracy depends on community structure and on the adversary's ability to target specific honest nodes means any consuming system needs an independent estimate of its social graph's modularity, or of an adversary's link-placement capability, to know whether the deployed scheme's accuracy is anywhere close to the near-1.0 AUC measured on low-modularity synthetic graphs rather than the near-random or below-random AUC measured on high-modularity or targeted-attack conditions. Because detection accuracy is measured relative to a trusted node and a fixed graph snapshot, any system needs a process for selecting and updating that trusted node and for refreshing the input graph, neither of which this paper specifies or evaluates.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus as of this batch regarding this paper's own reported numbers. This paper is itself the primary source for the finding, later reused and extended in ALVISI-SP-13 (also in this corpus), that community-structured honest regions and targeted attack-edge placement both degrade social-graph Sybil defense; ALVISI-SP-13's own targeted-attachment measurements (probabilities of 0.34-0.49 across five schemes under the RenRen-observed attack pattern) are a distinct, later experiment on a different attack model and should not be conflated with this paper's k-nearest-node targeting experiment (Figures 14-15), which measures a different construction. Cross-reference for later composition checking against GONG-TIFS-14 in this corpus: SybilBelief's own evaluation in that paper uses uniformly random attack-edge placement, not the targeted-attachment model this paper shows is materially more damaging; that gap is not closed by GONG-TIFS-14's results.

## [WANG-GLOBECOM-12] Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT

**Citation:** Liang Wang, Jussi Kangasharju. "Real-World Sybil Attacks in BitTorrent Mainline DHT." IEEE GLOBECOM, 2012. DOI 10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://doi.org/10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215
**Source URL:** https://doi.org/10.1109/GLOCOM.2012.6503215
**Domain:** J

### What it does
The paper identifies two routing-table attacks against BitTorrent's Mainline distributed hash table (MLDHT), a 160-bit Kademlia-based key-value store in which peer and content identifiers share one address space and each node keeps a k-bucket routing table (a fixed-size list of contacts grouped by numeric distance from the node's own identifier). A horizontal attack spreads a small number of forged identities (Sybils, meaning falsely distinct identities controlled by one attacker) widely across the network by answering every PING message with a random identifier and every FIND_NODE message by claiming sole ownership of the queried identifier, so querying nodes and the nodes those nodes tell about the attacker both come to treat the attacker as authoritative; the derivation the authors give is that a horizontal attack needs only N / max(k, log(N)) Sybils to intercept messages for an N-node network with bucket size k, because average lookup path length is O(log N) and eventually exceeds k as the network grows. A vertical attack instead inserts k Sybil identifiers numerically adjacent to one target identifier (a specific node or a specific content info hash), which lets the attacker intercept every query and every stored key-value pair addressed to that one target; the authors state this is a broader form of the previously known eclipse attack (an attack that fills a victim's routing table entirely with attacker-controlled entries) because it can also target a content identifier, not only a node. The authors detect real instances of both attacks with three honeypots: a detector that queries random, near-certainly-nonexistent node and content identifiers and marks any node that falsely claims ownership as an attacker; an MLDHT honeypot that places crafted content identifiers immediately adjacent to its own identifier so that any node performing a vertical attack against those identifiers is drawn toward the honeypot and revealed; and a BitTorrent-protocol honeypot that completes the BitTorrent handshake with any node that follows up a DHT-level probe with an actual download attempt, to confirm the probing node is truly monitoring content rather than only probing at the DHT level.

### Measured results
| Result | Conditions |
|---|---|
| Estimated Sybil count in MLDHT increasing throughout 2011, currently around 300,000 | Monitoring since December 2010, sampling a randomly selected 12-bit zone (a set of nodes sharing a 12-bit identifier prefix) every 30 minutes; per-attacker time series shown for the whole of 2011 with standard deviation, not a single point estimate; detailed methodology stated to be in a companion technical report not examined here |
| One identified attacker ("Mr. 50," IP prefix traced to Amazon EC2) injected an estimated 80,000 to 290,000 Sybils across 2011, holding roughly steady near 100,000 from mid-January through July before rising after August | Estimated from the same 30-minute zone-sampling monitoring system plus honeypot logging, not from a controlled experiment; identity based on shared, identically erroneous protocol implementation with a second, less active entity ("Mr. 184") |
| Attribution of observed Sybils in 2011: Mr. 50 56%, Mr. ISP 27%, other 14%, Mr. 184 3% | Same monitoring period and methodology as above |
| Traffic-localization test: for 6 popular files (top files on The Pirate Bay), the fraction of same-ISP ("native") nodes returned to an insider client connecting through a proxy inside the suspected ISP's network peaked at over 90%, versus a markedly lower fraction for an outsider client on the authors' own network; for 2 unpopular files (from a Chinese file-sharing site) both clients received a low native-node fraction, with the insider client still slightly higher | 8 total torrents tested (6 popular, 2 unpopular), one insider and one outsider instrumented client per file, requesting only the initial peer set from the suspected attacker ("Mr. ISP") without joining the actual file distribution |
| A cited prior result (Timpanaro et al., not this paper's own measurement): inserting 20 Sybils near a target causes a client to receive over 90% Sybils in its returned peer set | Attributed to reference [11] (Timpanaro, Cholez, Chrisment, Festor, IFIP NTMS 2011); reported here as a supporting citation, not reproduced experimentally in this paper |

### Parameters
- Node and content identifier length: 160 bits (MLDHT identifier space)
- Zone sampling granularity for the monitoring system: 12-bit zones (nodes sharing a common 12-bit identifier prefix), one zone selected at random per 30-minute sampling round
- Monitoring interval: fixed 30-minute sampling rounds, running from December 2010 through the 2011 measurement period reported in the figures
- Honeypot deployment start: September 2011 for the MLDHT and BitTorrent honeypots (so no direct observational record exists for "Mr. ISP" activity before that date, though "Mr. 50" traffic first appeared in the authors' logs in January 2011)
- Minimum Sybils for a successful horizontal attack, as derived (not separately measured): N / max(k, log(N)), where N is total network size and k is the routing table's bucket size

### Stated limitations
The authors state explicitly that they observed no overtly malicious behavior from either identified attacker and have no concrete proof of actual malicious activity; the paper's claim is that the scale of the observed activity is large enough to be a concern, not that harm occurred. The identity of "Mr. 50" and "Mr. 184" as the same controlling party rests on both nodes implementing an identical, protocol-incorrect message-handling pattern; the authors state they attempted to detect coordination between the two by feeding each a different fake info hash and observing whether the other later requested it, and never observed such sharing, so the shared-identity claim remains a conjecture, not a demonstrated fact. The authors do not know how various BitTorrent client implementations react to a Sybil's protocol-incorrect replies, so they cannot state how much real query traffic a horizontal attack actually captures in deployed clients as opposed to what the protocol alone would allow. The paper reviews defenses (a centrally issued identity authority, monetary or IP-based identity certificates, physical-network-fingerprint identity binding, social-network-based Sybil defenses, and statistical distribution analysis to detect anomalous node density) and states each has a specific weakness: a central authority raises processing and administrative overhead and creates a barrier to legitimate nodes joining; an IP-based certificate scheme needs a separate mechanism for nodes behind firewalls or network address translators; physical-network-fingerprint schemes fail when network conditions change; social-network-based defenses require a social graph to already exist in the deployment; and distribution-analysis detection can be evaded by an attacker who monitors the same statistic and stays under the alarm threshold, and in any case cannot detect a horizontal attack because that attack raises node density uniformly rather than locally. The authors state there is no complete solution among these, only ways to raise the resource cost of mounting the attacks.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Any content-location or measurement system built on MLDHT that assumes a node's claimed identifier reflects a genuine distinct participant is false in this deployment, because MLDHT lets a node choose its own identifier and never requires the identifier returned in a PONG message to match the one requested in the preceding PING; a system safe against this needs an explicit consistency check between the requested and returned identifier plus a per-request challenge value, which the authors propose as a low-overhead protocol fix but which is not present in deployed MLDHT. Measurement studies of MLDHT session lengths or churn that infer online duration from repeated responsiveness to the same identifier will be biased upward wherever a horizontal attacker is present, because the attacker answers every probe regardless of the identifier's real owner; the authors state they are unaware of any prior MLDHT measurement study that accounts for this. A system relying on a k-closest-neighbor response to locate content assumes those neighbors are not colluding to intercept the query; the vertical attack shows that assumption fails whenever an attacker can insert k adjacent Sybils near a target identifier, which the current protocol does not prevent.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus at the time of writing. Cross-check candidate: WOLCHOK-WOOT-10 crawls the separate Vuze DHT (not MLDHT) using a Sybil-based technique with a different goal (content-search bootstrapping and IP-to-content monitoring rather than routing-layer traffic interception); the two papers target different DHT instances and should not be merged into one combined MLDHT-plus-Vuze Sybil-vulnerability figure.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: Douceur, "The Sybil attack," IPTPS 2002 — defines the identity-forgery attack this paper's horizontal and vertical attacks both instantiate (already in corpus per BRIEF §7 baseline)
- foundational: Sit, Morris, "Security considerations for peer-to-peer distributed hash tables," IPTPS 2002 — cited as the origin of the free-identifier-choice vulnerability this paper exploits
- foundational: Urdaneta, Pierre, van Steen, "A survey of DHT security techniques," ACM Computing Surveys 43(2), 2011, pp. 8:1-8:49 — the survey this paper draws its defense catalogue from (already named as a dense bibliography in BRIEF §4.4)

- competing: Varvello, Steiner, "Traffic localization for DHT-based BitTorrent networks," IFIP/TC6 Networking 2011, and Steiner, Varvello, "Peer-to-peer traffic localization as a service," INFOCOM Demo 2011 — the traffic-localization methodology "Mr. ISP" is compared against, described by the authors as less aggressive than what was observed in the wild
- competing: Le Blond, Legout, Lefessant, Dabbous, Kaafar, "Spying the world from your laptop," USENIX LEET 2010 — prior demonstration of user-privacy compromise via BitTorrent portal monitoring, cited as showing this paper's attacks enable the same violation more easily and at larger scale
- foundational: Castro, Druschel, Ganesh, Rowstron, Wallach, "Secure routing for structured peer-to-peer overlay networks," ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 36 (SI), 2002, pp. 299-314 — proposes charging for identity certificates and embedding IP address in the certificate, cited as a candidate defense with a stated weakness for nodes behind firewalls
- competing/attack: Danezis, Lesniewski-Laas, Kaashoek, Anderson, "Sybil-resistant DHT routing," ESORICS 2005, pp. 305-318; Yu, Gibbons, Kaminsky, Xiao, "SybilLimit," IEEE S&P 2008; Yu, Kaminsky, Gibbons, Flaxman, "SybilGuard," ACM SIGCOMM 2006 — social-network-based Sybil defenses the authors state only apply where a social graph already exists in the deployment
- attack: Naoumov, Ross, "Exploiting P2P systems for DDoS attacks," InfoScale 2006; El Defrawy, Gjoka, Markopoulou, "BotTorrent: misusing BitTorrent to launch DDoS attacks," USENIX SRUTI 2007; Liang, Naoumov, Ross, "The index poisoning attack in P2P file sharing systems," IEEE Infocom 2006 — prior demonstrations that a compromised P2P routing layer enables denial-of-service, cited as the risk this paper's attack scale makes newly practical against MLDHT

## [WEI-INFOCOM-12] SybilDefender: Defend Against Sybil Attacks in Large Social Networks
**Citation:** Wei Wei, Fengyuan Xu, Chiu C. Tan, Qun Li. "SybilDefender: Defend Against Sybil Attacks in Large Social Networks." IEEE INFOCOM, 2012. DOI 10.1109/INFCOM.2012.6195572.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.cs.wm.edu/~liqun/paper/infocom12_1.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.cs.wm.edu/~liqun/paper/infocom12_1.pdf
**Domain:** F

### What it does
SybilDefender decides whether one specified suspect node in a social graph is a Sybil identity, and separately finds the whole cluster of Sybil nodes surrounding a known Sybil node, using only a bounded number of random walks rather than by processing the entire graph. It also proposes two measures for limiting how many attack edges (a link between a real user's node and a Sybil node) a real-world social network permits.

Mechanism, sybil identification: the social graph has a small cut of attack edges separating a large honest region from a smaller Sybil region. A random walk of a fixed length that starts inside the Sybil region tends to stay trapped inside it, so it visits (traverses) fewer distinct nodes than a same-length walk starting in the honest region. A pre-processing phase (run once per graph) picks a known honest node h, performs f short random walks of length log(n) from h to obtain f additional nodes that are honest with high probability under a fast-mixing assumption (defined below), and treats h plus those f nodes as judge nodes. For each candidate walk length l from a minimum l_min to a maximum l_max in steps of 100, the algorithm performs R random walks of length l from every judge node, counts for each judge node the number of nodes visited at least t times (t a small constant), and records the mean and standard deviation of that count across judges — producing one tuple (l, mean, stdDeviation) per length. To then test a suspect node u, the algorithm performs R random walks of length l starting from l_0 and doubles l on each iteration up to l_max; at each length it compares the suspect's own count of nodes visited at least t times against the judges' recorded mean for that length, and declares u a Sybil the first time the shortfall exceeds stdDeviation times a scaling constant alpha; if no length up to l_max triggers this, u is declared honest.

Mechanism, sybil community detection (finds the whole cluster around one already-known Sybil node s, rather than testing nodes one at a time): first estimate a suitable partial-walk length by repeatedly doubling a starting length and running R partial random walks from s at each candidate length until the fraction of "dead" walks (walks that exhaust the graph's reachable local region before reaching the target length) reaches a threshold beta close to 1. Then perform R partial random walks of that length from s, tally how often each node is visited, sort nodes by visit frequency, and greedily grow a candidate set S by adding nodes from the sorted list whenever doing so does not increase the set's conductance (the fraction of edge-endpoints in S that cross to outside S, a measure of how tight the boundary cut around S is); repeat sweeping the list until conductance stops improving across two full passes, and output the resulting S as the detected Sybil community.

Mechanism, limiting attack edges (two proposed techniques, evaluated only by a user survey, not by an attack simulation): (1) let users rate each of their existing relationships as "Friend" or "Stranger" through a purpose-built application, and drop "Stranger"-rated edges before running Sybil defense; (2) restrict the graph used for defense to an "activity network," where an edge exists only between users who have actually interacted (not merely declared a relationship), which is argued to naturally exclude unused attack edges.

### Measured results
All experiments use two full real-world social-graph data sets: Orkut (3,072,441 nodes, 117,185,083 edges, average degree 76.28) and Facebook (3,097,165 nodes, 28,377,481 edges, average degree 18.32) — described in the paper as the largest data sets ever used to evaluate topology-based Sybil defenses at the time. Sybil regions were synthetically attached to these real graphs using either a Preferential Attachment (PA, scale-free) model or an Erdos-Renyi (ER, random) model; the PA sybil region's average degree matches the host data set's average degree, while the ER sybil region's average degree ranges from 8 to 11 (a sparse topology by comparison). All experiments used the full published data sets with no small-degree-node pre-filtering (unlike some prior evaluations the paper cites).

| Experiment | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Random-walk coverage difference, honest vs. Sybil origin | PA-model Sybil region of 10,000 nodes, 1,000 attack edges, 1,000 random walks per source node, mean of 20 experiments per point, random-walk length swept to 10,000 hops | At walk length 10,000, the honest-origin curve exceeds the Sybil-origin curve by more than 200,000 nodes visited at frequency >= 5; observed standard deviation of the judge-node counts stayed under 1,500 |

### Parameters
| Parameter | Value used | Range/notes |
|---|---|---|
| l_min, l_max, l_0 (walk lengths, sybil identification) | 100, 10,000, 1,000 | not swept independently in the reported experiments |
| t (visit-frequency threshold) | 5 | fixed |
| alpha (standard-deviation multiplier for the sybil decision) | 20 | fixed; chosen large "to limit the number of falsely identified honest nodes" |
| l_s (short-walk length for judge-node selection) | 20 | equal to log(n) for the tested graph sizes |
| f (number of extra judge nodes derived from h) | 100 | fixed |
| R (random walks per node tested, sybil identification) | swept over {1000, 1500, 2000} | this is the one parameter varied across the main result table |
| l_0 (starting length, community detection) | 100 | fixed |
| beta (dead-walk-ratio threshold, community detection) | 0.95 | fixed |
| R (partial walks, community detection) | 2000 | fixed |
| Number of attack edges (main sybil-identification experiments) | 1,000 | held fixed while sybils-per-attack-edge was varied |
| SybilLimit comparison parameters | w=20 hops, r=10,000 random routes | taken from SybilLimit's own paper's stated optimum for this data set |
| Gatekeeper comparison parameters | m=100, f_admit=0.2 | taken from Gatekeeper's authors' recommendation |

### Stated limitations
SybilDefender is explicitly a centralized mechanism: "the administrator knows the social network topology," justified only by the observation that all current online social networks are already under centralized administrative control — it is not designed to run without a central party with full graph visibility. It assumes at least one node in the network is already known with certainty to be honest, as the starting point for the whole identification algorithm; the paper does not test what happens if that assumption is violated. It assumes the size of the Sybil region is not comparable to the size of the honest region, and states this is reasonable only by appeal to the large user bases of networks like Facebook, Twitter, and Orkut at the time and to account-creation friction (email verification, CAPTCHAs); the paper provides no bound on how close the two region sizes can get before the identification algorithm breaks down. It assumes the honest region is fast-mixing (a random walk of length Theta(log n) converges to the graph's stationary distribution with probability at least 1 - 1/n), citing prior work (Yu et al.) as having shown real social networks are fast-mixing, without re-validating that claim itself. It assumes the number of attack edges is limited, and the paper's own survey data shows this assumption is not automatically satisfied on real online social networks (Bilge et al.'s prior finding that roughly 20% of bogus friendship requests on Facebook are accepted, cited by the authors, and the authors' own survey finding 19.8% of rated relations are "Stranger"). Nodes that lie directly on the small cut (compromised nodes connected by attack edges) are the ones the algorithm systematically fails to identify correctly, in both the identification and community-detection algorithms — this is stated as the source of essentially all observed errors, not merely a hypothetical edge case. Finding the true minimum-size cut between honest and Sybil regions is NP-hard, which the paper states as the reason the community-detection algorithm approximates the cut with the greedy conductance heuristic instead of solving it exactly.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
Requires a single administrative party (or a coalition acting as one) with complete, current knowledge of the social graph's full edge set; the algorithm cannot run against a graph only partially visible to the party running it. Requires that party to already hold, from some external source, at least one node identity it is certain is honest, since the whole judge-node bootstrap in the pre-processing phase is derived by walking outward from that single node — the mechanism supplies no way to establish that certainty internally. Requires the graph to remain fast-mixing on the honest side, which depends on the honest population not being fragmented into many small, weakly-interconnected communities (the paper notes but does not test this failure mode; it is the same failure mode later measured directly against a related family of methods in GAO-CNS-18). Requires that the number of attack edges stays small relative to network size for the small-cut/conductance signal to exist at all — a network that does not maintain this (as the paper's own survey suggests real online social networks may not) removes the basis for both the identification and the community-detection algorithms. Supplies, but does not itself enforce, two techniques (manual relationship rating, or restricting to an interaction-derived activity network) intended to keep the attack-edge count low; each requires either a separate user-facing rating application or an independently available interaction log, neither of which SybilDefender's core algorithms provide.

### Contradicts
None found within this corpus regarding SybilDefender's own reported figures. This paper's own re-implementation and measurement of SybilLimit produce substantially higher false-negative rates for SybilLimit (up to 85.3% at low sybils-per-attack-edge) than SybilLimit's asymptotic O(log n)-sybils-per-attack-edge claim might suggest in isolation — a case where an independent re-measurement (by a competing paper's authors) diverges sharply from the originating paper's own framing, illustrating exactly the kind of re-measurement disagreement this corpus is built to preserve; no direct textual figure from the original SybilLimit paper is quoted here to compare against, so the two cannot be set side by side numerically without retrieving SybilLimit (Yu et al., IEEE S&P 2008) directly.

### References worth retrieving
- foundational: H. Yu, M. Kaminsky, P. B. Gibbons, A. Flaxman, "SybilGuard: defending against sybil attacks via social networks," SIGCOMM 2006 — origin of the fast-mixing random-route approach and the O(sqrt(n) log n)-sybils-per-attack-edge bound SybilDefender improves on.
- competing: H. Yu, P. B. Gibbons, M. Kaminsky, F. Xiao, "SybilLimit: A near-optimal social network defense against sybil attacks," IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2008 — the paper's primary baseline, re-implemented and measured directly; holds the comparison numbers this entry already reports, but should be retrieved to check its own reported figures against SybilDefender's re-measurement.
- competing: N. Tran, J. Li, L. Subramanian, S. S. M. Chow, "Optimal sybil-resilient node admission control" (Gatekeeper), IEEE INFOCOM 2011 — re-implemented and measured directly by this paper; relies on a random-expander assumption the authors state is unvalidated on real networks.
- competing: G. Danezis, P. Mittal, "SybilInfer: Detecting sybil nodes using social networks," NDSS 2009 — centralized Bayesian-inference alternative, cited with its own complexity bound O(|V|^2 log|V|) and a stated evaluation ceiling of 30K nodes.
- competing: L. Xu, S. Chainan, H. Takizawa, H. Kobayashi, "Resisting sybil attack by social network and network clustering," SAINT 2010 — computes shortest paths between every node pair per round, called impractical even for small networks by the authors.
- attack/measurement: L. Bilge, T. Strufe, D. Balzarotti, E. Kirda, "All your contacts are belong to us: automated identity theft attacks on social networks," WWW 2009 — source of the ~20% bogus-friend-request acceptance figure the paper cites as evidence against the "trusted relationships" assumption.
- foundational (analysis tool): R. Kannan, S. Vempala, A. Vetta, "On clusterings: Good, bad and spectral," FOCS 2000 — origin of the conductance metric used by the community-detection algorithm.
- competing (comparison basis, cited not retrieved in full here): B. Viswanath, A. Post, K. P. Gummadi, A. Mislove, "An analysis of social network-based sybil defenses," SIGCOMM 2010 — the community-detection ranking algorithm this paper directly re-implements and evaluates as a standalone method, finding it cannot self-select a cutoff point.

## [WEI-NSDI-24] The Eternal Tussle: Exploring the Role of Centralization in IPFS
**Citation:** Yiluo Wei, Dennis Trautwein, Yiannis Psaras, Ignacio Castro, Will Scott, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson. "The Eternal Tussle: Exploring the Role of Centralization in IPFS." USENIX/ACM NSDI, 2024.
**Retrieved:** full text via https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-wei.pdf
**Source URL:** https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/wei
**Domain:** A+J

### What it does
The paper, written by IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) core maintainers at Protocol Labs, reports on three centralized components deliberately added to the deployed IPFS system to compensate for measured weaknesses of the pure Kademlia-DHT (distributed hash table) design, and measures each component's effect using operational data from the live network. It is a measurement-and-engineering-experience paper, not a proposal of a new decentralized mechanism.

InterPlanetary Network Indexers (Indexers): a server-based key-value store that receives an announcement message from a content provider (containing a batch, or "advertisement," of many content-identifier-to-provider mappings, possibly 16,000-20,000 records at once) and answers CID-or-multihash lookup queries over a RESTful HTTP API, bypassing DHT traversal entirely. Advertisements form a hash-linked chain per provider, so an Indexer can reconstruct all of a provider's records by walking the chain and can audit what a provider has published. Indexers gossip announcement messages among themselves (over Gossipsub) and cache query results at a frontend server ahead of the backing Pebble database.

Hydra Boosters: a set of DHT-server nodes ("Hydra Heads") deliberately positioned across the Kademlia identifier space so that, in expectation, every ordinary peer has at least one Hydra Head within its 20-peer XOR-proximity bucket. All heads share one backing database (Amazon DynamoDB), so a query answered by any head can return provider records collected by every other head, collapsing what would otherwise require multiple DHT hops into fewer hops.

HTTP Gateways: a small set of HTTP-to-IPFS bridge servers that let an ordinary web client fetch IPFS content without installing IPFS software. A gateway runs Nginx with default web caching in front of a co-located IPFS node's own block-storage cache, so already-fetched or already-stored content is served without any DHT lookup.

### Measured results
| Metric | Figure | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Total provider records held | Indexer: 173,998,039,712 (~0.17 trillion); DHT: over 100x fewer | Indexer dataset snapshot 2023-04-24 UTC, from the Protocol-Labs-operated Indexer at cid.contact; DHT count from the paper's own Hydra Booster database |
| Number of distinct publishers | Indexer: 604 major providers (mostly NFT or storage services); DHT: ~56,000 providers | Same datasets |
| Query rate | Indexer: 2.5k lookup requests/second; DHT: ~5k GET-PROVIDER requests/second (estimated from Hydra Booster logs) | Operational logs |
| Advertisement synchronization time vs. DHT publication time | Indexer ~2x faster at the 50th percentile; per-record indexing time ~500 microseconds because most advertisements batch 16K-20K records | Sample of 16,757,817 provider records ingested 2023-04-24, out of ~5.3 billion processed/day; DHT publication time from separate active-measurement dataset |
| Indexer query performance | 62,611,156 successful HTTP requests over one day (2023-04-18 09:05 UTC to 2023-04-19 09:05 UTC), 246.77 GB served; average cache hit rate 65.22%; cache hits ~100x faster than DHT lookup at the 50th percentile; even the 34.78% cache-miss requests outperform DHT lookup | Amazon CloudFront request logs for the Indexer frontend |

### Parameters
- DHT replication factor for provider records, cited as the baseline the Indexer departs from: k=20 peers (paper cites Maymounkov and Mazières, [30]).
- Hydra Booster deployment: 135 nodes on Amazon ECS in us-east-1, 10-15 heads per node, 2,015 total heads.
- Active-retrieval test object size: 0.5 MB per published CID.
- Hydra-disabled condition (used as the "without" baseline): ADD-PROVIDER queries to Hydra Heads ignored (heads make up ~10-15% of the network, so this is described as "artificially decreasing the k-replication to 19"); GET-PROVIDER queries answered with closer-peer lists only, no provider records, because the shared database is disconnected.
- Nginx and IPFS-node caching layers at each gateway: default Nginx web cache in front of a co-located IPFS node's own block cache; no explicit cache-size or eviction-policy parameter is stated in the reviewed text.
- Number of publicly known Indexers at time of writing: 7. Number of gateways: over 80.

### Stated limitations
The authors state the Indexer introduces a single point of failure: some provider records exist only in the Indexer and are not replicated in the DHT, so a centralized Indexer failure can make "significant volumes" of provider records inaccessible; they state this risk is only partially mitigated by inter-Indexer Gossipsub announcement sharing, which "offers no hard guarantees on real-time synchronization." They state the Indexer's monetary operating cost ($5,000-10,000 capital, ~$1,000/month) contrasts with the DHT's load-spreading design, which needs no comparable individual hardware investment. They state Hydra Booster failure (of the shared DynamoDB database, or of the routing function itself) degrades performance (they measured up to 36.5%) but does not reduce content availability, because peers fall back to ordinary DHT routing; they state they observed no failed retrievals when Hydra Boosters were excluded from routing entirely. They state a centralized entity operating multiple Hydra Heads could theoretically attempt result poisoning or eclipse attacks, but argue (not measure) that IPFS's self-validating content identifiers (CIDs) limit a Hydra Head to, at most, forcing a re-query rather than delivering falsified content, and that the low mean Hydra-Head density in any single peer's proximity set (2.36) limits routing-manipulation leverage. They state gateways sacrifice IPFS's end-to-end cryptographic content validation, creating a man-in-the-middle exposure that would require additional client-side hash verification to close, which they say "may undermine the goal of improving adoption." They state that as centralized instances, Indexers, Hydra Boosters, and gateways let their operators monitor which content identifiers are queried by which clients, and that most clients' reliance on Protocol-Labs-operated instances of these three components is "not a sustainable solution" given the resulting dependency. They state privacy and censorship attacks are independently possible in the pure decentralized DHT routing layer as well (citing Balduf et al. [10] and Sridhar et al. [37]), so the centralized components are not the sole source of that exposure, though the paper does not quantify the DHT-only attack surface itself. They state none of the three types of incentive they identify for third-party Indexer/Gateway operators (storage-service self-interest, application self-interest, ecosystem-alignment interest) is a "formal incentive model," and that it is undetermined whether third-party uptake will be wide without one.

### Requirements it places on the rest of the system
A content-identifier-to-provider indexing layer that adds a centralized fast path (as the Indexer does) requires the content addressing scheme underneath it to be self-validating (a hash-derived content identifier) so that a compromised or malicious index operator cannot substitute false content, only false or withheld provider pointers — this paper's own security argument for Hydra-Booster safety depends specifically on that property and does not hold for an indexing layer sitting in front of a non-self-validating naming scheme. A fallback-to-DHT design for availability (as used for both Hydra Boosters and, implicitly, gateways) requires the DHT to remain independently reachable and populated at all times; the paper's own robustness argument for Hydra Boosters rests entirely on ordinary DHT routing continuing to function when the centralized accelerator is absent, so a design that lets the DHT's own participant population shrink (for example, by deprecating DHT-server responsibilities in favor of only using the Indexer) would remove the fallback this paper relies on for its no-availability-loss claim. Any accounting of "decentralization" for this class of system needs to state which of at least four separate observable channels it measures — content-provider count, publication volume, query volume, or entry-point traffic — because this paper's own data shows these four diverge sharply (56,000 DHT publishers vs. 604 Indexer publishers, but the Indexer holding over 100x more provider records).

### Contradicts
No claim commonly attributed to this paper was found unsupported by its text; the paper is explicit that Indexers "do not replace the DHT" and that the DHT "still plays a larger role" by publisher count and query volume even though the Indexer holds the numerical majority of provider records — a nuance a headline restatement of "one centralized indexer holds over 100x the DHT's location records" (as flagged by the target registry's why_needed note) risks flattening if the publisher-count and query-volume figures are dropped.
Disagrees with BALDUF-IMC-23 on IPFS cloud/DHT-node-hosting share: this paper does not itself report a DHT cloud-hosting percentage in the sections reviewed, but is the direct target of BALDUF-IMC-23's methodological critique — BALDUF-IMC-23 attributes the 2022 Trautwein-et-al. figure of "less than 3% of cloud nodes" (a predecessor measurement by overlapping authors, cited in this paper's own bibliography as [41], Trautwein et al., ACM SIGCOMM 2022) to a counting-methodology difference, not to network change; this NSDI-24 paper by largely the same author group does not revisit that cloud-hosting percentage, so the two papers' cloud-centralization findings are not directly comparable on the topology channel, only on the indexing/traffic channels this paper covers.

### References worth retrieving
- Maymounkov, Mazières, "Kademlia: A peer-to-peer information system based on the XOR metric" (cited as [30]) — foundational (already in corpus per BRIEF section 7).
- Trautwein, Raman, Tyson, Castro, Scott, Schubotz, Gipp, Psaras, "Design and evaluation of IPFS: a storage layer for the decentralized web," ACM SIGCOMM 2022 (cited as [41]) — foundational, prior measurement by an overlapping author group, source of the <3% cloud-node figure disputed in BALDUF-IMC-23.
- Balduf, Henningsen, Florian, Rust, Scheuermann (cited as [10]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper as showing privacy attacks are possible in the decentralized DHT routing subsystem independent of Indexers/gateways.
- Sridhar, Ascigil, Keizer, Genon, Pierre, et al. (cited as [37]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper as showing censorship is possible in the purely decentralized IPFS DHT.
- Vyzovitis, Napora, McCormick, Dias, et al. (cited as [42], likely the libp2p GossipSub specification/paper) — foundational, the protocol used for inter-Indexer announcement gossip.
- Singh, Castro, Druschel, Rowstron, "Defending against Eclipse attacks on overlay networks" (cited as [36]) — attack/critique, cited by this paper regarding the theoretical Hydra-Booster eclipse-attack concern.
- Kaashoek, Karger, "Koorde: A simple degree-optimal distributed hash table" (cited as [26]) — foundational, listed among prior DHT structures in related work.
- Rowstron, Druschel, "Pastry: Scalable, decentralized object location and routing" (cited as [34]) — foundational, listed among prior DHT structures in related work.
